en: First Daily Lesson. Having prostrated before Gaurīśa, who possesses inconceivable power, who is omniscient, and who is a lamp for the darkness of ignorance,
this commentary on the Sūtras of Kaṇāda is composed by me, a servant of Śaṅkara.
This is the commentary on the Sūtra taught by Mahādeva;
let it be studied by all for the sake of attaining knowledge of objects as they truly are.
Now, therefore, we shall expound upon Dharma. 1.1.1.

In this context, the word "atha" (now/thereupon) signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*). And that immediate succession cannot be conveyed by the word through reference to just anything whatsoever, because that would be redundant; for not every kind of immediate succession [is relevant here].
The explanation of the term *dharma* is useful in certain contexts;

therefore, it is logical that this word *atha*, although denoting mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*), follows specifically from the salutation to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇāma*), since the completion of the treatise is established by that very act.
This is because its purpose is to inform the disciples that the commencement of a work must be undertaken immediately after paying homage to one's chosen deity.

Otherwise, if one were to begin a treatise without bowing to the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the disciples—lacking the auxiliary cause known as *dharma* produced by that salutation which is the reason for the successful completion of the work—would find their undertaking fruitless. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the fact that the *dharma* produced by bowing to the chosen deity is the cause for the successful completion of a treatise; for the Veda, inferred from the uncontradicted practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), serves as the authority in this matter.
If it is asked, "How is it then that works such as the *Kādambarī* remain incomplete despite being preceded by salutations to one's chosen deity?"— the answer is: no,
for even when the merit (*dharma*) produced by the salutation exists,
the completion of the work may fail due to the deficiency of the author’s body or other factors that serve as causes for its completion.

For us, it is not merely the merit (*dharma*) produced by the act of salutation that is the cause for the completion of the work; rather, there is also the destruction of obstacles to the author’s body and so forth, because when there is a deficiency in the author’s body and so on, unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and the like are destroyed.

Furthermore, it is not correct to argue that because the completion of a work is observed without fail whenever the causes for its production—such as the author’s vision and the completeness of materials—are present, the merit (*dharma*) produced by the salutation cannot be the cause of the work’s completion. This is because, due to the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), inferring that merit produced by salutation lacks causality for the completion of a work would result in the invalidation of the authority of the gods inferred from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*); moreover, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the self (*ātman*), which produces the completion of a work but does not possess such merit.

As for the question of how merit produced by salutation could be destroyed where the work is not completed, since merit is perishable by virtue of its fruit, [the merit must perish even if the fruit is not realized].
If [it is argued that liberation occurs] due to the destruction of the body— the efficient cause— or from the direct realization of the Self which effects liberation—
[we reply: and yet, there is no absence of salutation even in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya and other such works.
It is logical that the completion [of a work] is not caused by the dharma produced by a salutation, because [in some cases] completion is observed even without it.
In that case as well—

Because it is impossible to ascertain the absence of mental salutation— which is inferred from the conduct of the learned and has the Veda as its authority— due to the lack of non-perception of something that is [otherwise] perceptible;
therefore, the meaning of the word *atha* is "immediately following the prostration to the Lord."
Alternatively,

the meaning of the word "atha" (then) is the immediate succession between the direct realization of Dharma and so forth attained through the grace of the Supreme Lord, and the injunction consisting of the instruction on the Dharma of the Supreme Lord.
If...
Immediately after [the two] have acquired the application of dharma and knowledge through the grace of the Supreme Lord, one should not fail to instruct them in dharma;
otherwise, by transgressing the command of the Supreme Guru, the Lord of Umā, one would incur sin. Not so.

Nor can it be said that there is no transgression for them due to their particular excellence of splendor; for the transgression of the Supreme Lord’s command overcomes the splendor of all beings in saṃsāra. And not...

There is no evidence for the claim that the venerable sage Kaṇāda was appointed by the Supreme Lord and possessed direct realization of dharma and other categories obtained through the grace of the Supreme Lord;
for this is established by the authority of the traditional practice of the school. Indeed, they teach:

[The traditionalists: The sage Kaṇāda, having received from the Supreme Lord— while He was wearing the guise of an owl— the command to directly perceive dharma and so forth and to teach that dharma, [proceeded to compose his work].
"He composed the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra. Now, let it be granted that there is an immediate sequence between the direct realization of dharma and the command (niyoga) of the Supreme Lord.
This is for the purpose of making known the authoritative status of the Vaiśeṣika treatise regarding the exposition of the Dharma;
for [the fact that it is] preceded by the direct realization of reality has not yet been understood.
The authority of the Vaiśeṣika treatise cannot be understood by its students,
because the quality of being a statement preceded by valid cognition is invariably concomitant with authority.
[The word "ataḥ" (hence) indicates the reason:
because] those who have studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-veda*), who seek the goals of heaven and liberation as understood therein,
who desire to know the means for attaining them, and who possess the capacity for grasping, retaining, and so forth [the teachings].
The meaning is that those who do not find the means to achieve that [heaven] through the Veda seek it from this [Dharma]; thus,
for one desiring heaven, Dharma is the means to attain heaven, as expressed in such passages as "let him sacrifice."
If it is argued that [this] is understood— no, for since the meaning of the verbal root, such as sacrifice (*yāga*), and the meaning of the suffix,
namely *bhāvanā*, have long since perished,
their being the means for attaining heaven, which occurs at a later time, cannot be established even by a thousand Vedas.

Because it is impossible to bring about [the result], there is a lack of fitness (*yogyatā*). Fitness, with respect to being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), consists in existing at the moment of the operation that occurs in the immediate antecedent moment.

Now, one might object: is not fitness, with respect to being the means (*sādhana*), either the state of having an operation occurring in the immediate antecedent moment of the fruit, or the possession of the power to produce the fruit?

If it is argued that fitness for being a means (*sādhanatva*) does not consist in existing in the moment immediately preceding the fruit, but rather fitness consists in existing at the moment of the operation of the means, or being the object of the means' capacity, or being one's own effect; and that fitness for being an end (*sādhyatva*) does not consist in existing in the moment immediately following the means—[we reply: no, because this [fitness] cannot exist prior to the comprehension of the relationship between the end and the means, such as heaven and the sacrifice.
Because it is impossible to ascertain [such] fitness (*yogyatā*); for indeed, as long as the prior operation is not known,
it is impossible to understand the state of possessing an operation existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven,
since the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is preceded by the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Nor can the capacity to produce that [cognition], which constitutes "possessing power" (*śaktimattva*), be understood from that very [capacity] while it remains unapprehended. Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that fitness (*yogyatā*) generates the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) while itself remaining unapprehended;
for, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the generation of the cognition of connection is established precisely upon the apprehension of fitness.

Because of the [necessity of] determination. Nor is there a cognition of fitness that occurs immediately after the comprehension of the relationship between the end and the means, because it lacks existence at the moment of the operation that brings about the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and because it is impossible; for the relationship between the end and the means is not comprehended in the case of heaven and sacrifice.

Because there would otherwise arise no cognition of the unprecedented (*apūrva*) produced by the fact that [the meaning] cannot be established otherwise. Now, it might be argued that the ascertainment of compatibility (*yogyatā*) is not the cause of the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), but rather that the ascertainment of the absence of compatibility is the obstacle to the cognition of syntactic connection.
And the absence of that [operation] is the cause for the cognition of the positive concomitance (anvaya);
for the absence of the sacrificial operation, which consists of the *apūrva* existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven,
is not established by perception or other means.

If you think that [the nature of the means] cannot be determined prior to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, that too is not correct, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*). To explain: does [the means] consist in possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*) existing in the moment immediately preceding the goal (*sādhya*), or...
Is fitness [yogyatā] the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*),

or is it the possession of an operation (*vyāpāra*) existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven for the sacrifice to be a means to heaven? It cannot be the first, because [in the case of the injunction] "one desiring rice should cook," [the fitness would apply even to one] desiring satisfaction...

For in such cases as "one should eat," there would be the consequence of a failure to perceive the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because it cannot be determined that the acts of cooking and eating possess the property of having operations occurring at the moments of [producing] rice and [achieving] satisfaction; this is because cooking and eating are the means for producing rice and satisfaction. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Since there is no apprehension of the absence of fitness— defined as the lack of an operation existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven—
the impossibility arises of such an apprehension obstructing the understanding of the relationship between heaven and sacrifice as the goal and the means;
or, if such an apprehension were present, it would render the understanding of the relationship between heaven and sacrifice as the goal and the means impossible.
If the state of possessing an operation occurring in the moment immediately preceding [the sacrifice] constitutes the fitness for being a means to heaven (*svarga-sādhanatva-yogyatā*) in sacrifices,
then some other means of achieving heaven must be stated for the sacrifice and so forth; for the property of being a means (*sādhanatva*) itself is not the means.

Cognitive fitness (*yogyatā*) is the cause for the cognition of a syntactic connection; yet, even in its absence—as in the case of "one should sprinkle with fire" (*agninā siñcet*)—the cognition of a connection still arises.
Therefore, this [cognition] is not valid knowledge (*pramā*), solely because it is not something previously unapprehended.

You may think that the cognition of the relationship between the means and the end— such as heaven and sacrifice— is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*) because there is no sublation (*bādha*). This is not so,
for there is sublation regarding the status of being a means to heaven [if it were defined] as existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven.

Because it is impossible to prevent [this consequence]. Furthermore, if the state of being an operation existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven were the "means" (*sādhana*), then the sacrifice—which teaches that [heaven] is the means to the means—would necessarily result in teaching an *apūrva*.
If you say, "Let it be so," we reply: no, because the *apūrva* was not previously understood [from the root *yaj*]. In that case, regarding the sacrifice...

If it is argued that because the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is not yet understood, one first understands the *apūrva* from the root *yaji*, and only thereafter understands the denotative capacity of *yaji* with respect to that [apūrva]— we say no, because this would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
For only when the *apūrva* is understood from the root *yaji* can there be knowledge of *yaji*'s denotative capacity for the *apūrva*.
And when there is the cognition that the verbal root *yaji* (to sacrifice) denotes the *apūrva*, the *apūrva* is understood from *yaji*. By this,

the view that the meaning of *yaji* is merely the sacrifice (*yāga*), while its status as a means belongs instead to the optative suffix (*liṅ*) which expresses being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*),
is also refuted.

Furthermore, if the *liṅ* suffix were to denote the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) consisting in possessing an operation existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven, it would entail the undesirable consequence that the *liṅ* suffix denotes the *apūrva*, which would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Because the *apūrva* is to be postulated only after the relationship between the means and the end has been understood;
as they say:
"An action enjoined for the sake of a result is momentary, yet it must lead to a future [result]."
Since its accomplishment cannot be otherwise, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is likewise postulated.
Thus [it is said].
Now, let it be granted that the sacrifice possesses the status of a means (*sādhana*) by virtue of existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven;
nor is that [status] contradicted for a sacrifice that has long since perished with respect to heaven.
If you argue that heaven follows immediately after the sacrifice because you accept this, that too is not correct,
because heaven does not exist in the moment immediately following the sacrifice.

Because it has been refuted by the non-apprehension of what is capable [of being perceived]. If it is argued that at that time it is unperceivable due to its subtlety, we say no; for then it would follow that it remains unperceivable even at another time. [For it would have to become] gross at another time.
If it is argued that [the object] is capable [of being perceived], we say no;
for subtlety and grossness, being contradictory properties, differentiate their substrata. And as for that which is capable of being perceived...
Because it does not exist at the moment immediately following the sacrifice,
that [result] is not produced by the sacrifice. Now,
if you argue that being a means (*sādhanatva*) does not consist in existing at the moment immediately preceding [the result], and so forth—
Rather, it is the state of being a producer (*utpādakatva*). And that is not denied of the sacrifice with respect to heaven,
because there is no certainty that the sacrifice lacks the capacity to produce heaven due to [the intervention of] the sense organs and so forth.

If you think that dharma is understood from the Veda because sacrifice and the like— which are the means to the highest good such as heaven, as known from the uncontradicted Veda— are themselves dharma, that too is not correct.

Because there is no evidence for the existence of a producer other than that which exists in the immediately preceding moment; thus, [the claim that] "that which is remote is the producer" is refuted.
For this is established simply by virtue of occurring in the immediately preceding moment.
Or, let it be that there is no distinct producer [of the effect], since it exists in the immediately preceding moment.
However, there is a lack of evidence for the claim that sacrifice produces heaven.
If it is argued that the Vedic injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) is the authority— no,
because the root *yaj* signifies merely the act of sacrificing, whereas the term "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*)...

And [the injunction] is so because it denotes a person characterized by the desire for heaven. Now, if it is argued that the injunctive force, in the form of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*), then, upon the inquiry "What is that desired end?"—
Heaven, which is not the object of desire for one who is free from limiting conditions (nirupādhika), is connected [to the injunction].
When there is an expectancy for the locus of the property of being a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatva), the sacrifice, which is the meaning of the verbal root, is connected; by that—

If it is argued that the meaning of the sentence is thus established as "sacrifice is the means to heaven"— no, for since the desired end (svarga) is already conveyed by the word *svarga*, the property of being a means qualified by that [end] would be redundant within the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Suppose it is argued: "Let the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) be simply instrumentality (*sādhanatva*); however, its limitation to what is desired (*iṣṭāvaccheda*) is indicated through its co-occurrence with the word 'heaven' (*svarga*). This is not so, because there is no evidence that instrumentality is the meaning of the optative suffix. Let it be [the case that it is].
The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). And heaven alone is that which is desired.
Nevertheless, when there arises an expectancy for the locus of that means-ness, the meaning of the suffix [is understood] as being proximate to the sacrifice, which is the meaning of the verbal root.

Only the efficient force (bhāvanā) is connected [with the result]. Therefore, since the meaning of the sentence is established as "the efficient force has heaven as its objective," how is it that the sacrifice's status as the means to heaven is proven?
Furthermore, in the Bhaṭṭa school’s view, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," an efficient force (bhāvanā) is perceived as the object of the impulsion; and that,
first of all, requires an object to be brought into being (vibhāvya).
Because it consists in the activity of an agent directed toward something yet to be brought into being (*bhāvya*),

and because that [activity] requires an object to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), why is heaven not understood as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of its connection with the accusative case, which has the same meaning as the second member of a compound?
Then, when there arises an expectancy for a means (*sādhana*) through the question "by what?", the meaning of the verbal root— such as sacrifice— is construed as that means. Consequently,
[the injunction] is characterized by the heaven to be attained (*bhāvya*) and characterized by the sacrifice which is the means (*sādhana*).

If the sentence-meaning is indeed the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) alone, how is the fact that sacrifice is the means for attaining heaven established? [One might argue: "Since the *bhāvanā* requires not only an end to be produced (*bhāvya*) but also a means to produce that end (*bhāvyasādhana*), it is by way of being such a means..."
The view that the connection belongs to the sacrifice is not tenable, because it has already been stated that the sacrifice cannot logically be the means for attaining heaven.
This remains the case even in the Prābhākara position regarding the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice."

By means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the eternal, unprecedented *apūrva* is denoted as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*), and not the sacrifice or other such acts. For that [sacrifice], having perished long ago,
cannot be the object to be accomplished by one desiring heaven, since it is the [apūrva] that serves as the means for attaining the desired heaven.
Because it is impossible to cognize [it as such]; for according to the logical principle that one who has a desire cognizes the desired object as a means to be accomplished (kārya),
and an "effect" (kārya) is defined by purposeful action (kṛti), since it is that which is aimed at by purposeful action and is achievable through purposeful action.
And "action" (kṛti) is effort; and since that,
like [the injunctions regarding] the sacrificial post and so forth, is defined by its object,
when there is an expectancy for an object, it is the sacrifice (yāga).

It is construed as being the object of effort (*prayatna*). Consequently, the meaning of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) results in the sense that the *apūrva* is either achievable by an effort directed toward the sacrifice, or is the intended goal of that effort. And as for the effort, just as...
Just as it depends upon an object, so too does it depend upon a substratum (āśraya). That alone is the substratum of the action which perceives the task as "this is my duty.
Therefore, there is a dependence upon one who understands the task.
By the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—who is the cognizer of the task—is presented.
And the task (*kārya*), although by its very nature something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), stands as a means to heaven because it is being desired. [The person] is one who desires.

According to the principle that "that which is desired as a means is understood as an effect," this very [activity] is called the "occurrence (or non-occurrence) of the probandum" (*sādhyavṛttir vivṛttiḥ*), because the probandum is something unprecedented (*apūrva*).
Because heaven is accepted as another thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Now, it might be argued that if sacrifice were not a means to heaven, it would not be the object of the volitional effort (*kṛti*) of one who desires heaven.
[No; because it is not a means to its own proof, but rather] by that [means],
the *apūrva*— which constitutes the very body of heaven and is synonymous with *niyoga*—
is distinguished by the cognizer who desires heaven.
Since the meaning of the sentence is that which is produced by an effort directed toward sacrifice, and that which is intended by the effort,
how can there be an understanding of sacrifice as the means to heaven?
Precisely by rejecting that [position],...
In our view, the first [alternative] is unrefuted, because it is established that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses something not previously known through its intended meaning (*tātparya*),
since "being an uncontradicted experience" is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is the second [alternative], for if [the optative] were to denote [such a thing],...

For, since the performance of the action [of cooking] arises from that very [cognition], it is not established that [the word "should"] denotes the effect. Now, if it is argued that [the action occurs] not merely from the fact that something is a means to a desired end, [we reply: no, for [action arises] precisely from the cognition that it is a means to a desired end produced by an effort.
For, if [the word] were to denote the occurrence of activity, it would follow that the purpose of the action and so forth must also be denotable.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the conceptual alternatives are untenable. Thus:

For—do the inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth denote the mandate (*niyoga*) without their relationship having been grasped, or with their relationship having been grasped? Not the first, because it would follow that even infants would comprehend it. As for the second [alternative]...
Is this apprehension [of the relationship] when the comprehension of the connection has not occurred, or when it has occurred?
Not the first, because the comprehension of the denoted object is the cause for the comprehension of its designator. Nor even the second.
The comprehension of that [niyoga] must arise either from a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) or from reasoning (tarka).
It cannot be the first, because you do not admit that a niyoga is cognizable by any other means of valid cognition. Nor can it be the second.

For *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) consists in the inference of a pervader (*vyāpaka*) through the attribution of a pervaded (*vyāpya*). However, prior to the cognition of the mandate (*niyoga*), nothing has been established as being pervaded by the mandate, such that the mandate could be inferred through the attribution of that [pervaded].
Now, one who holds that the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is paramount [argues] that,
upon considering the co-occurrence with the term "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the stable transcendental result (*sthāyyapūrva*) is what must be conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
If it is argued that the knowledge of the apūrva arises from inference—no;

for the knowledge that the optative suffix (liṅ) expresses a stable apūrva is derived from the fact that it must denote something stable in the absence of any other [stable entity]. Nor is there an apūrva...
It cannot occur without knowledge; and new knowledge does not arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that [apūrva] is not cognizable by any other means of knowledge.
Nor does it arise from reasoning (*tarka*), for that too—
Because, as before, if there were a dependence on another tarka, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "by considering the co-occurrence of words such as 'one who desires heaven'":

Is it intended that [the understanding arises] by reflecting upon the optative suffix (*liṅ*) uttered together with the words "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*) and "sacrifice" (*yajati*), whose syntactic relation (*saṃgati*) is not yet understood; or rather, by reflecting upon the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the words "desirous of heaven," "sacrifice," and so forth, whose syntactic relation is already understood?
Not the first, because it would follow that even children and others would have such a cognition.

Regarding the second [alternative] as well, is it intended that the optative suffix (*liṅ*), whose connection [to the meaning] is not yet understood, [arouses the cognition] through a consideration of its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*)?
Or [is it] for one who has understood the relation? Not the first, because of the previously mentioned defect.
As for the second, is it the case that the optative suffix (*liṅ*), having its relation understood through an unprecedented action...
Is it by means of reflection, or rather by means of reflecting on the optative suffix (liṅ) as the cognition of what is to be done through action? Not the first.

For it is impossible for the *liṅ* suffix to have its relationship [with the meaning] previously understood, because there is no reasoning (*tarka*) that presents something not previously known for the sake of grasping that relationship. Furthermore, in the second alternative as well, is it the action (*kriyā*) that is the object to be accomplished (*kārya*)?

Is it capable of being construed with a person enjoined who desires heaven, or not? In the first case, there would be the comprehension of the action as a task (kārya) conjoined with a person enjoined who desires heaven;
for the consideration of such a co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) is precisely what generates such a cognition.
However, there is no cognition of a permanent, unprecedented (apūrva) entity,

because there is no evidence that the investigation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), whose connection is understood through its co-occurrence with the verb *yaj* (to sacrifice), the word for the person enjoined who desires heaven (*svargakāma-niyojya*), and the action, generates a cognition distinct from perception and other means of knowledge. Now, whatever is co-occurrent with a word expressing a person enjoined who desires something...
The optative suffix denotes an effect that exists in the moment immediately preceding that [action],
because of the certainty of this pervasion.

Even when there is a general understanding of the pervasion— that from a sentence containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there arises a cognition of a stable *apūrva*— it does not follow that this optative suffix is the denoter of a stable *apūrva*.

Since a cognition terminating in a negation does not arise, and since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is uttered in co-referentiality with a word denoting an agent (*niyojya*) such as "one who desires heaven," the optative suffix consists of a certainty regarding pervasion accompanied by a cognition of the pervader (*vyāpya*) that terminates in a specific [object].

If it is argued that [the word] is the cause for the cognition of a denoter of a stable and unprecedented entity (*apūrva*), then this is indeed inference (*anumāna*), and not knowledge born of reasoning (*tarka*).
If it is said, "Let it be so," we reply: no, because of the unprecedented nature of the *apūrva*.
Because it is not cognizable through other means of knowledge (*māna*),

and even inference (*anumāna*) is not possible. This optative suffix (*liṅ-pratyaya*) denotes that which is the object of the volitional effort (*kṛti*) of a sacrifice, said to be produced by the volitional effort of a sacrifice existing in the moment immediately preceding heaven.

Because it is an optative suffix (*liṅ*) co-occurring with words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). Whatever is an optative suffix co-occurring with a word such as "desiring X," that [suffix] denotes an action existing in the moment immediately preceding that [desire]. For example:
Because the reason— namely, that the optative suffix in such expressions as "one desiring satisfaction should eat"—

is unestablished for us; for we do not accept that [the suffix] denotes either the object of the volition produced by the sacrifice which generates heaven, or the state of being the object of that volition.

Furthermore, even for the Prābhākaras, such denotative capacity [of the optative suffix] with respect to an action of this kind is unestablished prior to the apprehension of the linguistic convention. Whatever is an optative suffix co-occurring with words such as "desiring that" (yatkāma) is...
If it is argued that there is a general syntactic connection (anvaya) in the sense that [the word "kārya"] denotes an object that produces what is desired— [we reply: no,

because the words *yat* and *tat* refer to the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as it occurs in conjunction with the subject "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth, and thus denote an action (*kārya*) that brings about heaven.

Because the previously stated absence of syntactic connection remains as it was, and because, if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) co-occurring with the words "one whose desire is satisfied" (*tṛptakāma*) were intended to mean the expression of an action that is a means to satisfaction,
then the syntactic connection would be established between those two alone.

This is because the absence of a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the nature of the optative suffix (*liṅpratyaya*) as co-occurring with words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) and its denotation of an action that produces heaven remains as it was; furthermore, there is no evidence for any common property (*anugata*) to be expressed by the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.
Furthermore, such inferential knowledge (*tarka-jñāna*) lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

If it is argued that *tarka* is the logic (*nyāya*) that determines the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of words, and that "congruity" (*saṅgati*) occurs when that [meaning] is presented beforehand; [we reply:]...

Furthermore, regarding these two which have been set aside by the logical arguments, is it reasoning (*tarka*), direct experience (*anubhūti*), or memory (*smṛti*)? In the first case, it is indeed valid cognition (*pramā*), because being an uncontradicted direct experience is the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is not...
The second [alternative] is not tenable because it is not produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Now, if you mean that they have the same object, that is not so; for if "dependence on experience" means being produced by experience, that is not possible in the present case.
Because that which is yet to be (the future) lacks the state of existing in a preceding moment, it cannot be a cause;
furthermore, there is no evidence for the dependence on experience being anything other than the state of being produced. Nor is it the case that...
Inference (tarka) is distinct from memory and experience; for that which is produced by memory is an experience, while that cognition which is devoid of the nature of experience is memory.

Therefore, in the world, the linguistic convention for optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like is established with respect to an action as the object to be accomplished; however, in the Veda, it is indeed difficult to maintain that they refer to a lasting object to be accomplished (*kārya*) that is not previously known through other means of knowledge.

Others, however, maintain that the understanding of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as having action as their primary meaning arises from an examination of the linguistic usage of elders; subsequently, in the Veda, this is confirmed by the fact that such usage would otherwise be untenable given the co-occurrence with an agent (*niyojya*) who desires heaven.
There is no linguistic convention (*avyutpatti*) regarding the apūrva as the object to be accomplished,
with respect to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, which are synonymous with "denotative power" (*vācakatva*).
Subsequently, in common worldly usage, there is no such convention for the optative suffixes and so forth that denote the apūrva as the object to be accomplished.
It is determined that the capacity to convey an action (*kārya*) occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*);

for, since the application of words denoting an unprecedented action (*apūrva-kārya*) is possible even through secondary indication in the sense of "action" in general, there is no grounds for postulating that they are direct denoters (*vācaka*).

Expressive power (*vācakatva*) resides in the action to be performed (*kriyākārya*), whereas its presence in the *apūrva*—which is indicated only by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—is indeed extremely difficult to establish;
for since the *apūrva* is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible for the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. to signify it through secondary indication.
Because, when the primary meaning is sublated, that [cognition] takes the form of a recollection regarding what is connected to it;
or even if it is not a recollection, the comprehension of the connection with the denoted object is accepted as a constituent part of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, the linguistic usage occurs only with respect to a previously unknown form of dharma.

And as for the claim that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth possess authority [to denote the unseen force], that too is not correct; for it has already been demonstrated that there is no linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding the apūrva.

Furthermore, in common worldly usage, the denotative power of the optative suffixes and others is established through the force of the linguistic practice of elders as referring to something other than that.
Others, however, maintain that the understanding of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth arises from the observation of the usage of elders regarding the *kārya* (the "to-be-done"),

and not with respect to that which is qualified by "action-ness"— a term synonymous with the meaning of the verbal root— because such a qualification would be redundant due to the absence of anything further to be delimited; otherwise, it would follow that the optative suffixes could be understood to denote an action qualified by properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) or "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*).

And thus, by the power of linguistic derivation (*yogavyutpatti*), the *liṅ* and other suffixes in the Veda denote an action (*kārya*) that is connected to an agent (*niyojya*) who desires heaven— which is both required by the context and proximate— and which is capable of being performed. Furthermore, this [action] is not the transcendental potency (*apūrva*) of the verbal root such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*), because that [potency] perishes long ago.

Because it is impossible for [the act] to be a means for attaining the desired heaven occurring at a later time, there is an absence of fitness; consequently, there can be no syntactic connection with the person enjoined who desires heaven.
For one who desires [a result] understands the means to that which is desired as something to be accomplished.
According to this principle, that effect which is distinct from the sacrifice and is not within the scope of any means of knowledge other than verbal testimony is called *apūrva*.
It is termed *niyoga* because it enjoins— that is, impels— one toward its own self.

Thus it is explained. By virtue of that—namely, the power of understanding the effect as it is known in the world—the Veda possesses authority regarding the effect of the permanent [sentiment]. Whatever is an effect is produced by its inherent cause; this is established by the force of the pervasion (vyāpti) known from worldly experience.
And as for [the claim] that this applies to inference regarding atoms and so forth— that too is not tenable,
because even in common worldly usage, since an action such as "bringing" is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu), it is untenable for it to be the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya).
Furthermore, since the Prābhākaras do not accept in common worldly usage an effect distinct from the meaning of the verbal root,
either specific effects such as "bringing" and so forth are the meanings of the roots, or else there is a common [element].
If it is argued that "the object to be accomplished" (*kārya*) is for the purpose of providing a common referent (*pratyayārtha*), we say no;

for there is no inference of a persisting "object to be accomplished" that transcends the specific objects to be accomplished, such as "bringing" and so forth. There is no such persisting [concept] as "the object to be accomplished, the object to be accomplished."

If it is argued that the cognition [of the universal] is the means of knowledge (*māna*), we say no; for that is established simply by its being an effect. Otherwise, there would be no justification for a recurring referent of the word "cow" (*gopadārtha*) that is distinct from the cowness residing in particulars such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*).

Now, if the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in the world pertains to "task-ness" (*kāryatva*), then in the world that task-ness is denoted as being connected with the meaning of the verbal root— such as bringing— which is required, proximate, and capable; but in the Veda, it is not.
It is possible to express the state of being an obligation (kāryatva) as conjoined with the meaning of verbal roots such as "sacrifice" (yāga),
because it is untenable for that [obligation], having perished long ago, to be a means of attaining heaven which occurs at a later time.
Because it cannot be understood as something to be performed by one desiring heaven;

therefore, in the Veda, the status of the *kārya* (the thing to be done) as a lasting entity distinct from the meaning of the verbal root is established because the [injunction] does not terminate there. That too is not correct.
This is because there is no definition [of *nirukti*] that does not terminate in something other than the denotative function (*vācakatva*).

First of all, this is not *lakṣaṇā* (indication), because *lakṣaṇā* is accepted only when the object related to the denoted meaning is apprehended through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas the unprecedented action (*apūrva-kārya*) is not within the scope of other means of knowledge. Furthermore, for one who asserts *lakṣaṇā* in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), [the following applies]:
The Prābhākara view has been explained in detail, supported by the aphorism that "in an injunction, the word-meaning is not something else.
Nor is it figurative, because the quality of possessing the function of the expressed meaning...

Because an unprecedented effect (apūrvakārya) is not apprehended; nor is there a secondary function (gauṇī) characterized by denotative power (vācakatva), because there is no evidence for any other mode of operation (vṛtti) distinct from the secondary one. Now, as for the effect...

The intrinsic nature [of the optative suffix] is "being an effect" (kāryatva). And that, because it is incorporeal, is constituted by being an effect. Without expressing "being an effect," it cannot be expressed by the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth.
If it is argued that [the meaning] is thus obtainable without end—no;

for if the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) can be expressed without expressing the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then the status of being an effect would itself be non-expressible. It is not so.

[The nature of] "ness" (tva) is obtainable through [the suffix] -paryavasāna; thus, even in the world, the effect is indeed the denotable object. This concludes the [discussion on] the assumption that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the state of being an effect. Therefore, it is lost.
In the Prābhākara view as well, the Veda possesses authority regarding dharma.

Now, if the Veda does not possess authority regarding dharma, then where does the authority of the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" reside? [It resides] in that which is to be accomplished by dharma.

[This applies] to heaven and to the sacrifice that accomplishes it. And thus Praśastapāda says: "Its means, however, are those enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti," and so forth. But who, then, is the one desiring heaven?
The meaning of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is that "one who desires heaven should perform the sacrifice.
Now, if the sacrifice is not the means for attaining heaven, for what purpose then is it performed by one who desires heaven?
Understand that it is for the sake of the merit (*dharma*) that produces heaven;
the merit that produces heaven is generated by sacrifice and is further to be understood through inference as expounded in the Vaiśeṣika treatises.
Thus it is established: since dharma is not understood from the Veda, we shall therefore explain dharma. The prefix *vi-* signifies distinction (*viśeṣa*), and distinction is...

[The word *vi* denotes] preeminence. Therefore, we shall explain Dharma specifically by way of its preeminence; it follows that the six categories, beginning with substance (*dravya*), are its subordinate members. Alternatively, the word *vi* [denotes] manifoldness through various connections.
The meaning is that we shall explain the Dharma in its various forms, distinguished by such categories as that which prompts activity and that which causes cessation.

If it is argued that the prefix *ā-* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*) rather than exclusion (*maryādā*), because there is nothing to be excluded and thus the teaching would encompass every single phenomenon (*dharma*), we say no; for the term *dharma*, having fulfilled its purpose by conveying any given class of phenomena, does not thereby convey the totality of all phenomena.

Otherwise, in such cases as "Bring the cow" (*gām abhyāja*), there would be an inclination to bring all cows because the word "cow" (*go*) would denote all cows. We shall explain this; *khyā* in the phrase "we shall explain" (*vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*) is the form of the verbal root meaning "to tell. Its excellence (*prakṛṣṭatvam*)...

[It is] the quality of establishing that the Dharma is free from defects. And this [quality] does not exist in other treatises, because the defects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) propounded therein are pointed out in their respective places. However, when there are no other treatises...
If one were to insist that while other treatises teach the Dharma,
this Vaiśeṣika treatise alone teaches the Dharma, then [this would not be the case],
because other treatises do not lack the quality of expounding the Dharma. Therefore, this [is not the case].
The form *khyā* in the expression *prakathana* is not the substitute for the root *khyā* (meaning "to tell") as prescribed by the rule *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ*;

rather, it is the substitute for the root *cakṣiṅ*. If it is argued that this would entail the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), we say no, because there is no fruit of the action intended for the agent of the explanation. This is because [the rule] *svaritañitaḥ*...
This is because of the traditional rule of Pāṇini: "When the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

Since the Blessed Author of the Sūtras has attained all human goals through the grace of the Supreme Lord, there is no fruit for himself that he must attain. For what purpose, then, [did he compose the work]?

The exposition of the Dharma: know this to be for the sake of others. For when the Dharma is understood by others, it is practiced by them, leading to the attainment of heaven and liberation for those others.
If it is argued that heaven and liberation are not the fruit [of the teaching] because they pertain to others—no, for they are indeed the fruit for those very others.

If it is argued that [the Veda] does not have another as its fruit because it is "gone beyond" (paragata), we say no; for there is an absence of any such example, since the Blessed Lord, the Supreme God— who is eternally liberated and the author of the Vedas that teach the means for merit and demerit— has as his purpose the attainment of heaven and liberation by others.

If it is argued that for the author of the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra*, heaven and liberation are not the purpose [of the work] because they pertain to another [the Lord]— no, for it is accepted that the Lord is also the author of the ancient *Vaiśeṣika-mahāsūtra*.

If it is argued that for the author of these *Vaiśeṣika-sūtras*, heaven and liberation are not the purpose because they pertain to another— no, for it is accepted that the Lord is also the author of these sūtras.

"Because the teachings of non-Īśvara [systems] have two authors and because there is an absence of corroborative examples. Here, by eliding the vowel 'a' (in the compound *anīśvaropadeśānām*), the proposition regarding the exposition of *adharma* (unrighteousness) is also to be understood.
And thus, since those who desire to abandon hell and other such states resulting from ignorance of the meaning of the Veda...

Those desiring to know the means of achieving that [dharma] ask [the question]; therefore, the meaning is: "we shall explain adharma. If it is argued that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because the sentence has multiple referents—[we reply: no, for a syntactical split is accepted here through the elision or non-elision of the vowel 'a'.

Furthermore, even without the elision of the vowel *a*, there is no fault in the division of the sentences, because it is observed that the sūtras possess multiple meanings; for by the term "facing all directions" (*viśvatomukha*), it is intended to express that the sūtras convey manifold meanings. Thus, in this way...
By the first sūtra, dharma and adharma are shown to be the subjects expounded by the treatise. || 1 ||
Now, one might object: "If the Veda is not the authority regarding Dharma, then what is the authority?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"That from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is Dharma. (1.1.2)

Thus, "abhyudaya" (prosperity) is happiness such as that of heaven, and "niḥśreyasa" (the supreme good) is liberation. Their "siddhi" (accomplishment) is their arising; that from which this arises is Dharma. By stating "their accomplishment," he demonstrates that the property of being a predicate (pakṣadharmatva) belongs to the accomplishment.

But is it not the case that [the property of being a cause] consists in being the counter-positive of the prior non-existence of origination? Since *rūpa* (form) is unproduced (*ajanya*), how can it be so? For the ablative case is prescribed for the sense of "cause" (*yataḥ*) in the rule "from which the attainment of prosperity and the supreme good results," and the suffix *-tas* is intended to convey the meaning of the ablative.
And because a phenomenon (*dharma*) is not a cause with respect to its own arising,

it has been stated that that which possesses arising does so through a connection with a cause, as in "a cloth is produced from threads," and so forth; since [that cause] is what leads to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), it is *dharma*.

If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is redundant because Dharma has already been designated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the two effects— namely, worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)— we say no; for heaven and liberation are themselves Dharma, arising is its mark (*liṅga*), and the mark [is the means of cognition].
"Because it is a means of valid cognition.
And thus,
heaven and liberation are produced by qualities that lack the sub-class of "quality-ness" which is established in our own perception.

Because of its production. That which has production is produced by a quality that lacks the intermediate genus of "quality-ness" residing in our own perception, just like falling. And this [sound] is likewise; therefore, it is so. "Possessing production" is the logical reason (*hetu*).

If it is argued that it is not "origination" [that is meant], we say no; for since origination is never found to deviate [from fire], the possessive suffix (*matup*) would be redundant. If it is then argued that one should simply say "because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) and not "because of possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattvāt*), let it be so.

We shall examine this in the context of inference. Furthermore, falling [as an effect] is produced by the quality of gravity (gurutva), which is devoid of being a subordinate genus under the quality-ness (guṇatva) established by our perception;
and here, "being a fall" (patanatva) is the limiting condition (upādhi) in the case of the gravity of a whole (avayavin) which is produced by the gravity of its parts (avayava).

Because the pervasion of the probandum is violated; for even when the aforementioned probandum is present, the state of falling is absent there. Likewise, this applies to the cognition of a qualified heavy object produced by the heaviness of a qualifier, and to the impact and so forth produced by heaviness.
The failure of [the alleged upādhi] to pervade the probandum (sādhyāvyāpakatva) is to be observed.

Nor is "being produced by gravity" (gurutvajanyatva) an upādhi here, because the qualification "gravity" (gurutva) pervades only those things that are similar to the subject (pakṣatulya), and because non-produced things [are excluded] precisely by virtue of being produced.

Because it is excluded [from the subject]. Furthermore, a qualifying attribute that excludes only what is equivalent to the subject is not an "extraneous condition" (*upādhi*) when it serves as the means of proof for the subject, as in the case of "being produced by a body" being the reason for "having an agent.
[This applies to] heaven and liberation.

If it is argued: "The two [motions] are not produced by a quality that lacks the possession of a sub-class of the genus *guṇatva* (quality-ness) which is established by our perception, because they are not produced by gravity (*gurutva*), like space"—we say no, because even in the case of being unproduced (*ajanyatva*), there is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Nor is "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) the limiting adjunct here, because [it is absent] in the destruction of gravity.

Because the pervasion with the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*) is destroyed: for that [destruction] is produced by the quality of gravity (*gurutva*), which lacks the lower genus of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) residing in our perceptual experience, and because it is an absence (*abhāva*). The destruction of gravity is not produced by non-gravity. This...
If it is argued that "the destruction of gravity is not produced by that [prior] gravity, because it is a destruction and because it is a non-entity,

like the destruction of a pot"— [we reply that] this is not so, because the property to be proven (the probans), namely "being produced by gravity" and so forth, is unestablished due to its non-cognition anywhere.

The Teachers [the Bhaṭṭas] maintain that because the cognition of non-existence (abhāva) is preceded by the cognition of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), and because it is a form of perception accompanied by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and because in some cases of cognition there is sublation (bādhā) by the very subject under discussion, this [non-existence] must be depended upon for the establishment of the probandum (sādhya).
We, however, say: gravity is that which produces a state devoid of being produced by gravity.

This gravity produces a state devoid of being produced by that [gravity], because it is denotative, like a jar; thus, when it is established that there is a state produced by gravity, [the argument holds].

There is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) regarding destruction and the like, and a refutation of the direct pervasion of "existence" (*bhāvatva*), which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the root inference. Furthermore, in establishing that [destruction] is not produced by gravity (*gurutva*), there is sublation by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), since it is established precisely as being produced by gravity. By that—

The negation— that liberation (*mukti*) is not produced by a quality that lacks the sub-class of quality residing in what is established by our own perception, because it is a non-existence (*abhāva*), like mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)— is refuted;
for there is an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to non-existence as determined by its being destroyed by gravity, [and] with respect to its being unproduced (*ajanya*).

And because it possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*). Therefore, even Udayana’s argument—that liberation is not produced by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) because it is other than a means for experience—is refuted; for [liberation] has the state of being unproduced (*ajanyatva*) as its limiting condition once unseen merit has ceased.

And because of deviation; for through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the cause of destruction. Furthermore, Udayana also demonstrated that in the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*), the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the cause of the counter-positive.

Furthermore, since it is accepted that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is simply the unseen itself when that unseen has perished, [the definition] "being other than experience and its means" amounts to being other than pleasure, pain, and their means,
or else being other than the experience of pleasure and pain and their means.

Or [the definition might be] "being other than pleasure, pain, their cessation, and the means thereto. In the first and second cases, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the self-realization produced by the dharma born of yoga, for that too is a cause of pleasure and pain.

If it is argued that this [self-realization] is also a cause of pleasure and pain—that is not so, because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*). In the third case, however, there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

Since liberation consists in the cessation of suffering, it cannot be established as something other than that [suffering]. If it is argued that [the reason] "arising" is inconclusive because it applies to suffering and so forth, we say no; for being produced by dharma is not what is to be proven [in this context].

Because there is a certainty regarding the absence of the probandum— namely, being produced by a quality devoid of the subordinate genus of quality residing in our perception— the absence of suffering [is established];
for it is possible that [suffering] is produced by a quality that lacks the subordinate genus of quality residing in our perception and is non-dharma (adharma).
If it is argued that "arising" is an inconclusive reason because it occurs in cases where the probandum is doubtful, such as suffering and the like—
[we reply: no, for if residing in a case where the probandum is doubtful were a flaw,
all inference would collapse, since all reasons [would be flawed].

Because it resides in a subject (*pakṣa*) where the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful; otherwise, the establishment of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) would be unavoidable. If it is argued that the flaw consists in residing in a doubtful probandum that lacks the status of being a subject—[we reply: no.

Is being a subject (*pakṣatva*) the state of having a probandum that is doubted, or is it being presented as the locus (*dharmin*)? In the first case, even suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth would be subjects;
for it is untenable to claim that [the fallacy] is defective because it arises from residing in a doubted probandum that lacks the status of being a subject.

In the second case, even smoke and the like would be defective, because they would be suspected of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to their presence in another mountain where the probandum is doubted, which is distinct from the mountain presented as the locus (*dharmin*).

Now, if it is argued that "pakṣatulya" refers to something distinct from what is included as the subject (*dharmin*) and possesses a doubtful probandum (*sādhya*), because—like the *pakṣa*—it has a doubtful probandum; and if it is asked whether this state of having a doubtful probandum as its locus is qualified by the exclusion of being a *pakṣa*, or unqualified: [the answer is that it is neither].
The objection is stated that [the argument] would result in the collapse of inference as a whole; however, one should be satisfied with the fact that this applies equally to the case at hand.
Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding gravity here, because [it is accepted that] action and so forth are produced by gravity.
If it is argued that liberation and the like are produced by gravity because they are effects, just like falling—

this is not so, because the probans is overqualified by the property of being a non-substance (*adravyatva*). Since eternal substances constitute the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) from which the probans must be excluded, it is impossible for them to be included within the subject (*pakṣa*).

Now, if it is argued that while there may not be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by virtue of [the property] being a quality, there will nonetheless be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), we say: no.
For what is this inference? It is an inference regarding a quality that is devoid of possessing a sub-class of the genus "quality" (*guṇatva*) as established in our own perception.

The meaning would be either that it apprehends the universal of heaviness (*gurutvajāti*), or that it does not apprehend the absence of the universal of heaviness. It is not the first case, because the universal of heaviness has not been presented as a qualifier of the quality [of heaviness]. Even though it has not been presented...

If it is argued that the universal *gurutva-jāti* (the genus of gravity) is established by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), we say no; for in the case of being produced by a quality of gravity that lacks the lower-order genus of quality residing in our perceptual experience, there exists a limiting condition (*upādhi*) just as there is in the case of substantiality (*dravyatva*). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

If it is asked: "Since there is an absence of the universal *gurutva* (heaviness), and because that [universal] is not apprehended, how can there be an absence of heaviness in a quality that produces liberation— a quality which lacks the possession of a subordinate universal under the genus *guṇatva* (quality-ness) residing in our perception?"— listen.
This [entity] is devoid of the genus "heaviness" (gurutvajāti),
because it produces liberation, like the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra);
and there is no absence of the quality-ness (guṇatva) that is devoid of possessing a subordinate genus within the quality-ness residing in our perceptual objects.

The qualifying condition (*upādhi*)— namely, the absence of the specific property of being devoid of a sub-class of qualityhood that is perceptible to us— is absent because there is no exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since gravity itself constitutes such a counter-example.

Because it is excluded precisely by being included within the category of *guṇatva* (quality-ness); and because "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) possesses a qualifier that lacks both the thing to be excluded and any counter-example; nevertheless, in the case of "the mountain possesses fire," the state of not possessing fire in what is non-mountain...

The property of being other than the subject (*pakṣetaratva*) [is not a valid counter-example], because there is an absence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) to be excluded by the qualification "other than the mountain," and because those things devoid of fire are already excluded by virtue of being devoid of fire. Now, suppose this [subject] possesses the genus of gravity (*gurutvajāti*).

There is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on the reason: "because it possesses the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) that lacks any subordinate genus residing within the quality-ness that is established by our own perception," such as heaviness (*gurutva*). Nor is there here the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*) consisting in being a producer of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Because those causes that lack the universal of gravity (gurutvajāti) are excluded precisely by their being non-causes,

and because a non-cause— such as the final destruction (antyadhvaṃsa) and so forth— is not excluded even by the qualification "liberation" (mokṣa), [the definition] does not apply to a non-cause of liberation.
In a non-cause, there is no [liberating cause].

If you think that [the reason] is "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) because it exists and because it possesses a qualification devoid of exclusion from the form of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), that is not so;
for this falling is produced by a quality which lacks the genus of gravity (*gurutva*) that produces it, and which lacks the sub-genus of quality residing in our perceptual experience.
Because [the argument] "due to being an effect, like the falling of another" would result in a fallacy (vyabhicāra) with respect to that which is devoid of the universal of gravity (gurutvajāti),
yet is a substratum of quality that lacks the intermediate sub-universal of quality residing in our perceptual experience.

Nor is the first inference redundant because the property (*dharma*) is established by this [second inference] alone; for while this [second inference] is common to both *dharma* and *adharma*, it establishes *dharma* [specifically], whereas the first inference does not establish the *dharma* that generates heaven and liberation. Now, [if one objects]:
If it is argued that while there may not be a difference in meaning due to its being a *guṇa*, it will nonetheless be so by virtue of being *adharma*—
is this then an inference: "Liberation is produced by a *guṇa* that lacks the intermediate genus of being a quality residing in what is perceptible to us"?

Does it apprehend the quality that produces liberation as being non-dharma, or does it apprehend it as being dharma? It cannot be the first, because non-dharma-ness is not produced in the pervading portion [of the subject], for one who possesses the means of proof.

[The first alternative is rejected] because gravity and so forth are excluded [from the definition], and thus it would be non-pervasive. Nor is the second [alternative valid], because even when the property-ness (*dharmatva*) is not apprehended, that which possesses property-ness is still apprehended. If you ask, "How is there property-ness here?", listen: this is the substratum of property-ness.

[The probandum] is "the state of being devoid of heaviness that does not produce suffering and devoid of possessing a subordinate genus of quality residing in our perceptual experience," because it is a quality (*guṇatvāt*).

[Objection: The "state of being a producer of pleasure"—as in the case of what will be described as a producer of pleasure—is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). [Response: This is not so, because the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), which is the cause of liberation, is itself the cause of the eight great supernatural powers (*aṣṭamahāsiddhi*).
Because it is admitted that [the object] produces pleasure;
nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (asiddhaviśeṣaṇatā) due to the non-establishment of its being a dharma,
for [the subject] is "that which produces pleasure while lacking the possession of a sub-class of the genus *guṇatva* residing in our own perception."

A quality (*guṇa*) possesses the characteristic of being a property (*dharma*), because it is the locus of a property that resides in what is excluded from that which possesses the characteristic of a property, yet is devoid of residing in that which lacks the characteristic of a property; for it possesses a universal (*jāti*), like a cow—thus the status of being a property is established. And the characteristic of a property is as follows:

The definition [of quality] is: being a quality that is devoid of the universal "quality-ness" (guṇatva) which resides in qualities perceived by us and which lacks heaviness (gurutva) that does not produce suffering;

for, in our state as yogis, since heaviness, the property of dharma (dharmatva), and so forth are perceived by us, the sub-universal residing in those qualities is also resident in what is perceived by us, and thus heaviness, the property of dharma, and so forth would also possess the sub-universal of quality-ness residing in qualities perceived by us.

If it is argued that, because the quality ascribed to that [object] is untenable, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) and sublation (*bādha*) in the first inference—[we reply: no;
for our "perceptibility" (*asmatpratyakṣatva*) consists in being the object of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) that is not produced by yoga, and that...
"Because it does not exist in gravity, dharma, and so forth, there is no sublation (bādha) either.
Now, by the term "yogaja" (born of yoga), is it the dharma born of yoga that is intended, or its distinctness?

In the first case, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvam), since the dharma born of yoga is unestablished when [the existence of] dharma itself is unestablished.

Because [the reason] is even more unestablished. As for the second [alternative], the defects of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) and contradiction (*bādha*) remain as before, since even the yogic direct perception whose object is gravity,
dharma, and so forth, is not produced by yoga-born [dharma], the destruction of yoga, or the like.
If it is argued that [the reason] is invalid because properties such as heaviness (*gurutva*) are also perceived by us, we say no;

for what is intended is that which is produced by yoga (*yogaja*), provided that the qualifiers "having a property not grasped [by ordinary perception]" and "being other than that" are applied. When these qualifiers are intended, [the reason remains valid].

"Because all inference would collapse. Alternatively, "being an object of direct perception for us" means being an object of a direct perception produced by this [present] body. Nor should it be argued that being an object of a direct perception produced by this body is possible even for dharma and so forth.

Because by that very form which produces the direct perception of the body and so forth, the direct perception of the objects such as dharma is produced, it is precisely that [form] which is intended by the word "that" (tat). Or alternatively, Devadatta...

The proof of *dharma* is as follows: "The subject under discussion (the self) possesses a quality that produces pleasure and is devoid of the sub-class of qualities residing in our own direct perception that belong to Devadatta, because it is a self, like Yajñadatta.
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here.
Although the property of being a quality— lacking the subordinate genus of "quality" residing in our perception— is unestablished in the case of Yajñadatta and others,
[the definition] consists in the possession of a quality that produces pleasure, which resides in Yajñadatta and lacks the subordinate genus of "quality" residing in our perception.
Because it is well-established.
Nor is this "not being the locus of the contact between self and mind" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here,
because of the qualification [that it applies to] the self and the mind as well.
Because there is no counter-example to be excluded;
for substances are excluded precisely by virtue of being the locus of conjunction with counter-examples,
whereas non-substances are not excluded even by virtue of not being the locus of the conjunction between the self and the mind.

Nor is our [perceptual] cognition [of color, etc. non-counter-argued by the reason "not being the locus of the conjunction of self and mind," because it is subject to the condition (upādhi) of "not being the self";

nor is there any suspicion of proving something irrelevant (arthāntaratā), since qualities other than those such as form—which are distinct from the quality of demerit—possess the lower genus of "form-ness" and so forth residing in forms and the like that are perceptible to us.

This is because even mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possesses the genus of being a subordinate latent impression (*avāntara-saṃskāra-tva*), which is a quality established by the force of our own perception; furthermore,
[it is not a quality of the self] because it does not produce demerit, weight, or pleasure, and because weight is precluded from the self.

Nor will a twenty-fifth quality, distinct from form and the rest, be established; for it is not the case that [the object] is merely a property (dharma), which would imply a different meaning [than our position]. Rather, [what is meant] is simply the state of being a quality that produces pleasure, while lacking the subordinate genus of "quality-ness" (guṇatva) that resides in qualities perceived by us.

Because it possesses the characteristic of a phenomenon (*dharma*); and because, once the twenty-fourth phenomenon is established, it is impossible to manifest a distinct entity by means of a twenty-fifth. Or else, Devadatta...

The proof of the property [dharma] is as follows: "That which possesses a quality producing pleasure, yet is devoid of Devadatta’s cognition, desire, effort, and speed, exists because it possesses selfhood (ātmatva), like Yajñadatta.
The refutation of the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (arthāntara) and so forth is as before. And regarding the property of selfhood (ātmatva)...

By the statement "since validity [of cognition] results in the attainment of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*)," that which produces happiness is indicated as the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of implication.
[The reason for this is] the exclusion of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, due to the absence of the property of possessing a sub-class of quality (*guṇatva*) residing in our own perception.
And there is a qualification:

by stating that "dharma is that from which the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) results," it is implied that "adharma is that from which the non-attainment of prosperity results"; this is indicated by the first inference.

By treating [the object] as belonging to the side of suffering, and by substituting the term "producing suffering" for the term "producing happiness" in the second and third [definitions], the establishment of *adharma* is to be understood;
for if all objects were explicitly mentioned, the status of the work as a *sūtra* would be violated, as they say:
Those who know the sūtras understand a sūtra to be concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in its scope, devoid of filler, and irreproachable.
Thus [ends section] 2.

To refute the objection that the first inference suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish heaven and liberation, the Sūtra states: "The authority of the Veda (*āmnāya*) is established because it is the word of Him (the Lord). (1.1.3)

Thus, the word "that" (tad) refers back to heaven and liberation as they were mentioned in the context; for by means of that, there is the exposition— and consequently, the production of valid knowledge— of those two, namely heaven and liberation, [which constitutes] the purpose of the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
The authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and so forth, consists in their being instruments of valid cognition (*pramiti-karaṇatva*).

It is called "Āmnāya" because it is traditionally handed down (*āmnāyate*) and recited as the cause of Dharma. For instance, even if the Āmnāya were established as authoritative, if it were not a means of valid cognition regarding [matters such as] heaven and the like, [it would not be authoritative].

In that case, because there would be no other object to be established, it would simply not be a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*); and it has already been stated that the Veda is not a means of valid cognition regarding *dharma*. Furthermore, for that which is not a means of valid cognition with respect to heaven and so forth, it is impossible for it to possess validity either in establishing that [heaven] or in establishing the means to achieve it. Or, let it be so.

The authority of words such as "sacrifice" with respect to the sacrifice and so forth— their capacity to prompt performance— is indeed difficult to establish, because the wise do not engage in action without a purpose.
Therefore, [the knowledge of the result] is a necessary factor for performance.

Because it lacks the capacity to produce valid cognition, the invalidity of the Veda— characterized by its failure to prompt action— is unavoidable. And here, since the word "that" (tat) refers back to hell, [the injunction] applies to hell just as it does to heaven.
It should be understood that the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, by the first aphorism, *dharma* and *adharma*, which are the subjects to be expounded by the treatise, have been shown. By the second aphorism, however, heaven, liberation, and hell are made the [subject] positions.

The means of valid cognition regarding dharma and adharma have been shown; however, by the third aphorism, it is stated that for heaven, liberation, and hell, the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is the authority. Thus, the triad of aphorisms has been explained.

Alternatively, having stated the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of the treatise—namely, *dharma*—by means of the first sūtra, the second sūtra establishes the purpose (*prayojana*), stating: "That from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is *dharma*. For indeed, [the purpose] cannot be understood as long as the subject matter of the treatise is not known.
The engagement of listeners is possible only when dharma is the means for attaining heaven and liberation,
because engagement is preceded by the cognition that something is a means to a desired end; this would not occur in the absence of dharma being a means for heaven and liberation.
Because it is untenable that the understanding of dharma (*dharma-bodha*) produced by hearing the treatise (*śāstra-śravaṇa-janya*) is desirable,
as it is not an auxiliary factor (*anaṅga*) for the performance of the means to accomplish dharma that results in heaven (*svarga*) or liberation (*apavarga*). Therefore,
for those listeners who are being induced to act by means of the treatise, [the purpose is] dharma...
It must be established that [the Veda] is the means for attaining heaven and liberation.
Now, one might object: "How can heaven and liberation be the purposes [of the Veda] if they lack any means of valid cognition?
Anticipating this doubt, [the sūtra states]: "The authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is established because it speaks of those [two]."
By the third aphorism, it is established that the Veda is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding heaven and liberation, which constitute the purpose [of the treatise].
Now, if the aphorism is intent upon propounding *dharma*, which is the object of the treatise's ultimate purport—
[The objection that it is] useless [is incorrect], because that [dharma] is understood from the scripture alone; for if it were not understood,
it could not be the object of the scripture, and thus the first sūtra would fail to establish dharma as the intended subject matter of the scripture.
