Because, starting from the removal of obstacles, it generates an understanding of the means to dharma, heaven, and liberation— which are the objects of the treatise’s purport as residing in the listener—
thereby producing the motivation for the listener to engage with the treatise through that understanding of dharma.

Because it must have been anticipated beforehand; for it is not possible to comprehend that a dharma which has not been understood is a means to heaven and liberation, since a qualified cognition is produced by the cognition of the qualificand. Therefore, for the listeners—

This aphorism is purposeful because it establishes that an understanding of Dharma— which is produced by the treatise and so forth— must be cultivated for the sake of realizing that the limbs of hearing the treatise are the means to achieve Dharma, heaven, and liberation;
for without an engagement [with the subject] through its stated purpose, there would be no [interest] in the treatise for listeners.

Engagement [occurs]. For indeed, there is no engagement on the part of listeners toward a sūtra that sets forth the subject matter and so forth, without first having understood that subject matter and so forth;
therefore, in that case as well, another sūtra setting forth the subject matter and so forth would have to be commenced.

If it is argued that this leads to an infinite regress— thinking "it is thus there too, and it is thus there too as well"— we say no; for in the first sūtra, which introduces the inquiry into the dharma that is the subject matter of the scripture,
the very object to be established by this [treatise] itself has already been established, just like the object to be established by the scripture.
Because the Dharma itself is what is to be understood by both [teacher and listener],
once the meaning of the sūtra taught in the treatise has been understood,
the desire to know that which remains to be taught does not arise.
As for the objection that there would be an infinite regress due to the commencement of other sūtras to indicate that [purpose],
since the very fact of its being a purpose for itself is established by the same sūtra that establishes the purpose of the treatise, there is no need to commence another sūtra to establish that.
Because the purpose of the treatise itself is the purpose that brings about the understanding of the purpose of the treatise;
or alternatively, [the reason is as follows].
The aphorism "Now, therefore, we shall explain dharma" (athāto dharmaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ), which teaches dharma as the purpose of the treatise that expounds categories such as substance,
does not express the subject matter of the treatise itself, because sentences do not [directly] denote their own subject matter.
Because denotation (*abhidhā*) is a property of words; nor because it would follow that [the treatise] teaches something other than the substance taught by the treatise,
since *dharma* is taught by a treatise distinct from the three aphorisms (*trisūtrī*).
Because dharma and adharma are to be established by the *Guṇavibhāga-sūtra*,
and because there is no other means of knowledge (*māna*) to support the view that the particle "ca" (and) intends to include dharma and adharma as taught in another sūtra.

This is because such passages as "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial action of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)" [VS 5.2.14] establish causality by way of restating what is already observed.

Furthermore, because such statements as "Activity toward dharma and adharma is preceded by desire and aversion" (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.17) serve to establish that [activity] is produced by attachment and aversion, while referring back to dharma and adharma.

If it is argued that [the scriptures] serve to establish the nature of dharma and adharma as characterized by agency and being an effect— no, for through an examination of the context and other factors, it is precisely causality and so forth that are intended to be known. It is the causality of fire’s upward flaming and such that is sought to be understood.
If it is argued that [the treatise] does not concern itself with mere causality, we say no;
for dharma and adharma are already known from the very first sūtra. Since there is no other subject to be expounded, that sūtra has as its scope the essential nature of dharma and adharma.

If it is argued that even here, there exists something to be established as the subject matter of the treatise (*śāstra*) that is distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *dharma* and so forth— or if it is argued that, given its status as the subject matter, the *sūtra* which serves as the qualifier [of the treatise] must itself be the subject matter of the treatise—
we say: no, because the status of being the subject matter of the treatise...

Because it is not established by the treatise; or, if it were established by the treatise, it would follow that the treatise itself—which serves as its qualifier—would also have to be established by the treatise.
However, there exists another sūtra that establishes heaviness and fluidity.
Because of heaviness, there is falling. Here, fluidity is not the cause of flowing;

rather, it is the very sūtras beginning with [Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.5] that establish heaviness and fluidity as the causes of falling and flowing, respectively. Thus, the status of specific instances of heaviness, fluidity, and so forth is accepted.

Nor should it be argued that, just as gravity and other qualities are established by the sūtras explaining their causes such as falling, let the establishment of dharma and so forth be achieved by those very sūtras explaining their causes such as upward flaming; what then is the purpose of the first sūtra?
Furthermore, since the meaning of another sūtra could also be understood from the words of a commentator, it would follow that there is no need to begin another sūtra; [therefore,] the treatise,
by its primary purport, teaches Dharma through the exposition of substance and so forth.

If it is argued that [the scripture] teaches [them], we say no; for its purport lies only in [their] being substances and so forth, since substances and the like are not ends of human life in their own nature.
Rather, it is as the means for accomplishing *dharma* that substance-ness and the other categories are to be taught.
If it is argued that the purport of the treatise must be stated as being the establishment of properties such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth,

and that consequently— by the maxim of "the unperceived qualifier" (*nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*)— the purport of the treatise is established even regarding the property that qualifies the means of proof (*sādhanaviśeṣaṇadharma*), we say: no, whether the first aphorism exists or does not exist.
Because it would be impossible to determine that the treatise has the dharma as its scope and purpose;

for if the first sūtra exists, the dharma is established from that very source, and thus the treatise would have no purpose there. And if the first sūtra does not exist, the dharma is not established, and thus [the treatise]...
Because it is difficult to ascertain the intended meaning regarding its scope.

Furthermore, does this aphorism set forth the subject matter of the entire treatise, or does it set forth the subject matter of only a single part of the treatise? It cannot be the first [alternative].

Because it would follow that the treatise is purposeless. Nor is the second [alternative] correct, for even if this [particular point] were not explained— just as other parts of the treatise might remain unexplained— the engagement of the listener could still be accomplished.

If it is argued that the treatise (*śāstra*) exists for the sake of its detailed exposition— no, because if there is no addition to what is to be established, a detailed exposition is redundant. If it is argued that the treatise exists for the sake of explaining this aphorism (*sūtra*)— no, for what is the meaning of this aphorism without an explanation?

Is it known or not? In the first case, the commentary would be purposeless; in the second, the aphorism (*sūtra*) would be purposeless, because at the beginning of a treatise (*śāstra*), it generates the understanding of what is to be explained, and because a treatise generates understanding independently [of other means].

Therefore, the opinion of Ātreya-Ācārya— that [the treatise] is the expositor of that which is to be established by the scripture, namely, the substratum of various superior qualities that impel or restrain, along with its equipment, effects, causes, enjoyments, and the means of destruction— should be disregarded.
If it is argued that this sutra is solely intended to state the purpose [of the treatise],

and that it would be impossible for students to understand "this is its purpose" without first comprehending what is to be propounded by the treatise— [we reply: no, because [the purpose] arises from this very treatise...

If it is argued that since it is possible to understand that "the purpose of knowledge is dharma," and that even without understanding what is propounded by this scripture, one can understand that the knowledge produced by this scripture has that [dharma] as its object— [we reply: no, because [one cannot know] that "this is the knowledge produced by this scripture."

Because by means of the word, there is the production [of knowledge] even regarding that which is not delimited by its specific object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even by the word "knowledge," knowledge itself would not be understood. Or, let it be that he has a general understanding of something to be propounded by this treatise; yet, even if this were so, this [treatise] is not for that purpose alone.
It must be said that there is a Sūtra, because, precisely by virtue of being a sentence, it conveys some object of comprehension;
and because a Sūtra conveys a specific property (dharma) that is to be understood.
Now, [an objection may be raised: Dharma is neither happiness nor the cessation of suffering. How [can this be]?
To dispel the doubt regarding the purpose [of the treatise], the aphorism states:
"That from which the accomplishment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results is dharma" (1.1.2).
Since that which accomplishes it—just like pleasure and so forth—is desired by the person, it constitutes dharma.

The sense is that its purpose is like that of food, water, and so forth. Thus, the purpose has been established by these two sūtras. Furthermore, in response to the doubt as to what the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding unrighteousness (*adharma*) is, the second sūtra sets forth inference (*anumāna*).

The third aphorism, which establishes the authority of scripture, is: "The authority of tradition (āmnāya) is due to its being His word" (1.1.3). The word "that" (tat) refers back to the previously mentioned *dharma*, which is the means for attaining heaven and liberation. By that...
"The authority of the *āmnāya* (sacred tradition) arises from its teaching of the *dharma* that is the means to attain heaven and liberation (*apavarga*).
It is called *āmnāya* because it is handed down (*āmnāyate*) and recited as the authority for *dharma*;
it consists of the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). And there is also traditional practice (*ācāra*), as Yājñavalkya said:"
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vedāṅgas— these,
together with the Vedas, are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma.
Thus it is said; and likewise: "The conduct of the virtuous.
Thus it is said.

If it is asked how the Veda brings about the cognition of dharma, we reply: because the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth bring about the cognition of a means to a desired end. For instance, one who desires rice [is prompted by such injunctions].
Immediately after hearing the sentence "He went," etc., used by the eldest elder,
and observing the middle-aged elder proceeding to act accordingly,
the child reflects as follows: "This bodily movement..."
[The cognition] is produced by an effort generated by a desire produced by a cognition that makes known the means to a desired end, because it is an activity,
like my own activity. Immediately after that, this cognition of being a means to a desired end is not produced by the senses [but rather by something else].
This is because the reciter and others are not in sensory contact [with the object], and because past and present [actions]—

being devoid of the cause consisting of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)— cannot be established as effects. Nor is this [cognition] produced by inference, such as "this cooking is a means to a desired end because it is cooking," since [in that case] dharma would not be established.
Because the cooking to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is not apprehended through either perception or inference,

and because the mere verbal root *pacati* does not convey the cooking as something to be accomplished; and even if one were to infer that some kind of cooking is a means to a desired end, for the middle-aged elder...
Because activity directed toward the cooking to be accomplished would be impossible if the suffix alone,
denoting mere efficient force (*bhāvanā*), did not convey that cooking to be accomplished; and because,
in the absence of the understanding of cooking as a means to a desired end produced by an effort, [such activity would likewise be impossible] through both the stem and the suffix together.
Furthermore, the inference that cooking is a means to achieve a desired end is redundant,

since the fact that it is a means to achieve a desired end is already understood from verbal testimony and other sources. By this same reasoning, the argument that "this cooking is a means to achieve a desired end because it is the object of an injunction" is also refuted, as the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is unestablished.
Because the middle-aged elder does not understand the intention of the person who has reached the scope of the maturation of the sense organs and so forth;

if it is argued that [the meaning] is understood from the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) and so on— no, because at that time the middle-aged elder has not grasped the relationship (*saṃgati*) of the *liṅ* and other suffixes to that [intention], since he was in the stage of learning [the language].
Because it is subverting; and because, by means of the child's own case as an example,
even in the inference of the middle-aged man’s cognition of being a means to a desired end— which produces the effort that generates his activity— [the same subversion applies].

This is because [the existence of another] is inferred from their intention regarding the object-domain of their activity, whereas such [intention] is not perceived in oneself; for instance, people do not perceive—

through positive and negative concomitance— that their own activities, such as suckling at the breast or drinking, are preceded by an effort born of a desire produced by the cognition that those acts are means to a desired end.

Likewise, there is also the fact that [the cognition of the meaning] is preceded by the knowledge of the intended object of activity within its scope. Nor is it possible to have a cognition of the denotative capacity of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth with respect to an injunction (*praiṣa*) and the like if that injunction has not been cognized;
for it is accepted that the non-cognition of the denoted object is the cause of [failing to recognize] something as its denoter.

Now, regarding instruction (*upadeśa*), let it be granted that where the fruit of the action resides in the person being prompted (*prayojyapuruṣa*), there the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth possess the denotative power of expressing a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanavācakatva*), because the exclusion of the person being prompted from [the action] is preceded by the cognition of it as a means to a desired end. But where...
Furthermore, the fruit of the action does not reside in the person who is employed to act,

but rather in the person who employs them; just as in a king's command such as "Cook for the chef" or "Bring the elephant for the minister," [the result] pertains to the cooking performed by the chef and so forth.

Because rice and other such items are the means for accomplishing what the king desires, the understanding that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote "being a means to a desired end" does not arise in that context; for this is because a cook or similar person who is being prompted does not infer the cooking as a means to a desired end based on their own cognition. This is because the cooking [is already known].

Vācaspati and others maintain that [the word "cooking"] denotes the means for satisfying the cook, and in some cases, it denotes the intention of the person [who ordered the meal]. But that too is not correct, because while the rice is the means for the king's satisfaction, it is [the object] of both the king and the cook.

Because cooking is also a means to achieve what is desired— by virtue of being the means for the satisfaction of the owner who provides the food— the cook is likewise a means to achieve what is desired.
Now, how is it that the cooked rice, which is the means for the owner's satisfaction, [is so]?

If it is argued that [the action] has the quality of being a means to accomplish what is desired by the cook—understand this to mean that the master’s satisfaction is what is desired by the cook. But surely the master’s satisfaction is not the cook’s pleasure, because it resides in the master; nor is it a means to the cook’s pleasure.

Since the pleasure and so forth belonging to one person cannot be the means for producing the pleasure and so forth of another, how can it be desired by the cook? It is said in reply: because the satisfaction of the master is of the nature of happiness, it is desired by the cook by its very nature, just like the pleasure residing within himself. It is indeed [pleasure] residing within himself.

If it is argued that "pleasure is desired"—no, for even the pleasure of a son and so forth is desired. Otherwise, when a father performs a rite intended for his own pleasure on the occasion of a son's birth, there would follow the absurd consequence that the son’s purity and other such qualities would be the fruit [of the rite]. [This is true] in its essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*).

If it is argued that since happiness is desired, the happiness of an enemy or a neutral person would also be desired—no, because what is desired is the happiness that is the object of one's own cognition.

For just as the self and so forth, as well as sons and so forth, are desired because they are means to happiness, so too is the giver of the sensation [the master]; thus it is established that the cooking of rice, which is the means for satisfying the master, is a means to what is desired.

Otherwise, in the case of a cook engaged in cooking, since there would be an absence of the means for achieving a desired end within that domain, no desire produced by that [means] would arise; and in the absence of such a desire, no effort produced by it would occur.
If it is argued that one acts even without desiring it due to a royal command—no, for the activity of a conscious being is produced by desire. Not so.

If it is argued that while some activity arises from a desire produced by the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), other activities arise from an injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth— this is not so,
because the utterance of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) [denotes] a specific desire on the part of the prompter (*prayoktṛ*).
For it is impossible for exertion and the like— which have already perished— to be the generators of an activity that lacks the moment immediately preceding that activity;
thus, the cognition of the instigator’s command and so forth, produced by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, is the cause of activity.

If it is argued that the *praiṣa* (command) and so forth exist in their own form [as the cause of activity], we say no; for even when one perceives a command and so forth that are not to be carried out, there is no activity.
If it is argued that the knowledge of a command and so forth that are to be carried out is the cause of activity, we say no; why?
For even when there is an understanding of an injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth that is not delimited by a specific object, one does not act; [therefore,
what is required is] the knowledge of an injunction to be followed that is delimited by a specific object.

If it is argued that [the knowledge of an injunction] is the cause of activity— does the cognition of an impulsion (*praiṣa*) and so forth, unqualified by a specific object, serve as the cause of activity in its own right, or rather does the impulsion of one who is to be obeyed consist in being a means to a desired end?

[The opponent argues that the desire to act arises] through the generation of an inference regarding the means to achieve the desired object, by way of [the cognition of] being within the range of experience and being an object.

Not the first [alternative], because there is a lack of evidence (mānābhāva). If it is argued: "This activity is produced by the knowledge of an injunction toward this [object], because it arises immediately after that, just like a mental impression (saṃskāra)"—no.
Because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to what is produced immediately after [the object] but separated by an interval.

If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) is "being produced immediately after that [object] without an interval"—no, because there is deviation with respect to jars and the like, which are also produced immediately after that [object] without an interval. Those too...

If it is argued that they are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), we say no; for this would entail an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), and because the qualification "immediately preceding" (*avyavahita*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
[Furthermore,] from the cognition of a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth, there arises the cognition that [the action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

This is because it is accepted that desire arises from the cognition that something is a means to a desired end, and from that, activity follows; furthermore, in this case, activity itself serves as the probans (upādhi). Nor should there be any suspicion here of the fallacy of "being other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva).

Because it excludes the counter-example— namely, the activity of suckling at the breast and so forth, which is not produced by the knowledge of a command or the like— the following argument holds: this activity is not produced by the knowledge of a command or the like,
because it is an activity, just like the activity of suckling at the breast and so forth.
And because it is an antidote [to desire].

Nor is the second [alternative] correct, because [the action] arises from a desire produced by an inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), which itself is generated by the knowledge that the object is within the scope of a command from one who is to be obeyed.
Thus, since it is established that the cognition of an injunction (*praiṣa*) and the like is not the cause because activity has already arisen [by then],

and because the cognition of an injunction is destroyed at the moment the desire arises through the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), there is an absence of such cognition in the moment immediately preceding the activity.
And because of the faults in the previous position:

even if it were granted that the knowledge of a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth serves as a cause for a specific kind of activity, it would still be impossible to avoid the conclusion that the action is produced by a desire generated by the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanajñāna*). This...

Activity is produced by a desire generated by the cognition that a particular object is a means to achieve a desired end, because it possesses the nature of activity, like any commonly accepted instance of activity; and there is no deviation [from this rule] in the case of activity directed toward a demon or similar entity causing one's own house to burn, for that too...
This is because [the action] is preceded by a desire based on the cognition that burning one's own house and so forth is a means to achieve what is desired by the Piśāca;
for through the burning of one's own house and so forth, the pleasure desired by the Piśāca and others arises.
Nor is there any deviation [in the rule] regarding activity produced by water, wind, and so forth.
This is because there is an absence of activity in the form of effort (*prayatna*) in persons being carried along by water and the like;

and because there is an absence of activity—also known by the synonym *ceṣṭā* (volitional movement)—in their bodies. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule regarding human activity due to the movement of a stone on the ground by force, for that [movement]...

[The action of] carrying stones, which consists in avoiding the carrying of stones that are means to an undesirable end, is preceded by the cognition that [the opposite action] is a means to a desired end, because it is produced by desire. If it is asked how carrying stones is a means to an undesirable end, [the answer is:
because the absence of carrying stones—which is the object of the command—is caused by suffering.
Because it is a cause of harm (*bādhāhetutvāt*).

Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of engaging in activities such as consuming poison or jumping from a precipice, for even those are preceded by a desire born from the cognition that the destruction of the body— which is a means to desired ends— serves as a means to alleviate sufferings such as humiliation.
Nor is there any deviation from the rule regarding the activity of the Blessed Lord Mahādeva in [attaining] heaven and so forth;

for on the view that [such states] are effects produced by the effort of Īśvara, he too is equivalent to the subject of the argument (pakṣa). On the view that they are unproduced, [the objection applies] because of their being effects.

[This is] because the meaning of the word *pravṛtti* (inclination) is either "effort produced [by something] other than the life-force (*jīvanayoni*)" due to the qualification of the cause, or simply "effort. Therefore, it is established that in all cases of action,
the cognition of a task as a means to a desired end is the cause of inclination.
The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
If the optative suffixes did not denote being a means to a desired end,

then the rule *vidhinimantraṇāmantraṇādhīṣṭasampraśnaprārthaneṣu liṅ* [Pāṇini 3.3.161]— which prescribes the use of the optative in the senses of injunction, invitation, permission, request, inquiry, and entreaty— would be rendered meaningless.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the *Pāṇini-smṛti*, we say no; for by the word "injunction" (*vidhi*), the state of being a means to a desired end—
which is synonymous with "instigation" (*preraṇā*)— is denoted, and by the word "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*),
that [act] is meant whose rejection entails a transgression (*pratyavāya*).

Because it demonstrates that such [an act] is a means to achieve a desired end; because by the word "invitation" (*āmantraṇa*), there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in refusing it, since it is stated to be a means to achieve such a desired end; and by the term "request" (*adhīṣṭa*).
Because it expresses that [the action] is a means to achieve a desired end preceded by respect,
and because the *Pāṇinismṛti* is established as being based on reasoned principles (*nyāya*), it is untenable to postulate another basis for it.

Or let it be that only the *praiṣa* (command) and so forth are denoted by words such as "injunction" (*vidhi*) and the like; even so, there is no contradiction with the *smṛti* of Pāṇini. For even while he asserts that the *praiṣa* and so forth are denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, [he does not deny] the fact that the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) [is also conveyed].
Because there is no prohibition against its being denotable;

because there is no contradiction between its being the denoter of "being a means to a desired end"—which is established by logic—and its being the denoter of "command" (*praiṣa*) and so forth—established by traditional authority (*smṛti*);
and because Pāṇini did not state that the command itself or the knowledge thereof is the motivator of action.

Even in its negation, there is a contradiction with the Smṛti. By this, the argument that "this [word] is expressive because it is the means to achieve a desired end, since it falls within the scope of instigation (preraṇā)" is also refuted; for even if the term 'instigation' denotes the verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā), just as it denotes commands and the like.
For, just like the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the non-establishment of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is as indelible as diamond-paste.
This is because the middle-aged elder does not comprehend the verbal operation that is conducive to the activity directed toward the object of cooking.

And this is because, at the stage when [the child] lacks linguistic proficiency, even the middle-aged elder is still a "child"; and by means of the example of his own nature, the child infers for the middle-aged elder a cognition of the object as a means to a desired end, which produces an intention that generates effort—but this inference also fails to express a verbal operation whose scope is the object of the activity.

First, [the reason] is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because even when a child does not hear a word, they engage in activities such as suckling at the breast due to their failure to perceive that the cause of activity resides within themselves; furthermore, there is no evidence for a verbal operation conducive to activity. As for the argument: "This suffix, such as the optative (*liṅ*), possesses an operation conducive to activity, because it generates activity distinct from [any other] operation, like the self (*ātman*)," this is subject to the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), since [the suffix actually functions] through the cognition of a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*).
Furthermore, because the qualificand is unestablished, there is no evidence for the claim that a word generates activity.

If it is argued that the reason—"a word generates activity because it exists in the moment immediately preceding [the activity]"—is established, we say no; this is because the reason is inconclusive due to the case of space (*vyoman*) and other such entities.

Moreover, the qualification "immediately preceding" is itself unestablished. [Therefore,] from words and the like, there arises the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
If it is argued that the reason is established because this inclination (*pravṛtti*) is produced by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—
since it arises in the moment immediately following those [suffixes],
just like [an inclination] produced by the knowledge of them— [we reply: no.

Because there is a deviation [from the rule] due to jars and the like arising in the moment immediately following that [action], and because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*)— just as in the case of the self—
and because the qualification "being other than an operation" (*vyāpāretaratva*) is unestablished for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.
If it is argued that because the activity of an agent who employs [the word] is possible, and since activity is established through the word alone,

the employer is not the cause of the activity, and therefore the word does not have that as its operation— [we reply]: no, [for activity arises] precisely from what is produced by the cognition of the word.
Because activity is established [as being produced by the word], it is untenable to postulate an operation for the word itself if it does not produce activity. By this same reasoning,
the argument that "the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others possess an operation, because they are causes distinct from [their own] operations, like the self (*ātman*)" is also refuted.
This is refuted.

Now, regarding worldly sentences, the cognition of an impulsion (*preraṇā*) and so forth is the cause of activity, not the cognition of specific qualifiers such as a command (*praiṣa*), because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). And thus, for one who desires heaven...

It is inferred that the subsequent inclination following the hearing of sentences such as "one should sacrifice" is preceded by the cognition of an instigation (preraṇā) or the like, because it is an inclination,
just like an inclination produced by the cognition of a command (praiṣa). Not [otherwise].

There is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by means of the knowledge of an instigation (*preraṇā*) consisting in being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), because that [knowledge] does not have the object of activity as its domain. For being a means to what is desired is not determined by the object, as is the case with commands (*praiṣa*) and the like. However, the operation of the word...
It is described as being determined by its object and non-conceptual.
Furthermore, in this case, an injunction (*praiṣa*) and so forth are not possible, because such a thing is a specific intention of a person, and that is impossible in the impersonal Veda.

Now, let it be granted that the Blessed Lord Īśvara is indeed the teacher of Dharma, having directly realized the multitude of categories such as Dharma, which are the means for attaining heaven and liberation; what follows from this? To address this doubt:
The third sutra:
"On account of his word, the authority of the sacred tradition [is established]. (1.1.3)

Thus: by the pronoun "that" (*tad*), the omniscient teacher of Dharma mentioned in the word "Dharma" in the first sūtra is referred to. Furthermore, the expression "from speech" (*vacanāt*) is a statement emphasizing the abstract quality; it means "because of being speech" (*vacanatvāt*). "Āmnāya" refers to the Veda.
This is what is intended to be proven; the distinction here is that "authoritativeness" (prāmāṇyam) is what must be established.
The formal argument (prayoga), however, is as follows: Vedic statements are authoritative, because they are the words of God (īśvara).
It is like the case of someone who has accepted [the authority of] their own words. Nor is there an absence of an example,
for an example is established in the inferences proving the existence of God by including the qualification "composer of authoritative statements" [in the probans].

If it is argued that, because the specific qualification "author of unauthoritative statements" is employed in the inferences proving the existence of God (Īśvara), the status of being a statement by God is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the establishment of unauthoritative statements authored by God— [we reply: no.
Because the authorship of unauthoritative statements is not established due to the contradiction between being free from error and being the author of unauthoritative statements;
[and because] there is a contradiction between being the author of unauthoritative statements and being non-deluded.

If it is argued that, because of their mutual inseparability, let there also be no establishment of being an author of unauthoritative statements due to non-erroneousness— this is true; indeed, it does not occur,
precisely because of the qualification "being an author of unauthoritative statements."
Furthermore, once the establishment of error is achieved, who can prevent the subsequent establishment of non-error by means of that which is devoid of such [error]? Moreover,
regarding the two [cognitions] that lack the status of having as their object a property co-referential with error...

And because they are invariably concomitant with mutual non-existence: therein, "non-erroneousness" does not consist in being an author of unauthoritative statements regarding that [object], just as, for example, in the case of a jar or the like,
there is the absence of erroneousness in one who is non-erroneous regarding the jar.

Because of the absence, in a sentient being, of the authorship of unauthoritative statements, and because of the absence of knowledge of the meaning of such unauthoritative statements, as well as the intention to speak them and the effort directed toward that same object.
If it is argued that, because it would contradict his status as the author of authoritative scriptures, let there also be no establishment of his non-deludedness— this is true;
indeed, [non-deludedness] does not belong to one who possesses the qualification of being the author of unauthoritative scriptures.

The establishment of its being erroneous is also [admitted]. Furthermore, who can prevent the establishment of its being non-erroneous when it is established by means of that which is devoid of such [error]?
Now, [if it is argued that it is not so] because it lacks the qualification of being "devoid of having as its object a property co-located with error"—

If it is argued that the existence of the author of authoritative statements is established by such inferences as "Dharma is within the range of direct perception for the author of authoritative statements,
because it is an object of knowledge, like a jar," then we reply: no, for there is no one who [establishes] the authors of the most excellent authoritative statements.

Or else, [the proof may be formulated as]: "Persons such as ourselves also become possessors of direct perception of Dharma and so forth during the state of yoga-born merit (yogajadharma)," or "God is the author of authoritative statements because he is a person, just like me"—thus the example is established. Or, [one might argue]: "God is not the author of authoritative statements..."

If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) because [the opponent] is a human being, like an unreliable person— [and thus the reason "being a human"] is countered by "like one who is generally accepted [as reliable]"— we say no,
because [the distinction between] being an author of authoritative statements and being an author of non-authoritative statements does not apply to people such as ourselves.
Because two things that cannot coexist are mutually contradictory, and because [the reason] results in a mutual contradiction;
and also in the case of proving the absence of being an author of a valid statement whose probandum is a *mahāvidyā*.

Persons such as ourselves are not the example, because persons such as ourselves are authors of sentences based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that a jar is the example— no, because [the jar] lacks the property of being a person, which is a necessary part of the probans (*sādhana*).
And because [the reason] such as "being devoid of being a self distinct from Īśvara" is itself non-self, it is tainted by a *upādhi* (limiting condition).

If it is argued that once it is established that "Īśvara is the author of unauthoritative statements because he is a person, like me," there exists the property of "being the statement of Īśvara" in the statement of the Supreme Lord—[we reply: no.

Because "being the author of unmeasured statements" is a pseudo-reason (*upādhi*) for [proving] error; and because if that [error] were also proven, it would be contradicted by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*);
for it is precisely through the absence of error that God is established.
Furthermore, in the first inference proving the existence of God,
by employing the term "one who composes the instruction on dharma residing in a person who does not possess a quality residing in the author of unauthoritative statements," [the subject] is *dharma*.

The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is to be established by the following inference: "He is the object of a direct perception residing in the author of the teaching of properties that are devoid of being objects of properties residing in the author of unauthoritative statements, because He is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), like a jar. Furthermore, since the absence of the status of being an author of unauthoritative statements in the Lord is established by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends His existence as the subject (*dharmin*), the proof of the Lord as an author of unauthoritative statements is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject.
It is not the case that the status of being the word of God is inconclusive. Nor should it be argued that,

since the authority of the Veda is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehend its subject (the Veda itself), the argument "Vedic statements are authoritative because they are the word of God" is redundant.

This is because the proof for the authorship of the instruction on the Dharma qualified by the absence of being the author of unauthoritative statements does not establish the instruction on the Dharma qualified by being authoritative;
for the absence of non-authoritativeness and so forth does not constitute authoritativeness, but rather the state of being a means for valid cognition (*pramiti*).

Or, let it be that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is simply the absence of invalidity; and let it be established that the teaching of Dharma possesses that [validity]. Even so, the authority of the Veda is not established by that, because of that [absence of invalidity], the Veda’s...

Furthermore, because [the opponent's argument] fails to establish that it is an instruction in Dharma— since its purpose would be fulfilled even by an instruction in some trivial matter— and because it lacks both the absence of contradiction and the capacity characterized by fitness;

and because the argument "Vedic sentences are not authoritative, because Vedic sentences lack the property of being non-authoritative" is also fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," and because all counter-arguments are *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition) since they lack the property of being Vedic sentences.

If it is argued that this [example] does not belong to the same category [as the subject], because the illustrative instance—that an explanatory passage (arthavāda) such as "Fire is the remedy for cold" lacks validity according to its literal meaning—is deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala)—we say no;
for in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), the validity of the literal meaning cannot be avoided.
This remains true even if one accepts that the passage possesses validity elsewhere through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

And because, by the absence of any dispute regarding its validity, the deficiency of the example in respect of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) is avoided. [Objection: But if this were so, then the Buddha’s statement, "One desiring heaven should worship a *caitya*," would be authoritative (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: Since they are the words of the Buddha, just like the statement "non-violence is the means to dharma," the Buddhist scriptures (buddhāgama) would also possess authority. [Reply: No, because the status of being the Buddha's word does not apply to those statements that propound such doctrines as selflessness (nairātmya) and momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga).

Because of fallibility; and because the lack of authority in those various statements that propound selflessness, momentariness, dharmas, and so forth, is ascertained by the force of the subverting arguments (bādhaka) that will be stated here and there.
By this [same reasoning], the argument that "the statement regarding the worship of caityas and so forth is authoritative because it is the word of an omniscient being" [is refuted].

The argument that it is like the statement "non-violence is the means to dharma" is refuted; furthermore, there is deviation [from the rule] in the case of the speech of an untrustworthy person, since even such a person possesses omniscience during the state of yoga.
If it is argued that [the definition of scripture] is "being a sentence produced by a cognition whose object is everything and which is grounded in something"— no,
for this too is already subsumed under the previously mentioned refutation. By this, the statement "plucking out one's hair is a means to attain heaven" is not a valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that because it is the word of a Jina, it is the word of an omniscient being, and that this quality does not exist in the speech of an unreliable person—
[we reply: no,
for even the speech of an unreliable person is produced by a cognition of all objects residing in Īśvara.

Furthermore, because it is not accepted that the Buddha's knowledge has any limit, the qualification of the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). The nature of being the word of an omniscient being consists precisely in being a statement produced by knowledge whose object is everything; it does not, however, [consist in...]

If it is argued that [the definition] is "the state of being a statement produced by knowledge of all objects based on some particular basis"— no, for this too is seized by the same refutation as before. By this, [the argument] that "the statement 'plucking out the hair is a means to heaven' is a valid authority because it is a statement of the Jina" [is also refuted].

The argument that "it is like the statement of one who has attained realization" is also refuted, as it fails to establish the validity of the statements in the Jaina scriptures. Furthermore, the property of being the word of God is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the speech of an unreliable person.

If it is argued that even the speech of an unreliable person is the word of God because it is produced by God—no, for the word of God is defined as speech produced by the activity of the palate, lips, and other organs belonging to a body that constitutes God's own form; and such [activity] is absent in the case of the speech of an unreliable person. Now, what is...?

Does being the body of God consist in being directly presided over by God’s effort, or in being the locus of God’s experience, or in being the substratum of the sense organs produced by God’s knowledge?
In the first case, even the body of an untrustworthy person would be God’s body, as [all] things...

In the first case, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) remains exactly as it was, because [the object] is the direct objective of the effort of God (*īśvara*). In the second case, there would be the occurrence of pleasure and pain even for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). In the third case, [there would be the same] for the Supreme Lord.
If it is argued that this would entail [the attribution of] effects such as cognition [to the Supreme Lord], we say no;
for in the Purāṇas and other texts, it is accepted that the Supreme Lord possesses effects such as cognition, as well as pleasure and pain produced by union with or separation from Girijā,
and is endowed with sensory cognitions and so forth arising from union with or separation from Girijā.

This is because [the scriptures] speak of Candraśekhara as possessing a body. If it is asked, "In the absence of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), how can there be pleasure, pain, and so forth for the Lord?"—we reply: no, for merit and demerit are also accepted in the case of the Lord. This is evident from the Purāṇas and other sources regarding the Supreme Lord.
If it is argued that because of the scriptural mention of both merit arising from austerity and demerit arising from the decapitation of Brahmā,
there would be no distinction whatsoever between the Supreme Lord and beings such as ourselves regarding the possession of pleasure, pain, and so forth— [we reply: no.

Know that [the Lord] possesses such qualities as being free from error, being the agent of creation and dissolution, being the knower, being the fashioner, and being the sovereign of all worlds. Otherwise, if there were no distinction between pleasure and pain, even a king would have no distinction from commoners and the like regarding pleasures such as those arising from enjoying women, which are no different from those found in the forest.
If it is argued that the King is superior to commoners and the like—no;

for in that case, one must simply be content with the fact that the Supreme Lord is superior to kings and others in such matters as the bliss arising from union with the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), who is the mistress of the entire universe. By this same logic, regarding the composition of the Vedas and so forth...

The objection that there is an absence of a motivator for the Supreme Lord has been refuted; for it is accepted that the Supreme Lord possesses merit, happiness, and so forth, produced by the creation of the Vedas and other works.
However, the teacher Ātreya maintains that the Supreme Lord possesses merit, the body produced by that merit, happiness, and the like.

They maintain that [pleasure and so forth are produced by merit], but not that bodily pain and the like are produced by demerit. This is incorrect, because the inference and other means of knowledge that apprehend the substratum (dharmin) which establishes merit as the cause of pleasure and so forth are equally applicable to demerit and pain. The same applies to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are the causes of memory, and to aversion.
The Supreme Lord must be accepted on the strength of inference that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakānumāna*) and other such means.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord possesses intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Now, [regarding] this—

Since the Supreme Lord is established as the substratum of the effort that produces the dyad (dvyaṇuka) produced by a conjunction— which itself is produced by an action devoid of being simultaneous with the effort toward an effect— the Lord is established by the very means that apprehend the subject (*dharmigrāhaka*) as possessing both the effect and the effort; how then could it be [established] from the *dharmigrāhaka* alone?
If it is argued that the existence of the Supreme Lord as one who exerts effort toward an effect is not established—
because of the contradiction between exerting effort toward what is to be done and what is not to be done within a single agent— we reply: no,

for by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), [the inference establishes] the Lord as one who exerts effort toward both what is to be done and what is not to be done.

Because there is no contradiction between the effort directed toward what is to be accomplished and what is not, by means of the very proof that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). Now, in the statement "the Vedic sentence is a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "being a valid means of knowledge," which consists in being a generator of valid cognition; and likewise...

And [which one] has the status of the subject (*dharmin*) for the first Vedic sentence: is it that which begins it, or that which is in the middle produced by it, or the last one produced at the location of hearing according to the principle that "sound produces another sound"? Neither the first nor the second [options] are tenable, because they are contradicted by evidence (*bādhāt*).
The first [alternative] is not tenable because the initial and middle sentences, being unperceived, do not produce valid cognition (*pramiti*).

Nor is the third, because the final sentence, failing to produce the valid cognition that is the direct realization of its own object, is vitiated by the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*).

If it is argued: "Because you yourself have accepted that even the object is a cause of a directly apprehending cognition (*sākṣātkāri-jñāna*); or, even if you do not accept this, one could simply say that its establishment [as a cause] follows from this very fact"—we reply:
No, because [this applies only] to the sentence being heard.
Because it is taught as the subject (*dharmin*).
Nor is there the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*) by virtue of being a producer of a valid cognition that directly perceives its own object;
for this sentence does not produce a direct perception of this [object], because it is a sentence.

If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) based on a negative inference (vyatirekin)— namely, "this sentence is not a generator of a direct perceptual cognition regarding its own object, because it is a sentence, like other sentences"— we say no.

Because this [reason] is uncommon (asādhāraṇa), being excluded from its similar instance (sapakṣa)— namely, the sense organ and so forth that produce the direct perception whose object is this very thing— [the following argument is stated]:
"This sentence produces the direct perception whose object is this sentence, because it is either this sentence or the hearer of this sentence."
If it is argued that [the reason] is like "having ears," we say no; for it is subject to the fallacy of the "accidental" (sopādhitva) because it lacks the nature of being a sentence.

Nor is this reason "identical with the subject" (pakṣetaratā), because there exists a counter-example (vipakṣa)—namely, other sentences—which is excluded from the class of sentences and which does produce a direct perception (sākṣātkāra) regarding this very object. Alternatively:

To exclude the possibility of it having a different meaning, the statement of the probandum must be formulated as follows: "This Vedic sentence generates a cognition devoid of the nature of a direct realization produced by itself. Alternatively, [the probandum may be stated as]: "This Vedic sentence [generates] a valid cognition regarding its own causes and so forth, which is distinct from the direct realization of its own object."
If it is argued that the fault remains as before because the meaning would be different— namely, that [the Veda] produces [knowledge] by way of being a *liṅga* (logical mark)— we say no.

For in such inferences as "this Vedic sentence is produced by a cause or is of human origin, because it is a sentence," the sentence itself is the subject (*dharmin*), and it is precisely the property of being a sentence residing in that [subject] which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).
If it is argued that "space is distinct from other things because it is a Vedic statement; for whatever is not distinct from others is not a Vedic statement, as in the case of 'the pot' and so forth—
this being a Vedic statement produces valid cognition by way of a logical mark"— we say no, because [the mark] exists in each individual [instance].

In the production of the cognition "space is distinct from the others," there is no evidence for the claim that a collection of words— consisting of a collection of phonemes not delimited by a specific order, and accompanied by expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency—
is the generator of that cognition; otherwise, [the same would apply] to all [cognitions].

If it is argued that the Vedic sentence will generate the inference simply by virtue of being the subject (*dharmin*), lest there be the contingency of useless qualifiers (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇa*) generating the inference— [we reply that] the inference is established from each individual phoneme alone.

There is no evidence for the claim that a collection of words— consisting of a collection of phonemes and endowed with expectancy, proximity, and compatibility— functions as the locus (*dharmin*) by way of being the generator [of the inference];
for the inference is established through the cognition of the locus itself, since it is the locus that generates the inference.
If it is argued that, this being the case, since inference is established from the mere knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*), the mark itself must also be the producer of the inference—[we reply]:
no, because one experiences the smoke as the cause of the inference in the cognition "I infer fire from smoke. [One does not experience] "I infer fire from the mountain."

If it is argued that even a mark (*liṅga*) which is a property (*dharma*) would fail to produce an inference— [we reply]: no, because [the cognition] "I infer fire from smoke" and the aphorism "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" [establish its status].
Only the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been promised as that which is to be explained. For instance,
when the meaning of the Sūtra is the exposition of dharma and adharma, [the following applies].
Then,
[it is so] either by way of being dharma and adharma, or by way of being the producer of their production,
or by way of being the producer of that which produces them.

Or rather, only the object of cognition (*prameya*) should be explained. First, the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) and their cognition;
the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); and the body and so forth are [the instrumental causes].

The instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) consists of the action that produces the conjunction of the self and the mind, as well as the limbs of the body and so forth, which are the causes of the cause;
and it also includes disjunction and so forth, which produce the cessation of the prior conjunction that generates the conjunction of the self and the mind.

The cause of the cause of the cause. In this manner, by virtue of being that cause, everything from the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) down to the atom (*paramāṇu*) is to be included. And space (*ākāśa*) is the cause of the Vedas and so forth, which produce the knowledge of those qualities such as the *praṇava* that generate merit (*dharma*). Thus...
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and other such items that produce sacrifice, oblation, and giving are the causes of the cause.
Their constituent parts are also to be included as being the respective causes thereof.
Furthermore, color, taste, smell, and touch are the causes of the satisfaction of gods and Brahmins, which in turn generates merit (dharma).
Because it produces satisfaction through food and other items that are white, sweet, fragrant, and soft;
because it generates merit (*dharma*) through number and measure, such as the gift of a thousand cows or great golden jars and the like; and also [it produces] separateness (*pṛthaktva*).

It is a cause of dharma through a traditional succession, because the understanding of the means— such as rice grains— qualified by a distinctness produced by [prior] distinctness, generates sacrifices and other rites that produce dharma.

If it is argued that the performance of sacrifices and other rites proceeds solely from the cognition of rice and other materials as qualified by "otherness" (*anyonyābhāva*) through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and not from the cognition of them as qualified by "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), we say:
no; for when the inference of a substance is possible from the cognition of it as qualified by separateness...
Since it is impossible to restrict that performance will occur solely from a cognition qualified by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) or mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*),

even priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) possess causality toward dharma through a mediated succession, as in the case of one who possesses a cognition qualified by generality (*sāmānya*) and priority.

And because [space] produces merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) through one who addresses another as "distant" while possessing a cognition qualified by distance; and because the cognitions qualified by distance and proximity are produced by distance and proximity;
or because [space] generates the cognitions of direction, time, and so forth, which in turn produce merit, demerit, and the like.
The explanation of priority and posteriority [is concluded]. It is clearly evident that cognition, desire, aversion, and effort are causes of merit and demerit, either directly or indirectly.
Furthermore, gravity is indirectly a cause of merit, as in the case of water from a dripping vessel and the like.

Because gravity causes rain to fall upon the linga situated below, thereby producing dharma; and because water from clouds and other sources, falling downward due to gravity, produces the nourishment of rice and other crops; furthermore, fluidity is a cause of dharma through a mediated succession, since from fluidity [the water] flows everywhere.
Because flowing waters produce the means for the cultivation of rice and other grains,
moisture is an indirect cause of dharma; for it is through that which possesses cohesion produced by moisture that rice and other specific crops are brought forth.

This is because it produces the merit (*dharma*) that has the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth as its means; and because the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is a cause of merit through a mediated sequence,
since it generates the recollection of the ritual acts to be performed which produce that merit.
Furthermore, both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) possess a mediated causal efficacy toward merit,

because they serve as causes for the body and other factors that produce merit and demerit. And although merit itself produces both merit and demerit, it is nonetheless fruitful by virtue of being the means to achieve heaven and liberation.
And although unrighteousness (*adharma*) also produces both dharma and adharma,
it possesses fruitfulness by virtue of producing suffering, which in turn generates the detachment (*vairāgya*) that is useful for liberation.
Furthermore, sound (*śabda*), such as the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), is a cause of dharma, as is the Veda and so forth.
It is the cause of the cognition of dharma, adharma, Īśvara, and so forth;
and actions are the cause of dharma through a causal chain, because they produce conjunctions that generate the rice and other grains which are the means for accomplishing dharma.
And the universal, such as "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) and so forth, is the cause of dharma through a mediated sequence,
because the cognition qualified by "rice-ness" produced by "rice-ness"— namely, the cognition of rice— is the cause for the performance that generates dharma.
Furthermore, the specific qualities (*viśeṣas*) are to be explained as the means for the direct realization of the self, which is distinct from delusion and other factors that produce liberation,
even though they do not produce *dharma*.
Because it functions as a cooperative cause for the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), which produces the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the self as distinct from the body and so forth;

and because even *samavāya* [functions] by way of producing the cognition of rice and other grains as qualified by their status as being the specific kind of grain that is a constituent part of the ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
It is the means for establishing dharma, because it generates the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified in the case of specific cognition;

and because it generates the direct perception of the Vedas and so forth, which produce the knowledge of dharma, adharma, the Lord, liberation, and other such things, through the *praṇava* and other means that generate dharma.
Inherence (samavāya) must be explained, because the inherence of sound and the auditory organ is the cause of the direct perception of sound.
Non-existence (abhāva), both directly and indirectly, is the means for attaining merit, demerit, liberation, and so forth.
Because both the absence of an obstacle and antecedent non-existence produce all effects;
and because the destruction of a prior conjunction produces subsequent conjunctions that generate dharma and the like, as well as rice and other such products.
Furthermore, since the destruction of suffering is the means to liberation, the supreme goal of man, its non-existence must all the more be explained.

Therefore, because of its utility, [the categories] consisting of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and non-existence— Please note that the original text fragment ends abruptly; this translation reflects the logical conclusion of the argument presented. It is established that the object of cognition (prameya) is that which must be explained. Even when the meaning of the Sūtras consists in the exposition of the Vedas, it nevertheless serves as a means for the comprehension of Vedic categories.
Furthermore, the objects of cognition (prameya), such as substance and so forth, must indeed be explained. For instance,
in the view that words such as "rice" or "cow" denote the genus (jāti), the individual (vyakti), and their relation,
the categories (padārtha) consist of the genus, the substance, and inherence (samavāya).

In the view that [a word] denotes the individual which is the substratum of rice-ness (*vrīhitva*), the referent (*padārtha*) is simply the substance such as rice. And in the view that words such as "white" denote the universal (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*), and their relation (*sambandha*), the referents are the universal, the quality (*guṇa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
In the view that words denote individuals (*vyakti*), the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is simply the quality (*guṇa*) such as whiteness.

Furthermore, in the view that words for "going" and so forth denote the genus (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*), and their relation (*sambandha*), the word-meanings are respectively the genus (*jāti*), the action (*kriyā*), and inherence (*samavāya*).

Regarding the categories (padārthas): under the view that words denote individuals, the category is indeed action (karma). For words such as "inherence" (samavāya) and so forth, the category is inherence.
And for words such as "ultimate particularity" (viśeṣa) and so forth, the category is indeed ultimate particularity.
Furthermore, for words such as *samavāya* (inherence) and *sambandha* (relation), inherence is the word-meaning;
and for words such as the negative particle *nañ*, non-existence (*abhāva*) is the word-meaning. Therefore, by one who explains the Veda, the Vedic word-meanings [must be understood].

Furthermore, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence must indeed be explained; for without understanding them, it is impossible to grasp the linguistic convention (*saṅgati*) regarding them,
and it is impossible for those who have not grasped such conventions to derive cognition from words.
Even when the meaning of the Sūtra is the exposition of the teachings of the Dharma by the instructor,
then too, substances and the other categories must be explained as the referents of the words of the teaching of the Dharma, which is synonymous with the Veda. Thus...

Because only one who provides instruction in dharma is a teacher of dharma, and because the Veda alone is the instruction in dharma; for it is impossible to comprehend dharma from the Veda by those who have not understood its constituent words and meanings.
Even when the meaning of the Sūtra is an exposition of the dharma in the form of a *liṅga* (logical mark),
it nevertheless consists of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence, by virtue of being the nature of dharma and its substratum.
The object of cognition (prameya) must indeed be explained;
likewise, even in other commentaries on the Sūtras, only the objects of cognition, such as substance and the rest, are to be explained.
To distinguish these, the sūtra states:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—these are the substances. (1.2.4)
And here, the first division intended by the author of the Sūtras— within the nine chapters excluding the ninth— is that the object of cognition (*prameya*) is twofold: existent and non-existent.
Because of the subsequent exposition of "existent" (sat): immediately after that, the division of the existent into six categories— substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karma),
generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya)— is intended by the author of the Sūtras.
Because the six categories beginning with substance have already been explained at the outset,
this sūtra is intended for the classification of substances. As for the purpose of this classification:
If [it is asked], "What is the specific cognition? we reply: For when one says "substance," no specific cognition such as "earth, water, fire, air," and so forth, arises;
however, when one says "earth, water, fire," a specific cognition of earth and the others does arise.
Thus, the purpose of employing the sentence of classification (*vibhāga-vākya*) is to establish the status of "substance" (*dravyatva*) in earth and the other categories;

for when it is merely said that "it is a substance," the establishment of the status of substance in the nine [categories] beginning with earth does not arise, whereas it does arise from the sentence of classification.
Thus, there is either the occurrence of the specific characteristics of earth and so forth,
or the inference of properties residing in the specific instances of earth and so forth by virtue of their being substances. Not [otherwise].

When the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of earth and so forth are not yet cognized, neither the application of a definition nor the inference of properties residing therein by means of their being substances (*dravyatva*) is possible.
Because the specific instances of earth and so forth are established through perception and inference as far as possible,
and because the property of substantiality (dravyatva) residing in those specific instances of earth and so forth is thereby established.
If it is argued that the statement of division is useless— no,

for when the status of being a reliable authority (*āpta*) is not yet certain, the author of the aphorisms’ statement of division serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding such specific particulars as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
Because it is understood that [the Sūtra] does not culminate in perception or inference by way of generating an inquiry,
given that it is the word of the author of the Sūtras, whose status as a trustworthy authority is certain, and which provides a systematic classification.

This is because it is fruitful, insofar as it generates a valid cognition (*pramiti*) of a different genus from the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by perception and the inference (*anumiti*) produced by inference; otherwise, the specific nature of earth and the like, as well as the substance-ness (*dravyatva*) residing therein, would not be established merely through the statement of their classification.
Because the futility of both perception and inference is unavoidable, the statement of the author of the Sūtras is not a valid means of knowledge.
If [it is argued that it is not a means of knowledge], no;

for if it were to convey an object already understood through perception or inference, it would be impossible for the statement of classification to lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, since it conveys an object already known through perception and inference,
to assert its futility is nothing but the ravings of a madman. As for Udayana and others:
They say that the statement of division is for the purpose of excluding numbers less than or greater [than nine].
That is incorrect; because in the statement of division, the number nine is not presented as a qualifier of earth and the others, it is impossible to exclude numbers less than or greater than that.
Furthermore, because the number nine is difficult to establish in relation to earth and the other [elements],
since those distinct from space, time, and direction are infinite, a unity is untenable, and consequently, the intended number nine cannot be established.

Even though the number nine is possible with respect to each individual manifestation of earth and so forth, along with space, time, and ether, a higher number is nonetheless established in relation to a second manifestation of earth and so forth;
for it is difficult to establish the exclusion of such a higher number. And this applies to qualities and the rest as well.
Because even the discourse on number would be impossible.
Now, it might be argued: "Let it be that the exclusion of fewer or more numbers is not the result of the classification;
rather, the exclusion of the deficiency or excess of substances will be the result of the classification."
If it is argued that this is not so— no, because when the deficiency or excess of substances is not cognized,
their absence cannot be apprehended; and if they were cognized, the apprehension of their absence would be sublated,
since the absolute absence of substanceness and so forth in any one of the [nine] substances, such as earth, is impossible.

The exclusion [of the universal] will result in the exclusion of substantiality from that which is distinct from earth and the other [elements], as the fruit of the analysis; for the absolute absence of substantiality and substantiality itself have been established in relation to any one among earth and the others.

If it is argued that [the property] can be negated as being distinct from earth and the other [elements], we say: no; for is the absolute exclusion of substantiality (dravyatva) the absolute absence of the absolute absence of substantiality, or rather...

Is it the exclusion of the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence of substantiality (*dravyatvātyantābhāvātyantābhāvātyantābhāvavyavaccheda*), or rather the cognition of the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence of substantiality (*dravyatvātyantābhāvātyantābhāvapratyaya*)? It cannot be the first,
because the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence of substantiality would be beginningless (*anāditva*).

Because it is untenable for the result of the sentence of division [to be such]. In the second case as well, is it the absence of the absolute non-existence of substanceness, or is it substanceness itself, or is it something distinct from substance? In the first case, there is indeed agreement regarding earth and the other [elements].

Because we also accept that the result of the statement of division is the cognition of substantiality (*dravyatva*) with respect to [the categories] ending with mind (*manas*); and even in the second case,
one who is in disagreement regarding any one of earth and so forth would possess the cognition of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of substantiality.
The intended meaning is that its being the result of the sentence of distinction consists in its producing the sentence of distinction;

or else, the intended meaning is that its being the result of the sentence of distinction consists in its producing the "substance-ness" (dravyatva) understood from the sentence of distinction. It is not the first [alternative].
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the statement of exclusion— which has its purpose fulfilled by producing the cognition of "substance-ness" in earth and the other categories—
does not produce the cognition of the absolute absence of the absolute absence of substance-ness residing in earth and the others.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, precisely because there is agreement [on this point].

Since the result of the analytical statement (*vibhāgavākya*) is the exclusion of [substancehood] as a category distinct from earth and the other [elements], does this analytical statement also produce the cognition of the absolute absence of the absolute absence of substancehood in that which is distinct from earth and the others? Regarding that...

Is it intended that the result is the sentence of distinction itself, or rather, does the substantiality residing in earth and so forth— cognized through the sentence of distinction— produce the cognition of the absolute absence of substantiality in anything other than earth and so forth? Of each [of these alternatives]...
[The claim that] the result [of inference] is the connection with the sentence expressing exclusion (vibhāga) is not the first [option], because a sentence expressing exclusion,
which has fulfilled its purpose merely by making known the connection with substances such as earth,
does not convey the connection with the absolute non-existence of the nature of being a substance distinct from earth and so forth.

If it is argued that the statement of division (vibhāga-vākya) intends to establish the connection with the absolute absence of the nature of substance (dravyatva) distinct from earth and the other [elements], because the connection with the nature of substance as earth and so forth is established by another means— [we reply: no, because [it is] "by another means."

What is intended by the phrase "from the enunciation"? Is it from the enunciation itself, or from perception and inference? It cannot be the first, because [the categories are] substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because the enunciation sentence beginning with "the object of cognition" (*prameya*) merely conveys the relation between "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "object-of-cognition-ness" (*prameyatva*), and does not convey that earth and the other [substances] possess the status of being related to substance-ness.

Since the connection between earth and the other substances and the category of substantiality (*dravyatva*) is already known through perception and inference, if the sentence of exclusion (*vibhāga-vākya*) does not convey that [connection],
then it likewise [does not convey] the connection with the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of substantiality in anything distinct from earth and the others.

Because it would follow that the statement concerning the division [of means of knowledge] does not convey that [division], given that perception and inference have already been understood; and because, in the absence of a subverting factor regarding the primary meaning,
there is no evidence for either abandoning the literal sense of a sentence or imagining another meaning.
Since the mention [of the categories] is already implied by the statement of their classification,
