and because it is impossible to alter the statement of classification by the force of the statement of their enumeration; furthermore, a distinct substance such as earth and the like is not established by the definition-statement alone.

Because the status of earth and the other [elements] as substances is established. If it is argued that the statement concerning division is intended to negate the status of substance in something distinct from earth and the others— no,
because of the statements defining earth and the others.
Because [the sūtra] only establishes the definitions of earth and so forth,
it does not establish earth and so forth as substances; for the fact that earth and so forth are substances is established by the subsequent demonstration that they possess qualities (*guṇavattva*).

If it is argued that the sentence concerning division (vibhāga) is intended to negate substanceness (*dravyatva*) in something distinct from earth and the other [elements], we say no; for that sentence establishes [the property of] being a quality (*guṇatva*), and not the establishment of substanceness. Indeed, it is precisely the possession of the quality established therein [that is meant].

If it is argued that [the reason] establishes substanceness (*dravyatva*), we say no; for if the statement of division does not propose that earth and the others possess substanceness, there would be no occasion to state the reason of "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*). Or, if such a proposal were made, [the reason would be superfluous].
This is because the sentence of division, by its nature as a presentation of substances such as earth and so forth,
does not present a negation of substancehood distinct from earth and the like. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

Because the "substance-ness" (dravyatva) residing in earth and so forth—which is understood from the sentence concerning their division—cannot serve as a property of the subject (apakṣadharma) when proving "non-substance-ness" (adravyatva) in something distinct from earth and so forth;
furthermore, it would be contradictory (viruddha). This is because non-substance-ness...
Because of the absolute non-existence of substantiality (*dravyatva*), and because both substantiality and its absolute non-existence have ceased while [their opposites] have arisen.
Now, in the passage "earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind," the words "earth" and so forth—

Do they refer to individual instances that serve as the substrata for earthness and so forth, or do they refer to the universals (jāti) such as earthness? In the first case, do they refer to each individual instance that serves as the substratum for earthness and so forth, or what?

The [terms] "all-earthness" (*sarvapṛthivītva*) and so forth refer to the individual instances that serve as the substrata [of the universal]. In the first case, there is a deficiency in the analysis (*vibhāga*), because there is no differentiation of individual instances of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) other than each single instance of earthness,
and because the use of the plural number in the word "waters" (*āpaḥ*) would be untenable, since it refers to only a single instance of water.
Because plurality is impossible— since Pāṇini’s rule states that the plural is used for many—
and because this plural form is applied to a single entity by the force of grammatical instruction, as in the case of the word *dārāḥ*.
If it is argued that this is not so—[we reply] no, because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for the word *āpaḥ* (water) to denote singularity.

If it is argued that there is a rule stating "the word *āpaḥ* is always plural," we say no; for that [rule] does not establish [the word's meaning], as it is understood to denote plurality by necessity.
By the rule "the plural [is used] for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*), the fact that the plural number of the word *āpaḥ* expresses plurality is already established; therefore,
the further injunction that the word *āpaḥ* ends in the plural is intended to apply even when there is only one or two.

If it is argued that this is for the purpose of obtaining the plural number— no; for according to the maxim that "an undertaking is made when something is already established for the sake of restriction," the re-enactment of the rule that the word *āpaḥ* ends in the plural serves to restrict it such that it must end only in the plural, and not in the dual or the singular.

Regarding the phrase "because it is for the purpose of making known": the second [alternative] is not tenable, because the singular number in "earth," "fire," "air," and so forth would be untenable, since the nominal stems such as "earth" refer to an infinite number of individual instances. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable.

Because it would result in either a deficiency or an excess in the classification [of categories], if the words "earth" and so forth were intended to denote the universals (jāti) such as "earth-ness," there would be no presentation of the individual instances (vyakti) of earth and so on; thus,
there would be a deficiency in the classification of substances, since the universals such as "earth-ness" themselves would be included among the substances.

[The opponent argues: "Because it is divided by analysis (*vibhañjanāt*), there is an excess of division; furthermore, the plural number in the word 'waters' (*āpaḥ*) would be untenable because the nature of water (*aptva*) is a single entity.

This is not so, because by the words 'earth' (*pṛthivī*) and so forth, all individual instances that are the substrata of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like are expressed. Not... [the objection holds].
Nor is there an impossibility of the singular number [in the term "earth"],
for that is possible because it expresses the oneness residing in the universal (jāti) such as earthness (pṛthivītva).
Since universals such as earthness lack any object to be expressed [by themselves], they do not [function] by means of those [universals].

If it is argued that there is a grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with the singularity denoted by the suffix because the universal (*jāti*) is also the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [we reply: even if the universal were not the meaning of the nominal stem,
it would [still function] as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*) present in the mind.
The singular number expressed by the suffix will be construed with the meaning of the suffix itself;

for it is impossible for that singular number to be construed with the individuals denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If it is argued that the singular number expressed by the suffix is never seen to be construed with a genus (*jāti*) which serves merely as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*), we say: no.

For it is observed in such passages as "in this year, only barley was produced," that the author of the Sūtras intends to establish the oneness belonging to the genus (jāti) such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva).

If it is asked what the purpose is: it is the inclusion of all individual instances of earth and so forth. For if there were a plurality of "earth-nesses," then by the word "earth" one would only include that which is the locus of a single earth-ness; [therefore, this is done] so as to include all individual instances.
Because there would be no inclusion of individual manifestations that are substrata for different instances of "earth-ness," and because the deficiency in the classification would remain as it was;
[this applies] to those words such as "akṣa" whose grounds for application are the words "akṣa" themselves.

Even when the word *akṣa* includes all substrata of the property of being a *vibhītaka* within a single application— despite the existence of distinctions among those things whose forms consist of being a *vibhītaka*, being an *indriya*, or being the object of a sidelong glance (*kaṭākṣa*)— ...

Because it is universally accepted that the substrata of the sense faculties and so forth are not included [within the categories], the word "iti" (thus) indicates completion. The meaning is that by this, the substances are completed; there are none beyond these. As for the question, "What is the proof that there are only this many substances?"—[the answer follows].
If it is argued that the very word of the author of the Sūtras is the authority for that— no,
because validity, which consists in being the generator of uncontradicted experience, is not established merely by the word of Kaṇāda.
This is because it is established through inference, like the statement of Kaṇāda that fire is hot;

nor should it be argued that there is a "non-establishment of the qualifier" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā) on the grounds that the absence of sublation throughout the three periods of time— which constitutes non-sublatedness— is difficult to ascertain, for [the nature of] non-sublatedness...

Because the state of being free from sublation throughout the three periods of time is not accepted. If it is asked, "In that case, what is non-sublatedness?"—it is the absolute absence of sublatedness.
And if it is asked, "What indeed is sublatedness?"—it is established by a recurring cognition in the form: "This is to be sublated; this is to be sublated."

Whether it be a specific subordinate genus within the category of knowledge, namely that which resides in sublated knowledge, or a limiting adjunct (upādhi), its absolute absence constitutes "non-sublatability" (abādhyatva). Since this is established by mental perception itself, how can non-sublatability be difficult to ascertain?
Otherwise, if even for a cognition that has already arisen there were no ascertainment of its being uncontradicted,
it would follow that the authority of the Vedānta as well could not be ascertained.

If it is argued that "the capacity to produce an uncontradicted experience" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for validity (*prāmāṇya*), we say no; for that very [capacity] cannot be a limiting condition with respect to itself. Validity is the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting in the nature of the universal *pramātva* (truthhood), whereas the capacity to produce an uncontradicted experience is something distinct from that and thus constitutes a limiting condition.

If it is argued that this is not so because [the reason] pervades the probans—no, for it is a pervasive property of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*). If it is argued that "being spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) here—no, because in the case of perception and so forth, which possess validity, that condition does not exist despite their being valid;
furthermore, because it is a pervasive property of the probans.

If it is argued that since the author of the Sūtras is an authoritative source, all categories of reality are established by him alone, and therefore the exposition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establish atoms and so forth by the author of the Sūtras and others is redundant— [we reply]: no.

This is because the statement of the author of the Sūtras is intended to establish its status as the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*) by virtue of its possessing a foundational means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*), and also to demonstrate that its establishment occurs through other means of valid cognition as well; for it is not the case that the self (*ātman*) is established solely through scripture (*āgama*).
[Otherwise,] the exposition of perception and inference regarding that domain would be useless.

Furthermore, what is the proof that there are only this many substances? Is it by means of this much evidence for "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) [that you establish] substanceness as being excluded from qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth?

Is this excellent question a query regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the non-substantiality (*adravyatva*) of those things distinct from these [categories]? In the first case, the answer is simply the inference (*anumāna*) that establishes their substantiality (*dravyatva*). In the second case as well, this is the very same answer.

Because substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves it as being excluded precisely from qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the question "What is the proof for the non-substantiality (*adravyatva*) of that which is distinct from these [qualities]?", what is the meaning of the term "distinct from these" (*etāvadvyatirikta*)?
Are "quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence" intended [to be the categories],
or something distinct from those? In the first case, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence are devoid of substantiality (*dravyatva*).

Because they lack the property of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*). That which does not lack substantiality (*dravyatva*) does not lack the property of possessing qualities, as for example, a jar. And quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence lack the property of possessing qualities.
Therefore, the answer is that they are "devoid of substantiality" (*dravyatva*).
If it is argued that because "being devoid of substantiality" is unestablished, this constitutes the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*)—we say no;
for even if "being devoid of substantiality" were unestablished, what [would be affected] in the case of the statement, "Qualities and so forth are not substances"?

For the question "What is the means of valid cognition? itself is untenable. Substance-ness (dravyatva) is the counter-positive of an absence that is distinct from substance-ness and its mutual absence, and which lacks prior non-existence and destruction, because it is knowable (prameyatva), like a jar. Substance-ness is the counter-positive of absolute non-existence, because it is a genus (jātitva).

Because [the property of being a substance] is well-established as a qualifier—just like "cowness" (gotva) and so forth—and because the [property of] substancehood, which excludes qualities and so on, is established by the very means that prove [the existence of] substance, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). [For example: Qualities and so on possess fluidity, because they are objects of cognition (*meyatvāt*).

If it is argued that the inference "like a jar" constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) for the negative inference (*vyatirekin*), we say no; because it is not sublated by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes [the subject's] substantiality (*dravyatva*).
This is due to the genus (*jāti*) which is excluded from qualities (*guṇa*) and the like, yet is devoid of exclusion from things possessing qualities.

Because it is the referent of the word "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). Now, [the referent of the word "substance"] is the genus (*jāti*) that excludes qualities while being devoid of exclusion from that which possesses qualities; it is not [the genus] that excludes that which possesses qualities while being devoid of exclusion from qualities.

If it is argued that "the nature of being a genus (jātitva) as excluded from quality, action, particularity, inherence, and absence" refers only to action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence themselves as being taken up as the property (dharma),
and therefore there is no sublation by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes substantiality (dravyatva)— we say: no, for if this were the case...

Because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) in the quality (*guṇa*) itself; for, since the quality is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by virtue of being devoid of substantiality (*dravyatva*), it might be argued that the reason should be qualified by being devoid of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). This is not so, because [the reason] has a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the form of possessing qualities; for [the reason] is excluded from the counter-example—the quality—precisely by virtue of its being devoid of substantiality.
Because it is excluded [from others].

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of an absence residing in some locus, which is distinct from the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of substantiality and devoid of the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvatva*) and the nature of destruction (*pradhvaṃsatva*), because it is an object of knowledge (*meyatvāt*). Substantiality is the counter-correlative of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in some locus.

Because it is a genus (*jāti*), like "cowness" (*gotva*), and because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) since "knowability" (*meyatva*) exists even in that which possesses the absolute absence of substantiality (*dravyatvātyantābhāva*);
as for the second [position], the question itself is untenable.
If the term "distinct from quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and non-existence" denotes substances such as earth and so forth, which are established by both disputants,
then the inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes their status as substances is contradicted.
Furthermore, if it denotes something distinct from the substances such as earth and so forth that are established by both disputants, then in that case...

The means of proof must be stated; for a question regarding the means of proof that establishes the absence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) in something that lacks any basis in valid cognition is merely the ravings of a madman.
[It consists in] being distinct from quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), and non-existence (*abhāva*).

"It does not reside in substances such as earth that are established for neither disputant, because it is non-excluded from what is distinct from quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence, just like 'knowability' (meyatva). No; [this argument is invalid].
The state of being distinct from quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence,

and absence does not reside in anything other than the substances such as earth that are established by both disputants, because it resides in nothing other than quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence.

Because there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) starting with "possessing the nature of earth" (*pṛthivītvavat*), etc. Now, [the argument] "substance (*dravya*) resides in something distinct from the substances such as earth established by both disputants, because it is excluded from substance, like existence (*sattā*)," establishes another substance; therefore, there are only this many [categories].

If it is argued that [the term] "substances" (dravyāṇi) is thus appropriate—[we reply: no. For by the word "earth" and so forth, is a single individual instance of earth and so forth intended, or all the instances of earth and so forth as they are perceived, or indeed every single instance of earth and so forth?
Or is it of the same class as earth and so forth? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratā*);

for since its purpose is fulfilled by establishing individual instances of earth and so forth that are distinct from each [already known] instance of earth, it does not prove a different kind of substance (*dravyāntara*). In the second case as well...

There is the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntaratā*), because this [inference] achieves its purpose merely by establishing the existence of something distinct from the individual instances of earth and so forth that have been apprehended. Furthermore, in the third case as well, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

Because it is impossible to comprehend all individual instances of earth and so forth, the subsistence [of the probans] in anything other than those is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore, even in the fourth [alternative],
there is the fallacy of proving the irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*), since any instance whatsoever of earth and so forth would suffice for the establishment [of the probandum].
Is it that earth and the rest are distinct from something belonging to the class of earth and so forth?
Or, if in place of the term "distinct from earth and the rest," the term "devoid of the nature of earth and so forth" (pṛthivītvādirahita) is employed, then likewise [the objection does not apply].
If you think that earth and the other elements are distinct entities [from their nature],
and that even if such an entity were distinct from earth and the others, it would not be untenable for it to be devoid of "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) despite being pervaded by it— this is not so.

Even if one avoids the fallacy of proving something already established (siddhasādhanam) regarding the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth, it is difficult to avoid the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (arthāntaram) regarding ether, time, and direction;
for it is logically possible that there may exist further instances of ether and so on, distinct from the first instance of ether and the rest.
If it is argued that even another instance of space and so forth cannot be established as distinct from space and so forth because it is itself of the nature of space and so forth— [we reply:
no,
for even though another instance of space and so forth is of the nature of space and so forth...
Because it is established that [the subject] is distinct from ether and so forth by virtue of being distinct from the first ether;
for even the first ether possesses the nature of ether.
In order to avoid the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), the term "distinct from ether, time, and direction" is used in place of [the original term].
If it is further proposed that a term devoid of "space-ness" (ākāśatva), "time-ness" (kālatva), and "direction-ness" (dik-tva) be employed—that is not so;
for are space-ness, time-ness, and direction-ness universals (jāti), or are they the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of space, time, and direction? Which [is it]?
[These are] the grounds for the application of the terms "space," "time," and "direction.

In the first case, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because since universals such as "spaceness" (*ākāśatva*) are unestablished, their absence [from other things] is likewise unestablished. In the second case...
Space and the other [elements] are distinct entities [from sound],
because even space lacks the definition of space since it is merely the substratum for the word "space.
Nor does this imply that sound fails to be a property of the subject (apakṣadharma), as it resides in space.

Because of the absence of that [quality]; for space and time as well, they lack the definition of space and time because they are not the substrata of the absolute non-existence of the conjunctions that produce the specific qualities of "farness" and "nearness" (paratva-viśeṣa) which constitute the definitions of space and time. [This applies] to sound, conjunction, and so forth.

Because it is accepted that non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) consists in its co-occurrence with its own absolute non-existence. If it is argued that such a form of non-pervasive occurrence is intended— no,
for even if such a form of non-pervasive occurrence were established, the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) would be unavoidable.
If one does not admit that sound has non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), it would follow that all sounds would be perceived by everyone;

for this [consequence] would be established by the fact that all sounds reside within the auditory organs of all persons, thereby fulfilling the function of the pervasive entity. Thus, [the theory of non-pervasiveness] is necessary.

And because of remaining in that same state. Even in the third case, there is a difference in meaning for space and so forth, because space and the rest are themselves devoid of that which serves as the ground for the application of the terms "space" and so on;
for it is space itself that is the ground for the application of the term "space."

Because, due to the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), another property residing therein (*tadgatadharmāntara*) is not accepted as the probans (*nimitta*). Furthermore, "not being a substance" (*adravyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) with respect to [the property of] subsisting in something other than earth and so forth. Nor is this...

The state of being other than the subject (*pakṣetaratā*): because it is excluded from the counter-subject (*vipakṣa*)—namely, earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, which possess the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), such as "subsisting in what is distinct from earth and the rest"—substantiality (*dravyatva*) [is not a fallacious reason].
Furthermore, in cases such as "subsisting in what is distinct from earthness and the rest," substantiality is not [the probandum].

"It subsists in something distinct from earth and the other [elements], because it does not subsist in non-substances, like earth-ness"; by such arguments, there is a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*). By this, [the property] "subsisting in a substance distinct from earth and the others" [is established].

The proof for another substance—namely, "because it is not excluded from what is distinct from earth and so forth, like knowability"—is refuted; for the property of being distinct from earth and so forth is beset by the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), since it resides in other substances such as earth that are different [from the subject]. Therefore, in place of "distinctness from earth and so forth," [the reason must be qualified].
If one includes the absence of earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, selfhood, and mind-ness as the probans,
it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), namely the existence of substances such as ether and the internal space;
this remains true even if the phrase "distinct from ether, time, and direction" is substituted [for the probandum].
Even when the properties of being space, time, and direction are taken as the subject,

there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) regarding the categories of "spaceness," "timeness," and "directionness" under the view that these are universals (*jāti*), because the universals of spacenness, timeness, and directionness themselves are unestablished.
Furthermore, the absence of that [quality] is also unestablished;

moreover, in the view that the nature of space (*ākāśatva*), time (*kālatva*), and direction (*dik-tva*) constitute the definitions of space and so forth, space and the rest would be distinct entities (*arthāntara*).
Because space and the other [elements] are devoid of the characteristics of space and so forth, owing to their absolute absence of the words "space" and so forth as their defining characteristics;

because they are devoid of the characteristics of space and so forth which have been made the subject (pakṣa) by being devoid of the grounds for the application (pravṛttinimitta) of the words "space" and so forth;
and because they are distinct from the substances of space and so forth which have been made the subject by being devoid of the grounds for the application of the words "space" and so forth.
This is because even space and the like are devoid of that which serves as the ground for the application of the terms "space" and so forth;

and because, if [the probandum] were to reside in a substance, the state of being devoid of distinctness from space and the like would constitute a limiting condition (upādhi). Furthermore, this [probans] does not suffer from the fallacy of being "other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva).

Because there exists a counter-instance (vyāvartya) characterized by the absence of subsistence in substance—namely, the property of being a quality (guṇatva), the property of being an action (karmatva), and so forth.

[The argument is: "Being distinct from earth and the other [elements] does not subsist in substance, because it does not subsist in that which lacks the distinction from earth and the others, just like the property of being a quality," and so on.

"And because there is a counter-argument. Now, one might attempt to prove the existence of another substance by the following inference: "Ether is distinct from substances characterized by earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, selfhood, mind-ness, and direction-time-ness, because it possesses existence, like a jar. This is not [valid].
And here too, there is no "unestablished qualification" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva),

because the property of being distinct from the substance of space— which is the subject under discussion and is devoid of the characteristics of earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, self-hood, mind-hood, direction-hood, and time-hood—
is well-established in the case of a jar and so forth; nor is it...

If you think that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhārthāntaratā*)— since the goal would be merely to prove the difference from the substances such as space (which are themselves the subjects of the argument) that are devoid of earthness and so forth—

and that this is unavoidable because it would involve both contradiction (*vyāghāta*) and sublation (*bādha*) when attempting to prove the difference of the subject, space, from itself— that is not so.

If one accepts that [the subject] is excluded from the definitions of space and time, then the same objection remains: that there is the fallacy of proving something already established (*siddhārthāntara*), since the distinctness of the substances of space and time—which are devoid of the definitions of space and time—is already established by the proof of another space. This is because the purpose [of the argument] is fulfilled by the establishment of another space.
Because it would establish [the existence of] another substance.
Now, to exclude this [possibility], the qualification "being devoid of the nature of being other than the ether that has been made the subject" is employed.

That is not so, because the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). This is because, prior to the operation of this inference, an "ether" distinct from the ether that has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) is itself unestablished. Now, as for this pot...
"It is distinct from those substances characterized as earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, selfhood, mind-ness, direction, time, and space,
because it possesses existence (*sattva*), like a cloth"— thus [the opponent] attempts to prove it to be a different substance. This is not so,
because [existence] does not subsist by non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*).
Because the "other object" (arthāntara)— namely, the state of being distinct from substances such as space (ākāśa) which lack the characteristics of sound and so forth—

remains as it was [in the previous fallacy]. This pot is distinct from that substance which lacks the characteristics of earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, self-hood, mind-ness, direction, time, and space, other than this [pot].

Furthermore, because of this very [reason], there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) stating: "Whatever is not thus, is not so. Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here;

for [the subject] is distinct from that substance which is devoid of the characteristics of earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, self-hood, mind-ness, direction-ness, time-ness, and ether-ness, other than these.

"Because the qualification is established by the inference: 'That which has for its counter-positive an absence that is devoid of the nature of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) and devoid of the natures of antecedent absence (prāgabhāva) and destructive absence (pradhvaṃsābhāva) is an object of knowledge (meyatva), like a jar. (1-1-4)
Now follows the aphorism concerning the classification of qualities (guṇa):
color, taste, smell, touch, numbers, dimensions, separateness,
conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain.
Desire, aversion, and effort are the qualities. (1.1.5)

If it is asked what the purpose of the compound (*samāsa*) in the phrase "form, taste, smell, and touch" is, we reply: it is for the sake of brevity of case endings (*vibhakti-lāghava*). For if form, taste, smell, and touch were presented separately—as *rūpam*, *rasaḥ*, *gandhaḥ*, *sparśaḥ*—then a case ending would have to be applied to each one individually.

There is a heaviness of case endings in that four case endings must be employed; however, in the case of a compound, only a single case ending is used. But the teacher Ātreya [argues] that in the compound *rūpa-rasa-gandha-sparśāḥ*, [the case ending belongs to] *rūpa-rasa-gandha-sparśānām*.
They say that the purpose is to demonstrate the common properties (sādharmya) such as permanence, impermanence, and being produced by heat (pākaja); but that is not so, because [these properties],
including the permanence and impermanence of color, taste, smell, and touch, as well as their being produced by heat, will be discussed later.

Because the author of the Sūtras has already established this directly, indicating it again would be fruitless. If that is so, then [the same applies] to the qualities beginning with *rūpa* and ending with *prayatna*.
If it is asked why the author of the Sūtras does not employ compounds for the sake of brevity in inflection,
[the answer is] that it is for the sake of intermediate purposes; and we shall explain those in detail under each respective rule.
The plural form "numbers" (saṃkhyāḥ) is used for the purpose of including numberhood as well as its sub-types, such as oneness, duality, triplicity, and so forth. Therefore,
that which has been stated by some—
The claim that number is simply oneness, while duality and so forth are merely specific aggregations of oneness,
has been refuted;
for no such specific aggregation of oneness can be defined apart from the distinct universals (jāti) of duality, trinity, and the rest.
The plural number in the term "dimensions" (*parimāṇāni*) is intended to indicate the various sub-types of dimension, namely minuteness, largeness, shortness, and length.
Therefore, as for what has been stated by someone—
The claim that magnitude itself is dimension, that inferior magnitude is atomicity,
that this very [inferior magnitude] is shortness, and that a particular kind of magnitude is length— this has been refuted; for we shall establish this [our own position] later.
The use of the singular number in the term "pṛthaktvam" (separateness) is for the purpose of excluding sub-varieties of separateness, such as "dvi-pṛthaktva" (two-fold separateness) and so forth;
for the linguistic usage "two things are separate" and the like is accounted for by separateness as delimited by duality, and so on.
Some [hold this view].
That is not so, because there are distinct universals such as duality-inherence and triad-inherence, which are excluded from the separateness residing in single entities.

Because it is established by the same logic as other universals (*jātyantara*), the singular number in the term "separateness" (*pṛthaktvam*) is for the purpose of indicating the unity of the universal of separateness. Now, as for color (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*)...
If it is asked, "Why was the singular number not used in these and other instances?"— the answer is no; for in some cases,
when the unity of a genus is indicated by the singular number, it is possible to determine the unity of the genera of color and so forth by the same logical principle.
In cases such as "conjunction and disjunction," "remoteness and proximity," and so forth, the compound is likewise formed as before for the sake of brevity in the case endings.
The plural number in "cognitions" (buddhayaḥ) is intended to indicate the multiplicity of cognitions. By this—

The Māyā-Vedānta position— that there is only one intellect (*buddhi*) and that the conventional usage of distinct cognitions is as false as the conventional usage of multiple moons— is refuted. Alternatively, the plural form "cognitions" (*buddhayaḥ*) [is used].

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the multiplicity of universals (jāti), such as being a cognition (*buddhitva*), being a specific sub-class of cognition (*avāntara-pramātṛ-sākṣātkāritva*), being an inference (*anumititva*), being doubt (*saṃśayatva*), and being error (*viparyayatva*). By this, the Prābhākaras— who claim that there are no sub-universals within the universal of cognition (*jñānatva*)— are refuted.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and effort" (*prayatnaśca*) serves to include gravity (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), viscidity (*sneha*), the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and sound (*śabda*), which were not explicitly mentioned.
One might ask: even though they are equally unmentioned, why are only these many included?
If it is asked why there are only this many qualities—because only these many have been stated as such;
therefore, the qualities are those whose forms are explicitly mentioned, such as color (*rūpa*), as well as those conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*), such as gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth.
If it is asked how there are only this many qualities—the answer is: no, for there are only this many.
This is because [the objection] has already been answered by the principle that "substances [are eternal]. (1.1.5)
Now, for the purpose of classifying action, the aphorism: "Throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and going— these are the actions" (1.1.6).
Throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇatva*) is a specific genus (*jāti*). That which has this as its substratum is "throwing upward.
In the same way, throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*) and the others are also to be defined.
The use of the singular number in "throwing upward" and so forth is for the purpose of making known the oneness of the genus, such as "throwing upward-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*).
Because individual instances of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth are infinite, it is impossible for them to possess oneness.

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of demonstrating the oneness residing in the universal (*jāti*) of throwing upwards and so forth?"— it is not [without purpose], for there is a purpose in demonstrating the oneness residing in the universal in the case of "earth" (*pṛthivī*).

Because it has already been shown; for if it is argued that the classification is incomplete because whirling, evacuation, flowing, upward flaming, and so forth also exist, we say no, because whirling and the rest are included within "motion" (gamanatva).

Because motion characterized as "going" (gamanatva) is defined as being devoid of the properties of upward throwing (utkṣepaṇatva), downward throwing (avakṣepaṇatva), contraction (ākuñcanatva), and expansion (prasāraṇatva); and because the meaning of the word "going-ness" (gamanatva) is the universal (jāti) residing solely in that which possesses the aforementioned definition. And thus, the formal argument (prayoga): whirling and so forth are not [motions characterized as going].
[They] possess the property of being movements,
because they are actions devoid of the properties of throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, and expansion,
like the movement [of walking] which is commonly admitted. This is not so.

Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here, because "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) is established by inclusive perception (*anugata-pratyakṣa*) as "this is going, this is going. [The inference is:

Going is possessed of a genus (*jāti*) that resides in that which possesses the characteristic of going, resides in that which is excluded from that which possesses the characteristic of going, and is devoid of residing in that which lacks the characteristic of going.

Because it possesses the nature of a genus (*jātimattvāt*), like "cowness" (*gotva*); this is because the qualification [of the reason] is well-established. Nor can there be a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on the following: "Going (*gamana*) does not reside in that which possesses the characteristic of going, nor in that which possesses the characteristic of going that is excluded from [other things], nor in that which lacks the characteristic of going, nor is it devoid of a genus; because it lacks both the property of being 'going-ness' (*gamanatva*) and the property of being a genus (*jātitva*), like non-existence (*abhāva*). This is because [the reason in the original argument] is established as a qualification.
Because it is qualified by a limiting condition (*upādhi*)—namely, the absence of possessing a genus—and because there is a sublation (*bādha*) if that [absence] were also to be proven;

furthermore, this [condition] is not "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratā*), since even such a thing as possesses a genus is excluded from the subject, such as a jar. Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) may be "being denotable by the word 'motion'."
And likewise, whirling and the like are denotable by the word "going" (gamana),
because they possess the nature of action devoid of the properties of throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contracting, and expanding,
just like the [action of] going that is commonly accepted. Nor are whirling and the like possessed of the property of going (gamanatva), nor...

The two previous inferences are counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣatva*) by the following: "Those things denoted by the word 'going' do not possess action devoid of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇatva*), throwing downwards (*avakṣepaṇatva*), contraction (*ākuñcanatva*), and expansion (*prasāraṇatva*), because they are distinct from that which is commonly accepted as 'going,' just like a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth."
"Because it is qualified by an adjunct.

Alternatively, the nature of "going" (*gamanatva*) is simply the state of being an action devoid of the properties of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇatva*), downward throwing (*avakṣepaṇatva*), contraction (*ākuñcanatva*), and expansion (*prasāraṇatva*). And that [nature] is indeed established through perception in cases such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*).
In establishing the non-existence of that [universal], there is indeed a contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*); thus, everything is faultless.
Why was a compound not formed for *utkṣepaṇa*, *avakṣepaṇa*, *ākuñcana*, *prasāraṇa*, and *gamana* for the sake of brevity in the inflection?

If it is argued that [the singular number is used] because the grammatical simplicity of the case-ending is disregarded in accordance with the purpose of conveying the oneness residing in the genus (jāti) such as "throwing upwards" (utkṣepaṇatva), etc.— this is refuted by [Sūtra] 1.1.6.

Now, for the purpose of demonstrating the similarities and differences among substance and the other categories, the aphorism states: "Existent, non-eternal, possessing substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity."

"There is no distinction between substance, quality, and action" (1.1.7). The term "existent" (*sat*) is an indication that emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*); its meaning is "existence" (*sattva*). Likewise [apply this to the terms]: "non-eternal," "possessing substance," "effect," and "cause."
Expressions such as "possessing generalities and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*) are indeed designations where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant.

One should analyze "possessing generalities and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*) as "possessing generalities" (*sāmānyavat*), "possessing particulars" (*viśeṣavat*), and "possessing generalities and particulars. By that [analysis],...

It is stated that existence (*sattva*), impermanence (*anityatva*), substantiality (*dravyavattva*), being an effect (*kāryatva*), being a cause (*kāraṇatva*), possessing generality (*sāmānyavattva*), and possessing particularity (*viśeṣavattva*) are the common properties (*sādharmya*) of substances, qualities, and actions. The word "iti" is intended to include such categories as nameability (*abhidheyatva*) and knowability (*prameyatva*). Existence (*sattva*) means being (*astitva*).

It is a specific property residing in all categories of entities. If it is asked what the proof for this is, the answer is: perception itself. Now, if existence (*astitva*) is simply being (*sattā*), and that resides only in substances, qualities, and actions, then how is there the cognition "it exists" with respect to universals and the rest?

If it is argued that this is an error—no, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*). For no sublation arises to the effect that universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth do not exist. If it is argued that a sublation will arise at some other time—no, for even the cognition "the jar exists" would have a sublation at some other time.

Because it can be said that [the property] will exist; the inference "universals and so forth possess existence because they are objects of cognition (*prameya*), like a jar" is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that "possessing a universal" is the limiting condition (*upādhi*) here—no, because it pervades the probans (*sādhana*).

And because it is other than the subject (*pakṣetaratva*); for, since the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*) is unestablished, there exists no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) consisting of that which possesses the absence of the probandum, and thus [the reason] does not exclude itself from the counter-example. Nor is this...

The absence of the probandum (sādhya) in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayi) inference is unestablished because its qualification would be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Now, does existence reside in existence or not? In the first case, there is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
In the second case, it is untenable for existence to reside in all categories of things, since it [existence] resides in itself alone.
It is not [the case] that [existence is non-existent] because it is excluded; for even in the case of existence, existence is admitted.

Since there is no obstruction to its production or its cognition, we do not accept that self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) constitutes a fault in the present context. What [is the meaning] of "existence exists in existence"?

If it is argued that there is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, the state of being an object of cognition (prameyatva) and so forth—[we reply: no, because [the reason] is counterbalanced by a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) based on a negative inference (vyatirekin): "Universals (jāti) and the rest are devoid of existence (astitva), because they are devoid of substantiality (dravyatva), quality-ness (guṇatva), and action-ness (karmatva); for whatever is not thus, it is not thus, like a jar. If this is argued, we say: no.

Because the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvāt*). Now, where the probandum (*sādhya*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), there the "unestablished qualification" is a defect; for, since it is impossible to cognize [that probandum], it is impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the absence of a means of proof (*sādhana*). In the present case...

Furthermore, the probandum (sādhya) is of the nature of non-existence. In that case, the fault [of the reason] is "having an unestablished qualifier" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva). Even though the qualifier is unestablished, since the non-existence of that [qualifier] can be cognized as having the nature of a positive entity (bhūvarūpatayā), [the reason is not faulty].
If you think that the apprehension of non-pervasion is possible due to the absence of a means of proof— that is not so;

for when the qualifier is unestablished, it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion of the reason with it, and thus the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the pervaded (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) is unavoidable.

Even if it were possible to grasp the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by means of the absence of the probans, [the reason] would still lack the property of being a feature of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
This is because negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is accepted as a means for grasping positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*),
and this has already been established previously.

Furthermore, if the qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), it is included within the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) because the word conveying the probandum (*sādhya*) fails to express its meaning;
and because the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) is difficult to establish due to being sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhitatva*),
since those [categories] such as genus (*jāti*) are apprehended as existing by the very means of valid cognition that apprehend them.

Now, one might think: "If it is established that existence (*astitva*) is excluded from the object of cognition (*prameya*) because it is a genus (*jāti*), like 'cowness' (*gotva'), then the property of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), which is used to prove existence, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to an object of cognition that lacks existence. This is not so.

When "exclusion from the cognizable" (*prameyādvyāvṛttatva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), "exclusion from the existent" (*sadvyāvṛttitva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Furthermore, in its absence, there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*). Nor is this [condition] merely "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratā*), because it is excluded from "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, which lack exclusion from the cognizable.

By this, the objection is refuted: that because existence (*astitva*) is excluded from universals (*jāti*) since they possess the nature of being a universal—just like "cowness" (*gotva*)—the absence of existence is well-established; thus, for the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) stating that "universals and so forth are devoid of existence," there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

Now, is existence (*astitva*) a genus (*jāti*) or a distinct category (*dharmāntara*)? We say it is a genus. If it is argued that a genus cannot reside in a genus itself, we say no, because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) [to the contrary]. If it is argued that the acceptance of a genus within a genus leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say no, because [such an infinite regress does not arise] when existence is accepted in [higher categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*).

Because an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is impossible to establish; for if it is argued that even if existence exists, there must be another existence therein, and yet another existence in that one as well— [we reply] no, because existence does not require a further existence, and thus such an infinite regress is avoided by the absence of a "root-ruin" (*mūlakṣati*).

And because [the opponent] does not admit that [universals] possess the nature of being qualifiers (*dūṣaṇatva*). If it is argued that the absence of a relation is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the acceptance of universals in inherence (*samavāya*), we say no; for it is admitted that the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) exists between inherence and absences. In the case of inherence...

If it is argued that the absence of inherence (*samavāya*) is a subverting factor when the acceptance of universals (*jāti*) is maintained— no, for inherence itself can possess inherence. If it is argued that the acceptance of another inherence leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because there would be yet another inherence for that [second inherence] as well— no, because that very inherence [possesses itself].

If it is argued that there would be self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) because [the relation] is accepted therein—let it be so; for we do not accept self-dependence as a flaw when it does not obstruct origination or cognition. This is because inherence (*samavāya*) has inherence as its locus.

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of inherence being distinct [from its constituents], like a jar—no, because this is a fallacious argument (tarkābhāsa), as it does not result in a valid counter-implication (viparyaya). [The counter-implication would be:
"Inherence is neither the substratum of inherence nor is it dependent upon inherence."

Because [the reason] "due to being devoid of the state of being distinct from inherence," etc., lacks positive concomitance (anvaya), as its presence in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is not certain;
for [while] absence is not dependent on inherence, a jar and the like are dependent on inherence.
Furthermore, because it would be excluded even from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), its nature as a negative-only reason (*vyatirekin*) would be untenable.

Or, let there be another inherence (*samavāya*) in inherence; even so, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because in the second inherence, one simply accepts the first inherence itself. And it is not thus...

There is the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*), because even if there is no obstruction to production or cognition, mutual dependence is not accepted as a fault. For that which is dependent upon something else cannot be its support (*āśraya*), just as a cloth is not the support of its threads; and [the universal] is dependent upon its first inherence (*samavāya*).
[Objection: The second inherence is not dependent upon the first inherence. [Response:
No, because it is impossible to state what that commonality of the referent of the word "that" (i.e., the universal) is;

and because there would be a deviation in the case of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. [Furthermore,] it is dependent on an individual (*piṇḍa*) while being the substratum of another individual.

Furthermore, because there is a deviation [in the argument] with respect to horns and the like: that which is dependent upon the first inherence is not the substratum of the first inherence, just as existence (bhāva), which is dependent upon the first inherence, is not its substratum;
yet the second inherence is dependent upon the first inherence; therefore, it is not [the case that the second inherence is not the substratum of the first].

If it is argued that [the second inherence] has the first inherence as its substratum—no, because this is countered by a valid opposing argument (*satpratipakṣa*), such as: "The second inherence does not have the first inherence as its substratum, because it is an entity distinct from the first inherence, like a jar. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Furthermore, because inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished, the first reason suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Moreover, since one accepts the first inherence even in the absence of anything inhering in that first inherence, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). This applies equally to both existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).

This is because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes inherence (*samavāya*) is the same [in all cases], and there is an absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). Alternatively, let there be yet another inherence even in the second inherence; thus, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since one simply accepts the first inherence itself in the third inherence. And it is not so.

There is no fault of circularity (*cakraka*), because a circle is not a defect when it does not obstruct either production or cognition. Likewise, even if one accepts the fourth and fifth conjunctions (*samavāya*), there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Or, even if an infinite regress were to occur, it would still not be a fault.

Because, in the absence of being an obstacle to production or manifestation, even infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is not a defect. If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of an infinity of inherences (*samavāya*), we say no, because that is accepted.

If it is argued that the acceptance of existence (*sattā*) in the *viśeṣas* entails the consequence of the loss of their essential nature (*svarūpahāni*), we say no; for since there is no invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the acceptance of existence and the loss of essential nature, the reductio (*prasaṅga*) lacks a firm foundation. [This remains true] even if existence is accepted in the *viśeṣas*.

If it is argued that there is a loss of the defining characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), because "inherence in a single substance" is the defining characteristic of a *viśeṣa* when it is devoid of existence (*sattā*)— we say no;
for even if the definition of a final *viśeṣa* is untenable, [the definition holds] provided it is devoid of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*).

This is because it is logical for that which inheres in a single substance (*satya*) alone to have the character of a particular (*viśeṣa*); or else, because the universal (*jāti*) of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) constitutes the character of a particular. Furthermore, we shall state other definitions of particulars, so this [objection] amounts to nothing.

If non-existence were accepted as an existent category, it would be the object of the cognition "it exists," but this is not so, because one does not accept that it is the object of the cognition "the jar exists. This is because even the cognition "the jar does not exist" has the existence of the jar's absence as its scope; it does not mean merely "the jar is not."

Because of the demonstration of the absence of a jar; because by the word "jar" the counter-positive (pratiyogin) jar is denoted, and by the negative particle (nañ) the absence is denoted, and by the word "is" existence (sattā) is denoted. [Objection: If existence were admitted in the case of absence, then in the ninth chapter...

If it is argued that the conventional usage "because of the non-existence of the author of the Sūtra" is contradictory, we say no; for the usage "non-existent" (asat) is appropriate when intended in the sense of "absence" (abhāvatva). It is indeed existence [that is meant].

If it is asked: "How can 'being' (bhāvatva) be possible if existence (sattā) is admitted in non-existence (abhāva)?"—it is not so; for if existence is admitted as being a positive entity (bhāva), then being a positive entity consists precisely in being one or another of the six categories beginning with substance (dravya).
And because the absolute non-existence of the six categories beginning with substance possesses the nature of non-existence [itself].
When existence (sattā) is admitted among the universals (jāti), there is no universal or particular within those universals and particulars; therefore, cognition arises from that very [existence].

If it is argued that this contradicts the Sūtra— no, for by the statement "due to the absence of general and particular," [the Sūtra] negates an intermediate generality (sāmānyaviśeṣa) with respect to *sattā*.

Because there is no prohibition [of it]. Otherwise, since the negation of the universal would be established by the mere statement "due to the absence of a universal," the inclusion of the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) in the sūtra would result in redundancy.
Thus it is established that existence (*sattā*), as a universal (*jāti*), is indeed "being" (*astitva*) and the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of all categories of entities.
As stated by the authors of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*: "And because it is the sole cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛtti*), it is a universal alone."
Udayana,

however, argues that if existence were excluded from universals and the like, then because it would be the cause of the cognition of exclusion from universals and the like, it would be a particular universal (sāmānyaviśeṣa), just like substantiality and so forth.

It might be so; however, he [the author of the commentary] explained that it was stated by the Bhāṣyakāra that "it is the universal alone" because only the continuity (anuvṛtti) serves as the cause. That is incorrect, because [continuity] is excluded from genus (jāti) and the other categories.
If existence were to differentiate its own substratum from universals such as "beingness" (jāti) and so forth,

it would follow that substances and the like— which are themselves differentiated from qualities and so forth— would lack the capacity to differentiate their own substrata from qualities and the like.

If it is argued that substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth possess the quality of being differentiators because they specifically produce, in their own substratum, a cognition that excludes the absolute non-existence of themselves— this is not so, even if such existence were granted.
Regarding the phrase "because of being equal":

non-eternality (*anityatva*) is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of destruction; it is a specific property residing in effects, substances, qualities, actions, and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is the dependence upon substance; it is a specific property residing in effects, substances, qualities, actions, universals, particulars, inherence, substances [themselves], and non-existence.

Being an effect (kāryatva) is the state of being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva); it is impermanence (anityatva), a specific property residing in impermanent substances, impermanent qualities, actions, and destructions.
Causality is the state of being a generator; it is a specific property residing in all things.
Now, what is this "state of being a generator"? It cannot be merely "occurring prior [to the effect]," for even things that perished long ago would then [be considered causes] at present.
Because it would follow that [the cause] is the cause of things such as a jar at the very moment they are being produced;
nor is it "existing in the immediately preceding moment," since this would apply even to donkeys and other such things existing in the moment immediately preceding a jar.

Because it would follow that [the cause] would be the cause of the pot and so forth; nor is it the case that [causality] consists in necessarily occurring in the immediately preceding moment, since there are many things that necessarily occur in the moment prior to that specific pot.

Otherwise, it would follow that donkeys and the like could also be the producers of this jar. Nor can it be defined as the property of belonging to a genus that exists in the immediately preceding moment of the same kind [as the effect], because this would fail for things devoid of a genus, such as destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) and the prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) which themselves lack a genus.

Because it would follow that [the cause] is not a cause in the case of a jar and so forth; and because it would follow that even the ether (*ākāśa*) is not a cause in the case of sound, since the ether, being eternal,
lacks the property of belonging to the same class as [an effect] existing in a preceding moment.

Furthermore, because [the opponent] holds that being of the same class as that which occurs in the immediately preceding moment is necessarily the cause, it would follow that space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities produce all effects.
Nor do space and the like possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Because it would follow that sound and other such things lack causality; because there is no temporal exclusion [of the cause] due to its eternity; because there is no spatial exclusion due to its omnipresence;
and because it would follow that the color of the threads and so forth would be the producer of the jar and other such effects.

Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [its] being a cause? It is certainly not the sense faculty, because that is not apprehended upon the first contact with the sense organ.
Nor is it [apprehended] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
For those who lack the reflection upon that [invariable concomitance], causality is not cognized even though positive and negative concomitance exist;
nor is it [cognized] when accompanied by the reflection upon positive and negative concomitance.

For even when there is contact with the senses accompanied by the investigation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the causality of threads and their colors toward a cloth and so forth is not perceived;
whereas in the case of space and such, it is not perceived even in the absence of positive and negative concomitance and the investigation thereof.

Furthermore, because [the cognition] is perceived as having a cause; for it follows that the sense organ would not be a cause, since the perception of causality is established solely through the investigation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Nor is it an inferential mark (liṅga), because such a mark is absent. If it is argued that "positive and negative concomitance themselves are the inferential marks"—no, because of those two...
Because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its presence in the color and other qualities of the threads that do not produce the cloth.
If it is argued that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that are not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*) constitute the inferential mark (*liṅga*), we say no;
for what does "not otherwise established" mean? Does it mean residing in the cause, or rather...

[The definition of being a cause is] "the state of being devoid of the nature of not being a cause. It is not the first [alternative], because the colors of the threads and so forth are devoid of the nature of being the cause of the cause of the cloth,
and thus [the concomitance and exclusion] of those [properties] would [not hold].
The fallacy of inconclusiveness remains in the same state because [the reason] is not restricted to being the cause of the cause and so forth.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*), since the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) residing in the threads and other materials are not established prior to the establishment of those threads and others as the causes of the cloth.

Because it is not established that being a cause of cloth is something undesirable; nor is there another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since none can be defined. Therefore, causality is impossible to distinguish and is without any proof.

To this it is replied: Is "causality" (kāraṇatva) itself impossible to distinguish, or is it its specific instance, namely "being the cause of a jar" and so forth? Not the first, because causality is simply the state of being a generator (janakatva). If it is asked, "What is this state of being a generator?"—it is simply the state of being a generator. When the state of being a generator is questioned...

If it is argued that the answer "it is precisely the state of being a producer" is untenable—no, for this very answer is tenable. This is because, if one were to state something else, there would be a contradiction and a shift to a different subject matter; for when asked "What is cloth-ness?", the answer "cloth-ness" is not contradictory, whereas [stating something else] would constitute a shift to a different subject matter.

It is possible that it "transcends. If one asks, "What is the definition of causality?"—it is the absolute absence of non-causality (*akāraṇatvātyantābhāva*). If one asks, "How is this the definition of causality?"—it is because, while being distinct from causality, it does not reside in what is undesired [as a cause].

Because it resides in the state of being a cause. If it is asked, "What is the substratum of causality?"—it is simply substance and so forth. If it is asked, "How much [of these]?"—it is all of them. If it is asked, "What is the proof for causality?"—it is simply perception, namely, the cognition: "This is a cause; this is a cause."
Just as the perception "this exists, this exists" is the means of valid cognition for existence (*sattā*),

so too the perception "this is a cause, this is a cause" is the means of valid cognition for causality (*kāraṇatva*). This is because there is no difference between the two cases regarding their producing an uncontradicted experience.

If it is asked how uncontradicted experience itself is established—[the answer is] because it is a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). This is because the absolute absence of contradiction by experience is cognizable through mental perception; and also because of non-discrepant worldly usage such as "this is the cause" and "that is the cause," [as observed] in the case of the sky and so forth.

If it is asked what the proof is for its being a cause—the answer is simply "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the state of being a producer of a jar is itself the causality of the jar, and the state of being a producer of a cloth is itself the causality of the cloth. And as for other objections, they are to be treated just as before.
Regarding the phrase "because of exclusion":
if it is asked what the definition of a cause is— does the definition of a cause intend to express a property of the cause, or something that is not excluded from the cause?

Or [the definition] is the ground for the application of the term "cause," or it is a property that does not reside in non-causes and is excluded from non-causes. In the first case, it is simply "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and so forth; in the second case, it is simply "causality" (kāraṇatva), "existence" (astitva), "knowability" (prameyatva), and so forth.

In the third case, it is simply a cause. In the fourth, there is no proof; for if there is no cognition of that which is not a cause, one does not engage with it, since it is impossible to ask about dharma when it has not been cognized. Or, even if it were possible [to ask], the answer would simply be "nothing at all."
Because we do not accept that dharma functions without a cause;
for if absolute liberation itself were the cause,
it would be impossible for an effect to arise immediately following it, as is well known.
You may think that the impossibility of [the world] being a cause follows, and consequently the impossibility of its being an effect,
because of the absence of both a creator and a purposeful unseen force (adṛṣṭa) for all things that arise—
but that is not so, even after ultimate liberation.
Because one must accept that atomic action and the conjunctions produced by it [exist], and because such conjunctions—
being neither enjoyment nor its means— are not produced by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) and are devoid of purpose; [if they were] the cause of final liberation, what [would be the point]?
If it is argued that [the reason] is valid— such as "final liberation is caused because it is an object of knowledge (*meyatva*),
like a jar," and so forth— and that no *upādhi* (limiting condition) is possible here, because there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) from which it could be excluded; for whomsoever...
Because that which is being designated as a qualifying condition (upādhi) for something is itself the "otherness of the subject" (pakṣetaratva).

Furthermore, there is an absence of a counter-example (vipakṣa), because since the absence of the probandum (sādhya) in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayi) inference is unestablished, a counter-example possessing such an absence is impossible. Nor is there any possibility of a counter-argument (pratipakṣa) here.

Because the absence of a probandum that is purely positive (kevalānvayi) is unestablished, there can be no counter-example (vipakṣa) possessing it; nor is there any possibility of a counter-argument (pratipakṣa) here,
because the absence of a purely positive probandum is unestablished, and thus [there is no such thing as] its pervader.

Because it is impossible to understand [it] anywhere; for, on the view that absolute liberation is not a cause, the very definition of a cause is simply being other than absolute liberation. Now, what is the definition of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)? It is precisely the state of being dependent upon an effect.

The specific definitions of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), however, should be understood according to their respective possibilities. For instance, if it is argued that [the definition] is "being a cause while not being conjoined with the jar"—
no, for that would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka), as it would apply to jars and other things which are the inherent causes of color and so forth.
Even for [qualities such as] the color of a jar and so forth,

their being the substratum of the jar consists in their inhering in the parts of the jar which are the causes of the jar's color; furthermore, the definition of the inherent cause of a jar is that it is the substratum of the jar while not being conjoined with a cloth.

The definition of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a cloth is its being the substratum (*āśraya*) of the color and other qualities of the cloth; likewise, the definition of the inherent cause of the color and other qualities of a jar is its being the substratum of the color and other qualities of the jar. Alternatively, the definition of the inherent cause of the color of a jar is its being the cause of that which is the inherent cause of the color of the jar, and so forth.
Now, what is the definition of a non-inherent cause? It is not [simply] being proximate while being a cause by virtue of inhering in the inherent cause.
Furthermore, [the definition] is over-extensive with respect to dharma and so forth, which produce pleasure, pain, and the like;
for while dharma, adharma, and so on are producers of pleasure and the like, they also reside in the self (ātman) as their cause.

Because, like the inherence in a single object with the cause (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāya*), inherence in a single object with the effect (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*) also constitutes proximity; and because [the definition] would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) in the case of the dimension of atoms (*paramāṇuparimāṇa*) and so forth,
since those too possess the status of being producers by virtue of generating specific cognitions and the like.
Furthermore, [the universal "substance-ness"] is proximate by virtue of being inherent in the dyads (dvyaṇuka) which are the causes of the triads (tryaṇuka) and so forth;
and because both the universal and the particular are over-pervasive,
since they too produce cognitions of persistence and exclusion respectively.
Furthermore, [the definition fails] because of the inherence in a single object that is the effect of conjunction and so forth.

Moreover, if one qualifies [the definition] by excluding that which lacks the capacity to produce only a specific quality of the self (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇa*), then the conjunction between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*) would result in being under-defined (*avyāpaka*).

If it is argued that "whatever is a cause of something while being in proximity to it is its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)," we say no; for if the words "whatever" (*yat*) and "that" (*tat*) are intended to convey a general, inclusive meaning, the flaw of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition remains as before.

Furthermore, if the definition were intended to refer to those specific [types of inherence], it would suffer from the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpaka*), because the terms "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*)—meaning both "inherence in the same object as the cause" (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāya*) and "inherence in the same object as the effect" (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*)—do not subsume all cases;
thus, the definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is untenable. To this we reply:

that is not so, because the general definition of a non-inherent cause is: "an entity that is devoid of being a substance, devoid of being a self-attribute (*ātma-guṇa*), devoid of being a specific attribute (*viśeṣaguṇa*), and devoid of being the producer of mere specific attributes such as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)."

And thus the aforementioned fault does not arise, because [the definition] excludes jars and the like by specifying that they lack the nature of being substances (*dravyatva*), and it refutes merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*),
and so forth by specifying that they lack the nature of being specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self.

This is because [the definition] excludes those things that produce only other specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self— such as non-existence (*dhvaṃsa*) and so forth— as well as number, plurality, separateness, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, the color, taste, smell, and touch of the ultimate composite, universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*), by including the phrase "devoid of producing only other specific qualities of the self such as non-existence. This applies to those things which produce [qualities] distinct from the specific qualities of the self other than non-existence.

And because of the inclusion [of the following] among the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, and action;
and because prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the absence of an obstructer, and final liberation are included under the term "existence" (*bhāva*).

Because of its exclusion [from the definition]. Nor does this result in the non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the conjunction between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*), because that [conjunction] is the cause of mental activity (*manaḥ-kriyā*) distinct from destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self.
This is because there is no other non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the action of the mind.

[The definition applies to] existence (*bhāvatva*) which is devoid of being a substance, which resides in substances such as space (*ākāśa*) that do not originate [other] substances, which is devoid of the specific quality of viscidity (*sneha*) and of being a substance, and which is devoid of being the generator of mere non-cognition (*ajñāna-mātra*) such as destruction.
Because it is the general definition of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
