By the inclusion of the phrase "devoid of specific qualities other than the quality of viscidity residing in substances that do not originate [other] substances such as space," the specific qualities of the self, which is a composite substance, are excluded. Furthermore, what is intended by "non-inherent causes" (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)?
Does the recurring linguistic usage— "this is a non-inherent cause," "this is a non-inherent cause"— which excludes everything else,
exist or not? If it does exist,
then that very thing will be established as the definition of a non-inherent cause.
If it does not exist— then what is the point of a definition of non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*),
since there is no need for a definition for the sake of establishing it due to the absence of a uniform linguistic usage? This is because of the absence of a recurring universal (*anugatajāti*).
Because for the sake of establishing that [universal], there is no dependence on the definition of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

If it is argued that the definition of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is for the purpose of producing the cognition of the difference from others—[we reply: no, because the cognition of the difference of that individual from others is established by the very definition of that specific individual.

If it is argued that the definition of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* is intended for the sake of producing, simultaneously, the cognition of the difference of all individual instances of what is intended as an *asamavāyikāraṇa* from others— [we reply: no.

Because it is accepted that a cognition which excludes everything other than its intended scope of all individual instances of simultaneous non-inherent causes would contradict the purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [one must say]:
"This is the non-inherent cause here; this is the non-inherent cause here."
Furthermore, since the conventional usage of the term "specific non-inherent cause" (*asamavāyikāraṇaviśeṣa*) is established solely from the definition of that specific non-inherent cause itself,
it is incorrect to define the non-inherent cause as dependent upon the definition of a "specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because no such definition of a specific quality exists.
If it is argued that this is not so—no;

for the definition of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is "the possession of a genus residing in a quality which resides in that which resides in earth, while being devoid of the natures of color, taste, smell, and touch. And this [is not the case].

It does not over-extend to natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*), because that too possesses a subordinate genus denoted by the word "quality" which is devoid of the properties of color-ness, taste-ness, smell-ness, touch-ness, and the artificial fluidity residing in earth.
Nor is it over-extensive with respect to the state of being a fiery substance (*taijasadravyatva*), because of that...

Because it lacks the universal subordinate to the property of quality (*guṇatva*) that is devoid of earthness, colorness, tasteness, smellness, touchness, and the state of residing in earth or residing in adventitious fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*);
and because the universal denotable by the term "adventitious fluidity" resides in what resides in earth while not residing in what does not reside in earth.

Alternatively, the definition of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is that of possessing a sub-class of the genus "quality" which does not reside in that which resides in the earth. Nor should it be argued that this definition is under-extended (*avyāpti*) to color and other qualities;
for while the property of "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth do reside in that which resides in the earth...

Even though [qualities] such as blueness and yellowness— which are subordinates of those [earth-qualities]— reside in what resides in earth (i.e., they reside in earth), they are devoid of residing in what does not reside in earth; [this is the case] with respect to the color and other qualities of earth and so forth.

Because blueness and other qualities exist [in earth], and while they reside in what resides in earth, they lack residence in what does not reside in earth; for water and fire lack forms such as blue and yellow; and even in the case of the white form of earth...
This is because one accepts subordinate universals (*avāntarajāti*) such as "whiteness" which are excluded from water, fire, and color;
and because, in the case of the taste of earth, one accepts universals such as "distinct sweetness," "bitterness," and so forth, which are excluded from the taste of water.
And because, in the case of the touch of earth,
one accepts a genus such as "touch produced by maturation" (*pākaja-sparśatva*) which is a sub-class of touch excluded from the touches of water and so forth;
and likewise in the case of the color of water.
This is because [the Vaiśeṣikas] accept a specific clarity that is a sub-type of whiteness, which is excluded from the colors of earth and so forth;
and because they accept a non-manifest sweetness that is a sub-type of sweetness, which is excluded from the tastes of earth, within the taste of water.
And because, in the case of the nature of fire (*tejas*), one accepts a specific whiteness and luminosity that is excluded from the natures of water and so forth;
this is not [uncontested] regarding the touch of earth and the like.

Because there is an inference [of the universal] from touch-ness and so forth, based on those universals which reside in what resides in earth while being devoid of residing in what does not reside in earth. Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*), because in that case...

Because there is no intermediate magnitude or supreme magnitude; or, even if such existed, they would be distinguished by being distinct from that [magnitude]. However, the specific definitions of the non-inherent causes are as follows:
the state of being the conjunction between the parts of a jar and the jar itself, which produces the jar.

The definition of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of a jar: the definition of the non-inherent cause of the color of a jar is either being a color that produces the color of the jar, or being the color of the parts of the jar;
and likewise, [the definition of the non-inherent cause of its taste] is being a taste that produces the taste of the jar, and so forth.

The definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of [qualities such as] the taste of a jar and so forth is the oneness (*ekatva*) that is the producer of a single [substance]. Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) of oneness itself is the definition of the non-inherent cause of oneness. The definition of the non-inherent cause of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth is likewise [the oneness that produces them].

The single separateness that produces [another] single separateness is the definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of single separateness. The very genus (*jāti*) of single separateness is the definition of the non-inherent cause of dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of remoteness (*paratva*)— namely, "the state of being a conjunction that produces remoteness"— is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as it would apply to the conjunction between the self and the locus of remoteness in a pot,
since that conjunction does not produce [that specific] remoteness. Alternatively, if it were to produce it, then that [conjunction] too would necessarily be a non-inherent cause.
The definition of the non-inherent cause of *aparatva* (proximity) is the nature of conjunction that produces *aparatva*;
the definition of the first non-inherent cause [of cognition] is the nature of the conjunction between the self and the mind that produces cognition. Regarding the production of sound:
The definition of sound’s non-inherent cause is its subsistence in true space (*satyākāśa*).
And the definition of [the non-inherent cause of] action is its being the non-inherent cause of action.
This [latter] being the non-inherent cause of action is the non-inherent cause of action.

"Karma is the non-inherent cause" is established by the existence of a uniform linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*). And in the absence of such uniform usage, one does not even accept a definition. Thus, wherever there is an inability to specify a particular definition, yet a uniform usage exists, [the category is accepted].
In each respective case, it must be established that the very property (dharma) which is established through pervasive linguistic usage is the definition (lakṣaṇa).
If it is asked, "What is the definition of an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa)?", the answer is: its very nature as a cause (kāraṇatva).

Because both inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) and non-inherent causality (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) also function as instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) in the production of cognition and other such effects; however, the specific definition of an instrumental cause is that which,
while being devoid of the definitions of the inherent cause and the non-inherent cause of a jar, [is nevertheless a cause].
The status of being the cause of a jar, and so forth—enough with this elaboration.
Possessing a universal (*sāmānyavattva*) is having a recurring substratum; possessing particularity (*viśeṣavattva*) is having a particular substratum;
and possessing both universal and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattva*) is having both recurring and non-recurring substrata. And these three [characteristics]...

The commonality of all categories (*sarvapadārthasādharmya*) exists because the properties of inclusion (*anuvṛtta*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*) are present everywhere. "Knowability" (*prameyatva*) means being the object of valid cognition (*pramā*). "Cognizability" (*jñeyatva*) means being the object of knowledge (*jñāna*). "Nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) means, in short, being the object of verbal designation (*abhidhāna*).

And these [properties] are the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) of all categories (*padārtha*). If it is argued that [properties] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) do not possess the nature of being a property of all categories because they are excluded from themselves—[we reply:
no, for knowability and the like are the substrata of knowability and the like. Knowability...

The locus of knowability (*prameyatva*) is the locus of nameability (*abhidheyatva*), because it is nameable; nameability is the locus of nameability, because it is knowable, like a jar—since such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist.
Furthermore, circularity (*ātmāśraya*) is not a flaw, as it does not obstruct either the production or the cognition [of the property].

Now, [properties] such as impermanence, being an effect, and subsistence in a substance are not substances, because they lack qualities (*guṇa*), and because they subsist in qualities and subsist in actions (*karman*). Nor are they qualities or actions, because they themselves subsist in qualities. Nor are they universals (*jāti*), because they subsist in absences (*abhāva*).
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (*jāti-saṃkara*) with respect to substantiality (*dravyatva*),
because substantiality exists in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth while excluding impermanence, being an effect, and subsistence in a substance;
whereas impermanence, being an effect, subsistence in a substance, and so forth [do not exist there].

It is not substance (*dravya*), because it exists in action (*karma*) and so forth while excluding the nature of substance; nor is it quality (*guṇa*), because that would entail the fallacy of confusion between universals (*jāti-saṃkara*); and as for [the other categories] such as possessing a universal (*sāmānyavattva*), they are afflicted by the same defect regarding their instances as *sattā*. It is not inherence (*samavāya*), because [it also exists] in non-existence (*abhāva*).
Because it exists [as a positive entity] and because it lacks a relation [to its locus]; nor is it a particular (viśeṣa), because it does not reside in many;
nor is it a non-existence (abhāva), because it cannot be defined by a counter-correlative (pratiyogin); nor is it a separate category of reality (padārthāntara), because such is not admitted.

It is said: these are indeed universals (*jāti*), because the property of being dependent on non-existence (*abhāvāśritatva*) is found to deviate (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of existence (*sattā*); and because the confusion of universals (*jātisaṃkara*) is not a fault; or, if it were a fault, then even substantiality (*dravyatva*) would be abolished; and because there is no apprehension of any specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). Those...
If it is argued that these two are not universals (jāti) because they are co-located while being mutually exclusive—

just as the universal "element-hood" (bhūtatva) and the universal "sensory organ-hood" (indriyatva) are, or as "substance-hood" (dravyatva) and "impermanence" (anityatva) are co-located while being mutually exclusive— and therefore they do not belong to the category of universals: we say no.
Because there is sublation (*bādha*) regarding the aspect of substantiality (*dravyatva*).

If it is argued that impermanence (*anityatva*) and so forth are not universals (*jāti*), because while being co-located with substantiality, they reside in the absence of substantiality— just like the absence of color (*rūpa*)— we say no.

Because there is deviation [from the probandum] in the case of existence (*sattā*), and because if the reason is qualified by "being other than existence," there is sublation (*bādha*); for in the present context, the definition of a genus (*jāti*)— either as "being a state residing in multiple things while being eternal" or "being inherent in multiple things while being eternal"— is established by valid means of knowledge.
For even the property of having an identical manifestation is not accepted as a refutation of the universal (jāti). Or,
let there be other categories such as eternality and subsistence in a substance,
since they lack the defining characteristics of substance and so forth.

Nor does this contradict the restriction that there are only six categories, because we do not accept the restriction that there are only six categories since a seventh category is also established by valid cognition. Furthermore, it does not follow that categories are infinite, even though [properties] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) are infinite.
Is the definition of the category of *dharma* simply its nature as *dharmatva*?

It is precisely the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) while being devoid of the six characteristics such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; or rather, let [qualities] such as permanence and subsistence in a substance be merely specific types of entities.

If it is argued that properties such as impermanence and subsistence-in-a-substance (dravyāśritatva) are non-entities because they cannot be defined by their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), like a jar—[we reply: no; for what is this "being-an-entity" (*bhāvatva*)? Is it existence (*sattā*), or is it being one of the six characteristics (*ṣallakṣaṇa*), or is it simply "this is an entity, this is an entity"?

This is a specific property established by the inclusive cognition "this," or it is the state of not being defined by a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or the state of having no counter-correlate. In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because existence (*sattā*) is admitted in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). In the second case, there is a contradiction (*bādha*).

In the third [case], there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because the qualifying attribute of the property (*dharma*) is itself unestablished, given that the inclusive cognition "this is existence, this is existence" is not established;
even if it were established, the reason (*hetu*) would remain unestablished. In the fourth [case], there is the fallacy of being identical with the probandum (*sādhyaviśiṣṭatva*).

There is the fallacy of the reason not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*) and the contradiction (*bādha*); for since sense organs and the like—which determine [the property of] knowability and so forth—are themselves the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) by their very nature, knowability and the like are determined by their own counter-correlates. Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*), because even jars and other such things [are likewise].

Because it cannot be defined by a sense organ that is its own counter-correlative (*svabhāvapratiyogin*). Furthermore, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) consists in being the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*). And that is defined by the valid cognition itself, just as the absence of a jar is defined by the jar, because it is perceived as delimited by that [cognition]. The same applies to "cognisability" (*jñeyatva*).

Knowability is defined by cognition. The state of being denotable is the state of being an object of denotation. The state of being an effect is defined by an effect. Impermanence is defined by the impermanent. The state of being dependent on a substance is defined by that which is dependent on a substance. [This applies] to knowability and the like.

The claim that "not being definable by a counter-correlative" (*pratiyogyanirūpyatva*) is unestablished; for even in the fifth [reason], the reason is unestablished and there is sublation (*bādha*), because it is established by experience that properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) have "knowing" (*pramā*) and so forth as their counter-correlatives. What [is the point] regarding knowability and the rest?

If it is argued that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being an entity (*bhāvatva*), we say no. For if "being an absence" (*abhāvatva*) means either the absence of the property of being an object characterized as an entity, or the state of being denotable by the word "absence," then the very fact of possessing the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the characteristics of substance (*dravya*) and so forth is the proof for that. Or else, [if it means something else]...

If [non-existence] is defined as possessing the absolute absence of the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), then it should be accepted that when its perceptibility is under discussion—as in the case of the non-existence of a jar—it is indeed perceived;
and when its inferability is under discussion, it is indeed inferred. Now, as for knowability (*prameyatva*)...

Of what is there non-existence? Of valid cognition (pramā) itself. Now, the state of being an object of valid cognition (prameyatva) does not have prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) with respect to valid cognition because it is not subject to destruction; nor does it have non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) because it is devoid of origination;
nor does it have absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) because it is co-located with valid cognition.

If you think that it is not "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva) because it exists even in valid cognition (*pramā*), that is not so; for you have admitted that the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is a form of non-existence within valid cognition.
Others, however, [hold a different view].

They say that "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of valid cognition (*pramā*), because the definition of the absolute non-existence of valid cognition is "being a non-existence of valid cognition while residing in valid cognition. This is not correct,
because this definition of valid cognition is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as it applies even to the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of valid cognition.

If it is argued that the definition must be qualified by its true nature as being characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), we say no; for that very [nature] cannot be stated. Or, even if it could be stated, it is because one does not accept that the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is included within the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of knowledge (*pramā*).
In this same manner, "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) and the other [categories] are also to be defined.

Alternatively, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of valid cognition (*pramā*). Now, by the term "absolute non-existence of valid cognition," is it meant the absolute non-existence of each individual instance of valid cognition?

Is what is intended the absolute non-existence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it a single absolute non-existence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is all means of valid cognition? Not the first,
because the absolute non-existence of each individual means of valid cognition does not exist even in the locus of that very individual means of valid cognition.

Because it would result in the destruction of the status of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) as being purely positive (*kevalānvayi*). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because since all absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva*) of all cognitions—which are the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of every cognition—do not exist anywhere, it would result in the destruction of their status as purely positive. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable.

If you think that this is because a single absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) having all cognitions as its counter-correlates is impossible, since the difference between absences follows from the difference between their counter-correlates— this is not so, because we accept that the absolute non-existence of each individual cognition is itself the object of knowledge (prameyatva). Nor does this [entail] the [reductio] regarding objectivity (*prameyatva*).

There is a refutation of the status of being a purely positive (kevalānvayi) [property], because even in the locus of each respective valid cognition (*pramā*), the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of that very cognition is admitted; furthermore, cognitions and the like are themselves non-occurrent (*avṛtti*). This being the case, since individual instances of valid cognition are infinite, properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth would also be infinite.
If it is argued that this must be so— this is true,
for all parties accept the absolute non-existence of infinite cognitions having infinite counter-correlates. Or, let there be a single [non-existence] having all cognitions as its counter-correlate.

Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is the state of being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatva*). Nor is there any logical inconsistency in its being a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayin*),
because it is possible for a single absolute non-existence— having all cognitions as its counter-correlate— to exist in all selves, even those that possess only a few cognitions.

Thus, the absolute absence of cognition is knowability (*jñeyatva*); the absolute absence of sound is nameability (*abhidheyatva*). Alternatively, the absolute absence in time is cognizability (*prameyatva*);
the absolute absence in space is knowability (*jñeyatva*); [and] the absolute absence in ether is...
Regarding "the state of being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*): alternatively, the state of being cognizable (*prameyatva*) is the possession of the absolute non-existence of valid cognition;
the state of being knowable (*jñeyatva*) is the possession of the absolute non-existence of knowledge;
and the state of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is the possession of the absolute non-existence of words.
Now, is "possessing the absolute absence of valid cognition" (1) the absolute absence of specific instances of valid cognition,
or (2) the state of being the locus of the absolute absence of specific instances of valid cognition,
or (3) all absolute absences having every instance of valid cognition as their counter-positive, or (4) the state of possessing such [absences]?
[The definition] is either an absolute non-existence of each [instance] having all means of valid cognition (*pramā*) as its counter-correlate, or the possession of that [non-existence].
Not the first, because its meaning is already covered [by a previous refutation]. Not the second, because the suffix *-vat* would be redundant.
Not the third, because it has been refuted in the same manner as before. Nor the fourth, for the very same reason.

And because the meaning of the suffix -vat would be redundant, the fifth [alternative] is not tenable; for it is already included in what has been stated. Nor is the sixth, because the meaning of the suffix -vat would be redundant. That is not so, because [the definition refers to] that which resides in a locus possessing the absolute absence of a particular type of valid cognition (*pramā*).
This is because what is intended by "possessing the absolute non-existence of valid cognition" is [the absence of] being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatva*).

Nor is it the case that "possessing the absolute non-existence of valid cognition" is impossible in the self (*ātman*), which possesses valid cognition, due to the impossibility of the absolute non-existence of valid cognition therein.

It should not be argued that the universal concomitance (*kevalānvayitva*) of knowability (*prameyatva*) is untenable because "knowability is not a jar"; for [knowability] also exists in Devadatta who possesses valid cognition (*pramā*).

Because the absolute absence of valid cognition (pramā) residing in Yajñadatta is possible [in Devadatta]. For just as Devadatta possesses validity (pramāvattva), since valid cognition residing in Devadatta is possible even though valid cognition residing in Yajñadatta and others is possible; so too...
Even though an absolute absence of valid cognition (*pramā*) residing in Devadatta is impossible, an absolute absence of valid cognition residing in Yajñadatta is possible; therefore,
the state of possessing an absolute absence of valid cognition is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) residing in Yajñadatta.

Because even those [entities] that possess the absolute absence of truth (pramā) possess the absolute absence of truth, it follows that even for that which possesses truth, the state of being an object of knowledge (prameyatva)— defined as possessing the absolute absence of truth— is unavoidable. Nor is the suffix -vat redundant, since it applies to all absolute absences of truth whatsoever.
Because it is impossible for [the absence] to be co-located with its own counter-positive, the status of being a purely positive (kevalānvayi) is untenable;
for in this view, consciousness and the like are not admitted to be non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). If not...
If it is argued that the absolute absence of a valid cognition (*pramā*) is *kevalānvayin* (universally present),
and therefore its possession (*tadvattva*) is also *kevalānvayitva*, because wherever there is the exclusion of that [absence], there too the possession of it is excluded—
[we reply: no, for in a case where there is the exclusion of the absence of a single instance of valid cognition...
Even though the state of possessing that [absence] is excluded,
the state of possessing the absolute absence of truth is not excluded, because another absolute absence of truth is possible; as in the case of that which lacks a particular instance of smoke.

For it is established by everyone in the world that when that particular possession of smoke (*dhūmavattva*) is excluded, the possession of smoke is not thereby excluded as a whole, because other instances of smoke are possible;
otherwise, if upon the exclusion of one instance of smoke the possession of smoke were excluded from the mountain, [the inference would fail].

Because it would follow that [the reason] is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*); and because, in the kitchen, if a single instance of smoke were excluded, the state of possessing smoke (*dhūmavattva*) would also be excluded, which would entail the absence of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*). This is because the absolute absences of valid cognition (*pramātyantābhāva*) would themselves be excluded.

If it is asked what the proof is for the fact that "possessing the absolute absence of valid cognition" (pramātyantābhāvavattva) is a recurring property—[the answer is] perception itself, in the form: "this possesses the absolute absence of valid cognition," and "this possesses the absolute absence of valid cognition. This is just like the perception: "this is smoky," and "this is smoky."

If it is argued that, since the presence of smoke has not been excluded, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of the contradiction between possessing validity (*prāmāṇya*) and its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), because both would coexist in one and the same locus—
[we reply: no, for [the reason is] the state of possessing the absolute absence of validity.
Because the state of possessing the absolute absence of possessing validity is not admitted as possessing the absolute absence of possessing validity;
and because the absolute absence of possessing validity [cannot coexist] with possessing validity in one and the same locus.

And because [the opponent] does not accept [the relation of] "inherence" (samāveśa). If it is argued that its non-existence consists in the state of possessing the absolute absence of valid cognition (*pramā*), we say no; for the absolute absence of valid cognition is not the same as the thing itself, just as the possession of smoke is not the same as the smoke, or as "pot-ness" is not the same as the pot.
Alternatively, knowability (*prameyatva*) consists in possessing the mutual absence of valid cognition;
knowableness (*jñeyatva*) consists in possessing the mutual absence of knowledge;
and nameability (*abhidheyatva*) consists in possessing the mutual absence of words. Nor is there...

The meaning of the suffix *vat* would be redundant, because mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) of specific types of valid cognitions (*pramā*) cannot be established as purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), since they are excluded from their own counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
Furthermore, the property of possessing the mutual absence of valid cognition— such that "this possesses the mutual absence of this valid cognition"— [would be untenable].

This is because its status as a purely positive (kevalānvayin) property is established by the fact that it possesses a recurring cognition in the form "possessing the mutual absence of validity. The same should be stated regarding the nature of the mutual absence of sound and so forth.
Alternatively, knowability (*prameyatva*) is the state of being an object of God’s valid cognition; cognizability (*jñeyatva*) is the state of being an object of God’s knowledge;
and nameability (*abhidheyatva*) is the state of being an object of God’s will. Furthermore, when existence (*astitva*)...
If [existence] is distinct from the existent, then its existence must be defined as either the state of having an absolute absence of the existent,
or the state of having a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of the existent, or the absolute absence of conjunction,
or the object of an effort directed toward God.
Alternatively, knowability (*prameyatva*) is the state of possessing a means of valid cognition (*pramā*);

cognizability (*jñeyatva*) is the state of possessing knowledge (*jñāna*); and nameability (*abhidheyatva*) is the state of possessing a word (*śabda*). Nor is there any inconsistency in the status of these—knowability and the rest—as being purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), for they are present in all things whatsoever.
Because the prior non-existence and the subsequent destruction of the self’s valid cognition exist elsewhere, as do the absolute non-existence and mutual non-existence of valid cognition,
the state of possessing the absence of valid cognition exists everywhere. Thus...
The same should be stated regarding "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth.

Likewise, [the same applies to] being the object of valid cognition (*pramā*), being the object of doubt, being the object of error, being the object of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), being the object of memory, being the object of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), being the object of inference (*anumiti*), and so on.
The common characteristics of all categories:

existence (*bhāvatva*) belongs to substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. Now, what is this "existence"? Is it the absence of being definable by a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)?
Alternatively, [the definition of substance is] being characterized by any one of the six [qualities], or being the object of affirmative cognition,
or being the object of non-conceptual cognition,
while being devoid of the characteristics of separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and inherence.
[The definition of existence (*sattā*) is] either the absence of being an object of mere conceptual cognition,

or the absence of being devoid of the six characteristics such as substance (*dravya*), or the state of being the object of the cognition "this is a division," or some other property (*dharmāntara*). Not the first, because of [the non-exclusion of] substances and so forth.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it would entail the absence of that [negation], since it is defined by its dependence on a sense organ and so forth as the counter-positive of its own nature (*svabhāva-pratiyogin*).

Nor is the second, because it is impossible to define "the possession of any one of those other than the six characteristics beginning with substance" (*dravyādi-ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa-atirikta-tad-anyatama-vattva*). Nor is the third, because a positive cognition (*vidhi-pratyaya*) cannot be established.

Or rather, it is a specific sub-class of being a cause (*pratyayatva*) belonging to disjunction (*vibhāga*), because disjunction is defined by that which is being disjoined, while separateness (*pṛthaktva*), priority (*paratva*), and posteriority (*aparatva*) are defined by a limiting relation (*avadhi*).
Because it is impossible for that which lacks the state of being definable by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) to be the object of a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
If it is argued that [the absence] is the object of a positive cognition (*vidhipratyaya*), we say no; for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for that.

Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because it would not apply to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatva*), and inherence (*samavāya*); for conjunction and inherence are defined by their relata, while disjunction is defined by that which is being divided, and thus [the definition] would fail in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).

And because [the reason] is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*). For it is established by the inference: "Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the object of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), like a jar. Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the status of] inherence (*samavāya*) and non-existence, for those too are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*). Now, regarding the non-existences of jars and so forth...

If it is argued that its status as an object of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is sublated because it is necessarily an object of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) due to its nature being constituted by a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—
we say no; for what is this "nature constituted by a counter-correlate"?

Is it the absence of difference from the counter-positive, or is it being delimited by the counter-positive? Not the first, because the difference between the counter-positive and its absence is established by perception.
Regarding the second [option] as well, is "being delimited by the counter-positive" a property of the absence, or is it its very nature?

Not the first, because even when that [qualifier] is not cognized, it is possible for non-existence to be the object of a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), since things such as a jar can be objects of non-conceptual cognition even without being delimited by attributes (*dharma*). Not the second, either.

Because there is no evidence that the nature of absence consists in being delimited by its counter-positive, since the property of not having a jar as its counter-positive resides in the absence of all jars.
Furthermore, it is untenable for the nature of the absence of a jar to consist in its being mutually exclusive [of other absences].

Nor is the fifth [alternative] possible, because since an absence cannot be an object of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), it is impossible for it to be an object of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) alone.
Because the non-existence of that [gravity] would be seized by the impossibility [of its definition],
and because it pervades the absence of gravity, magnitude, and length—
as in the cases of "this is heavier than that" and "this is larger than that."
Because they are defined by their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*),

they cannot be objects of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) and can only be objects of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*). If it is argued that even though these [directions] are defined by their limits (*avadhi*), they are nonetheless objects of indeterminate cognition— no, that is not so.

Furthermore, since even properties such as distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), which are themselves defined in relation to the objects of non-perception (*avadhi*) and so forth, could potentially be objects of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*),
it would follow that the specific qualifiers intended to differentiate them would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, [the definition] is non-pervasive with respect to the genus (*jāti*) of pleasure, sound, and so forth, due to their excellence (*utkarṣa*), inferiority (*nikarṣa*), and the like; for excellence, inferiority, and so on, being defined by a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)— as in "this is superior to that" or "this is inferior to that"— are not objects of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
Nor is it the sixth [alternative], because since that [absence] is possible only as an object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*),
its non-existence would be undermined by the impossibility of such an absence existing everywhere while being devoid of the six characteristics beginning with substance (*dravya*).
Even though substance and the other categories each possess their own individual characteristics, [the category of existence] is not [identical to them] because it lacks those six characteristics.

Nor is it the seventh [alternative], for regarding the expression "this is existence" (*bhāvaḥ ayam iti*), do you intend by the word "cognition" (*buddhi*) mere cognition of existence, or a specific cognition that "this is existence"?

Not the first, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence: since the existence of an object is defined by cognition, and cognition is defined by that object. Nor the second, because it would entail the fallacy of being non-pervasive, as past and future existents cannot possibly be its objects.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for this cognition to have itself as its own object, the self-luminosity of knowledge is negated;
nor is the eighth [alternative] possible, as there is no evidence for it— this is not so.

Because existence (*bhāvatva*) consists precisely in possessing at least one of the six characteristics, such as substancehood (*dravyatva*), etc.; nor is it impossible to define "possessing at least one of the six characteristics," since this is defined as the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the possession of the six mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are the six characteristics beginning with substancehood.
Because it is one of the six characteristics beginning with substance (*dravya*).

Alternatively, the definition of existence (*bhāvatva*) is the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence that has the six characteristics beginning with substance as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Nor is this [definition] co-extensive with non-existence (*abhāva*) in substances and the like.

Because it is impossible for substance and the other categories to possess the absolute non-existence of the six counter-correlates—namely, the six characteristics such as substanceness—and even if one were to grant that "existence" (*bhāvatva*) is a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), there is no lack of evidence; for there is indeed the perception: "This is existence," "This is existence."

In this regard, it is established because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is this [existence] unestablished even as a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for its establishment follows precisely from the uniform linguistic usage "this is an entity. Alternatively, inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition in that case:
"This is a jar..."

"This [subject] possesses that which has as its locus the non-locus of the exclusion from the qualities residing in this [subject], which in turn are not the loci of the exclusion from the substances functioning in this [subject]; it possesses that which has as its locus the non-locus of the exclusion from the actions residing in this [subject]; it possesses that which has as its locus the non-locus of the exclusion from the universals residing in this [subject]; it possesses that which has as its locus the non-locus of the exclusion from the specificities residing in this [subject]; and it possesses that which has as its locus the non-locus of the exclusion from the inherence in the absence of that which functions in this [subject]—because it is knowable (*meyatva*), like a jar. Nor is there here the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), given that [the subject] possesses these properties.

Furthermore, because this—such as the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of this pot—is well-established in relation to cloth and other things, by virtue of being either the exclusion from substance (*dravyavyāvṛttatva*) or one of the others. Nor is "being that pot" (*tadghaṭatva*) a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here, because it is a mere "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*).

For [the probandum] is established simply by this much: "the locus of that which is not devoid of the exclusion from substance, not devoid of the exclusion from quality, not devoid of the exclusion from action, not devoid of the exclusion from genus, not devoid of the exclusion from particularity (*viśeṣa*), not devoid of the exclusion from inherence (*samavāya*), and not devoid of the exclusion from absence (*abhāva*)."
If it is argued that since existence (*bhāvatva*) is already established, this inclusion of "occurrence" (*pravṛtti*) for each [term] is redundant—
[we reply: no, because since such a property is not established, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
This is for the purpose of avoiding that [fault], because of the employment of the term "occurrence in this" (*etad-vṛtti-pada*).
Even though that which is devoid of the occurrence in the absence of the non-exclusion from substances and so forth is unestablished,

there exists that which is devoid of the exclusion from substance and so forth as qualified by occurrence in this, and that which is devoid of the occurrence in the absence as qualified by occurrence in this.

If it is argued that this [reason] is redundant (*arthāntara*) because the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar and so forth is well-established, and because [the subject] possesses one of the six categories such as substance (*dravya*), we say: no, for there is disagreement regarding a property that is common to the six categories such as substance, which are excluded from non-existence (*abhāva*).
Because of the presentation of a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*),

and because the probandum is qualified by being distinct from both the state of possessing any one of the six characteristics such as substance (*dravya*) and the absolute non-existence of possessing those six characteristics.

This is because [the definition] fulfills its purpose by merely following the property common to the six categories, such as substance (*dravya*), which are excluded from non-existence (*abhāva*), and because it maintains indifference toward [the specific definition of each category], such as "possessing any one of the six characteristics beginning with substance.
Nor is it thus...
There would be the consequence of establishing a property that subsists in only two, three, four, or five categories, such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth;

however, this is acceptable because it is what is intended. Alternatively, [the definition is]: "This pot possesses a genus (*jāti*) that subsists in it and is not devoid of exclusion from those [genuses] that subsist in it."

[The inference is as follows: "That which possesses a genus (jāti) that is devoid of [the property of] residing in an absence which is itself devoid of [the property of] residing in this [substratum], while being devoid of [the property of] residing in a particular residing in this [substratum] which is itself devoid of [the property of] being excluded from what is excluded from it, and while being devoid of [the property of] residing in an inherence which is itself excluded from what is excluded from this [substratum], because it possesses a genus, like a cloth. This establishes the genus, which is another synonym for existence (bhāvatva).
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here, because the probandum is not unestablished in the case of "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and other such instances.
Nor is there a deviation (vyabhicāra) of the property "possessing a genus" (jātimattva) when existence (sattā) is admitted in [the category of] genus and so forth,

because those [categories] are equivalent to the subject (pakṣa), since one accepts such genera as "genus-ness" (jātitva) and "particularity-ness" (viśeṣatva). Nor is there a deviation of "possessing a genus" in the case of absence (abhāva) when existence is admitted therein, because in the case of absence...
For one who accepts [the existence of] being (*sattva*), the nature of the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāvatva*) and so forth must be admitted therein;
for the status of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "absence of cloth-ness" (*paṭābhāvatva*) are subject to the same logical fate. Nor can it be argued by this very same reasoning...

There would follow the undesirable consequence of establishing categories such as substance, or those subsisting in only two, three, four, or five categories; or universals (*jāti*) and so forth that subsist in only two, three, or more of the [nine] categories beginning with earth; or forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that subsist in only two, three, or more of the [twenty-four] categories beginning with earth.
For, in the absence of a sublation (*bādha*), the establishment of such things is accepted; whereas, when a sublation exists, it is precisely therein that they are precluded.

This is the nature of being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*), and its absence is the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*). Among the five categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), the nature of being a positive entity consists in their being devoid of the characteristic of inherence (*samavāya*).
Furthermore, these five, beginning with substance, possess the quality of being inherent (*samavāyitva*) and plurality (*anekatva*).
Praśastapāda says that it is "homogeneity" (sādharmya). That is not correct. Is "inherence-ness" (samavāyitva) inherence itself, or is it the state of being a substratum of inherence?
It cannot be the first, because [the property] would also exist in inherence and so forth.

Because it would result in the modification of inherence (*samavāya*). Not the second [alternative], for by that very reason it would follow that inherence itself possesses the property of similarity (*sādharmya*), and furthermore, the qualification "substratum" (*āśrayatva*) would be redundant. [As for] multiplicity...
And is this [universality] a number, or is it a difference in essential nature? Not the first, because it is impossible in the case of qualities and so forth.

Not the second, because since a difference in essential nature is excluded [from its own locus], it cannot logically be a pervasive [universal]; furthermore, it is impossible for it to be a property (dharma).

If it is argued that the suffix *vat* is redundant because the property [of being a non-substance] can be established simply as the absence of qualities—namely, the absence of quality-ness, the absence of being a substratum for effects, and so forth, with respect to qualities, actions, universals, particulars, inherence, and non-existence—we say: no, because of the absence of qualities... [the suffix is not redundant].

Because they exist even in substances, and because the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of qualities belonging to their own substrate are possible everywhere; [and] because qualities residing in one substance [do not exist] in another substance.
And because of their absolute non-existence:

the common property [of the remaining categories] is the absence of possession of action, since they are distinct from substances that have not yet produced action or those already destroyed, and distinct from corporeal things.
Dependence belongs to those things that are distinct from eternal substances.
If it is argued that atoms possess dependence upon a substrate, such as the earth, in the same manner as jars and other objects—this is not so, because there is a lack of evidence.
First of all, there is no perception regarding the dependence of atoms.
Because no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted [to establish it]; nor is there inference (*anumāna*), due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

If it is argued: "Atoms (*paramāṇu*) are dependent (*āśrita*), because they possess form (*mūrtatva*), like a cloth"—this is not so, because the probans is rendered fallacious by the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), namely, the absence of being an eternal substance (*nityadravyatva*). Atoms are not dependent...

Furthermore, because it possesses the nature of an eternal substance, like the ether (*gagana*), there is also a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*). Alternatively, being dependent (*āśritatva*) is a property of all categories of entities, because the ether and so forth are dependent, or because they are dependent upon time. Nor is there a lack of proof for this, since the ether and so forth [are indeed established as such].

[They] are dependent, or else dependent on time, because they are objects of cognition (*prameya*), like a quality of time; this follows from inference. Nor is "the absence of being an eternal substance" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, because it is a case of "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), since there is no instance excluded [from the reason] that lacks the probandum. Nor is it time...
Thus, there is an inconsistency, because time itself is dependent upon time.

Nor is there the fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), since self-dependence is not a defect unless it obstructs production or cognition. That is not so, for [the definition applies] to that which is not dependent on time.
Because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of temporal mutual non-existence (*kālānyonyābhāva*), temporal absolute non-existence (*kālaguṇātyantābhāva*), and so forth;

and because if the reason is qualified by "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*), it would result in the fallacy of a superfluous qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣyatva*). If it is argued that "being an entity" alone is the reason here—no, for there is deviation in the case of sound, cognition, and so forth; those too...
If it is argued that [these qualities] are indeed dependent on time— no,
for this would entail the consequence that the characteristics of space and so forth are all-pervasive.
Therefore, the dependence of space and the like upon time is without proof.

And it is established that being dependent is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked, "Upon what are space (*gagana*) and the others dependent?"—it is upon corporeal things (*mūrta*) alone. For this very reason, the Teachers maintain that space and the others are all-pervading (*sarvagata*).

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) is their connection with existence (*sattā*), their possession of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattva*), and their being denotable by words whose meanings are established by convention (*svasamayārthaśabdābhidheyatva*); for [the first of these] applies even to existence itself.

Because it exists, because a relation must reside in both relata, and because it exists even in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth; for inherence (*samavāya*) residing in existence (*sattā*) is admitted there as well.
If it is argued that the relation is the state of being a substratum of existence (*sattāśrayatva*), and not inherence in existence—no, [that is not correct].

Because that [universal] would also have to be admitted in respect to genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and because the word "relation" (*sambandha*) would be redundant. If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) itself is the common property (*sādharmya*), we say no; for that belongs as a property to all categories (*padārtha*). Now, this jar...

Existence (*sattā*) is established by the following inference: "That which possesses a genus (jāti) that is devoid of the exclusion from substances residing therein, devoid of the exclusion from qualities residing therein, devoid of the exclusion from actions residing therein, and devoid of the genera of substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness residing therein, because it possesses a genus, like a cloth.
You maintain that this [existence] is the common property (*sādharmya*) of the three categories beginning with substance; however, that is not so, because of that [existence].

Because it is not accepted that [existence] is denotable by the word "existent" (sattā) on the grounds of being the cause for the linguistic usage of "existent," and because the state of being the cause for the linguistic usage of "existent" is observed even in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth despite the absence of that [existence]. Otherwise, [this would apply] to substances (*dravya*) and so forth as well.
Because it would follow that [the three categories] would become the cause for the linguistic usage of "existent," they would consequently fall under the denotation of the term "existence" (sattā).

Furthermore, the possession of universals and particulars does not belong to these three alone; for even in the case of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, there is the possibility of the existence of further universals and particulars, such as "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) and "particularity-ness" (*viśeṣatva*).

It is also not tenable that [the term "existent"] is denotable by a word according to one's own convention (*svasamaya*), because it has been established above that its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) consists solely in the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*);
furthermore, the author of the Sūtras did not establish such a convention.

If it is argued that such a convention was established by the disciples of the author of the Sūtras— no, for there is a lack of evidence; moreover, even if a basis for application were possible, the establishment of a convention would be nothing more than the ravings of a madman.
Furthermore, even though there is no possibility of a basis for application that exists solely within the triad of substance and so forth,

it is possible for the word "object" (*artha*) to have multiple referents— just like words such as "akṣa"— due to the existence of the bases [of application] namely *dravyatva*, *guṇatva*, and *karmatva*.
And the property of being a producer of merit (*dharma*) belongs only to those things which are producers of merit.
The property of producing demerit belongs only to those things that produce demerit;
the property of being an effect belongs only to those things that possess causes; the property of impermanence belongs only to those things that possess causes of destruction;
and the property of being characterized by cognition belongs only to universals and the like—such is their common characteristic (*sādharmya*).
Praśastapāda [says]:
That is not so, because since universals and the like do not reside in cognition, it is untenable for cognition to have the characteristics of universals and the like.

Furthermore, because it would be over-extensive due to its application to the self (*ātman*). If it is argued that by the word "cognition" (*buddhi*) one intends "being an object of cognition"—this is not so, because it would be over-extensive with respect to substances (*dravya*) and the like.
Now, if the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is "being the object of a recurring cognition" (*anuvṛttabuddhiviṣayatva*), [then...]

If you maintain that the definition of a particular (*viśeṣa*) is being the object of a cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtta-buddhi*), and that the definition of inherence (*samavāya*) is being the object of a cognition of "this is here" (*ihedam iti buddhi*), that is not so;
for [properties] such as being the object of a pervasive cognition (*anugata-buddhi*) reside individually in each of the various universals (*sāmānya*).

Because it is impossible for [the universal and the particular] to possess common properties such as being general or specific; or, even if such were possible, it would be impossible for them to have the defining characteristics of a universal and so forth.
Or else, [they are distinguished] by being the objects of inclusive cognition and exclusive cognition respectively, as in the case of "this" [and "that"].

If it is intended that the definition of cognition (*buddhi*) is "being one or another among the objects of cognition," that too is not correct, because that [property] is also possible in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth;
for the recurring cognition "this is a jar" apprehends both the jar and its exclusion [from others].

Because [the cognition] "an atom is excluded" and so forth has as its object the apprehension of atoms and the like, and because the cognition "there is a cloth here in these threads" and so forth has as its object the apprehension of threads, cloth, and the like; thus,
by virtue of being the object of an inclusive cognition and the object of an exclusive cognition, this is [the definition].
If you think that by the phrase "having cognition as its characteristic" what is intended is the state of lacking any characteristic distinct from the object of cognition— that is not so,
because other characteristics, such as those of universals (sāmānya) and so forth, will be stated [later]. || 7 ||
Substances originate another substance. (VS 1.1.8)

Now, if "being the initiator of a substance" here means "being the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of a substance," then by the term "substances," are all substances intended, or only those that are corporeal,
or those that possess touch, or those that possess touch while being devoid of the state of being a final whole? Not the first [option].

Because it would follow that ether, time, space, self, mind, and [material objects] such as pots would all be inherent causes of substances. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it would follow that the mind also would be an inherent cause of substances. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable.

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that even jars and the like would be inherent causes of substances (*dravya-samavāyikāraṇa*). Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because "being the final constituent" (*antyāvayavitva*) cannot be defined, and because it would follow that space (*dik*), time (*kāla*), and the self (*ātman*) are generators of substances. To this we reply: no, for when [the definition of] being a generator of a substance...
In that case,

by the phrase "those which are substances" (*dravyāṇi*), there is the inclusion of those possessing touch that are devoid of being ultimate wholes (*antyāvayavin*); nor is there a failure to define "ultimate whole-ness."

Because that which lacks the state of being a part possesses the state of being a whole, it is the ultimate whole (*antyāvayavin*). However, when "substance" (*dravya*) is used in the sense of including substances other than ether (*ākāśa*) and mind (*manas*), let there be no further subsuming category for the substances already mentioned under the term "substances."

Nevertheless, the state of being an inherent cause of a substance is [excluded] by the phrase "those which are substances," because this includes those possessing touch that are devoid of the nature of being ultimate composite wholes (*antyāvayavin*). Nor is there a failure to define "ultimate composite wholeness."

Because the state of being a whole (avayavin) devoid of [the state of being] parts (avayava) constitutes the state of being a final whole (antyāvayavin). But if it is asked, "In what case does the common property (sādharmya) of being the initiator of a substance (dravyārambhakatva) or being the cause of a substance (dravyakāraṇatva) indeed apply, and to which things?"—we reply: "To threads and so forth. To how many?
If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply: no, because the specific knowledge of the number is not a defect.
If it is asked, "Of what is there inclusion?"—no, because no further inclusive category is admitted. If it is asked, "What is the proof for this?"—no.
"This is the inherent cause of the substance, this is the inherent cause of the substance;
this is the cause of the substance, this is the cause of the substance"—this is indeed a matter of direct perception.
And if, regarding the causality of a substance, "substance-ness" (dravyatva) other than that of ether and the mind is accepted as the inclusive property, [then it follows].
In that case, qualities would not be the cause of substances;
for if the unifier itself were to require another unifier, there would be an infinite regress.
Moreover, it is possible to comprehend that [unifier] even without another unifier.

If it is argued that this infinite regress is not a defect— because [the universal] can likewise be established through scripture even for [universals such as] being an inherent cause of a substance (*dravyasamavāyikāraṇatva*), and thus there is no destruction of the root— [we reply: no,
because if the preceding preceding subsumers are not apprehended, those that follow them cannot be apprehended.

If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "intermediate" (antara) is redundant— since the purpose is fulfilled simply by stating that "substances originate substances," as the destruction of the root [cause] is necessarily implied— we say no;
for its purpose is to demonstrate the distinction between the substance that is originated and the substance that originates.
For the Sāṃkhyas maintain the non-difference of cause and effect, and they provide this proof:
"The threads are not different from the cloth, because they are the cause of the cloth; that which is different from the cloth [is not its cause]."

[The opponent claims: "That which is the cause of the cloth, such as a jar and so forth. [The author replies: That is not correct, because the property of being the cause of the cloth is found to deviate in the case of the weaver and others. [The opponent objects: "But they too are equivalent to the subject of the argument (pakṣa). [The author replies: No, because that would be contradicted by direct perception; for the weaver and others are perceived to be distinct from the cloth.

This is because immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) is established for everyone in the world. Furthermore, is the difference of jars and the like from cloth unapprehended or apprehended? Not the first, because that would entail the impossibility of grasping their distinction (*vyatireka*). Nor the second, by that very same reasoning.
Furthermore, it would be impossible to avoid the conclusion that there is a difference between threads and cloth;

for the property of being the cause of cloth is excluded from what is distinct from cloth, and thus, by virtue of its exclusion, it is a unique (asādhāraṇa) reason. By this [argument], it is shown that cloth is not different from threads, because it is the effect of threads; whereas that which is different from threads...
Arguments such as "it is not the effect of those threads, just like a jar" have been refuted.
If it is asked what the proof is for the difference between the produced and the producer, [the answer is]:
"this thread is different from this cloth; this cloth is different from this thread," and so forth.
Is it through perception or inference? For example: "This yarn is distinct from this cloth, because it is yarn, like another yarn";
or "This cloth is distinct from this yarn, because it is cloth, like another cloth," and so forth. That...

The inclusion of the term "internal" (antara) is purposeful because it indicates that the relationship between the produced and the producer is made known by perceiving a difference [between them]. [Objection: Since the relationship between the produced and the producer is already understood through perception and inference alone, the inclusion of the term "internal" is redundant.
If [it is argued that it is unnecessary], we say no; for since the relationship between the initiated and the initiator is also established through perception and inference,
the inclusion of the word "internal" (*antara*) intended to demonstrate that [relationship] would render the Sūtra itself redundant.
Because it is purposeless.
And qualities [produce] other qualities. (1.1.9)

The word "they begin" (ārabhante) is to be supplied [from the previous rule]. Here, according to the author of the Sūtras, there are two sūtras: the first is "and the qualities" (guṇāśca), and the second is "another quality" (guṇāntaram).
This is what is intended to be said. Therefore,
the meaning of the first sūtra is that not only substances initiate another substance, but qualities do so as well.
This is because the conjunction that initiates a substance, the knowledge of God, and so forth,
are generators of substances such as cloth; the word "and" (ca) serves to include the non-existence of the prior absence of unmentioned substances and the absence of obstructions.
Since both the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a substance and the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakābhāva*) are also causes of a substance,
the purport of the two sūtras is that the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of substances, qualities, and absences that produce a substance is their being generators of a substance.
But when "the qualities and the other quality" constitutes a single sūtra, then "being a commencing cause" (ārambhakatva) means being a producer (janakatva).

The word "ca" (and) serves to include substances and other categories not explicitly mentioned; thus, the meaning of the aphorism is that the common property (*sādharmya*) of all categories is their capacity to produce qualities. Of all categories...

Because it produces a quality by way of generating a qualified cognition either as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In that case, "origination" (*ārambhakatva*) here means being an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*); and the word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including action (*karman*). Thus, at that time—
The meaning of the sūtra is that the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*karman*) is their status as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*).
Now, just as in the case of the word "commencement" (*ārambha*), so too regarding the intermediate term (*antara-pada*):

If it is argued that the mention of "intermediate" (*antara*) is redundant because its connection [to the preceding rule] is possible here as well, we say: no, for the word "immediately following" (*anantara*) would be inapplicable to the word "substance" (*dravya*). Or else:

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and qualities" (*guṇāśca*) should be repeated immediately after the phrase "another quality" (*guṇāntaram*). By that means, the "and" in "and qualities" serves the purpose of collecting what has not been mentioned, whereas the "and" in "another quality" [serves a different purpose].

This is for the purpose of accumulating [the definitions of] action. By this, the meaning of the sūtra is established as follows: just as there is the production of substance from quality and substance, so too is there the production of quality and action. || 9 ||

Just as the production of substances is a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of substances, and the production of qualities (*guṇa*) is [a common characteristic] of qualities, why should the production of action (*karman*) not likewise be a characteristic of actions?
Or, just as substances and qualities possess the capacity to produce action, so too let action possess it.
Thus, in order to avoid the logical consequence [of infinite regress] regarding action, the Sūtra states:
"Action is not found to be achievable by action" (1.1.10).

Thus: first of all, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that an action generates another action, because there is an absence of direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) such as "this action is the generator of an action. Nor is there inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, [it might be argued that] the first action is the generator of an action, because it is invariably...

If it is argued that [the probans] is like an arrow because it exists in the moment immediately preceding that [destruction], we say no; for this argument is vitiated by the presence of an extraneous condition (*upādhi*), namely, the absence of being an action (*karmatva*). Nor is this [probans] "identical with the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), because it is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—namely, absolute non-action which lacks the capacity to produce [an effect]—by virtue of being an action. By means of being an action...

And because there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*). Furthermore, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is the proof for the fact that one action does not produce another action: "The first action does not produce an action, because it is an action, like the final action. Now, [one might object] that this much alone—that an action is not something to be accomplished by an action—is sufficient.
If it is argued that [the statement] "it exists" is redundant because its purpose has already been fulfilled, we say no;

for it serves to establish a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). In response to the inquiry as to why action is not something to be accomplished by action, there exists a means of valid cognition regarding that.
This is also evident from the commentary on the Sūtra: "The state of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth.
Now, it is not correct to say that "action is not something to be accomplished by action," for at the point of negating that action is the producer of action—

Because the negation of an action's capacity to produce another action is not the subject under discussion. If it is argued that by negating [the former], the negation of an action's capacity to produce an action is established by implication— no,
for there is a direct negation of an action's capacity to produce an action.

Because it would be overly cumbersome to establish that [the action does not produce another action] by way of negating the action's status as a producer of an action due to its being impossible to perform, one might suggest that the aphorism should instead state: "An action is not found to be a producer of an action. But that is not correct.
This is because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

"That which has action as its object" (*karmasādhya*) means that which is produced by action; it is that which generates action. By this, the negation of being a direct generator of action is established.

Alternatively, by the sūtra "That which exists is non-eternal, possesses substance, and is an effect" (1.1.7) and so forth, the common properties of substance and the other categories—such as being causes and so on—have been stated. To establish that, it is said:
"Substances originate another substance" (1.1.8), and "qualities originate another quality."
[1-1-9] These are two sūtras.

Now, let it be granted that substances (*dravya*) and so forth possess causality because they produce substances and so forth; however, action (*karman*) does not have an effect. For, first of all, there is no effect of action...
[The action] is not itself the effect, precisely because it is an action; nor is it another effect, because that does not exist.
To resolve this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"Action is not something to be accomplished by action" (1-1-10). Although action is not something to be accomplished by action, nevertheless, conjunction is possible as the cause of action;
such is the meaning of the sūtra. || 10 ||
Substance is not incompatible with its effect, nor is it incompatible with its cause. (1.1.11)
That whose effect is non-contradictory—that is, not destructive—is "non-contradictory with respect to its effect" (*kāryāvirodhi*);

the meaning is that it is not destroyed by its effect. That whose cause is non-contradictory is "non-contradictory with respect to its cause" (*kāraṇāvirodhi*). By this, [the author] indicates the state of being non-contradictory with respect to both effect and cause.
The authors of the *Bhāṣya* and others maintain that the common properties (*sādharmya*) of substances have been stated;
however, that is incorrect, because all effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) are destroyed by the destruction of their inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Because it is impossible for that [destruction] to be absent given that [destruction] is destroyed by its effect;

since both the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) are themselves effects, they lack the property of being destroyed by their own effects— this is what is meant by "not being destroyed by its effect."
If [it is argued that it is not so]—no; for by the word "own" (sva), what is intended:
the cause in general, the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the inherent cause of a substance, or a specific type of inherent cause? Not the first, because [the fault] follows from that very [point].
This is because both the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) are also produced by substances such as God (*īśvara*) and time (*kāla*).

Nor is it the third [alternative], for precisely for that same reason, the destruction of the inherent cause of a substance is also produced by the inherent cause of that substance; this applies even to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in the case of destruction.

Because it is a cause. Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because since the destruction of its effect is unestablished anywhere, its absence is likewise unestablished, and thus the possession of a common property (samānadharmatva) cannot be established. [This is so] because the destruction of the conjunction that is its effect occurs in action (karman) and so forth.
Furthermore, if [non-existence] were well-known as such, then because its absence exists even in sound and so forth,
it would follow that sound and the rest would also not be incompatible with their effects.
By this, the claim that "the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of substances is non-incompatibility with their causes" is refuted.
Because all effects that are substances—
which are destroyed by the destruction of their inherent causes or non-inherent causes—
must be destroyed by the destruction of their [material] causes, it is logically impossible for them to be devoid of such [causal] destruction.
This is because both the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and destruction are themselves causes of their own effects.
If it is argued that "not being destructible by the substances that are its own respective causes" constitutes "non-opposition to its cause," we say no;
for all effect-substances are destructible by the substances that are their own respective causes, such as God (*īśvara*) and others.
Because its separation from that [substratum] is untenable.

If it is argued that "the state of not being destructible by the respective causes of its own constituent substances— excluding God, space, and time" constitutes "non-opposition to its cause"— we say no.
Because the property of being destructible by its own respective causal substance— distinct from God, space, and time— is unestablished anywhere, it is impossible to apprehend its absence;
therefore, the possession of a common property (samānadharmatva) is untenable.
Furthermore, because it exists in the final sound and so forth—which are contrary to the cause you accept—just like a jar;

for, since the final sound, like a jar, is destroyed by the destruction of its own cause, its "non-destruction by the cause of sound" constitutes its "non-contrariety to the cause. And that [property] exists in the final sound.
If it is argued that [sound] does not exist—no; for since all effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) are destructible by causes of sound such as the Lord (*Īśvara*), their absence is untenable.
[Rather,] it is [the case that sound is] indestructible by causes of sound other than the Lord and so forth.
If it is argued that [the reason] is "not being contradicted by its own cause"— no, for that is possible even in the case of the final sound.
If it is argued that the final sound is destroyed by its own cause, namely the penultimate sound, which is distinct from God and other such factors— no, because that [position] will be refuted later.
Sūtra:
In both cases, there is a merit. 1.1.12.

"Both ways" should be explained as "contradictory to the effect" and "contradictory to the cause," and not as "non-contradictory to the effect" and "non-contradictory to the cause. This is because non-contradiction with the effect is sublated in the case of the first word in a series and in cognitions that produce other cognitions, such as knowledge and so forth.
