Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding the property of "not being opposed by its cause" in the case of the final sound, which is destroyed by the penultimate sound;

for since the properties of "not being opposed by its effect" and "not being opposed by its cause" are also under discussion here as the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) of "being opposed by its effect" and "being opposed by its cause," respectively.
[The followers] of Praśastapāda’s disciples [say]:
"That is not so, because the property of being opposed to its own effect is possible even in substances;
for both the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) are themselves effects."
Furthermore, because the property of being destroyed by its own respective effect resides in each specific instance,

it would be impossible for sound, cognition, and so forth to share that commonality. Moreover, since destruction by the cause is also possible in the case of substances— given that even that which is destroyed by a substance can serve as a cause [of another]— [the proposed definition fails].
Because even in the case of substances, it is possible for them to be destroyed by their own respective causes,
since effect-substances and their qualities are destroyed by their own respective causes, such as God;
and because [it is possible] for them to be destroyed by the destruction of their own respective inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Because it is impossible for them to possess a common property by virtue of being restricted solely to their specific differences; because [the property] cannot exist in a quality; and because there is no evidence that the final sound is destroyed by the penultimate sound. [Thesis: The final sound is destroyed by another sound, because it is a sound.

If it is argued that it is like the first sound—no; because this [argument] is refuted by the fact that its own destruction is established, and thus it is vitiated by proving something other than the intended point.
For the final sound, by virtue of being self-destructible, immediately after its own production...

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of momentariness due to destruction—[we reply] no; for even if the penultimate sound were destroyed by the final sound, this [consequence] would be unavoidable. [The inference is:
"The final sound is destructible by something other than itself, because it is a sound, like the first sound."

If it is argued that this is not so because of the deviation regarding the penultimate sound— if it is claimed that the penultimate sound is destroyed by that very [final] sound or by the sound occurring immediately prior to it— [we reply]: no,
for the penultimate sound would [otherwise] lack dependence on a destroyer produced in the moment immediately following its own production.

Because it would entail momentariness; and because, given the dependence on the sound that is its effect, the destruction of the penultimate sound is established from that very cause, thereby determining that those two [the preceding sounds] are not the causes [of the final sound's destruction];
thus, by virtue of being destructible by a sound other than the final one—

Furthermore, because the property of being a generator of sound is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and because its absence constitutes a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*). Nor does this [property] constitute the fallacy of "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratā*),
since it is absent in color and so forth, which are not destroyed by sounds other than the final sound.

Because it is excluded [from the class of non-sounds]. Now, this final sound is destroyed by a sound distinct from itself, because it is a sound, like the first sound. Nor is "being a producer of sound" a limiting adjunct (upādhi) here, because it does not pervade the probandum in the case of another final sound.
If you maintain that, because it is destroyed by itself, this sound is destroyed by sounds other than itself— that is not so; for even another final sound lacks self-destruction,
and if it did not depend on any other cause of destruction, it would follow that it is non-momentary (akṣaṇika).
And since its destruction is established as occurring from that very [condition] when there is dependence upon it,
its status as a cause is fixed. If it is asked, "How can momentariness be established when it has not yet been apprehended?"— it is not so.
This is because it is to be established that [the subject] is the counter-positive of a destruction produced in the moment immediately following the moment of its own production;

and this [property] is well-known in the case of jars and other things destroyed in the moment immediately following their existence. Nor should it be argued that such momentariness is indeed already accepted in the case of the final sound and so forth.
For even that [sound] is inferred to be related to a moment distinct from its own moment of origination by virtue of its being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*);
furthermore, because it is established as being destructible by some sound other than itself, this does not prove that it is destructible by the penultimate sound.

If it is argued that no other sound is perceived as the destroyer of the final sound—this is not so, because the penultimate sound is likewise not perceived. If it is argued that the penultimate sound is not perceived because it has gone to another location—that applies equally to the other sound as well. This [is] the final sound...

This [sound] is not something destroyed by the penultimate sound, because it does not produce that [penultimate sound], just like color; furthermore, it is subverted by a counter-argument. Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the penultimate sound itself, because even though it does not produce that [final sound], it lacks the property of being destroyed by it.
By this, the following formal arguments are refuted: "This destruction of the final sound is produced by a sound distinct from this [final] sound,
because it is a destroyer of sound, like the destruction of the initial sound," and so forth.
Because this [conclusion] is established by the fact that it is produced by some sound other than these [two], it does not prove that it is produced by the penultimate sound; furthermore,

there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the destruction of sound at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), since that very [destruction] lacks being produced by a sound distinct from that [specific] sound, immediately following which—
Because sound is not produced [again], and because its counter-positive lacks the nature of being a cause for its own destruction;

and because it is impossible for a penultimate sound or the like to be the destroyer of the final sound; otherwise, there would follow the consequence of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga). This is the destruction of the final sound.

This [sound] is not produced by the penultimate sound, because it is the destruction of the sound that produces it, just like any other well-established instance; furthermore, this is a case of counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).
As for the question, "What is the proof that the penultimate sound does not cause the destruction of the final sound?"—[the answer follows].
If [it is argued]: "The penultimate sound is not the cause of the destruction of the final sound, because it is a sound, like the first sound;
this penultimate sound is not the cause of the destruction of this final sound, because it is a sound."
The inference begins with "like the first sound" and so forth. If it is asked, "What, then, is the cause of the destruction of the final sound?
the teacher Ātreya says: "It is a specific conjunction with a substance possessing touch."

For just as the velocity residing in an arrow is destroyed by its contact with a wall or similar object possessing resistance, so too is sound [destroyed], because sound is not perceived when it is obstructed by a wall or the like.

That is incorrect: the disputed conjunction with a substance possessing touch is not the cause of the destruction of sound, because it is a conjunction, like a [conjunction] that is admitted [to be such]. The disputed [conjunction] is not the cause of the destruction of this final sound, because it is a conjunction.

This is because it is negated by the passage beginning with "as in the case of one who has accepted [the view]," and because there is no evidence for a specific conjunction with a tangible substance being the destroyer of the final sound. If it is argued that the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) is the proof— no, for even in that case...

"Because a negation has already been stated. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the cause of the destruction of the final sound?"—[the answer is] God's knowledge, will, effort, space, time, and unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
If it is asked, "What is the cause of the destruction of the final sound other than God and the rest?"—[the answer follows].

If it is argued: "This final sound is produced by a cause distinct from God and other such factors, because it is an effect, like a jar"—thus established by inference as a specific category of object—then [the opponent might say]: "Let this very thing be specifically pointed out as 'this is that'.
[The reply is: No, because there is no purpose in specifying it in detail.
And because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine that [specificity].

If it is argued, "In that case, it would not be established," we say: no. Do you mean that it would not be established in general, or that it would not be established in its particularity? It is not the first case.
Because that [conclusion] is established by the very inference stated previously. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it is accepted [by us]. For instance:

"This substance is not the destroyer of the final sound, because it is a substance, like any other admitted substance. And: "This quality is not the cause of the destruction of the final sound, because it is a quality."

If it is argued that the inference under discussion is uncontradicted because [the text] denies that substances and all other categories are the cause of the destruction of the final sound— by means of the phrase "like those already accepted" (*sampratipannavat*) and so forth— we say: no.
If things other than those established by the inference under discussion were taken as the subject (*dharmin*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Furthermore, that which is established by the inference under discussion would be sublated by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its subject.

And there is an absence of any means of valid cognition that determines [the subject] as being a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth, in the case of that which is established by the inference under discussion.

Furthermore, [the reasons] such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) are unestablished due to doubt; and because all of these fail to prove the absence of the probandum in the present inference, they are afflicted by the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntara*). Moreover, as far as it is understood...
Furthermore, because the inference under discussion— when the destruction of substances, qualities, and so forth by the final sound is denied—
concludes with respect to what is distinct from those [substances,
etc.], and because it is impossible to take things distinct from those as the subject (dharmin) since they have not been established [as such].

Therefore, the sūtra "In both ways, it is a quality" (1.1.12) is intended to demonstrate the common characteristic of being non-opposed to both cause and effect. What then is the definition? "Substance is that which is not opposed to its effects and not opposed to its causes" (1.1.11).
The meaning of the sūtra "There is a quality in both ways" (1.1.12) is stated as follows: [Sound] is existent, non-eternal,
possesses substance, is an effect, is a cause, and possesses generality and particularity.
In the sūtra *dravyaguṇakarmaṇāmaviśeṣaḥ* (1.1.7), the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of substances, qualities, and actions is stated. Non-eternality consists in perishability (*vināśitva*).
And since destruction is an effect, it is produced by a cause.

In considering the causes for the destruction of substances and so forth, is it the respective effects of those substances and so forth that are the cause for their destruction, or rather the respective causes of those substances and so forth, or perhaps the destruction of the respective causes of those substances and so forth, or what?

"The destruction [of a substance] consists in its ceasing to perform the functions of its respective substances and so forth. In that regard, the aphorism for the purpose of refuting the first position is: "A substance is not incompatible with its effects."
[1-1-11] Thus. To refute the second and third positions, the sūtra states:

"And it is not opposed to its own causes" (kāraṇāvirodhi ca) [1-1-11]. Here, by the word *kārya* (effect), each respective effect is intended; by the word *kāraṇa* (cause), each respective cause—excluding God, knowledge, will, effort, space, time, and so forth—is intended.

If it is argued that effects and the like are the destroyers of substances— this is not so, because there is no evidence to prove it. Furthermore, since perception determines that they lack the causality for the destruction of substances— on the grounds that [the effect] arises even without them— and because of [the nature of] substances themselves.

If [things] were destroyed by their own respective effects, it would follow that the atom would be destroyed in the second moment by the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and threads and the like would be destroyed by the cloth and so forth.
Furthermore, if they were destroyed by their own respective causes, [it would follow for] the cloth and so forth...
For it would follow that the threads and so forth perish at the very second moment,

since there is no other factor to be depended upon; or, if such a factor were present, the destruction of the cloth and so forth would be established by that alone, and thus the threads and so forth could not be proven to be the causes of their own destruction.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include the fact that, apart from the destruction of the effect and the cause, there is no other cause for the destruction of a substance; for if threads, cloth,
and so forth were destructible by any [cause whatsoever], it would follow that they would be destroyed in the very second moment [of their production].
Having established that upon the destruction of various substances, those respective effects and causes do not stand in a relationship of cause and effect,

[the author now proceeds] for the purpose of establishing that upon the destruction of various qualities as well, those respective effects and causes likewise do not stand in a relationship of cause and effect.
The Sūtra states:
"In both ways, there is a quality" (1.1.12). "In both ways" means that which is not opposed to the effect and not opposed to the cause.
This is the meaning. And here, by the word "quality" (guṇa), a quality distinct from the specific qualities of sound that are destroyed by their respective effects is intended.
[The first sound] refers to cognition and so forth.
Because they are destructible by the respective effects, such as sound and cognition;
the sūtra is for the purpose of supporting the fourth position:
"The absence of the effect follows from the absence of the cause" (1.2.1).
The following sūtra— "but not the absence of the cause from the absence of the effect" (1.2.2)— is intended to refute the fifth position.

If it is asked, "How can there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) here between two sūtras separated by many other sūtras?", we reply: "Because of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic competency (*yogyatā*).
For proximity (*sannidhi*), like expectancy and the rest, is also a cause of syntactic connection; yet that [proximity] does not exist here.
If you say this is not so—no, because the presence of being situated in the intellect exists here as well;
for it is possible to perform even an uninterrupted utterance. Therefore, it is in this very sūtra...

If it is argued that [the term] should be recited [in both places], we say no, because the purpose is possible even there. If it is argued that it should be recited both there and here, we say no, because even when recited in one place, its connection with the other is still possible. If it is asked why it is not recited here, we say no.
In this reading, it can be argued: "Why is it not recited there?

Or alternatively, let it be so: [the definitions] are precisely those of the sūtras, "A substance is non-opposed to its effects and non-opposed to its causes" (1.1.11) and "A quality is both ways" (1.1.12).

The intended meaning here is that from the destruction of the cause follows the destruction of the effect, whether it be a substance, a quality, or an action. Regarding the fact that a quality can be the cause of the destruction of another quality, this is established by the [sūtra] beginning with "and from contact with fire," which demonstrates the destruction of color and other qualities through contact with fire.
This is established by the aforementioned sūtra.
That action is destroyed by its own qualities will be addressed in the very next sūtra.

Therefore, in the destruction of a substance, the cause is either the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). In the destruction of a quality,
the cause is either the destruction of its inherent cause, the destruction of its inherent cause [of that inherent cause], or another quality.

The cause [of destruction] is as follows: upon the destruction of an action, the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause; such is the established rule. That the destruction of a substance results from the destruction of its inherent cause is not tenable, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). And regarding the effect...

This is because [the destruction of the effect] is established solely through the destruction of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), which is itself produced by the destruction of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
Thus, the disputed destruction of a substance is produced by the destruction of the conjunction of its parts,
because it is the destruction of a substance, just like the destruction of a cloth produced by the destruction of the conjunction of its threads.
If you say this is not so—no, because that would contradict perception, namely the observation that "the destruction of the cloth follows from the destruction of the threads.

Or, if there were no such contradiction, one would have to admit that in all cases the cause of the destruction of a substance is simply the destruction of the conjunction of its parts. [Furthermore,] an action (karman) arises that is opposed to its effect.
It is established by perception that [motion] ceases having initiated disjunction, conjunction, and velocity.

Furthermore, this cessation of action is not produced by the destruction of its substrate, because the substrate is established by perception. Nor is it produced by the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), even though...
Because the cessation of action is observed even in cases where gravity, fluidity, velocity, and so forth serve as non-inherent causes;
for although the cessation of action produced by gravity and the like is indeed caused by the destruction of its non-inherent cause.

If it is argued that the cessation of motion produced by pushing or striking will be caused by a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)—we say no; because the cessation of motion produced by gravity and other such factors is established as being caused by conjunction (saṃyoga). The disputed cessation of motion is not...

[The cessation of action] produced by the cessation of impulsion and impact [is not the cause of the cessation of action], because it is a cessation of action, like the cessation of action not caused by gravity. The cessation of impulsion and impact under dispute is not the cause of the cessation of action, because it is a cessation of conjunction, like that which is commonly admitted. This...
The cessation of this action is not produced by the cessation of the impulsion, because it is a cessation of action,
like the cessation of any other action. This cessation of impulsion is not the cause of the cessation of this action, because it is a cessation of impulsion.
Because it is prohibited by such statements as "like the cessation of another's rice-offering" (*anyanodananivṛttivat*);

nor [can it be] from a conjunction produced by disjunction, because [the effect] would cease at the very moment of the cessation of the prior conjunction, with the consequence that no subsequent conjunction could arise immediately thereafter.

If it is argued that disjunction, accompanied by the cessation of the prior conjunction, is the cause of the cessation of action—and therefore the cessation of action does not occur at the very moment the prior conjunction ceases—this is not so;
for the cessation of the prior conjunction is not the producer of the cessation of action. Or, if it were indeed the producer, [then...]
For if that were the case, it would follow that disjunction (*vibhāga*) is not the cause [of the cessation].
This disjunction is not the cause for the cessation of this sequence, because it is a disjunction, like any other disjunction.
This cessation of action is not produced by this disjunction, because it is a cessation of action.

And because there is a prohibition, as in the case of the cessation of other actions. If it is argued that "there is a subsequent conjunction following from disjunction," we say no; this disjunction is not the cause of this conjunction, because it is a disjunction, like the disjunction of other things. This conjunction is not produced by this disjunction, because it is a conjunction.
Because of the prohibition [of such a view] by the statement "like conjunction with another. If it is argued that disjunction itself is produced by action as the subsequent conjunction— no,
because the cessation of the prior conjunction produced by disjunction is also a cause of the subsequent conjunction.

Because it is established by direct perception: this cessation of the prior conjunction is not the cause of this subsequent conjunction, because it is a cessation of conjunction, like the cessation of any other conjunction. This conjunction is not produced by the cessation of that [prior] conjunction.
If it is argued that [the prior conjunction] is the cause [of the subsequent one] because it is a conjunction, like any other conjunction—this is not so;

for as long as the causality of this specific conjunction has not been established anywhere, its absence cannot be proven. Or, if it were established, it would be contradicted by the very same reasoning that proves the cessation of the prior conjunction is the cause of the subsequent conjunction.

The same applies to the second inference as well: since the cessation of the prior conjunction is also produced by the action at the very moment of disjunction, the cessation of the action occurs from disjunction at the moment immediately following disjunction,
and the subsequent conjunction will then follow from the action.
If it is argued: no, the prior conjunction is not destroyed by this action, because it is a quality (*guṇa*), like color (*rūpa*).

This prior conjunction is not destroyed by this [present] action, because it is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), like any other conjunction. This action is the destroyer of this conjunction, because it is an action (*karman*).
Because of the prohibition [implied by the phrase] "like any other action.

Nor is it momentum (*vega*), because if the action were to cease due to momentum at the very moment when the previous conjunction is destroyed following a disjunction, it would follow that no subsequent conjunction could arise immediately thereafter.
This momentum is not the cause for the cessation of this action, because it is momentum, like any other momentum;
and because of the following refutation: "This cessation of action is not produced by this momentum, because it is a cessation of action, like the cessation of any other action."

Nor does it occur at the very moment of the division of color and so forth, because if the action were to cease immediately after the division from color and so forth, it would follow that no subsequent conjunction could arise.
Therefore, by process of elimination, subsequent conjunction is the cause of the cessation of action. This...
If it is argued: "This conjunction is not the cause for the cessation of this action, because it is a conjunction, like any other conjunction;
and this cessation of action is not produced by this conjunction, because it is a cessation of action, like the cessation of any other action"—[we reply: no.

The reason for the cessation of action is unestablished, because its absence is not established; or, if it were established, then by that same logic, the subsequent conjunction would also be established as a cause for the cessation of action, which contradicts [your position]. [Action] ceases due to the subsequent conjunction.

[The opponent argues: "And because [the existence of] action is sublated by direct perception; furthermore, the proofs establishing that disjunction and so forth do not possess the capacity to destroy action are themselves sublated by perception. [We reply: No, for there is no such direct perception as "action has ceased due to disjunction," and so on.
Or, even in the case of [the destruction of action by] disjunction or velocity, since it is admitted that these too are destroyers of action; nor does it follow that,
because action ceases in the very moment following disjunction, a subsequent conjunction would be impossible.
Because it is accepted that even the cessation of the prior conjunction produced by disjunction is a cause for the destruction of action; therefore, the Blessed One [states]:
"Action is opposed by its effect" (NS 1.1.13).

Thus he formulated [the definition], but not as "an action that is opposed to conjunction. Once it is established—by the inference: "The cessation of other actions, being produced and devoid of the non-existence of the conjunction that produces it, is like a cloth"—that this is the cessation of an action produced by conjunction;
Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to conjunction that produces the cessation of action.
Regarding the fact that the cessation of action is produced by conjunction, there is both perception and inference as proof:
"This cessation of action is produced by something other than this [specific] conjunction and devoid of any other producer thereof."
Because it is an effect, like a cloth;
or alternatively,
it is produced in the moment immediately preceding this action and is the generator of the cessation of this action.

This conjunction [is so] because it is produced in the moment immediately preceding the cessation of that action; for whatever is not thus is not thus, like a jar. This conjunction is produced in the moment immediately preceding the cessation of that action.

This [reason] is the producer of the cessation of the action that produces this [effect]. It is not the case that what is not so is not so, just as a cloth [is not the producer of its own cessation]; thus it is established by a negative inference (*vyatirekin*). Nor is there a fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because the producer of this [effect] existing in the moment immediately preceding the cessation of that action is not unestablished.

And it must be stated that the qualification [of the subject] is established by the first inference in the second inference: "This cessation of action is produced by what arose in the moment immediately preceding this moment, because it arises in this moment, like a cloth arising in this moment. Thus, its establishment is secured.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of birth occurring even before the cessation of this karma;
for there would be no required condition produced in the immediately preceding moment.
If it is argued that these two [reasons] are "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because they belong to the existing class of similar instances (sapakṣa), we say: no.

Even though the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) exist, there is no certainty regarding the reason's exclusion from them; and because the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇa*) fallacy is a defect precisely due to the certainty of its exclusion from similar instances.
By this same logic, [the same applies] to the cessation of division, velocity, and prior conjunction.

If it is argued that [the self exists] because its status as the cause of the cessation of karma is established—no, for that establishment is accepted when there is no sublation; however, when such sublation exists, its establishment is precluded. || 13 ||

Now begins the section on the definitions of substance and so forth. Herein is the aphorism defining substance: "That which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause—this is the definition of substance."
[If it is argued: "It is improper to state the definitions at the occasion of [discussing] similarity"—[we reply:
no, because the definitions of substance and so forth are also common properties shared by all substances and so forth.
This is because, after the classification of substances and so forth, there arises a desire to know their properties.

Furthermore, since both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) have been introduced [as topics], one might ask: "Why was dissimilarity not explained previously? This is not a valid objection, because there is no contradiction in explaining it now even though it was not explained previously.

Furthermore, because all the similarities previously established—excluding those that are purely positive—are in the nature of dissimilarities. The statement "it possesses action, it possesses qualities, and it is an inherent cause" is an expression where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus; [it refers to] the state of possessing action and the state of possessing qualities.

The meaning is "the state of being an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇatva*). If it is argued that "possessing action" (*kriyāvattva*) is not the definition of substance (*dravya*), because it is non-pervasive due to its exclusion from [substances] such as space (*ākāśa*), etc.—[we reply: no, for possessing action is the definition of a substance that possesses action. And it is not thus...

The definition of substance is untenable because even those substances that possess action (kriyāvat) are substances, and thus that [action] would also constitute the definition of substance. Nor does it follow that the definitions of earth and so forth would thereby become the definition of substance; for this is accepted.

Alternatively, by the word "action" (kriyā), action in the sense of an object is not intended; rather, it refers to arising and perishing, because these are what is to be accomplished (sādhya). Furthermore, grammarians employ the term "action" for the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha). [An objection: How can arising and perishing be the meaning of a verbal root?

If it is argued that [existence] arises and perishes, as seen in such usages as "it is produced" and "it is destroyed," and since production is merely prior non-existence, how can an existent substance possess action? To this we reply:
the suffix *vati* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī-artha*), meaning "that in which action exists"; thus, it is called "possessing action."
The meaning would be "the locus of prior non-existence" and "the locus of destruction.

And thus, two definitions are established: "substance is the locus of prior non-existence" and "substance is the locus of destruction. Nor is there any lack of pervasiveness (avyāpakatva) in these two.

Because all substances (*dravya*) are the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), mutual non-existence (*saṃyoga-prāgabhāva*), and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of [their qualities] and so forth;

nor is there the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since it is accepted that prior non-existence and destructive non-existence reside solely in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). [The definition of substance is] "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*).

If it is argued that [the definition] is non-pervasive regarding quality (*guṇatva*), because even that possesses quality by virtue of being inherent in qualities— on the grounds that the suffix *vat* is prescribed merely to express a relationship in the sense "this belongs to this"— we say no, because by the term "possessing quality" (*guṇavattva*)...

Because it is intended that [the locus] is the substratum of qualities; for there is an injunction regarding the suffix *vat* in the sense of "that which has this" (*tad asmin asti*) even when it refers to being the substratum of that. Furthermore, since quality-ness (*guṇatva*) itself resides in qualities, it lacks the status of being a substratum of qualities; thus, even though it is dependent on qualities, it is not the substratum of qualities.

The teacher Ātreya maintains that since "being a quality" (guṇatva) is also the locus of qualities, the state of being the locus of qualities (guṇāśrayatva) is the pervader [of the definition of substance].
That is not correct, because there is no proof for the state of being a quality being the locus of qualities, as in the case of "the pot is white."

This is because, unlike the case of "this pot is conjoined [with color]," there is no such experience as "the property of being a quality (guṇatva) is conjoined with the quality-ness," and because there is an absence of a logical mark (liṅga). If it is argued that "the property of being a quality has a substratum in qualities because it inheres in qualities,
just like substance"— no, for what is this "inherence in qualities"?

Is it inherence in that which has qualities as its locus (*guṇaniṣṭhasamavāya*), or the state of being the substratum of inherence in that which has qualities as its locus (*guṇaniṣṭhasamavāyāśrayatva*), or simply the state of being a substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*)? Not the first, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to qualities; for inherence in qualities exists in qualities just as the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*) does.
This is because inherence resides in both [relata], and because there is deviation in the case of action (*karman*) and so forth;

since inherence is unitary, the inherence of a quality exists there [in action] as well. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, for precisely that reason there is no exclusion [of action from being a substance], and because the term "substratum" (*āśrayatva*) would be redundant.

Not the third [alternative], because it is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*) and because it contradicts perception (*pratyakṣa*), as in the case of "the quality-ness of a non-quality. Therefore, quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is not over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*). Thus say the teachers of the Ātreya lineage.

Some say that the author of the Sūtras included the qualification "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*) in order to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the quality-ness of the sun, which is also possessed of qualities;
however, that is not correct, because [the definition of substance as] "possessing qualities" (*guṇavat*) would be contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*).

For one who accepts that [substance] possesses qualities, it is impossible to deny that it also possesses action; thus, the fault of over-extension remains as it was. Even if the over-extension were avoided by [defining substance] as possessing qualities through [the qualification of] possessing action, [the fault would persist].

Because the definition would still be over-extensive with respect to *sattā* (existence), as that fault remains; and if it is argued that the term "inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*) should be added as a qualification to avoid this— no, for even in the case of *sattā*, there exists the state of being an inherent substratum (*samavāyin*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
Because it is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) by virtue of being the cause that brings about its own specific cognition;

for being an inherent cause consists in being the substratum of the effect. If it is argued that this [status of being a substratum] does not exist in *sattā* (existence), we say no, because *sattā*, like being the substratum of qualities, is also the substratum of effects.
Because it is impossible for existence (*sattā*) to be inherent (*samavāya*) with its effect in the same way as it is with its quality. If it is argued that "existence resides in the effect,
but is not the substratum of the effect"— then [it follows that] existence resides in the quality, but is not the substratum of the quality.

In order to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the state of being a substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*), the state of being a substratum of effects (*kāryāśrayatva*) need not be included [in the definition]. Therefore, it is established that just as being a substratum of effects is the definition of substance (*dravya*), so too is being a substratum of qualities.

The word "iti" (thus) is intended to include other such definitions; for example: substance is that which is the substratum of number; substance is that which is the substratum of dimension; substance is that which is the substratum of separateness; substance is that which is the substratum of conjunction; substance is that which is the substratum of disjunction.
Regarding number as well: substance is the substratum of oneness; substance is the substratum of duality;

substance is the substratum of triadness, and so forth. Regarding separateness as well: substance is the substratum of unitary separateness; substance is the substratum of dual separateness; substance is the substratum of triple separateness.
If it is argued that the inclusion of "oneness" and so forth is redundant because the definition of substance as "the substratum of separateness" (pṛthaktva) alone would suffice—
[we reply: no.

In this context, because singularity and separateness are not denoted by the two words "one" (*eka*) and "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), and because duality and separateness are not denoted by the two words "two" (*dvi*) and "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*);
furthermore, [this is so] by means of the indivisible word "duality-separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so forth.

Because of the non-mention of "duality" and so forth [in the definition]. For if the word *pṛthaktva* (separateness) were to denote separateness itself, then the definition of substance would be established by the mere statement that "substance is the substratum of separateness"; thus, the qualification of "duality" expressed by the word *dvi* [would be redundant].

It would be redundant. However, when the word "dvi-pṛthaktva" (two-fold distinctness) denotes a specific sub-genus of distinctness characterized by particularity, then there is no fault of a redundant qualification. Furthermore, this is because the number two is not being expressed by the word "dvi" [in the sense of a numerical quality].
Furthermore, because "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) is not included by the word "separateness" itself; if "duality of separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) were meant as the separateness of two things,
then the meaning of the sentence would be that the definition is "substance is the substratum of duality of separateness," and thus the qualification "in two" (*dviṣu*) is employed.
If you say "it is so," we reply: no, because this is merely a conventional derivation.

For the definition of a substance (*dravya*) is being the substratum of a genus that resides only in the genus of separateness (*pṛthaktva-jāti*) existing in two things. Otherwise, being a lotus-born (*paṅkajatva*) would be the definition of a lotus (*kamala*).

If one relies on the etymological derivation that "a lotus (*paṅkaja*) is that which is born from mud (*paṅka*)," the definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), as it would apply to frogs and the like. Furthermore, if one relies on the etymological derivation that "cowness (*gotva*) is the characteristic of cows, [and] a cow is that which goes (*gacchati*)," it would be over-extensive, as it would apply to jars and other such things.

It might be argued: "If it is merely a matter of etymological derivation— that 'paṅkaja' means 'born from mud' and 'go' means 'that which goes'— and what is intended is that the universal *paṅkajatva* (mud-bornness) is the defining characteristic of lotuses and the universal *gotva* (cowness) is the defining characteristic of cows, then [the same applies] to both."
The definition of a substance as the locus of that which possesses a genus residing solely in separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is merely an etymological derivation;
for [the definition] consists in being the locus of that which possesses a genus residing solely in separateness.
If it is argued that the qualifier "residing in two" (dviṣṭha) is redundant because the definition of substance is already established [by the presence of number], we say no;
for by the term "genus residing solely in separateness that resides in two," a specific genus is indicated, and being the locus of that [genus] constitutes the definition of substance.

Furthermore, since the definition of substance (*dravya*) is established as being the substratum of the category of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), which resides in two things and possesses a universal that inheres only in those two,
the inclusion of the phrase "possessing a universal that resides only in two things" (in the opponent's definition) remains redundant. Thus, its uselessness persists.

If it is argued: no, for in the definition "a substance is the substratum of a genus residing solely in duality and separateness," the word "separateness" (pṛthaktva), which is used in conjunction with the word "duality" (dviṣṭha) and denotes a specific sub-genus of separateness—

Because there is no denotation of [the quality] distinctness as qualified by a genus; or, even if there were such a denotation, because the substratum of distinctness would not be perceived; and because the word "distinctness" [is distinct] from the two preceding and following words which denote both [relata].

Because there is no syntactic connection (anvaya) between the word "substratum" (*āśraya*)— which has no expectancy for anything else— and the word "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), nor between the word "pervasion"— which has no expectancy for the word "possessing a genus" (*jātimat*)— and the word "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*).

If it is argued that the definition of substance is established by the mere statement "substance is the substratum of genus," and thus the phrase "subsisting only in separateness residing in two" is redundant— [we reply: no, for the word "genus" (jāti) when used in conjunction with the phrase "subsisting only in separateness residing in two" [serves a specific purpose].
Because it intends to convey a specific type of genus, it does not convey genus in general; otherwise,

even in the case of "substance is the locus of qualities," if the word "quality" were to denote that which is devoid of generality, substancehood, and action, then [the definition] would apply to the locus of generality as well.

Since the definition of substance (*dravya*) is established by the mere term "substance" itself, the phrase "devoid of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*)" would be redundant. Furthermore, if the word "quality" (*guṇa*) denotes that which possesses quality-ness, and if the word "quality" denotes a genus (*jāti*) residing only in those things devoid of generality (*sāmānya*), quality-ness, and action-ness— [then the definition remains flawed].

Since the definition of a substance (*dravya*) is established by this much alone— that it is a real entity (*dravya*) which is the substratum of genus (*jāti*)— the phrase "subsisting in that which is devoid of generality (*sāmānya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action-ness (*karmatva*)" would be redundant. Alternatively, if by the word "genus" (*jāti*) in conjunction with the word "subsisting only in that which is devoid of generality, quality, and action-ness," one intends not genus in general, but a specific genus (*jātiviśeṣa*), then the aforementioned fault does not apply.

If you think that the same [objection] applies here as well, then one should be satisfied with that. As for the two definitions— that substance has existence (*sattā*) as its locus, and that substance has a genus (*jāti*) as its locus— that is not correct, because they are over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), applying to qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth.
If it is argued that the definition of substance exists as "that which is the substratum of qualities, actions, and so forth,
because they always have a substratum and because they have a substratum possessing a genus," [we reply:
no, because quality-ness and the like are themselves genera subordinate to existence (sattā), and thus possess the property of having a genus.
Because the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth remains as it was; for there is the inference:
"The disputed [entities] possess intermediate genera such as quality-ness (*guṇatva*), because they are knowable (*meyatva*), like a jar.
Furthermore, the definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which possesses a genus that does not reside in qualities or actions" is also not a valid definition of substance.

Because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; for those possess universals such as "being a universal residing in qualities and actions" (*guṇakarmavṛttijātijātitva*), and so on.
[The definition of substance is: a substance is that which possesses a universal residing in what does not reside in qualities and resides in space (*gaganavṛttijātimaddravya*).
The definition of substance as "that which possesses a genus residing in qualities and residing in time," and so forth, is also not a valid definition of substance,

because it is over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to action and other categories. For instance, space [would absurdly follow as being a substance] because it possesses a genus that resides in a quality residing in space, while lacking the state of being devoid of a genus that excludes actions residing in space.

"Like a jar," and so forth. Nor is there any possibility here of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) or similar fallacies, because [the reason] is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). By this, [the following] definitions of substance (*dravya*) are [refuted]: "a substance possessing a genus that does not reside in action but resides in space," "a substance possessing a genus that does not reside in action but resides in time," and so on.

Refuted. Furthermore, the definition of substance as "a substance possessing a subordinate genus of existence residing in ether" is also not a valid definition of substance, because it is over-extensive (ativyāpaka), applying to qualities and so forth as well. And thus, ether possesses a genus that is excluded from all [other things] except for those qualities residing in ether.

Because it possesses genus (*jāti*), because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), and like a pot; and because it is not devoid of the exclusion from qualities residing in space (*gagana*). [The subject must be] either devoid of residing in space, or devoid of the exclusion from qualities. The first alternative is contradicted in the case of space.

And it is devoid of the exclusion from qualities (*guṇavyāvṛttatva*). This [exclusion] is either existence (*sattā*) itself or a subordinate genus thereof (*tadavāntarajāti*). The first alternative is refuted by the mention of "exclusion from the existent" (*sadvyāvṛtta*).
Therefore, there is established a subordinate genus of existence that is devoid of the exclusion from qualities.
This [objection] too is refuted by our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the author of the Sūtras did not teach the absence of a genus residing in qualities or in space; rather,
the author of the Sūtras [taught] that there is a genus residing in qualities and space.

If it is argued that since [the definition] was not established [by the Sūtrakāra], its establishment constitutes a departure from the tenet (*apasiddhānta*), we say no; for then it would follow that establishing [properties such as] "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth would also result in a departure from the tenet.
This is because one would be stating something contrary to what was established by the author of the Sūtras.

If it is argued that [the distinction between substance and quality] is not an unestablished tenet because it was not explicitly taught by the author of the Sūtras—[we reply: the same applies [to other cases]. Therefore, regarding substance and quality...

Since existence (*sattā*) as a subordinate genus is indeed admitted to be excluded from action (*karman*) while being non-excluded from substance (*dravya*), and excluded from quality (*guṇa*) and action while being non-excluded from quality and action, and since it is excluded from substance, this [existence] is a quality.
Or rather, this is a quality.
"This possesses the universal of the exclusion from existence (sattva) that is devoid of the exclusion from the ether residing in it, because it possesses a universal, like a jar.
By this, the definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which possesses a universal distinct from existence residing in the ether" is refuted.

The definitions of substance (*dravya*) that proceed by substituting terms such as "time" (*kāla*) for the term "space" (*ākāśa*) in the definition of substance must be rejected. Furthermore, the definition "a substance is that which is fit for a genus directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and residing in the same locus as action (*kriyā*)" is also not a valid definition of substance, because it overextends (*ativyāpaka*) to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. And thus:

Qualities and the like possess a genus that is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and is co-locus with action, because they possess a genus, like a jar; thus, there is established in qualities and the like a genus directly pervaded by existence that is co-locus with action. [This follows] from [the inference regarding] existence itself.
Furthermore, because qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*),
and because they possess a genus that is directly pervaded by existence and is co-located with action (*kriyā*),
how could it be said that "existence is pervaded by existence"?

If it is argued that—since the absence of subsistence in that which possesses the absolute non-existence of existence (i.e., the state of not being a substratum for the absolute non-existence of existence) is established for both disputants as being pervaded by existence in the case of "existence" (sattā)—let existence be pervaded by existence, but not directly;
[we reply: no, because [the reason] is the absence of being pervaded by the genus (jāti) that excludes the existent.

This is because directness (*sākṣāttva*) is present even in existence (*sattā*), and no other [definition of] directness can be formulated. Even for those who hold that [directness] is not pervaded by existence— so as to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth— for them too, the inclusion of the term "direct" (*sākṣāt*) is entirely redundant.
Because the state of possessing a genus that is pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and co-located with action (*kriyā*) avoids both under-extension and over-extension,
it does not require any further qualification. Let it be,
then, that substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by existence and co-located with action.
If it is argued that this is the definition of a substance— no,

for the absence of occurrence in that which possesses the absolute non-existence of existence (*sattātyantābhāvavadvṛttitvābhāva*), which is pervaded by existence (*sattāvyāpya*), exists in existence itself (*sattā*) and thus over-extends (*ativyāpaka*) to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

If it is argued that "pervasion by existence" (sattāvyāpyatva) consists in the absence of occurrence in that which possesses the absolute non-existence of existence, while being distinct from existence— and that this [pervasion] does not exist in existence itself— [we reply]: no,
because the qualification "absence of occurrence in that which possesses the absolute non-existence of existence" is redundant.

Since the definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which possesses a genus pervaded by existence (*sattā*) that is co-locative with action" is thus established, the alternative definition— "substance is that which possesses a sub-genus of existence residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*)"— is also not a valid definition, according to the reasoning previously stated.

Because it would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to qualities, actions, and so forth; and because the definition of substance is established by the mere statement "a substance possesses conjunction," making the inclusion of "that which possesses a subordinate genus of existence residing therein" redundant.

Furthermore, the definition "a substance is that which possesses a genus residing in ether and which is the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence residing in that which possesses a genus" is also not a valid definition of substance, because it over-extends to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. And thus, qualities and the like...
"Substances possess a genus that resides in ether and is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in that which possesses a genus,
because they possess a genus, like a cloth. By this [it is shown that] substance is the locus of a sub-genus of existence (sattā) that is co-locative with its effects.

The definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which is the locus of a sub-class of existence (*sattā*) that is co-located with qualities" and so forth is refuted; for the definition of substance is established by merely stating that "substance is the locus of effects" and "substance is the locus of qualities."
Furthermore, it would be redundant to include the mention of a subordinate genus of existence that is co-ordinate with [the definition].
Nor is "being any one of the nine [substances] beginning with earth" a definition of substance;
for if the nine individual entities beginning with earth are intended, this fails to extend to substances beyond those nine.
Furthermore, when there is the intention to express the nine characteristics beginning with earth, [the term "substance"] applies because it exists in all substances,
and because the nine characteristics exist in those things that lack the nature of substance.

Therefore, the definition of substance (*dravya*) is that it is the substratum of any one of the nine characteristics beginning with earth. And "being any one of the nine characteristics" is the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of those nine, which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) the set of nine characteristics.

Vidyādharamiśra holds that substance is the locus of the property of being a conjunction that does not reside in the loci of other conjunctions. That is not correct; for what is this "not residing in the loci of others that possess conjunction"?

What is intended is either (1) the state of not having as its locus anything other than conjunction, or (2) the state of not having as its locus anything other than that which possesses conjunction and that which does not possess conjunction? It cannot be the first, because the mention of "that which possesses conjunction" would be redundant; for [the definition would apply to] all things that possess conjunction.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it is impossible for the properties to be devoid of that [conjunction], since they are either identical with conjunction or different from it, and since they cannot reside in a locus other than that which possesses conjunction; furthermore, the definition would be unfeasible. Nor is the second [alternative] correct, because the mention of "possessing conjunction" and the mention of "properties possessing conjunction" would be redundant.

Because it is logically consistent that the definition of substance (*dravya*) is simply "not being the locus of anything other than what possesses conjunction," since all things possessing conjunction are "other than those possessing conjunction with something else," their properties [are likewise established].

Because it is impossible for that [absence] to be devoid of conjunctions—given that it is not the locus of others possessing conjunctions, just as conjunction itself is not—and because the definition would be unestablished.
By the phrase "others possessing conjunctions," what is intended is that which is devoid of the nature of conjunction (saṃyogatva). By that...

If it is argued that the definition of substance (*dravya*) is "that which is not the locus of what lacks conjunction," we say no; for since being possessed of conjunction (*saṃyogavattva*) suffices as the definition of substance, the inclusion of the phrase "not the locus of what lacks" is redundant.

Since the definition of substance (*dravya*) is established by the mere statement "substance is the locus of conjunction," the inclusion of the term "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) without the suffix *-vat* would be redundant. By this [same reasoning], in place of the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*),...

The definitions of substance (*dravya*) have been refuted by the addition of terms such as "having division," "number," "dimension" (*parimāṇa*), "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), "quality" (*guṇa*), and "effect.
Furthermore, the definition that "substance is the substratum of that which does not reside in what is devoid of possession of conjunction" is also not tenable.

Regarding the definition of substance (*dravya*): since the definition of substance is established by the mere statement that "substance is the locus of conjunction," the inclusion of the phrase "that which exists in what does not exist in that which lacks the cognition of *vatimat*" is redundant.

If it is argued that there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the word *saṃyoga*, which ends in the suffix *vat*, and the word *adhikaraṇa*—we say no; for since the suffix *vat* has been removed because it serves no purpose, the word *saṃyoga* can indeed be connected with the word *adhikaraṇa*. [In the event of] such impossibility...

This is because [the author] accepts that these and other such qualities possess the characteristic of being substances. By this same principle, one may substitute the term "disjunction" (*vibhāga*) for the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), and insert the terms "number" (*saṃkhyā*), "dimension" (*parimāṇa*), and "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*).

The definitions of substance have been refuted. However, when it is established that there is no possession of a genus (jātimattva) for things distinct from substance, quality, and action, then [the following definitions hold]:
substance is that which has existence as its locus; substance is that which has a genus as its locus; substance is that which possesses a genus that does not reside in qualities or actions.
Substance is that which possesses a genus residing in qualities but not residing in space; substance is that which possesses a genus residing in time but not residing in qualities;
substance is that which possesses a genus residing in direction but not residing in qualities.
Substance is that which possesses a genus residing in qualities and residing in pots. Thus, there are as many definitions of substance as there are individual substances.
Likewise, substance is that which possesses a genus subordinate to existence (sattā) residing in the ether.

Substance is that which possesses a genus distinct from existence as it occurs in space (*gaganavṛtti-sattā*). By substituting the term "space" with "time" and so forth, there are as many definitions of substance as there are individual instances of substance.
Likewise, substance is that which possesses a sub-genus of existence co-located with action;
substance is that which possesses a sub-genus of existence co-located with substance.

Because of the previously established futility [of other definitions], and given the capacity for persistence, substance is that which possesses a subordinate genus of existence co-located with its effects;
substance is that which possesses a subordinate genus of existence co-located with qualities; and likewise...
By substituting terms such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth for the place of the verb,

and by substituting terms for specific instances of form and so forth, and likewise by substituting terms such as "number," "dimension," "separateness," "conjunction," and "disjunction" for the place of the term "quality" (*guṇa*), there are infinite [variations].

The definitions of substance (*dravya*): likewise, by substituting terms other than "existence" (*sattā*) in place of the term "existence" [in the definition of existence], there are infinite definitions of substance. Similarly:
"A substance is that which possesses a genus residing in ether and which is capable of being the locus of an absolute non-existence residing in a genus."

Furthermore, by substituting terms such as "time" (kāla) and others in place of "space" (ākāśa) and so forth, one should understand that there are as many definitions of substance (dravya-lakṣaṇa) as there are individual instances of substance.
In our own view, however, substance is that which is the substratum of effects, and substance is that which is the substratum of qualities.

Substance is the locus of prior non-existence; substance is the locus of posterior non-existence; substance is the locus of number; substance is the locus of dimension; substance is the locus of separateness;
substance is the locus of conjunction; likewise [it is the locus] in place of the terms "number" and so forth.

By adding one term at a time, such as "oneness" and so forth, there are infinite definitions of substance (*dravya*). Likewise, substance is that which is the substratum of any one of the nine characteristics beginning with earth.
However, some [hold a different view]:

They consider that substance is the substratum of that which does not occur in what is devoid of "effectness," substance is the substratum of that which does not occur in what is devoid of "qualityness," and substance is the substratum of that which does not occur in what is devoid of "numberness."
Substance is that which is the substratum of what does not occur in what is devoid of dimension;

substance is that which is the substratum of what does not occur in what is devoid of separateness; [substance is] that which is the substratum of what does not occur in what is devoid of the nature of conjunction.
Substance: Substance is the substratum of that which does not reside in what is devoid of the nature of being a division;
and by substituting "oneness" and "singleness" for "number" and "separateness" respectively, there are infinite definitions of substance.
Likewise, substance is that which does not reside in what is devoid of having an effect, and substance is that which does not reside in what is devoid of being a quality (*guṇatva*). Similarly,
by substituting the word "quality" with words such as "number" (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, there are infinite definitions of substance.

If it is argued that [the definitions] are "to be seen" [as too narrow], because the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) do not exist in a jar and so forth at the moment of their production and are therefore non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*)— we say no, for in the case of jars and the like...

Even though [the cause] is the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of effects and qualities, it is not excluded from the meaning of the word "non-pervasive" (*avyāpaka*), because it lacks the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of being possessed of effects or qualities, and because it possesses the property of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in that which is intended to be the definiendum (*lakṣya*). And as for effects and qualities...
Because the status of being a substance-characteristic is not accepted; or, even if it were not accepted,
because the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the effect and its qualities residing in a cloth would be possible at the very moment of the production of a jar or similar object.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for there to be an absolute non-existence [of the property], it is untenable for it to be non-pervasive;
for the meaning of the term "non-pervasiveness" consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in that which is intended to be the locus of the definition.
This applies to jars and the like at the moment of their production.

The absence of both "possessing an effect" (*kāryavattva*) and "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*)—as in the case of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the qualities of an effect—is indeed present [in the Primal Cause].

And that absence is precisely an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), because since possessing an effect and possessing qualities are beginningless, their prior non-existence is impossible. Consequently, the definition is under-extended (*avyāpaka*).
If you say this, it is not so, because absolute non-existence cannot logically occupy the same locus as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

[Objection: Does it then follow that even in the first moment, a jar and the like possess the state of having an effect (*kāryavattva*) and the state of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*)? [Reply: Certainly; for how could there be the state of having an effect in the absence of an effect and qualities?

If it is argued that [the definition] consists in possessing qualities (guṇavattva), [we reply: because it does not pervade [all substances] due to its being a quality of an effect (kāryaguṇa), all is well. But what is the purpose of a definition? Is it the knowledge of substance (dravyajñāna)?
Is it the cognition of being denotable by the word "substance" (dravya), or the removal of [the status of] substance, or the cognition of a substance as excluded from other substances,
or the state of being a cognition qualified by the absence of qualities such as "quality-ness" (guṇatva)? Not the first.
Because the direct perception of substantiality (dravyatva) is established through the sense organ alone,
and the inference of substantiality is established through a logical mark (liṅga) alone. If it is argued that the definition of substance itself is the logical mark for substantiality— no.

The first [alternative] is not tenable because, even if "substance-ness" and so forth were well-known, the qualification would be unestablished; or, if they were established, the proof would be redundant. Nor is the second [alternative], because if being denotable by the word "substance" is unestablished, the qualification is unestablished; or, if it were established, the proof would be redundant.
Because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) due to its exclusion from non-substancehood (*adravyatva*), which is denoted by the word "substance" (*dravya*).

If it is argued that substancehood (*dravyatva*) is also the subject (*pakṣa*) itself, we say no; for in that case, the state of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) is not established, and because the status of being denotable by the word "substance" is established solely through well-known usage (*prasiddhavyavahāra*). It is not [the case that substancehood is the subject].
The third [alternative] is not tenable, because for one who seeks a substance, activity is established through the cognition of the substance itself;
and because the application of the word "substance" and the cognition produced by it are accounted for through the cognition of the word "substance" alone.
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because by the word "other," [one does not denote] that which possesses substance...
Even if it possesses the characteristics [of a substance], this is because there is a contradiction in its being the material cause (*upādāna*), and because it is sublated; and furthermore,

even from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as color (*rūpa*), which is excluded from taste (*rasa*) and so forth that lack the characteristics of a substance, [the probans would deviate] if the material cause were devoid of the characteristics of a substance.
Because it would follow that the definition of substance (*dravya-lakṣaṇa*) would be non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) due to its being excluded [from all other things].

If it is argued that by the phrase "devoid of the definition of substance" one intends to refer to everything that is devoid of the definition of substance—[we reply: no, because of the word "everything" (*sarva*).
When there is the intention to express merely that which has been apprehended by you,
[the reason] excludes that which lacks the characteristics of a substance as apprehended by you,
because it lacks the characteristics of a substance as apprehended by us and others; this applies even to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Because it would follow that being the definition of substance [would be] unique [to it] by virtue of its exclusion [from others];

and because, in the case of the intention to speak of what is either already understood or not yet understood by you, an intention regarding what is not yet understood is untenable, since the exclusion from what is not yet understood [has not been established].
And because it is impossible to apprehend [such a thing], the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*).

If you argue, "I apprehend everything that is devoid of the characteristics of a substance," we say no; for your sense organs do not operate with respect to what is not in contact [with them], nor [do they operate] when the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has not been perceived.
Because inference regarding you is impossible;
furthermore, is it being proved here that there is a single exclusion (avyāvṛtti) whose counter-correlates (pratiyogin) are all individual instances devoid of the definition of a substance?
Or, [the definition] is all exclusions (vyāvṛtti) that have as their counter-correlatives (pratiyogin) every individual thing devoid of the characteristic of substance.
Not the first, because it is impossible for there to be a single exclusion whose counter-correlative is something devoid of the characteristic of substance. Nor the second.
Because it is impossible for the absences of all exclusions to coexist in a single locus, there can be no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the absence of the probandum and the absence of the probans.
Now, [if it is argued that] the absences of the exclusions from all individuals lacking the definition of substance [coexist] in one place...

If it is argued that [this is] impossible—[we reply: even for all things, although they lack the definition of a substance and lack their own specific exclusions (*svavyāvṛtti*), it is impossible for them to lack that [exclusion], because they possess an exclusion from what is other than themselves (*svānyavyāvṛtti*). And of this...

This is because there is no evidence for the absence of all exclusions (vyāvṛtti) that relate to every individual thing devoid of the characteristic of being a substance; and furthermore, because in the system of Udayana and others, the difference between absences is necessarily determined by the difference between their counter-correlates (pratiyogin).
And because non-existence, by virtue of being an existence,
lacks the exclusion from all individual instances that are devoid of the definition of substance,
it lacks the state of being distinct from all individual instances that are devoid of the definition of substance.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the absence of the probandum to be pervaded by the absence of the probans in that which lacks the definition of a substance. Moreover, is every individual instance devoid of the definition of a substance unapprehended or apprehended somewhere? Not the first, because it would entail the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

[The reason] must be either other than the subject (*pakṣa*) or within the subject itself. Not the first [alternative], because if the reason occurs there, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be possible, thereby destroying its status as a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason;
and if it were excluded from it, it would result in the fallacy of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) due to being excluded even from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Not...
The second [alternative] is untenable because it would entail the futility of the proof;
for in the case of perceptible substances, their distinction from others is already established by perception.
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), since this applies even to imperceptible substances.
If it is argued that the means of proof is not redundant because it establishes difference from others— no,
for since the concomitance of properties such as possessing qualities with difference from others is already ascertained among perceptible substances,
the status of the reason as a *kevalavyatirekin* (exclusively negative) is destroyed, given the operation of inference.

Because the meaning of the word "kevala" (exclusive) is either the absence of a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) established previously, or the absence of a certainty of positive concomitance that is not produced by a certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); [in the case of the "exclusive" reason], there is an absence of certainty of positive concomitance in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

If it is argued that this is the meaning of the word "only" (*kevala*), we say no; for the qualification of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) would be redundant, and moreover, the similar instance itself remains undefined. If it is argued that the similar instance is that in which the probandum is ascertained, we say no;
because even a locus where the qualification by possession of the probandum is already established would then also be a similar instance.

If it is argued that the "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is that which is distinct from the subject (pakṣa) and possesses the proven property (sādhyavān) with certainty—this is not so; for the qualification "distinct from the subject" is redundant, and because this [definition] would render the subject itself a similar instance, thereby resulting in the fallacy of the "limiting condition" (upādhi). This is because the locus where the qualification is established is precisely the subject itself.
Because it is ascertained to be a pervader of the probandum,
and because it is not a pervader of the probans, since it excludes substances that are not perceptible, like the definition of substance.
Furthermore, because there is no "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) due to its exclusion from atoms and forms that lack other distinctions; and because, among perceptible substances,
it is impossible to ascertain through perception the exclusion of perceptible individuals that lack the definition of a substance.
Among perceptible substances,
there are exclusions of perceptible individuals that lack the definition of a substance, established by perception;
and there are exclusions of imperceptible individuals that lack the definition of a substance, established by inference.
If it is argued that they are ascertained— no,
because there is no recollection of infinite inferential marks (liṅgas) restricted to the exclusion of infinite unperceived individuals that lack the defining characteristics of substance;
this holds true even for perceptible substances.

Furthermore, since the ascertainment of the exclusions of individual instances— whether perceptible or imperceptible— that are devoid of the characteristics of a substance (*dravya*) is established by perception and inference alone, the futility of negative-only (*vyatirekin*) reasoning remains as it was. Moreover, an absence residing in that which is imperceptible is not itself perceptible.
If you say this is not so— no, because the absence of a jar and so forth, which resides in imperceptible entities such as the sky,
is itself perceptible on a ground surface. If you argue that an absence is perceptible even when its locus (*dharmin*) is imperceptible—
no, because [otherwise] the perceptibility of the absence of color in air would follow.

This is because it has been accepted even by Udayana and others; furthermore, it is merely the ravings of a madman, for even when the causal complex for the perception of an absence—consisting of the knowledge of the locus, the knowledge of the counter-positive, the sense-organ contact, and so forth—is complete, the perception [of that absence] does not occur. This is especially true in the case of substances that are themselves imperceptible.
Even if the exclusions of perceptible and imperceptible [entities] that lack the definition of substance are themselves imperceptible,
and even if there is a determination of the exclusion of substance,

one may infer [the object] as being like the exclusion of the imperceptible which lacks both the state of being a perceptible individual lacking the definition of substance and the exclusion [of substance].
Furthermore, because it is possible [to establish the probans] in the case of perceptible substances, the futility of the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) remains as it was;
this is so when all substances are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*).

If it is argued that the fact that *dravyatva* (substanceness) is pervaded by the difference from others (*itarabheda-vyāpyatva*) and the fact that the difference from others is pervasive of *dravyatva* (*itarabheda-vyāpakatva*) are established by a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), and therefore the negative inference is not redundant—[we reply: no;
for [this would require] *dravyatva* to be pervaded by the difference from others precisely through that very difference from others, and likewise for the difference from others...
