Because there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) due to its being a pervader of substantiality (*dravyatva*); and because a property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) cannot be a prover unless it establishes a connection between the pervader and the subject;
[and] the qualifier of the subject delimited by the word "all" must be pervaded by the property being affirmed.
If it is argued that, for example, in the statement "every cloth is red," the property of being a cloth (*paṭatva*) is pervaded by the property of being red;

and that the property of being the predicate of what is being predicated (*vidhīyamānadharmatva*), which is the qualifier of the property delimited by every cloth, is pervaded by the property of being red—as in the case of "the cloth is red"—[we reply]: No, because of this...

If it is argued that there is no redundancy in the negative inference (vyatirekin) because it is a distinct means of knowledge— since, when all substances are taken as the subject, the connection of the "difference from others" with all substances, which is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge, is established by the negative inference— [we reply: no.
Because the various relations with all other substances are manifold due to the difference between the related substance and the other [substances];
for it is precisely these relations with all other substances that constitute both the differentiation from others and the relation of possessing qualities and so forth.

If it is argued that—since there is no determination of substances through direct perception, and since their non-difference is established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—the difference of all substances from one another cannot be established simultaneously without a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), and therefore the negative inference is not redundant; [we reply: no, because [this would apply only] to that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
Furthermore, since a term for "simultaneity" (*yogapada*) that is distinct from the relation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva-saṃsarga*) is not established even by a negative inference (*vyatirekin*),

there can be no single cognition directed toward all substances as qualified by their distinction from others, without a negative inference that proceeds by taking all non-complete substances as its subject (*pakṣa*).
If it is argued that there is no lack of purpose for the distinct entity because the cognition [of identity] does not arise, we say no;

for since the object of the distinct inference is already understood through another means of knowledge, and since the unity [of the substance] has been apprehended, the distinct entity would be purposeless, and thus its distinction [from the substance] is redundant.

Because it remains in that state; because each [individual] alone serves as the subject (*dharmin*), and since the cognitions of the exclusion of others (*itarabheda*)—which terminate in individual substances—are manifold, a single cognition whose object is all substances qualified by the exclusion of others is impossible.
Furthermore, if the direct perception of the exclusion of others in perceptible substances were produced by perception...

If it is argued that the negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) is useless because the result— the differentiation from others— does not arise since [the probandum] already exists, we say no; for perceptible substances cannot function as the subject (*pakṣa*) due to the absence of any doubt regarding the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and thus its property would not qualify as a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

Because it would be untenable for [the cognition] to have inference as its result. If it is argued that being a subject (*pakṣatva*) does not consist in having a doubtful probandum (*sandigdhasādhyatva*), but rather in being the object of a conflicting dispute (*vipratipattigocaratva*)—we say no; because in the case of perceptible substances whose difference from others is already ascertained, there is an absence of any conflicting dispute regarding their difference from others.

If it is argued that [the subject] must be taken as the locus (*dharmin*) and nothing else—[we reply: no, because it is impossible for perceptible substances, which possess the probandum (*sādhya*) as admitted by both parties, to be taken as the locus for the sake of another person. If this is argued—[we reply: no.

Since perceptible substances cannot function as the subject (*pakṣa*)— because they lack the state of having a doubtful probandum— the property residing in them cannot be a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), and thus it is impossible for it to result in an inference.

Because it would be impossible to prevent the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). Furthermore, in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), since there would be no mention of a locus (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*) would result in the fallacy of not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
If you argue that being a locus (*dharmitva*) is itself the state of being the subject (*pakṣatva*), we say no; for this would apply even to fire already ascertained through perception.

Because no inference of fire arises from the presence of smoke in a kitchen and similar places; if it is argued that the inference of fire is indeed established there— no, because there is a lack of evidence, and because there is no subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I infer fire in the kitchen," nor is there any conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding fire [in that context].
And because [the existence of fire] is established through perception itself. If it is argued that the inference of fire occurs through the causal complex for the inference of fire—
no, because neither doubt regarding the probandum nor certainty regarding the probandum, which are the causes of inference, are possible [in this case].

If it is argued that there is no "unestablished qualification" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) because the exclusions from all individuals devoid of the characteristic of substance are well-established precisely within all those individuals that are themselves excluded from other substances and devoid of their characteristics; and that there is no "futility of the means of proof" (sādhanavaiyarthyam) because the proof is applied to substances—[we reply: no, for while the exclusions from others may be established, [the point remains].
Furthermore, because those exclusions cannot coexist in a single locus,
it is impossible for the absence of the probandum to be pervaded by the absence of the probans at the time of apprehending the exclusion of one individual from others.

Furthermore, since it is possible to apprehend the exclusion of others (itaravyāvṛtti) regarding substances by means of the very same instrument of knowledge that apprehends such exclusion in other cases, the futility of the *vyatirekin* [inference] remains as it was.

If it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is "the state of possessing a universal exclusion from all individuals that are counter-correlatives of every individual devoid of the characteristic of being a substance," and that because this absence is unitary, its pervasion by the absence of the probans is established— [we reply: no.
Because the property of possessing a universal exclusion from all individuals— which would have as its counter-correlates all individuals devoid of the definition of a substance— is unestablished;

and even though the difference from others (itarabheda) is unestablished, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualification here, because the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) is possible since the absence of that [difference] is itself a positive entity (bhāva).
If it is argued that this is a fault— no;

because it is impossible for a single locus to be simultaneously devoid of the characteristics of substance as denoted by the term "different from others," and yet to possess all exclusions (vyāvṛtti) relative to every individual instance,
there is the fifth [type of] non-establishment of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*).

Because qualities-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), the universal of [quality-ness] (*jātitva*), particularity-ness (*viśeṣatva*), inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*), absence-ness (*abhāvatva*), and the absence of absence— namely,
qualities-ness and the others— are not one, it is impossible for the absence of the probandum to be pervaded by the absence of the probans.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to apprehend the absence of the six absolute absences— namely those whose counter-correlates are quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), genus-ness (*jātitva*), particularity-ness (*viśeṣatva*), inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*), and non-existence-ness (*abhāvatva*)— without first establishing the existence of their respective counter-correlates (such as quality-ness itself), which are distinct from the entities [like substance] that possess them, it is impossible to grasp the pervasion due to the lack of a probans (*sādhana*).

If it is argued that one infers the probandum in the subject by means of a demonstrated *vyatirekin* (negative-only inference), having first understood the probandum from the very statement of the thesis— "devoid of substance-ness, quality-ness, and so forth"— and having ascertained the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans— [we reply: no.

Because no connection is understood from the two components of the proposition when they are uttered as referring respectively to the subject and the probandum without being mutually connected; even if a connection were understood...
Because there is only the comprehension of the absence of the conjunction of "being a single quality" (*guṇatva*) and so forth;

for there is no comprehension of the probandum as being the possession of the sixfold absence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so on. Or, even if such a comprehension were to occur, the probandum understood from the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) would lack any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because the absence of that [probandum] is likewise devoid of any means of valid cognition; and because if the statement of the thesis were itself a means of valid cognition, the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) would be redundant. It is the negative inference that establishes the probandum which is entirely unestablished, whereas it is the positive inference (*anvayin*) that establishes the connection with the probandum which is likewise unestablished.

If you say this, it is not so; for when the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, its absence is likewise unestablished, and thus the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is impossible.
Furthermore, because the absence of a probandum that lacks epistemic warrant exists everywhere...
Furthermore, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is broken by the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) precisely where there is the counter-instance to the probans.

If it is argued that [the probandum] is unestablished by valid means (*aprāmāṇika*) due to the absence of that [probans], since the probandum is established through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), we say no; for the validity of negative concomitance itself remains unproven.
Śrīkara, however,

is that which possesses the absolute absence of quality (guṇatvātyantābhāva), because it is devoid of the property of residing in something other than the co-occurrence with the five [absences], such as the absolute absence of action (karmatvātyantābhāva) and so forth.

Because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatvāt*), like a jar; having thus established that the absolute absence of quality-ness (*guṇatvātyantābhāva*) is co-located with the fivefold absolute absences of action-ness (*karmatvātyantābhāva*), [it follows that] substance (*dravya*) possesses the absolute absence of quality-ness which is co-located with the fivefold absolute absences of action-ness.

Because it is a quality (*guṇatva*). One might argue that what is not thus should not be applied as "it is thus"; to this he says: "That is not so, because [the reason] such as 'possessing a quality' (*guṇavattva*) is excluded even from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as action (*karman*) and the like, which possess the absolute absence of the five [absences] co-located with the absolute absence of being a quality."
Because it is impossible to avoid [the fallacy of] over-extension (*sādhāraṇatva*),
and because the proof would be futile once the fivefold absolute non-existence of "objectness" (*karmatva*) has been established in the subject (*pakṣa*).
[This is so] even where there is the absence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) somewhere or other.

Furthermore, the property of "coexistence with the five absolute non-existences of action-ness" is established for the subject (pakṣa) by the very same means of valid cognition that establishes the qualifier [in the probandum]. This is because [the property] is coextensive with the five absolute non-existences of action-ness.
Furthermore, regarding the position that [the subject] is the absolute absence of quality-ness (*guṇatva*),

since this is established by the mere statement "that which possesses the absolute absence of quality-ness," the qualification "being co-locatable with the fivefold absolute absence of action-ness" (*karmatva*) is redundant; thus, [the definition fails] because of the possession of the absolute absence of quality-ness.

If it is argued that, because [the reason] such as "possessing qualities" (guṇavattva) is excluded from the sapakṣa as well as from the subject (sādhya), it would follow that it is an "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason— [we reply: no,
for even when this qualification is adopted, the state of being an uncommon reason remains unchanged.
Because the futility of the qualification attached to the probandum (sādhya) is as indelible as adamantine cement:

"The absolute absence of qualities possesses the property of being devoid of residing in the absolute absence of the nature of quality— which is itself distinct from the absolute absence of co-occurrence with the absolute absence of the nature of action."
"Because it is an object of knowledge, like a cloth"— this is because the probans that establishes the qualification is countered by an opposing argument (satpratipakṣa).
As for Śivādityamiśra, however...
By means of the inference that the absolute absence of qualityness (guṇatva) is co-located with the absolute absence of actionness (karmatva),
[it is established as] not delimited by any specific substance.

Having established that [the subject] possesses the nature of being a sixfold absolute absence whose counter-correlate is "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so forth, one employs a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) as follows: "Substance possesses the sixfold absolute absence whose counter-correlate is quality-ness and so forth, because it possesses quality-ness; for whatever is not thus is not so. But even that is not [correct].

This is because the inference that establishes the qualification is beset by all possible fallacies, such as being countered by an equally valid opposing argument (satpratipakṣa); and this has been explained in detail in the *Mahāvidyāviḍambana*.
Therefore, the sūtras that set forth definitions are purposeless and should not be undertaken. That is incorrect, because the existence of substance (dravyatva) is established.

Because it serves as the purpose for defining substance, the direct perception of substantiality (*dravyatva*) in perceptible substances is produced by the sense organs together with the cognition of qualities (*guṇavattva*) and so forth;

for even when the cognition of qualities and so forth is absent, [the cognition] "this is a substance" occurs in relation to jars, cloths, and the like, despite the presence of the sense organs and other factors.
Because there arises no corresponding immediate cognition (aparokṣapratīti) of the form "this is a substance" [in the case of imperceptible substances];

and because, in the case of imperceptible substances, the inference of substanceness (*dravyatva*) is produced by the definition of substance—such as possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*), which is a mark based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*).
Nor, in this case, do earthness (*pṛthivītva*), possession of odor (*gandhavattva*), possession of taste (*rasavattva*), or possession of whiteness (*śuklavattva*) [serve as the basis].

The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—such as being a substance perceived by the senses, or [qualities like] motion—are excluded because they fail to pervade the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor are [the following] applicable:
possessing color, possessing touch, being an element (*bhūta*), being a sense organ (*indriya*), possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), being an effect (*kārya*), or being perceptible to us.

Time possesses [the property of] being devoid of residing in a time that is distinct from the category of substance (dravyatva), because it is knowable (meyatva); thus, since the existence of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) residing in time is established, the pervasion of the probandum (sādhya) in time is broken. Nor is the previous inference rendered useless in this way, for it applies only to those things other than that [time].

Because it is taken as the subject (*dharmin*). Alternatively, by means of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), such as: "Time possesses the property of being devoid of residing in a time distinct from [the category of] substantiality (*dravyatva*)," because it is a quality (*guṇatva*), like a cloth, and so forth.

Because, by means of the definition of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*), one infers substanceness (*dravyatva*) in those substances that are not perceptible; nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here,
since in a jar and the like, color and other qualities are devoid of temporality qualified by being distinct from substanceness.

Because it is established by perception. Nor is the means of proof (sādhana) redundant, since substanceness (*dravyatva*) is not established by perception in the case of substances that are not perceptible. Furthermore, there is no possibility of this [reason] being fallacious due to a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and so forth, precisely because it is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) reason. Or, let it be granted that substanceness is established by perception in the case of perceptible substances.

[This is established] by means of a purely negative definition of substance (*kevalavyatireki-dravyalakṣaṇa*). Nor is there here the fault of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), because [the reason] such as "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) is not excluded from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Nor is there a collapse of the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) due to the possibility of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Since the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) does not depend upon the very establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*),
it is necessarily present prior to the operation of the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*); therefore, at the stage when positive concomitance has been ascertained—

This is because its status as a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) is established. Alternatively, let the proof of all substances (*sarvadravya*) proceed from a purely negative inference based on the very definition of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*).
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
This is because the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) does not constitute a deficiency in the members of an inference,
nor does it induce a deficiency in the members of an inference. Furthermore, the non-establishment of the probandum,
by undermining doubt regarding the probandum, ultimately results in the failure of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
If it is argued that [the subject] must be a *pakṣa* because there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), we say no;
for doubt about the probandum is not a constituent factor of inference,
since inference is established precisely through the ascertainment of the probandum, and it is only when the probandum remains unascertained that [it qualifies as a *pakṣa*].

Because it is the subject (*pakṣa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that inference would arise even for those who are already learned or for those who are mistaken.

If it is argued that—since the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be apprehended through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans, and thus the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) does not proceed—[we reply]: no.
This is because it has already been established that the pervasion of the absence of the probans residing in the absence of the probandum does not produce the inference of the probandum,
since only the pervasion of the probandum residing in the probans produces the inference of the probandum.

If it is argued that, because there is no means [other than inference], the pervasion of "possessing qualities" by "substance-ness" cannot be grasped even if negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is not understood— [we reply]: no,
for just as in the case of perception, the pervasion of substance-ness residing in the possession of qualities serves as the means.
Because perception is admitted [to function] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth;

for if one does not grasp substanceness (*dravyatva*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of qualityness (*guṇatva*) by means of substanceness is not grasped by perception—if this is argued, [we ask]: is it because it is not grasped due to its being dependent on a substance (*dravyāśritatva*) that it is not grasped?

It is intended [to mean] either because it is not delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*), or because it is the object of a cognition produced by the cognition of "substance-cognition-ness," or because it is not the object of a cognition not produced by the cognition of substantiality.

Either because it is the object of a cognition whose object is substanceness (*dravyatva*), or because it is not the object of a cognition whose object is not substanceness. It is not the first [case], because the pervasion by substanceness—
which is synonymous with being resident in the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) that are themselves pervaded by substanceness— is [established].

Because it is a substance and because it is non-dependent. Regarding the second [alternative] as well, does "being delimited by substanceness" mean being qualified by substanceness (*dravyatvaviśiṣṭatva*) or having the nature of being characterized by substanceness (*dravyatvavaiśiṣṭhyarūpatva*)?
It cannot be the first, because even in the case of jars and so forth—which are qualified by substanceness—there is no apprehension of substanceness [when they are not themselves perceived].
Nor is it the second [alternative], because it would apply only to substance (*dravya*).

This is because "pervadedness" (*vyāpyatva*), which subsists in both substance and quality, is distinct [from the former]. Nor is it the third, because even that which is the object of a cognition qualified by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—which is produced by the cognition of a substance—is [included].
[It is] not [the case that it is] the fourth [alternative], because there is no proof and thus it is unestablished;

and because of the inference: "The state of being pervaded by substantiality (dravyatva) does not arise from the cognition of substantiality, because it is an object of knowledge (prameyatva), like a cloth. Nor...

The fifth [alternative] is not tenable, because, like a jar or similar objects, even that which is the object of a cognition whose object is substanceness (dravyatva) is itself an object of a cognition whose object is substanceness. Nor is the sixth [alternative] tenable, because it is unestablished due to a lack of evidence. [As for] "being pervaded by substanceness" (dravyatvavyāpyatva)...
Furthermore, from the inference: "The object of a cognition that does not have substanceness as its object is distinct from substanceness, because it is other than substanceness, like a cloth";

and "The object of a cognition that does not have non-pervasion of substanceness as its object is the object of the cognition of knowability, because it is knowable, like a cloth. And if such [objects] were thus devoid of substanceness...

If it is argued that there is an inconsistency because, since it is equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and thus where could pervasion (*vyāpti*) be apprehended?—we say no. To the question regarding the locus of pervasion, the answer is "in possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*);
and to the question regarding the locus of its apprehension, the answer is "in the self" (*ātman*).

If it is argued that "possessing qualities" (guṇavattva) is either the subject (pakṣa) or the similar instance (sapakṣa)—we say no; for, by virtue of being devoid of the substancehood that is to be proven (sādhyadravyatva), it constitutes a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
If it is further argued that pervasion (vyāpti) is grasped in the similar instance and not in the subject—we say no, even in the case of the position that [the reason] is positive (anvayin).

Because the absence of substantiality (*dravyatvābhāva*) is grasped as being pervaded by the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) alone; because it exists elsewhere [in the counter-example]; and because it is well-known that pervasion is grasped in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), which is logically consistent with the intention of grasping the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) as residing in the similar instance.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended as residing in the probans (*sādhana*) as known in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and not as residing in that probans as known in the subject (*pakṣa*)— we say no; for when the apprehension of pervasion is possible through its residence in the probans as already known, [there is no need for the other].

Because being a member of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) as it pertains to the means of proof (*sādhana*) is useless. "Being pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyatva*) means either subsisting only in that which possesses substantiality, or the absolute non-existence of the existence of the absolute non-existence of substantiality. In this regard, both [definitions] apply.

If it is argued that [the property] cannot be apprehended because it is impossible to apprehend it through the apprehension of substantiality (*dravyatva*), we say no; for this objection has already been answered.

Furthermore, since these two [properties] are not accepted as having the nature of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*)—due to their non-existence in the case of purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) inference—what then is "being pervaded by substantiality"? It is that which generates the inferential cognition of substantiality.

It is a specific property (dharmaviśeṣa) that culminates in the possession of qualities (guṇavattva). And that can indeed be apprehended even when substantiality (dravyatva) is not apprehended, just as [the presence of fire] can be apprehended even when the specific fire residing on a mountain is not apprehended.

It possesses the property of being pervaded by fire residing on the mountain, as residing in a specific smoke residing on that same mountain, which generates an inference of a specific fire residing on the mountain;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that an inference of a specific fire residing on the mountain could arise through a purely negative-only (kevalavyatirekin) inference based on a specific smoke residing on that mountain. [This is] by means of a positive concomitant (anvayin).
Because the establishment of a specific fire residing on the mountain— by virtue of the property of being present in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) through the mark of possessing smoke—
is something that will be refuted later.

Alternatively, by way of providing the specific property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*), the definition of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*) generates the inference of substantiality (*dravyatva*), not by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*). This pot possesses a genus that does not reside in that which is excluded from the definition of substance residing in it, and which is not the locus of residing in that which lacks the definition of substance residing in it.

In cases such as "because of possessing birth" (*jātimattvāt*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is included within the definition of substance (*dravya*). Nor is the perception [of the reason] rendered useless by virtue of being established through another mode [of cognition], because that [other mode] is not its basis (*anupajīvyatvāt*); otherwise, substantiality (*dravyatva*) would be established by this very mode as well.

For in another way, the futility [of the definition] remains difficult to avoid. Even if "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the definition of substance, even then the purpose of the definition is the establishment of substance-ness, because the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of substance-ness is produced by substance-ness itself. As for the conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) of substance-ness...

And [this is so] because it is produced by the cognition of substanceness (*dravyatva*); and because, in the case of substances that are not perceptible, there is an inference of substanceness which is likewise produced by the cognition of substanceness. Alternatively, the purpose [of the definition] is the establishment of [the fact that the object] is denotable by the word "substance" (*dravya*).
Therefore, the purpose of the definition of substance (*dravya*) is the establishment of its status as a substance;

or rather, the purpose of the definition of substance is the establishment of its being denotable by the word "substance. And thus, earth and the others are denotable by the word "substance" because they possess qualities (*guṇavat*). Whatever does not have this [quality] is not [denotable by that word].

Thus, it is as follows: "just as 'form' (rūpa)," and so forth. Nor is there here the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because the qualification is established by the inference: "the word 'substance' (*dravya*) has a denotable object, because it is a word, like the word 'cow'. And it is not thus...

Because there exists a similar instance (sapakṣa), the definition of substance lacks exclusivity (asādhāraṇatva) due to the uncertainty of its non-exclusion from the similar instance. Nor is the status of being a purely negative reason (kevalavyatirekin) destroyed by the possibility of positive concomitance (anvaya), because the presence of the probans in a similar instance is not ascertained. Nor...

The negative inference (vyatirekin) is redundant because the property of being denotable by the word "substance" (dravya-śabda-vācyatva) has not been ascertained in the subject (pakṣa) by means of the inferential proof of its differentiators. Nor is the negative inference redundant because the status of being denotable by the word "substance" is established through the linguistic usage of elders alone.

Because that [reason] cannot serve as a basis for reliance; otherwise, since the status of being denotable by the word "substance" would be established by the negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) alone, the futility of the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) would be difficult to avoid. Or, let it be so in the case of perceptible substances.
The establishment of the denotability of the word "substance" (dravya) arises from the linguistic usage of elders.

However, the establishment of the denotability of the word "substance" does not occur with respect to substances that are imperceptible, because the definition of substance consists solely of negative concomitance (kevalavyatirekin). Nor is there [such a case] here.
Because there exists a similar instance (sapakṣa), the reason is not "uniquely inconclusive" (asādhāraṇa), since [the probandum] is ascertained from that reason;

nor is its status as a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason destroyed by the possibility of positive concomitance (anvaya), because the establishment of positive concomitance is not a necessary precondition for the application of the qualification, just as it is not for the application of the qualifier itself.

Because the status of being a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is possible in the state where that [positive instance] is absent; nor is there futility of the probans (*sādhanavaiyarthyam*), because among substances that are not perceptible, there is an absence of usage by elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
Even if such usage were present, it would not be something upon which [the inference] depends. Nor is the previously mentioned [objection] applicable here.
The limiting adjuncts [are established] from the very reasoning previously stated;
or rather, let there be the establishment of the denotability by the word "substance" (dravya) in perceptible substances through the definition of substance as an anvaya-vyatireka [reason]. Not so.
And here, our own perceptions and other such factors do not serve as limiting conditions (upādhi), for the same reason stated previously.

Nor does the presence of a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) arise from the absence of a limiting condition; for even in the absence of the definition of a substance, it is not [invalidated] because of the presence of a limiting condition. Or, let it be so in the case of perceptible substances.

The establishment of [the property] being denotable by the word "substance" (dravya) follows from the definition of substance as that which possesses only positive concomitance (kevalānvayin). For instance, in all perceptible substances, one may argue: "An atom possesses that which is devoid of residing in an atom other than what is denoted by the word 'atom-substance', because it possesses qualities, like a jar," and so forth.

The phrase "because it is easily accessible" establishes the possession of exclusion (*vyāvṛttimatva*)— which is another synonym for differentiation (*bheda*)— as being devoid of the characteristics of a substance (*dravya*).
Nor is it impossible to comprehend all individual instances that lack the characteristics of a substance.
Because the state of possessing the exclusion from that [unestablished thing] is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*),
since what is to be proven is precisely the state of possessing the exclusion from those individuals that lack the characteristics of a substance as far as they are cognized. Nor...

Furthermore, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because the property of "possessing an exclusion from individuals devoid of the characteristic of being a substance that is currently undergoing realization" is unestablished anywhere; for it is established only in things such as a jar.
Because the exclusion of individual instances of perception that lack the definition of a substance is established by inference;
and [those instances] themselves do not possess the exclusion of individuals lacking the definition of a substance as understood through either perception or inference.

Because it lacks the characteristic of a substance as understood by others, and because it is excluded even from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is the fault of being "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇatā*);
for since that [subject] itself is not understood to possess the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*), one cannot ascertain the exclusion of the reason (*hetu*) from it. Not so.
Furthermore, for one who accepts that a jar possesses the exclusion of infinite imperceptible individuals devoid of the definition of a substance,
it is impossible for there to be a fixed gender based on the exclusion of those infinite imperceptible individuals devoid of the definition of a jar-substance.
Furthermore, that which possesses its fixed characteristic must necessarily be stated by another [means of knowledge]. Nor is the means of proof (sādhana) redundant,

because [the existence of the universal] is established through both perception and inference, based on the exclusion of individual instances— both perceptible and imperceptible— that lack the characteristic of being a substance residing in things such as jars.

Because, among perceptible substances, there is no certainty regarding the exclusion from the individual instances of the definition of substance that are themselves perceptible; and because it is impossible to rely upon a certainty regarding the exclusion from all perceptible and imperceptible instances— both those residing in perceptible substances and those devoid of the definition of substance.

Alternatively, let the probandum (sādhya) be simply the possession of exclusion from those individual perceptual instances that lack the characteristic of being a substance (*dravya*). Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because the probandum is established in the case of a jar itself. Nor is there the fallacy of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatā*) due to the existence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Because the reason does not exclude the similar instances (sapakṣa); nor is there a collapse of its status as a purely negative reason (kevalavyatirekin) due to the possibility of determining positive concomitance (anvaya) in the similar instances, since the determination of positive concomitance— unlike the establishment of the probandum— is not a necessary prerequisite.

Because there is no necessity for the operation of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) prior [to the establishment of the probandum], its operation cannot be avoided in the absence of that [prior certainty]. Nor is the means of proof (*sādhana*) redundant, with respect to perceptible substances.

Because, by means of a perception that establishes the possession of exclusion from all individual instances devoid of the definition of substance, one cannot ascertain— in those substances that are not perceived— the possession of exclusion from all perceived individual instances that are devoid of the definition of substance.
Regarding substances that are not perceived...

Furthermore, because the possession of exclusion from perceptual individuals that lack the characteristic of being a substance (*dravya*) is not apprehended by non-perception; or even if it were apprehended, it would not be something upon which [the inference] depends. Nor is there any pointlessness in the negative-only (*vyatirekin*) inference regarding jars and the like, because those are not depended upon as the subjects (*dharmin*). Or, let it be so.
Even if one were to grant that all perceptible substances other than the jar possess the status of being the subject (*dharmin*),
the proof remains redundant;
for there is an immediate experience of the exclusion of all perceptual instances that lack the definition of substance as residing in the jar.
And because it is not the object of any perceptual manifestation that is devoid of the characteristic of substance residing in jars and the like;
or, even if the jar were admitted as the subject (*dharmin*), nevertheless, the means of proof (*sādhana*) would not be futile.
Because the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) as residing in a jar is not something to be depended upon;

and even if the establishment of the state of being the probandum as residing in a jar and so forth were to be depended upon, it does not have the probandum residing in a jar as its object. Nor is it the case that...
Since it is impossible to comprehend all individual instances that lack the definition of substance,
the property of being excluded from them remains unestablished; thus, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*),
even though all individual instances lacking the definition of substance have not been comprehended.

For it is possible to perceive those exclusions (vyāvṛtti) which are in contact with the sense organs as residing in the jar; this is because it has been established that even without the perception of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), the nature of non-existence (abhāva) is logically accounted for.
Or rather, because what is to be proven is simply the possession of exclusion from individual instances that lack the characteristics of a substance as perceived by another's direct perception;
and there is no fault in proving the possession of exclusion from perceptible individuals that lack the characteristics of a substance.
The definition of substance is over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa) because it is excluded even from the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as the form of an atom;
furthermore, like imperceptible substances, imperceptible qualities also lack the certainty of possessing the property to be proven.

Because it is impossible for there to be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and because if its possession of the property to be proven were ascertained through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the operation of the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) prior to that [ascertainment] would be unavoidable. Nor is it the case that...

Because the absence of exclusion from all individual instances of direct perception— which lack the definition of a substance— is possible in a single locus, there is no impossibility of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*);
for the probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of possessing exclusion from all individual instances that lack the definition of a substance.

Because that absence, being a single entity, is possible everywhere, including in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; by this, it is also shown that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is untenable, since it is impossible for the absences of the exclusion from all individuals lacking the definition of substance— which are themselves of the nature of all those individuals lacking the definition of substance— to reside in a single location.

This is not tenable. A single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is being proven as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to all individual instances perceived as lacking the characteristics of a substance (*dravya*). Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because such a probandum (*sādhya*) is not unestablished; this is so—
The exclusion of form (*rūpavyāv� knowability* (*prameyatva*), like a jar; thus, the probandum is established by such [inferences]. Or, let it be so:

The probandum consists of all exclusions (vyāvṛtti) that are counter-correlates to every individual instance of perception devoid of the characteristics of substance. Nor is there a fallacy of an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā),
because even if the exclusions from all individual instances of perception devoid of the characteristics of substance are not established in a single locus, [the probandum remains valid].
Furthermore,

because [the property] is established by perception precisely within those perceptual exclusions that lack the characteristic of mutually distinct substances, the fault of the impossibility of its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not apply.

Because that [reason] is not a constituent part of inference; and because it is impossible to apprehend through perception the state of being pervaded by the exclusion from all things— which has as its counter-correlates (pratiyogin) all individual instances perceived as devoid of the definition of substance— since the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) would be impossible.

Furthermore, it has already been established that even when the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, the apprehension of its pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) is possible; nor do the previously mentioned *upādhis* apply here, for the same reason stated before. Moreover, there exists a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) which has as its counter-correlates all individual instances of perceptible objects that lack the definition of substance (*dravya*).
Because the probandum is established even without the exclusion of specific properties, and because there is no certainty regarding the pervasion of the probandum by the limiting condition (upādhi);

for it is impossible for all exclusions— each having as its counter-correlate every individual thing devoid of the definition of substance— to reside in a single locus, and thus the limiting condition [cannot be established].

And because there is certainty regarding its being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*). Nor is there a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*) here by means of [properties] such as cognisability (*prameyatva*), because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar and so forth, where the probandum is already established.
Nor is there a counter-balanced opposition due to the absence of our own perception and other means of knowledge.

Because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*) due to the absence of the characteristic of a substance (*dravya*). Nor does this [condition] constitute the "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), because it is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as a jar and so forth, which are instances where the probandum (*sādhya*) is established.
Therefore, substances are imperceptible.

All individual instances possess exclusions from everything that is counter-correlative to them and is devoid of the definition of a substance, because they are qualities; for whatever is not thus is not so, just as color (rūpa) is not [devoid of the definition of a substance]. This is how it should be stated.

Alternatively, the purpose of the definition of substance (*dravya*) is the establishment of the possession of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the six counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), namely: quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), genus-ness (*jātitva*), particularity-ness (*viśeṣatva*), inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*), and absence-ness (*abhāvatva*).
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) here, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is well-established in the case of a jar and other such things.

Nor are there such faults as the futility of the proof (sādhanavaiyarthyādi), for the same reason stated previously. Or, let it be that only one [property], such as the absolute absence of possessing qualities (guṇavattvātyantābhāva), is the probandum (sādhya). And in this case, the fault of having an unestablished qualifier (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) does not apply, even though the probandum itself is unestablished.
Because that absence [of the universal] is itself a quality, it can be apprehended by you,
and thus the apprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is possible. Nor is there an impossibility of negative concomitance,
because the absolute absence of the absolute absence of being a quality...

Since each [of the properties] such as *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality) is possible in [each of] the qualities and so forth individually, nor is there an "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) of the definition of substance— which is excluded even from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as a single property— by means of proving the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of *guṇatva*.

Furthermore, since karma and the like are not determined as being the probandum (*sādhya*), they are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*) and thus cannot constitute similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Nor is the means of proof (*sādhana*) redundant;
for the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) in substances that are not perceptible cannot be apprehended through perception.
Even in the case of perceptible substances,
since the perception that establishes the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) does not depend [on the prior perception of the substance],
at the time when that [perception] is absent...

This is because the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) is fruitful insofar as it generates the cognition that establishes the conventional usage of the absence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*); furthermore, on the view that "quality-ness" is not perceptible, the absence of "quality-ness" in jars and the like would also not be perceptible.

For it is precisely the absence of being a counter-correlative to perception that constitutes perceptibility; nor is this [reason] subject to a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) by means of "knowability" (prameyatva) and so forth, which would otherwise establish its status as a quality (guṇatva).
Because it is weak, being sublated by the perception of the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) residing in the jar;

nor is there any futility of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through that very perception which proves the absence of the property of being a quality has already been refuted. Not so.
Its status as a foundational premise (*upajīvyatva*) is due to its establishing the absence of a counter-argument;

for even though the perception that proves the absence of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) in a jar is a foundational premise, it nonetheless establishes the absence of quality-ness in cloth and other things. And by the term "quality-ness," what [is meant]?
The genus intended is one that is devoid of exclusion from that which possesses the characteristics of a quality;

or, while possessing exclusion from that which possesses the characteristics of a quality, it is excluded from "being" (*sat*). Not the first [alternative], because it would result in the fallacy of proving something other than the intended object (*arthāntara*) due to the existence of the counter-reason (*pratipakṣahetu*). Nor the second.

Because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of [the reason] such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) precisely in the locus of exclusion. Or, let it be that even in all substances, the probandum is the state of being an absolute absence (*atyantābhāvatva*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*); and in this case, there is no fault of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

This is established by such arguments as: "Because it possesses the property of being devoid of the state of residing in anything other than that which co-exists with the five absolute absences of *guṇatva* (quality-ness), because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like a jar. Nor is there any possibility of [the fallacy of] being the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth, because the absence of a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) probandum is unestablished.
Because it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of any reason whatsoever with that [subject],
and because when proving a different object (*arthāntara*), that different object cannot be avoided;
[this applies] to the other refutations of *mahāvidyā*.
And because [the fault] is removed according to its specific location, therefore,
wherever among people such as ourselves the possibility of removing a refutation exists,
one should establish the negative-only inference (vyatirekin) by resorting to each respective path.

Therefore, since it produces knowledge of substance, produces knowledge of the fact that [the term] "substance" is denotable, produces knowledge of substance as excluded from qualities and so forth, and produces knowledge of substance as devoid of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and the like, the definition of substance is purposeful; thus, the commencement of the Sūtra is justified.
Furthermore, the knowledge of substanceness (*dravyatva*) is precisely that which generates the knowledge of substance as excluded from qualities and so forth.

Substance is distinct from qualities and so forth, because it possesses the nature of substance (dravyatva); for there is the application of a negative inference (*vyatireki*) such that "whatever is not thus [i.e., does not possess the nature of substance] is not thus [i.e., is not distinct from qualities]. Likewise, even the cognition of a substance devoid of qualities and so forth is precisely what generates a cognition of a substance as excluded from qualities and so forth. Substance [is distinct] from qualities and so forth...

Because the inference "it is differentiated because it lacks the nature of a quality" proceeds, there arises a cognition excluded from qualities and so forth, and this is the cause for the meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) that is likewise excluded from qualities and so forth.
Furthermore, meditation upon substance as distinguished from qualities and so forth is the cause of the direct perception of substance as distinguished from qualities and so forth;
and the direct perception of substance as distinguished from qualities and so forth is the cause of liberation.
The direct realization of the Self, which is distinguished from the eight substances beginning with earth, as well as from qualities and so forth,
is the cause of liberation.

And that [realization] is produced by the meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) of the Self as distinguished from the eight substances beginning with earth, as well as from qualities and so forth.
If it is argued that this [knowledge] arises from the contemplation of the Self as distinct from the eight substances such as earth and from qualities and so forth,
and since that [distinction] follows simply from the definition of the Self, the definition of substance is redundant— [we reply]: no,
because the nature of the Self as a substance, which is excluded from qualities and so forth, is understood through the definition of substance.
Furthermore, since the distinctness [of the Self] from the eight substances beginning with earth is understood through another inference,
the contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) of the nature of the Self as distinct from the characteristics of the eight substances beginning with earth is established; thus,
the definition of "substance" (*dravya*) also possesses purposefulness.
That which subsists in a substance, does not possess qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions independently—this is the definition of a quality (guṇa). (1.1.15)
That which has a substratum (*āśraya*) is a "possessor of a substratum" (*āśrayin*), meaning it is "supported" (*āśrita*).

[The compound] *dravyāśrayī* means that which has a substance as its substratum, i.e., supported by a substance (*dravyāśrita*). Alternatively, that which is both a substance and a substratum is a "substance-substratum" (*dravyāśraya*); that which possesses this is a "possessor of a substance-substratum," i.e., supported by a substance.

This is the meaning. Therefore, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) is: that which is dependent on a substance (*dravya*), devoid of qualities, and lacking the status of being a cause independent of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*). This is established by the qualification "dependent on a substance."
By the exclusion of [substances] such as space which do not depend on other substances, by the qualification "devoid of qualities" which excludes things like jars that possess qualities,
and by the qualification "devoid of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction."
Some say that this is for the purpose of excluding actions that are causes independent of conjunction and disjunction.

That is not correct, because it would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to substances, inherence, universals, and absences, and because the qualification "residing in a substance" (dravyāśrita) would be redundant. [This applies] to ether and so forth...

Because [the definition] is already excluded by the very mention of "devoid of qualities" (guṇarahita). Now, if it is argued that a qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa) that excludes universals and so forth must be provided by the word occurring in the defining statement, since that alone is required; and that "possessing a universal" (sāmānyavattva) indeed excludes universals and so forth—[we reply:]...
And since that [quality] cannot be established by the literal meaning of the words "substance" and so forth, the term "dependent on substance" indicates the possession of a universal;
therefore, the term "dependent on substance" is not redundant. Nor does this definition apply to universals and the like.
A distinguishing qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) that serves as an exclusion (*vyāvartaka*) must be provided, because it is precisely that which is required.

You might think that "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavattva*) excludes universals and the like, and that this [definition] does not suffer from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*) according to its literal sense; but even that is not correct.

Since the exclusion of action (*karman*) is already established by the mere fact of being devoid of the causality of conjunction and disjunction, the qualification "independence" (*anapekṣatva*) is redundant.
If it is argued that "being devoid of the causality of conjunction and disjunction" alone constitutes the qualification— no, for in that case...
The qualification "devoid of being a quality" is redundant,

because substances are already excluded by the mere absence of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction; this applies equally to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), God, knowledge, desire, and effort, which [are also excluded] by that very same [criterion].

If it is argued that the defining characteristic is simply "the state of being devoid of being a cause of conjunction and disjunction," which is established by the exclusion of karma— no, for in that case, the qualification "devoid of qualities" would be redundant.
This is because substances are excluded by the very fact that they lack the status of being causes of conjunction and disjunction; furthermore,
the definition would be under-extensive (*avyāpaka*) with respect to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the knowledge, will, and effort of the Lord (*īśvara*),
since these are causes of conjunction and disjunction by virtue of being the generators of all produced things.

Furthermore, in order to avoid the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to the knowledge of God (*īśvara*) and the like, and to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to karma,
the qualification "devoid of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction" is included.
Although the knowledge of God and so forth are causes of conjunction and disjunction, they lack the status of being causes independent of conjunction and disjunction,
because they are causes that depend upon conjunction and disjunction. And this is also the case for action.

This is because of the qualification "being devoid of being a cause that is independent of conjunction and disjunction. Nor is the qualification "devoid of qualities" redundant, since substances are already excluded by the qualification "being devoid of being a cause that is independent of conjunction and disjunction."
If you think that [the definition] cannot be refuted because it is impossible to do so— this too is not correct;

for since the refutation is established by the fact that [the definition] is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) in the case of action (*karman*), precisely because it lacks the nature of being a cause independent of disjunction (*vibhāga*), and under-extensive (*avyāpti*) in the case of God’s knowledge and so forth.
The qualification "being a cause independent of conjunction" is redundant,
and because it has already been established that universals and so forth also possess universality, the fault of over-extension remains as it was.

The teachers of the Ātreya school, however, maintain that the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) is simply this: "a quality is that which is not a cause of conjunction or disjunction. They further state that the remainder [of the definition] is intended merely to describe its essential nature. That too is incorrect.

If it is argued that the qualification "being a cause" (*kāraṇatva*) must be employed in order to exclude [the definition] from being over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth— which also possess the property of being causes of conjunction and disjunction— we say: no, for even universals and the like...
Because they are the cause of producing a cognition qualified by themselves;

because a qualified cognition is produced by its qualifiers; and because of the inference: "Universals and so forth are [real] entities, because they are causes, like a jar. Now, [the opponent objects]:
The qualification "being the cause of that which lacks the nature of cognition" (jñānatvarahita) should be adopted;

and thus there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the dimension (parimāṇa) of the ultimate composite (antyāvayavin) and so forth, because even this [dimension] is the cause of the destruction (pradhvaṃsa) and so on of that which lacks the nature of cognition. Nor...
If you think that there is no pervasion [of the definition] by the dimension of an atom, because even that has action as its cause—
since it is determined through positive and negative concomitance that the dimension of a corporeal object is the cause of action— that is not so.

Because [the definition] would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) that produces a jar and so forth—which lacks the nature of knowledge—as well as the destruction of a cloth (paṭapradhvaṃsa) and so forth, which produces the destruction of the color and other qualities of that cloth.
If it is argued that the qualification "being an entity" (bhāvatva) should be added in order to exclude those cases—[we reply]: no.

Even when over-extension (*ativyāpti*) has been avoided in this way, the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the knowledge, will, and effort of God (*īśvara*) remains difficult to avoid;
for these [latter] are the generators of all effects.
Because it is untenable for it to be a non-producer of conjunction and disjunction,

and because it would lack pervasion in the case of the dimension of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth; for although those [dimensions] do not produce conjunction and disjunction, they are not non-producers of that which lacks the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*).
Others, however,
maintain that "residing in a substance" is one [definition],
while "being an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" is another, and thus it does not possess qualities.

They describe the meaning of the sūtra as follows; however, that too is not correct, because the property of "residing in a substance" (dravyāśritatva) is over-extensive (ativyāpaka), as it applies to action (karman) and so forth as well. For the purpose of excluding action...

If it is argued that what is intended is "being dependent on all substances"— no, because this would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to existence (sattā), substantiality (dravyatva), and so forth. If it is argued that what is intended is "being dependent on all substances while not being dependent on non-substances"— no.

[The definition] "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is too broad. If it is argued that [the definition should be] "that which, while being distinct from substance-ness..."—no, because it would still be too broad with respect to other definitions of substance.
If it is argued that the qualification "being distinct from the definition of substance" should be included—no.

Even if over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is thus avoided, the failure to include all qualities (*avyāpti*) remains unavoidable; for the property of "residing in all substances" cannot possibly exist in any [quality] whatsoever. Therefore, [the definition must be: "the state of possessing a subordinate genus (*avāntarajāti*) that resides in all substances."
If it is argued that [the definition] consists in "subsisting in all substances"— no;

for since the status of possessing a subordinate genus residing in what subsists in space (ākāśa) and so forth can serve as a valid definition, the inclusion of the word "all" (sarva) is not redundant, as it excludes the status of subsisting in other substances.

The definition that "a quality (guṇa) is that which is devoid of qualities and lacks the status of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction" is also not valid, because it over-extends to universals (sāmānya) and the like. If it is argued that the qualification "possessing a universal" (sāmānyavattva) should be included [in the definition], we say no; for even universals and the like possess universals.
Because the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpakatva*) remains as it was.

If you say, "provided that [the object] is distinct from generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), and absence (*abhāva*)"—no, because that would entail the necessity of supplying words not present in the original definition (*adhyāhāra*). Even if the over-extension is thus avoided, as for the definition...
And because it is difficult to comprehend: for if the absence of qualities is known, then the definition of a quality is known;
and if the definition of a quality is known, then the absence of qualities is known—thus there is a mutual dependence.
Others, however,
maintain that in the phrase "possessing qualities" (*guṇavān*), what is intended is contact with specific qualities; therefore,
[the subject] is devoid of touch that is dependent on substance.

They describe the definition as: "A quality is that which lacks the nature of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction. That too is not correct, because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) with respect to substances, inherence, universals, and so forth.
To exclude those, [the definition must include] the state of possessing existence while being distinct from universals, particulars, and inherence.
If it is argued that a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) must be supplied, we say no; for that would entail the fault of textual interpolation (*adhyāhāra*).

Furthermore, in the phrase "inherent in substance" (*dravyāśrita*), the qualification "substance" (*dravya*) is redundant, because by the very fact of being inherent, things such as space (*ākāśa*), which are not inherent, are already excluded.

Furthermore, in the definition "that which lacks the status of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction," the qualification "lacking the status of being a cause dependent on conjunction and disjunction" is redundant;
for action is already excluded by the phrase "being a cause independent of disjunction" alone.
Furthermore, because action cannot be excluded on the grounds that it lacks the status of being a cause independent of conjunction,
since action is devoid of being a cause independent of conjunction.
Because action produces conjunction immediately after the cessation of the previous conjunction following disjunction, the sūtra defining a quality (guṇa) is therefore untenable.
To this it is replied: that which has a substance as its substratum is "substance-dependent" (dravyāśraya).

In order to exclude [the categories of] substance, quality, action, and the universals (jāti) that reside therein, there is a generality (sāmānya)— a synonym for which is "objecthood" (arthatva)— which is called "existence" (sattā) by Udayana and others; it is "residing in substance" (dravyāśrayī), meaning that it exists in this [substance] as its substratum.
The meaning is "possessing an object," and its status as an object has already been established. In the phrase "not possessing qualities" (*na guṇavān*),
by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), specific qualities— namely number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction— are intended.

In the phrase "not a cause with regard to conjunctions and disjunctions" (*saṃyogavibhāgeṣvakāraṇam*), what is intended is the state of being devoid of causality that is independent [of others] (*anapekṣa*),
because the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is construed with the word "independent" (*anapekṣa*) by means of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Because that which has the same meaning as "samāna" (equal/same) is connected with a cause that is not a [logical] reason (*akāraṇa*), and because "a-" has the same meaning as "samāna" according to the grammatical rule: "The negative particle *nañ* [expresses] 'not-measure' (*amāna*), 'not' (*na*), and negation. Not.
Furthermore, if one accepts the compound *akāraṇam* as "non-cause" (na-kāraṇam),
then the definition of a quality (*guṇa*)— namely, that it is "not a cause of conjunction or disjunction"—

would result in the fallacy of being non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) with respect to the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara-jñāna*) and other such qualities. This is because the knowledge of the Lord and so forth...

Because it is the cause of conjunction and disjunction; and being the cause of conjunction and disjunction independently means that, while being a cause of conjunction, it is a cause of disjunction without depending [on anything else], since the word "independently" (anapekṣa) is construed only with "disjunction. [This is so] because it would also be construed with "conjunction."
Because it would follow that conjunction arises at the very moment of disjunction;
furthermore, since the definition is established by the mere fact of being a cause of conjunction,
the qualification "independence" (anapekṣatva) is redundant.

If it is argued that the inclusion of "having conjunction as its cause" is redundant— because [the definition] would over-apply to action (karman) simply by virtue of being devoid of a cause independent of disjunction, and because it would fail to apply (avyāpti) to the will, effort, and unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the Lord (Īśvara)— we say: no.
This is because it is intended to exclude the under-extension (*avyāpti*) that would otherwise apply to the disjunction between the hand and the wall,

which produces the disjunction between the body and the wall; for it is impossible for the disjunction between the hand and the wall to be devoid of [the quality of] being a cause independent of the disjunction between the body and the wall, provided that it is a cause of conjunction.

Furthermore, the property of "being devoid of being a cause that does not depend on disjunction" is also possible in cases such as the disjunction of a hand from a wall, which produces the disjunction of the body from the wall;
nor does this result in circular reasoning, because [the definition] involves the absence of qualities (*guṇarahitatva*).
Because the state of being a qualifier characterized by qualities is not admitted, and because number and the like are defined solely as "number-ness" and so forth;
therefore, that which is the substratum of objecthood is not the substratum of number and the like in its capacity as a cause of conjunction.

The definition "a quality is that which lacks the nature of being a cause independent of [other] divisions" is thus established. Likewise, by substituting the word "number" (saṃkhyā) with the words "dimension" (parimāṇa), "separateness" (pṛthaktva), "conjunction" (saṃyoga), or "disjunction" (vibhāga), [the same definition applies].
The fourfold definition should be understood as follows:

alternatively, in the phrase "possessing qualities" (*guṇavān*), the absence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) is indicated by the absence of the absence of qualities (*guṇarahitatva*). Thus, there is no mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*), because [the absence of substantiality] is [established] through the absence of the absence of qualities.

Because there is an absence of the qualification of being a specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇaviśeṣaṇatva*), and because *dravyatva* (substantiality) can be defined even without a quality simply by its being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, that which is the substratum of objecthood (*arthatva*) while devoid of substantiality, and which is a cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)...
The meaning of the sūtra is that a quality (guṇa) is that which lacks the nature of being a cause independent of disjunction (vibhāga).
Alternatively, the phrase "not possessing qualities" intends to exclude the absence of contact with specific qualities,
for the purpose of excluding non-dependent entities such as space (ākāśa) and the like.

And in order to obtain the qualification of "residing in substance" (*dravyāśritatva*), the term *dravyāśrayī* must be repeated. It is a "substance-residence" (*dravyāśraya*) because it is both a substance (*dravya*) and a residence (*āśraya*).
That which possesses this [quality] is "resident in substance" (*dravyāśrayī*); thus, by this, the state of residing in substance is obtained. Nor is it...

There is no thing to be excluded from the definition of substance (*dravya*), because such a thing would not be included within the definition itself. Nor is the mention of "substance" redundant, as it serves to dispel the doubt that qualities (*guṇa*) might not reside in substances. And so:

There is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because the absence of qualities (*guṇarahitatva*) is not a qualifying attribute of the definition, and because touch is defined solely by touch itself. Therefore, that which is the substratum of the object is devoid of the touch that is dependent upon it.
The meaning of the aphorism is that the definition [of action] is a quality (guṇa) devoid of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction.
Alternatively, the phrase "not possessing qualities" (na guṇavān) serves as a specific qualification of the definition, meaning that action itself is devoid of qualities.

Nor is there a circularity in this way; for even when a quality is defined by its being devoid of qualities, it is not by means of that definition—such as "being devoid of qualities"—that the quality itself is defined, since that [definition] merely establishes its difference from others. By means of the quality...
Furthermore, even when defining characteristics such as being devoid of qualities (*guṇarahitatva*),
qualities are defined simply as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) even without those specific characteristics;
and this is because of quality-ness itself.

Because it is defined as a genus that does not reside in any genus, being devoid of the twenty-four genera such as "form-ness" (rūpatva) which are excluded from form and so forth; and because, even when the definition of a quality— such as its being devoid of qualities— is not apprehended, it is still "form."

Furthermore, the nature of *guṇatva* (the quality-ness) can be understood through such inferences as: "That which possesses a universal (*jāti*) that does not reside in anything devoid of the universals residing in color, nor in anything devoid of the exclusions from taste and so forth residing in color, nor in anything devoid of the twenty-four universals such as color-ness itself; because it possesses a universal, like a jar.
Alternatively, let the definition of *guṇatva* be established by the very definition of a quality (*guṇa*).

Nevertheless, there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because the definition of substance is established precisely through the definition of quality, by means of such formulations as: "that which is the cause of conjunction while being devoid of the causality of disjunction, and so forth, excluding [the properties of] being devoid of qualities and the like. Thus, it is based on the objecthood [of substance] as distinguished from those [qualities].

If it is argued that, since this [other definition] exists, let this alone suffice—what is the use of that? We say no; for even that [definition] does not lose its status as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) due to its being faultless.
This is because, in order to avoid mutual dependence (parasparāśraya), one must necessarily rely upon this very [definition].

If it is argued that the definition consisting of "being devoid of qualities" and so forth is useless because the exclusion of others (itarabheda) and other properties are established by other means—[we reply: no, for this [definition] is not useless, as it generates an inference of the exclusion of others that is not produced by other definitions of quality.
This is so even when there exists a definition of quality distinct from this one.
Furthermore, because this [definition] is not necessarily required for the establishment of the definition of a quality (*guṇa*),

one should not say that "only this [definition] exists" as such; for the definition of a quality can be established by other definitions as well, and thus that [other definition] would be what is required.

If it is argued that [the definition] must depend upon [other definitions] for the sake of its own determination—no; for by the reasoning already stated, it is established that not all [definitions] necessarily require such dependence. The plural number in the phrase "in conjunctions and disjunctions" (*saṃyogavibhāgeṣu*) is for the purpose of stating their essential nature, and is not included within the definition itself.
Because there is no [other] thing to be excluded.

Alternatively, what is intended is the state of being devoid of being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction, or the state of being devoid of being a non-inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction.

And being devoid of non-inherent causality for conjunction and disjunction means either: (1) being a cause while lacking non-inherent causality for disjunction; or (2) being a cause of disjunction while lacking non-inherent causality for conjunction; or (3) the absence of both [non-inherent causality for conjunction and disjunction].
If there were an intention to specify the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in both cases, the qualification would be redundant.

The qualification "being a cause of conjunction" is included in order to avoid the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) to such things as the hand or a wall, which are the non-inherent causes of the disjunction between the body and a wall.

Furthermore, the qualification "being the cause of disjunction" (*vibhāgakāraṇatve sati*) is added in order to avoid the over-extension (*avyāpti*) [of the definition] to cases such as the contact between the hand and the wall, which serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the contact between the body and the wall.
Regarding this, one should either exert effort to avoid the objections arising from an examination of the definition of a non-inherent cause,
or else disregard them.
And the word "iti" in such a sūtra is for the purpose of excluding other definitions;
thus, a quality (guṇa) is an object that does not reside in substances or actions.
A quality (*guṇa*) is an object devoid of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*).
