A quality is an object that is the substratum of that which is devoid of subsisting in what possesses number and devoid of subsisting in action.
An object that possesses [the property of] being devoid of subsisting in what possesses number, yet does not subsist in throwing upward, contraction, expansion, or going, is [a quality].

This is the quality [definition]. Likewise, by substituting the term "number" with the terms "dimension," "separateness," "conjunction," and "disjunction," and by adopting the qualification "being devoid of subsistence in action," there are four definitions.

Likewise, by substituting the term "functioning as action" (*karmavṛttitva*) with the terms "functioning as throwing upward," "throwing downward," "contracting," "extending," and "going," four definitions are to be understood.

A quality (*guṇa*) is that which is the substratum of that which does not reside in what possesses conjunction (*saṃyoga*), yet resides in action (*karman*), and which is devoid of residing in that which resides in action.
[It is] that which resides in what possesses conjunction, yet is devoid of [residing in] throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.
A substance possessing a function is a quality.
A quality is that which is the locus of something that resides in [substances] possessing division, yet does not reside in actions.

A substance (guṇa) is that entity which is the substratum of what is devoid of subsistence in what possesses division and is also devoid of subsistence in action. A substance is that entity which is the substratum of what is devoid of subsistence in dimension and is also devoid of subsistence in action.

Quality (*guṇa*). A category that does not reside in that which possesses dimension, and which does not reside in throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, or locomotion, is quality. A category that does not reside in that which possesses separateness, and which does not reside in action (*karman*), is quality.

A substance that possesses the qualities of upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*), downward motion (*avakṣepaṇa*), contraction (*ākuñcana*), expansion (*prasāraṇa*), and locomotion (*gamana*), while being devoid of the state of possessing qualities, is a quality (*guṇa*).

Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) between these two [definitions], because it is possible to define something as a quality even without a formal definition of "quality. Nor...
In all cases, the inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*) is redundant, because it serves the purpose of excluding universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

As for what was stated by Vidhādhara Miśra and others—that [the definition of quality] is: "a quality possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and is non-co-instantaneous with conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is not co-instantaneous with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*)"—[this is incorrect].

This is not tenable, because it overextends to universals (*jāti*) and so forth; for the universal "universal-ness" (*jātitva*), the qualifier "universal-ness," and other such universals— which do not reside in upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*), which are co-instantaneous with conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and which are directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*)— also exist within universals and the like.

Because [the definition] would be unavoidable in cases such as "that which possesses a genus not occurring at a moment, because it is an object of cognition," and because it would be over-extensive in the case of throwing downwards (*avakṣepaṇa*), since it lacks the property of being co-located with conjunction (*saṃyoga*) while not occurring in throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*).
Because only [qualities] such as throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*), which are directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), actually exist there.

If it is argued that "throwing downward-ness" (*avakṣepaṇatva*) and so forth do not constitute being directly pervaded by existence—[we reply: no, for [the definition of] being directly pervaded by existence is...
Is it intended that [the property] is directly pervaded by manifest existence (*aparokṣasattā*),
or rather that it is pervaded by existence while not being pervaded by a genus excluded from the substrata of existence,
or that it is pervaded by existence while lacking pervasion by a genus excluded from the substrata of existence?
Or [is it the first]? Not the first, because even throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*) and so forth are directly perceived as being pervaded by existence (*sattā*).
Nor the second, because even throwing downward and so forth do not fail to be pervaded by potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, which are excluded from the substrata of existence. Nor the third.

Furthermore, since the property of possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) is pervaded by "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), which is excluded from the substrata of existence (*sattāśraya*), it would follow that it lacks the property of being pervaded by a genus (*jāti*) excluded from the substrata of existence; consequently, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) would be impossible. This would apply to substance (*dravya*) and the others as well.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for [the property] to be devoid of that [universal], given that it is pervaded by substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth which are excluded from the substrata of existence (*sattā*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that it is not directly pervaded by existence itself.
This is provided that it lacks pervasion by any universal excluded from the substrata of existence and distinct from quality-ness (*guṇatva*).
If it is argued that being directly pervaded by existence (sattā) is possible in the case of quality-ness (guṇatva), because it is directly pervaded by existence— [we reply: no,
because action-ness (karmatva) and so forth are pervaded by actions and the like, which are excluded from the substrates of existence other than quality-ness.

If it is argued that because the impossibility of being devoid of that [quality] entails the possibility of the absence of being directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), there must be only one [such quality]— we say no,
because it would follow that the qualification "not residing in throwing upward" (*utkṣepaṇāvṛttitva*) is redundant for the sake of [defining] action-ness (*karmatva*).

This is because [the unwanted case] is already excluded by the qualification "directly pervaded" (*sākṣād-vyāpyatva*) itself. By this, the following definition is also refuted: "Being directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) is being directly pervaded by existence while lacking the state of being a sub-class of a sub-class of existence."

Because the meaning of the term "subordinate genus of existence" (sattāvāntarajātī) is precisely the exclusion from the substratum of existence and the exclusion from the substratum of the genus [of being], and because that has already been refuted previously.
If it is argued that [the definition of a quality] is "being directly pervaded by existence (sattā) while being distinct from either quality-ness (guṇatva) or action-ness (karmatva)," we say no;

for the definition of a quality is established by the mere statement "a quality is that which possesses quality-ness," and thus the futility of the additional qualifiers is as indelible as adamantine glue.

Furthermore, because it is possible for there to exist a genus that is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), which resides in color (*rūpa*) and so forth, and which coexists with the action of throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*)—the latter being coextensive with the action of throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*)—[as follows]:

"That which possesses a genus that does not reside in throwing downward, yet is excluded from color and so forth (which, while coexisting with conjunction, lack the property of residing in throwing downward), and is itself not non-resident in throwing downward, is [such a thing], because it is knowable (*prameya*), like a jar. This is established through inference. Moreover, the inclusion of the term "genus" (*jāti*) would otherwise be redundant.

If it is argued that the term "universal" (*jāti*) is included in the definition in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to throwing downward (*avakṣepaṇa*) and other such actions—which possess an absolute absence of a form directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) that is co-located with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), returning motion (*āvṛtti*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—we say no. For what is this "universality" (*jātitva*): is it a universal (*jāti*), or is it [defined by] eternality?
Or [is it] "being inherent in many" and so forth?
Not the first, because you do not accept that. Not the second, because the avoidance of over-extension is established by the very fact of being inherence; for if [inherence] were non-eternal...

Because the property of depending on many [substances] is redundant; for, given that it is inherence (*samavāya*), the state of being an inherent category (*samaveta-padārtha*) consists precisely in its being dependent. By this, [it is shown that] a quality (*guṇa*) is that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and residing in a conjunction that is not produced by a conjunction non-residing in a jar.
Thus, that definition is refuted.

Furthermore, the definition "a quality which possesses a genus that does not reside in conjunction, does not reside in the non-inherent cause of conjunction, and is devoid of being produced by conjunction" is also not a valid definition, because it over-extends to universals (*jāti*) and other categories.
Furthermore, because of the futility of what was stated previously:

Is "being the non-inherent cause of conjunction" defined as being a cause of conjunction while lacking the status of being an inherent locus of conjunction, or [is it] being a non-inherent cause while...
Or [is it] being the cause of conjunction? Not the first,
because it would result in the lack of pervasion (*avyāpakatva*) regarding the qualities of God’s knowledge, will, effort, and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*),
since God’s knowledge and the rest do not have conjunction as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Because, if the universals residing in those [qualities] were non-inherent causes of conjunction by virtue of being causes of conjunction, it would be untenable for them not to subsist in the cause of conjunction. Nor is the second [alternative] correct,
because [the definition] "the state of being devoid of the specific qualities of the self and of substance-ness" [is flawed].

In the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) by means of a quality— namely, the definition characterized as "being a non-inherent cause that lacks the property of being a producer solely of specific qualities of the self"— and in the determination of a quality by means of the definition of a quality, [the definition] is unsuitable because it lacks the state of being an entity devoid of the production of only the specific qualities of the self.

It is a great oversight on the part of the modern logicians— who, in order to avoid mutual dependence, have formulated definitions of qualities that include non-inherent causality— as that very same [fallacy] has presented itself before them.
Even when mutual dependence is avoided by our method,
[it remains necessary] upon considering the definition of the first particularity included within the definition of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Because its redundancy is difficult to avoid; for, given that it resides in itself, the meaning of the term "specific quality of the self" is the state of being a specific quality of the self. And thus, [the definition] is: that which does not reside in the self, is not the cause of a conjunction not produced by [another] conjunction, and does not coexist with conjunction.
Thus, it is refuted.

It is not tenable to define [velocity] as "a quality that possesses a genus which does not reside in velocity produced by [another] velocity and does not reside in the same locus as velocity," because of the previously mentioned defects and because it would be over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to the self (ātman).
Because [the property] residing in the non-inherent cause of velocity— which is not produced by velocity—
is possible in the self, given that "selfhood" (ātmatva) is co-located with velocity;
and because the qualification of being directly pervaded by existence has already been refuted.

Nor is it correct to define [action] as "a quality that possesses a genus which does not reside in conjunction and does not reside in that which is not the non-inherent cause of velocity produced by velocity," because this definition is over-extensive (ativyāpaka) with respect to space and time;
for, in the view that admits multiple spaces and times, one must accept genera such as "spatiality" (dikkālatva) and so forth.

And because that [substance] does not have its formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as a common substratum; and because in space, time, and ether, there is the acceptance of a genus manifested by supreme magnitude devoid of cognition; and because in space and time, there is no acceptance of a genus for that magnitude which is devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Time.

[The definition: "That which possesses a genus residing in a quality that does not coexist with [the genus] residing in time—which is devoid of the property of residing in time that is co-locus with *saṃskāra* (disposition)—and which does not have as its non-inherent cause a velocity produced by velocity, because it is knowable (*prameyatva*), etc."—this [definition] is not difficult to avoid [as being too narrow]. Furthermore, due to the previously mentioned defects, [the definition]: "A quality that possesses a genus which does not coexist with a genus similar to the genus of the non-inherent cause of the non-inherent cause of cognition" [is also flawed].
This also is not a definition, because of the previously mentioned fault;
for it over-extends to the action of impact (*abhighātakarman*),

since it possesses a genus that is non-co-instantaneous with a genus which is the non-inherent cause of a cognition occurring as produced by impact, while being excluded from the action of the mind produced [by that impact].

And mental action, because it is devoid of contact, cannot result from impact; furthermore, since mental action is not produced by impact, [the definition] excludes it. For one who is in disagreement, [the definition] is: that which possesses a genus devoid of being produced by impact or being devoid of subsistence.
The inference "because it possesses a genus, like a jar" is [untenable],

since the exclusion of action is already established by the fact that [the property in question] does not reside in that which is the non-inherent cause of a disjunction qualified by being the non-inherent cause of a conjunction.
The definition "a quality is that which possesses a genus residing in itself or elsewhere" is also not correct, because it overextends to particulars (*viśeṣa*) and so forth;
for even those possess a genus such as "particularity" which resides in themselves or in other particulars.

Nor is it correct to say that a quality (guṇa) is that which possesses a genus residing in a function (vṛtti) that does not reside in a pot; for this definition is over-extensive (ativyāpaka), as it would include motion (karman), since it has already been established that there exists a genus residing in both qualities and motions that does not reside in substances.
Furthermore, [the definition] is over-extensive with respect to genus (*jāti*) and so forth,

because one accepts that even in those [categories], there exist genera that subsist only in non-substances (*adravyamātravṛtti*). Nor is it the case that "a quality is that which possesses another genus subsisting in *saṃskāra*."
The definition [of action] is too broad, because it overextends to substances and actions;
for a genus that resides only in qualities and actions is admitted to exist even in action, as it subsists in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). The same applies to other [definitions] as well.
The objections conceived by modern logicians based on the priority of genus have been refuted.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that "quality" is any one of the twenty-four categories.
Because it is impossible to know all individual forms, it is likewise impossible to know even any one of them;
for [the object] would have to possess the property of being any one among those forms already apprehended.
Furthermore, [the definition] fails because it does not encompass those things whose form and so forth have not been apprehended.
Nor is "a quality being a possessor of properties distinct from form and so forth" a valid definition, because it is impossible to know all forms and other such properties.
Because it is impossible to know even the state of being distinct from that which is distinct from those properties;
namely, the state of possessing properties distinct from all known properties such as form and so forth.
Furthermore, this is because it does not pervade [the category of] color and so forth as understood by you.

However, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*)— namely, "that which is the substratum of that which is devoid of being distinct from the twenty-four universals such as color-ness (*rūpatva*)"— is indeed perfectly correct.
Therefore, this is the secret here:
wherever the possibility of removing the refutations we have [previously] desired exists.
Let each of these characteristics of the qualities be as desired.
And since the purpose of the definition has already been stated, everything is entirely satisfactory. || 15 ||
Action is defined as that which inheres in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. (1.1.16)

"Subsisting in a single substance" (*ekadravyam*) means that which has a single substance as its substratum; that is to say, the state of being pervaded by a single substance. "Not a quality" (*aguṇam*) means the absence of qualities; that is to say, the state of being non-qualitative. And the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*)...
It is connected with conjunction and disjunction.
The plural number in the phrase "in conjunctions and disjunctions" is used because action produces many conjunctions and disjunctions with substances, qualities, and so forth.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity to produce many conjunctions and disjunctions; for, since there is nothing to be excluded, it is impossible for the plurality of conjunctions and disjunctions to be included within the definition. As for the word "independent" (anapekṣa), however...

It is connected only by non-separation (avibhāga). For even if there were a connection by way of conjunction (saṃyoga), since action would be the cause of conjunction without depending on [another] conjunction,
it would follow that conjunction would arise at the very moment of separation.
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras has no intention to define a cause that is independent of conjunction and yet useless for the purpose of defining characteristics.

Therefore, action is that which is pervaded by oneness and is independent of disjunction as its cause; it is that which, being devoid of the quality of "quality-ness," is independent of disjunction as its cause,
while possessing conjunction as its cause.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that action (karman) has three defining characteristics: it is a cause independent of disjunction (vibhāga),
and [it is a cause] while being a cause of conjunction (saṃyoga).
If it is argued that action (*karman*) alone may be the cause of disjunction (*vibhāga*), and what is the use of the specific qualification of "independence" (*anapekṣatva*)— we say no;
for [the qualification] is intended to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the Lord’s knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth.
Now, what is this "being a cause independent of disjunction"? It is certainly not the state of being a cause of disjunction while being independent of other causes.
Because it does not depend upon an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); nor [is it so] because,
while not depending on causes distinct from the inherent cause and the others, [it arises].
It is not the cause of division (*vibhāga*), because it depends upon God’s knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth;
nor is it [the cause] in the sense of being independent of any cause other than the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)— namely, God’s knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit, space, time, and the self.

The definition of action (karma) as "being the cause of disjunction" is over-extensive with respect to objects such as a jar, because it would also apply to the prior non-existence of disjunction, which is required [as a cause].
And because, in the analysis of that which is produced by the action of both [agent and object], there is no dependence on a second action;
nor [is it possible] given the independence from causes other than substance-ness, the Lord’s knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), prior non-existence, and action.
If it were the cause of disjunction,
then time, the inherent cause, and God would also necessarily follow as causes that do not depend on [other] disjunctions; for they too—
Because it does not depend on any cause other than substance-lessness, the knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), prior non-existence, and action of God;
nor does it depend on any cause other than substance-lessness, the knowledge, will, effort, unseen merit, prior non-existence, and the second action of God.

If it were the state of being a cause of disjunction, then there would be the undesirable consequence that even inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and the like would not depend on [further] disjunctions. Nor is it [the state of being a cause of disjunction] in the sense of not depending on a cause that arises in the moment immediately following its own production.

And [the definition of a cause] as the cause of division would result in the fallacy of non-pervasion (ananugama) of the definition if the word "own" (sva) did not denote specific individuals; for if action were denoted [instead], [the definition would fail to apply].
Because if the Lord’s will and knowledge were the non-inherent causes,
it would follow that they are causes independent of disjunction; for even those [will and knowledge] produce disjunction.

Because it does not depend on a cause that arises immediately after the action; nor is it the state of being the final cause of disjunction, since that too cannot be defined. Is the state of being the final cause of disjunction [defined as] being the final [cause] with respect to disjunction?
[The definition of the cause of disjunction is] either being a cause, or being a cause of disjunction while being the final [moment],
or being a cause of disjunction while having arisen in the moment immediately preceding the disjunction. Not the first [alternative].

Because it is impossible for [the disjunction] to be the final one since it has already arisen prior to the [subsequent] disjunction; for the meaning of the word "final" (carama) is that which occurs subsequently. Nor is the second [alternative], because:
Otherwise, for some reason or other, even a jar or similar object would result in being the final cause of disjunction;
and if [disjunction] were the final cause of disjunction...

For it would follow that even a cloth or other object produced immediately after a pot— which itself is the cause of a disjunction— would be a cause of disjunction independently of any other disjunction;
furthermore, it is impossible for anything to possess the status of being the final cause of all disjunctions.

The first [alternative] is untenable because it is impossible for an action to be the final [cause], as it is impossible for it to be the final cause of disjunction. Nor is the third [alternative] valid, because it would over-extend to jars and other such things; for those too...

"Because, while being produced in the moment immediately preceding the disjunction of a pillar and so forth that arises in the moment immediately following the moment of the jar and so forth, it is the cause of its own inherent disjunction"— this is incorrect,
because [the reason] consists in having the nature of producing disjunction, which is synonymous with *vibhāga-kurvad-rūpa* (the state of being currently performing the act of disjoining).
Because the meaning of the word "non-dependent cause" (*anapekṣakāraṇatva*) is a specific kind of action (*karmaviśeṣa*),
and because that [action], being excluded from other categories of things,
is a non-cause that does not produce disjunction (*vibhāga*).

[The subject] is the locus of that which is devoid of the state of being an effect of the disjunction of causes, and is devoid of subsisting in that [disjunction], because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*),
like a jar; thus, from this inference, [it follows that] the nature of being a cause independent of disjunction [is established].

And it is indeed a genus (jāti). Nor is there a confusion of genera (jātisaṃkara) due to qualities and so forth, because that is not a defect. [The objection that it would be] a property (upādhi) is refuted, because, like knowability (prameyatva) and the like, it is included within non-existence (abhāva). Let it be so, then.

If it is asked whether the definition of action (*karman*) as a cause independent of disjunction is incorrect because it is also a cause of conjunction— [we reply: no, for [the definition applies even to] the disjunction between the hand and the wall which does not produce disjunction in the body.
"Because it is a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction.

Alternatively, the definition of action (karma) is "that which is a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction"; thus, the definition is "action is action. It is not [the case that this definition is redundant].

And thus, because action is defined by means of action itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); furthermore, since it is impossible for an action to reside within another action, [action] cannot serve as its own definition. [For if one says] "action, action," [the term] "action" refers to that which is the locus of the property of being an action (*karmatva*).
Because it is explained [otherwise]. Nor is there a circularity (*parasparāśraya*) such that the action is defined by its "action-ness" (*karmatva*), and "action-ness" is defined by the action;
for even if the action were defined by its "action-ness," [it would still be defined] by the action...
If it is argued that "action-ness" (karmatva) is the universal residing in what is not defined by anything else,
and that this [universal] is defined by action itself— [we reply: no.

Because [the definition] is established by defining throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and movement as being devoid of deviation, and because action is not defined by "action-ness" (karmatva) itself.
For it has been stated that the definiendum is not defined by its definition;
rather, [the definition] is established through its distinction from others. This is because "action-ness" (karmatva) is appropriately a definition of action by virtue of being the locus of action.
Alternatively, [the reason] is for the purpose of negating the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of action (*karman*).
Thus, action is not a substance, because it inheres in a single substance and because it is devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), like color (*rūpa*). Now, as for its inherence in a single substance—

If [the definition] is "residing in a substance that is the locus of unity," then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to jars and the like, because those are not so resident. Alternatively, if it is "not residing in multiple substances," then...
There is an inconclusiveness regarding space and so forth,
because they, being non-dependent, are dependent upon more than one [substratum].
Now, if [the definition] is "not being dependent on more than one while not being dependent on a substance," then...
This is unestablished, because the action [of moving] has the sense of negation.
Some say that when a jar moves, its color and other qualities move; it is for the purpose of refuting that [view].
The apprehension that action (karman) is dependent upon a substance (dravya). And thus, color and the like do not possess action, because they are not substances, just like action itself.
Action is a substance, provided it possesses a universal (sāmānya).
If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) because [the subject] is the cause of producing conjunction and disjunction, like a jar— [we reply: no,
because the probans is overqualified by the condition (upādhi) of "not being the cause independent of disjunction."

And because it is sublated by that proof, the word "substance" (dravya) has as its meaning a universal that— while being excluded from those things where the word functions as denoting an action or a substance—
is not excluded from the nine characteristics beginning with earth; for such is the referent of the word "substance."

If it is argued that "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is the nature of a genus that does not reside in qualityless [entities] and is devoid of exclusion from those possessing qualities, and that this definition is not contradicted— [we reply: no, because [it would apply] to action (*karman*), which is devoid of qualities.
"Because it is not so"—
or rather, some maintain that conjunction and disjunction themselves are action;
to refute that, it was stated [in the definition] that action "resides in a single substance and is devoid of qualities."

Conjunction and disjunction possess multiple substances and are qualities; however, action possesses a single substance. Furthermore, these [conjunctions and disjunctions] are not actions, because they are qualities and disjunctions. Therefore...
Because it possesses conjunction and disjunction resulting from that action,
like the conjunction and disjunction of other things; or rather, as Bhūṣaṇa says, action is a quality.

To refute that [objection], it is stated that [the Self] is "without qualities" (*aguṇa*), explaining it as "that which does not possess qualities. This is because, while [qualities] exist, they reside in the threads, like a cloth [residing in its threads].
[The Self] is the substratum devoid of being a locus for the operation of action and qualities, and devoid of being a locus for the operation of action itself.
Because it is an object of cognition (*meyatvāt*), like a jar; or, a quality (*guṇa*) is like action (*karman*), because it is a cause independent of disjunction (*vibhāga*), like disjunction itself;
or, because it possesses generality (*sāmānyavattva*) while being dependent on a single substratum, like color (*rūpa*).

Is "sapratipakṣa" intended to mean "jāti" (a futile rejoinder) or something else? Not the first, because there would be a contradiction in establishing the definition of a quality (*guṇa*)—such as being devoid of the causality that does not depend on conjunction or disjunction—and so forth. Nor the second.
In the proof of a genus that exists only in qualities and possesses the characteristic of being a quality,

there is sublation precisely because one accepts a genus that does not reside in substances but resides in qualities, as well as a genus that resides in actions; even if such [genuses] were not accepted.
Because it would be impossible to prevent such other objects as "genus" (*jāti*) or "thing-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) [from being included].
The word *iti* is intended to include other such definitions; thus, for example, "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is an object devoid of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). Action...
Action is that which is the locus of being distinct from throwing upward, contracting, expanding, and moving forward, and so forth.

Action is defined as that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*) and not co-located with conjunction (*saṃyoga*) while being devoid of the property of exclusion from number (*saṃkhyāvyāvṛttitva*);
for these [qualities] possess the genus "dimensionality" (*parimāṇatva*) and others, which are devoid of the property of exclusion from number yet are co-located with conjunction.
If it is argued that the term "directly pervaded by existence" (sattāsākṣādvyāpya) is included for the purpose of excluding that [fallacy], we say no; for this has already been refuted.

Furthermore, "action is that which possesses a genus not co-located with the conjunction of the non-occurrence of [subsidiary] functions" is also not a definition, because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like,
and because it is over-extensive with respect to color (*rūpa*) and the like; for these too [possess such a genus].
Because it possesses a genus that resides in conjunction and action, while being devoid of the state of having a common substratum with conjunction;
for even in the case of qualities and actions, a non-exclusive genus is admitted. By this, [the objection is refuted].

The two definitions— "action which possesses a genus that resides in the inherent cause of a disjunction not produced by [another] disjunction, and does not reside in the same locus as that disjunction," and "action which possesses a genus that has speed as its non-inherent cause, and is not produced by speed"— are both refuted.

The definition "action possessing a genus that resides in the inherent cause and non-inherent cause of a jar, but does not reside in the jar" is also not a valid definition, because of the previously mentioned faults and because it over-extends to [qualities such as] color and so forth. Ghaṭā...
Because it is possible for the conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*) also to be a cause,
and because the quality of being a quality (*guṇatva*), which resides in that [conjunction], is unestablished in color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which do not reside in a pot.
Because there is the fault that [the definition] would exclude [qualities] residing in a genus that inheres in a disjunction which is qualified by being an inherent cause of conjunction;
and because, in the phrase "qualified by being an inherent cause of conjunction," the qualification "inherent cause" (asamavāyi) is redundant.

The definition "action possessing a genus that resides in the non-inherent cause and inherent cause of eternal earth-form, but does not reside in atoms" is also not a valid definition, because it is redundant;
for by the very fact of being the non-inherent cause of eternal form, the required conjunction is already excluded.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "supreme" (parama) would be redundant; for existence (*sattā*) is already excluded by the fact that [the property in question] does not reside in atoms, and because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) with respect to color and other qualities. [This is so] because the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the color of an atom...

Because it is possible for the conjunction of the fire-particle with the earth-atom to also be a cause; and because the quality-ness residing therein exists in color and other qualities residing in the atom.

Furthermore, the definition "action is that which possesses the genus of having the nature of moving toward time, upward throwing, or downward throwing" is also not a valid definition, because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) with respect to effects, substances, and qualities;
for the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) exists in those as well.

Because it accepts a genus that resides in action alone; and because, while not residing in time, it does not reside in upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*). By this, the definition "action is that which possesses a genus residing in upward motion, other than existence" is also [established].
Refuted; for among the qualities of an effect-substance, one accepts a genus that is manifested by the effect. Against one who is in disagreement, [the argument is]:
"The jar..."
[The definition is] "possessing a genus that is devoid of both the exclusion from products and the exclusion from jars, and is devoid of subsistence in products and subsistence in jars,
because it possesses genus, like a cloth"— this inference [is invalid],
because it over-extends to impermanent substances and qualities.
Because even a genus that subsists only in impermanent things is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), given that it subsists only in impermanent things;
and because the state of being directly pervaded by existence has already been refuted.
This is the secret here:
wherever it is possible for those like us to remove the faults of the desired [definition], let each such case be as one wishes; this is the defining characteristic of actions in this context.
Alternatively, substantiality is the definition of substance; quality-ness is the definition of quality; action-ness is the definition of action;
and [the remaining definitions] are the specific definitions of substances such as earth, which are distinct from ether, time, and space.
The universals such as earthness and waterhood,
as well as the universals such as colorness belonging to specific qualities like color,
are the defining characteristics; likewise for specific actions such as upward throwing and so forth.

The universals such as "upward motion-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) are the defining characteristics of generality, and generality itself consists precisely in possessing a universal. In that regard, [the universal] may be either a genus (*jāti*) or a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) is characterized by being an eternal relation and being a relation distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Or else, it is the state of being related to a non-substance, or the state of being related to a quality, or the state of being related to an action, or the state of being related to a genus,
or the state of being related to a particular; and this is the state of being related.

It is simply "genus" (jāti), because genus is admitted even in the case of inherence in specific genera. And the definition of non-existence (abhāva) is simply its state as non-existence; this applies to prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) as well.

The defining characteristic of antecedent non-existence is its being antecedent non-existence; that of destruction is its being destruction; that of mutual non-existence is its being mutual non-existence; and that of absolute non-existence is its being absolute non-existence.
Furthermore, properties such as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) are indeed universals (*jāti*), because they share the same logical status as *gotva* (cowness) and other such universals.
Alternatively, [the definition applies] to earth’s possession of odor, or to that which possesses coldness...
The definition of water is: being the substratum of gravity; possessing color while being devoid of heat and cold; and possessing a touch that is neither hot nor cold while being distinct from air.
And [the characteristics of water are] possession of cold touch, possession of viscidity, being the substratum of natural fluidity, possession of taste while being devoid of smell,
and being the substratum of gravity while being devoid of smell.
The definition [of fire] is as follows: heat is the characteristic of fire; possessing luminous form is its characteristic;

possessing form while being devoid of taste is its characteristic; and possessing form while being devoid of weight is its characteristic. As for air, however, it is characterized by being devoid of form.
Possession of touch; possession of a touch that is neither hot nor cold while being odorless; possession of a touch that is neither hot nor cold while being weightless.

The definition of touch is the possession of touch that manifests touch. For space, the definitions are sound, being an all-pervasive sense organ, being the auditory faculty, and the absolute non-existence of anything other than space. For time—

And all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) consists in being devoid of a conjunction that produces eternal posteriority, while possessing a conjunction that produces non-eternal posteriority; and in that state,
it is devoid of a conjunction that produces eternal posteriority.

The definition of space (dik) is: being large (mahattva), while possessing conjunction that produces the notion of "remoteness" (paratva), while being distinct from all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) and so forth, while being devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa), and while being the absolute non-existence of difference from time (kālānyatvātyantābhāva). As for direction (diś):

[The definition of space is] all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) while possessing a conjunction that produces the quality of "remoteness" (paratva) culminating in an atom; [the definition of time is] magnitude greater than that of the other [substances] while being devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa). [While being devoid of specific qualities...]

The defining characteristics of space are its omnipresence throughout time and its absolute absence from other directions; the defining characteristics of the self are its being the substratum of cognition and so forth, provided that it is distinct from space.
The definition [of Ākāśa] is being all-pervasive (vibhutva) while possessing specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇavat).
As for the mind (manas), its definitions are: being the sense organ that apprehends pleasure, being the sense organ that apprehends pain, and being a sense organ that apprehends [objects].
The state of being an atom that produces memory; the state of being an atom devoid of touch;
the state of being an atom devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa);
and the state of being minute while being the substratum of a conjunction that produces cognition and so forth.
The definition [of form]:
being a quality perceptible by the eye, while not being graspable by touch.

The definition of taste is the possession of a genus that is not graspable by touch but is graspable by the eye; the definition of taste is the state of being a quality not graspable by the sense of taste [in the case of the object] and possessing a genus of taste that is not graspable by the sense of touch.

The definition of odor (*gandha*) is its being a quality perceivable by the olfactory organ; specifically, it is the possession of a genus that is perceivable by the olfactory organ but not perceivable by the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*). As for touch (*sparśa*), however—

The definition [of touch] is the state of being a quality graspable by the tactile organ but not by the visual organ, or the state of possessing a genus graspable by the tactile organ but not by the visual organ. As for number, however—
The state of possessing a genus that does not reside in separateness but resides in oneness; the state of possessing a genus that does not reside in conjunction but resides in oneness;
the state of possessing a genus that does not reside in disjunction but resides in oneness.
The state of possessing a genus that resides in duality but does not reside in separateness; the state of possessing a genus that resides in duality but does not reside in conjunction;
the state of possessing a genus that resides in duality but does not reside in disjunction.

The definition [of substance] is: possessing a genus that does not reside in separateness (*pṛthaktva*), but resides in plurality; possessing a genus that does not reside in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but resides in plurality; and possessing a genus that does not reside in disjunction (*vibhāga*), but resides in plurality.
Dimension, however, consists in possessing a genus that occurs in number and occurs in magnitude,
or possessing a genus that occurs in number and occurs in minuteness.

The definition of [the quality of] length is: possessing a genus that resides in number and resides in length; the definition of [the quality of] shortness is: possessing a genus that resides in number and resides in shortness.
As for distinctness (pṛthaktva), however—

The definition of a quality (*guṇatva*) is that which possesses a genus residing in many substrates, while not residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*). However, in the case of conjunction,
it is that which possesses a genus residing in many substrates, while not residing in number (*saṃkhyā*) or separateness (*pṛthaktva*).

The nature of substance is truth; the nature of quality is the state of being a quality while possessing a genus that resides in more than one thing, excluding number, separateness, disjunction, and inherence.
The definition of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the possession of a genus residing in the threads that constitute a number-series. As for disjunction (*vibhāga*),
however, it is the possession of a genus residing in multiple substrata, which resides in distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction, and number.
The definition of truth-substancehood (*satyadravyatva*) is:

being a quality (*guṇatva*) while possessing a genus that resides in more than one and resides in the occurrence of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*). As for "remoteness" (*paratva*), however...
The definition [of time] is: possessing a genus residing in number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, velocity, remoteness, action, non-existence, and mind;
or, being produced by the conjunction with an all-pervading substance (vibhu) while lacking any specific quality other than conjunction and remoteness. As for remoteness (*aparatva*), however...
The definition [of cognition] is: possessing a genus residing in number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, velocity, separateness, priority, action, non-existence, and mind;
or, being produced by a conjunction that is devoid of any specific quality of an all-pervading substance other than conjunction and priority. As for cognition (buddhi), however—
The definition [of intellect] is the possession of desire-vrtti, knowledge-vrtti, and genus.

In this same way, by substituting the word "desire" (*icchā*) with words such as "effort" (*prayatna*) and so forth, many definitions of intellect (*buddhi*) are to be understood. [This applies likewise] to pleasure (*sukha*).

The definition [of pleasure] is: possessing a genus that resides in a quality of the self produced by eating, which does not reside in unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and is distinct from knowledge (*jñāna*). As for suffering, however, [it is defined as possessing a genus that resides in a quality of the self produced by eating, which does not reside in unseen demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and is distinct from knowledge].
The definition [of desire] is: possessing a genus that resides in a quality of the self which is produced [by effort].
However, for desire, it is:
possessing a genus that resides in a quality of Devadatta, which is the producer of a jar, does not reside in the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and resides in a quality of the self.

The definition [of hatred]: the definition of hatred (*dveṣa*) is the possession of a genus residing in a quality of Devadatta that produces violence which is opposed to the occurrence [of an object] when that [object] is not perceived. [The definition] of effort (*prayatna*):
The definition is: "possessing a genus residing in a quality of Devadatta that produces a jar, which does not reside in adṛṣṭa (unseen merit/demerit).
And [the definition] of gravity is:
[possessing a genus residing in a quality of Devadatta that produces] a pearl-oyster shell released from clarified butter, which does not reside in adṛṣṭa...

The definition of *phala* (fruit) is the possession of a genus that resides in qualities and functions. The definition of *dravatva* (fluidity), however, is the possession of a genus that resides in water—which is distinct from that which does not reside in the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—and which produces downward flow.
The definition of *sneha* (viscosity) is as follows: [the possession of a genus residing in water].

The definition of the quality of water (*udakaguṇatva*)— excluding conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and fluidity (*dravatva*) that produce cohesion (*saṃgraha*) and reside in a genus (*jāti*) inherent in qualities produced by effort (*prayatna*), unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), or fluidity, and which generates impetus (*saṃrambha*)—
is *saṃskāra* (disposition).
The definition [of *bhāvanā*] is the possession of a class of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) that arise from a modification [of the mind] which has the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its object.

As for *bhāvanā* itself, it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that produces an effect distinct from memory— which is produced by knowledge having an object other than the unseen— and which produces an effect distinct from the unseen itself.
The definition [of momentum]:
momentum is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) distinct from elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) and mental impression (*bhāvanā*), or it is a latent impression that produces action distinct from elasticity.
The definition [of elasticity] is:
the state of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that produces action not caused by velocity (*vega*). As for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), its definition is...

The definition of merit (*dharma*) is: being a quality of the self that possesses a subordinate genus of quality which does not reside in what is perceptible to us and resides directly [in the self]. The definition of demerit (*adharma*) is: possessing a genus that resides in that which produces pleasure and does not reside in that which produces pain.

The definition [of dharma] is either the characteristic of being a quality (guṇatva) that excludes the class of qualities producing suffering and does not reside in those [qualities], or it is the state of being a quality that produces pleasure while being excluded from the class of qualities that produce suffering. As for adharma, however—
The definition [of pleasure] is either: possessing a genus that does not reside in that which produces happiness and does reside in that which produces pain;

or, being a quality that lacks a genus residing in that which produces happiness—which is excluded from qualities—and yet resides in that which produces pain. As for sound, however, its definition is: being a quality perceptible by the auditory organ.
Alternatively, the definition of upward motion (*utkṣepaṇa*) is the possession of a genus that is not perceptible by the sense of touch but is perceptible by the sense of hearing.
The definition of throwing upward (utkṣepaṇa) is being an action produced by an effort generated by the desire "I shall throw upward.
The definition of throwing downward (avakṣepaṇa),
however, is being an action produced by an effort generated by the desire "I shall throw downward."
Contraction, however, is an action produced by an effort generated by the desire "I shall contract";
whereas extension is—
The definition [of *prasāraṇa*] is being an action produced by an effort (*prayatna*) which is itself produced by the desire "I shall extend. As for movement (*gamana*), however,
its definition is being an action distinct from upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), downward throwing (*avakṣepaṇa*), contraction (*ākuñcana*), and extension (*prasāraṇa*).
The definition [of a universal] is:
being inherent in many while being eternal;
or, being inherent in many while being eternal.
The definition of absence (*abhāva*) is being distinct from inherence (*samavāya*).

The definition of particularity (*viśeṣa*), however, is either the state of being inherent in that which lacks existence residing in multiple substrates, or the state of being an entity that lacks existence not residing in multiple substrates.

But for non-existence (abhāva), there is the absolute absence of being an entity (bhāvatva). As for antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), its definition is perishability while being beginningless. As for emergent non-existence (pradhvaṃsa), however, it is being an effect.

The definition [of non-existence] is either the state of being destructible by truth, or the state of being an absence that is the counter-positive of prior non-existence. As for absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), however,
its definition is the state of being an absence distinct from prior non-existence, posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

As for its definition: the definition of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is its very nature as mutual non-existence. Nor is there a lack of evidence regarding this nature of mutual non-existence.

This is because the difference from a pot, the difference from a cloth, and so forth, are all mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*). Furthermore, among these differences such as "difference from a cloth," the universal property of difference—
which is established by the continuous experience "this is different" and "that is different"— is not established by perception.

Just as in the case of "remoteness" (*paratva*), "nearness" (*aparatva*), and so forth, there exists a specific property such as remoteness that is established by experience in the form "this is remoteness," "this is nearness"; likewise, it is the same in the case of the difference between a jar and a cloth, and so on.

The specific property of distinctness (*anyatva*) is an object established by direct perception and is difficult to deny; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of denying properties such as "remoteness" (*paratva*) and so forth in relation to other things as well.

Nor should it be suspected that these definitions are not based upon the Sūtras, for [the Sūtras state]: "This is the definition of substance," "this is the definition of quality," and "this is the definition of action."
By the word "ca" (and), there is a collection of such characteristics;
for the word "iti" denotes such a manner,
[including] substances, specific qualities, and specific actions.
Because they are substances, qualities, and actions;
for the definitions of universals and so forth are also of this same nature. This does not apply to the second chapter and those that follow.
Furthermore, those [sūtras] that set forth definitions are not redundant, because they are intent upon the critical examination of those definitions. || 16 ||
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravārtika*, composed by the illustrious servant of Lord Hara, the supreme scholar, Nyāyācārya Bhaṭṭa Vādīndra.

Now begins the section on the general nature of causes.
Substance is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions. (1.1.17)
Substances, qualities,
and actions are "substance-quality-actions"; among these, a single substance is the cause, just as a single atom of earth.

In succession, there are infinite substances through the sequence beginning with dyads and so forth; and there are infinite instances of fluidity, velocity, priority, posteriority, conjunction, disjunction, unity, and plurality.
And although one undertakes infinite qualities and actions in succession,
nevertheless, the non-luminous and non-aerial atoms also [undertake] infinite [qualities] in succession.

The fiery atoms do not initiate dyads, dispositional tendencies, priority and posteriority, disjunction, multiple numbers, multiple separateness, or actions; rather, they initiate fluidity and so forth.

And effect-substances— namely, many substances such as dyads and threads, in their respective orders— originate [other] substances, qualities such as color and so forth, and motions; this applies even to those [substances] like threads which are only two.

Even those [causes], such as the two threads and so forth, which either produce a single dyad (dvitantuka) and so forth, or cease without producing a dyad and so forth at all, likewise possess the quality of being producers of many substances.

It is to be inferred precisely from its nature as a thread. As for the non-production of many substances, that occurs simply due to the destruction of the threads. Or rather, those [causes] such as threads which, having produced exactly two substances, cease to exist—of those...

[The quality of being] the producer of two substances [belongs to those qualities which produce a substance]. However, those which cease after producing only one [substance] possess the state of having only one substance [as their substrate].
But as for those which cease without even producing a substance, their...
[The atoms] do not produce substances at all; however, the ultimate composite parts (antyāvayavin) originate qualities and actions, while space originates only qualities.
As for transmigrating beings...

[The atoms] initiate intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, as well as various numbers, manifoldness, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction, and also substances such as jars, their qualities, and their actions. Therefore, whatever effects a jar-substance produces, [the atoms produce them all].
The meaning of the sutra is that one of these is the cause.
At this point, which concerns similarity (*sādharmya*),
the investigation of a common cause is irrelevant, because [the definition] of a cause...
If it is argued that this is because it is impossible for [the cause] to possess the property of being an effect— [we reply: no,
because the determination of common causes is intended to demonstrate the property of those effects not being produced by non-causes.

And likewise, in the context of demonstrating common properties (*samānadharmapratipādana*), such as: "Whatever substance, quality, or action a single atom initiates, the fact that those [substances, qualities, and actions] are produced from that atom constitutes their common property (*sādharmya*)," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is possible to investigate [the nature of] a cause by means of an application of the same logic;
others maintain that even a cause possesses the very characteristics of its effect.

This is because there is the cognition that "this is the cause here. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that in the case of dyads and the like, one could not infer causes such as God or atoms on the basis of their being effects, since it would be impossible for the cause to reside within the subject (*pakṣa*). Regarding the subject...

Because it would contradict the probandum (*sādhyabādhāt*), and because it would entail the absence of positive concomitance (*anvayābhāva*) for the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) due to the impossibility of its residing in similar instances (*sapakṣaniṣṭhatvāsambhava*),
[this applies] to God (*īśvara*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth.

If it is argued that because [the property] does not reside in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), it is impossible for it to be their attribute (*dharmatva*)— we say no; for even though it does not reside in them, it is still a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of them, since the definition of an attribute (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely that which qualifies something.
If it is argued that this [point] has already been established by the sūtra, "Substances originate another substance" (VS 1.1.8)—
we say no, because of that [sūtra's]...
Because this [sūtra] establishes common properties such as being the ultimate constituent of a substance that initiates another substance,

it aims to demonstrate common properties such as the state of being produced by a specific substance, which resides in the substances, qualities, and actions produced by those respective specific substances. The same applies to the subsequent sūtra.
The tautology regarding the statement "qualities also originate further qualities" (VS 1.1.9) must be avoided. 17.
Likewise, [the word] *guṇa*. 1.1.18.
Just as substance is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions, so too is quality [the common cause] through God’s knowledge, will, effort, merit, and demerit.
Because it produces substance, quality, and action: by means of the quality of conjunction existing in two tufts of cotton, which consists of accumulation (*pracaya*) and nodana,
there is the production of the two-tufted substance, the magnitude residing therein, and the action of the tuft of cotton.

And because it is produced [by conjunction]. For just as the conjunction called "accumulation and impulsion" existing between two balls of cotton produces a substance consisting of two balls of cotton from those two balls of cotton, because it is an originating conjunction; so too is it here.

In the case of two tufts of cotton, largeness arises from accumulation (*pracaya*), because the largeness produced by two equal [quantities of] largeness is superior to the largeness of a single tuft;
likewise, the largeness of three tufts is superior to that of two. Thus...
"Action [arises] within a tuft of cotton due to impulsion";
therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that whichever quality produces which substances, qualities, and actions is the common cause (sādhāraṇa) of those.

But that which produces only substance and quality is the common cause of those two; for example, [the contact] with the inherent cause is the common cause of the touch residing in the [substance] and the touch [itself]. Of the touch—

The state of being a producer of substance [belongs to qualities], because minds, which are devoid of touch, do not produce substances. However, that quality which produces only qualities and actions is a common cause for both; for example:

The gravity, fluidity, and magnitude of the parts [give rise to these qualities] in the whole, because they originate the gravity, fluidity, and magnitude of the whole, and because they originate motion in their own substratum;
this applies to the dimension of material objects.
Because it produces action, and since action does not arise in formless entities such as space,
velocity also initiates action in its own substratum; thus,
there is velocity in the composite water-molecule (avayavin) which is composed of water-particles possessing velocity.
The teachers beginning with Praśastapāda;
however, the teachers beginning with Ātreya do not accept this, because there is a lack of valid evidence.

If it is argued that velocity itself is the proof for the existence of a composite water-substance produced from parts possessing velocity— no, for that is accounted for by the motion produced by fluidity (*dravatva*) alone. This being the case:

If it is argued that velocity could not exist at the very time of fluidity— this is true; it simply does not arise because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it, nor is there any perception such as "the water possesses velocity."
Because it is otherwise established by the velocity produced from a subsequent action arising from fluidity;

for if the velocity of a part did not produce velocity in the whole, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such velocity existing even in a whole composed of parts devoid of velocity.

If this is argued—[we reply] no, because it is accepted [as such]. For even action produced by impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth gives rise to such velocity (*vega*). Velocity-ness (*vegatva*) resides in that which is produced by velocity, because it resides in velocity, like existence (*sattā*). Velocity-ness resides in that which is produced by velocity.

If it is argued that the inference "because of the non-cessation of velocity, like existence (*sattā*)" is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for it is vitiated by the presence of a logical adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting in the occurrence of non-velocity. Furthermore, due to the absence of that [adjunct], there is a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣatva*). This is because the velocity of the water-particles...
This is because [the reason] is vitiated by proving something else (arthāntara), as it fails to establish that [the motion] is produced by the force of the parts of water;

and also because of the following inference: "This velocity is not produced by velocity, because it is a velocity. Nor is there any possibility of a counter-argument here, since [the subject] is not produced from velocity.

Because it possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhitvāt*); and because, if it were not produced by action (*karmājanyatva*), it would follow that it lacks the nature of velocity (*vegatvābhāvaprasaṅga*). This is because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is determined that action is the generator of velocity. As for that quality which...
It produces only qualities; it is the common cause of qualities,
just as the color of an atom is the cause of the many colors of the dyads produced from it, as are taste and the other qualities.
Regarding the phrase "of taste, etc.": the word "etc. refers to sounds in all directions, mental impressions (bhāvanā) among memories, and momentum (vega) among actions, and so forth. || 18 ||
Action is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. (1.1.19)

The term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is understood to mean "universal" (*sāmānya*), and this is merely an illustration; for velocity (*vega*) is also a cause of action (*karman*). Therefore, all conjunctions, disjunctions, and velocities produced by a particular action [are its causes].
To the extent that they are produced by it, that karma is common [to them];
and the fact of being produced by that is their common characteristic—
this is the meaning of the sūtra.

This sutra is indeed not to be undertaken, because since conjunctions and disjunctions are merely conjunctions and disjunctions, the additional property here— that they are produced by specific actions— is superfluous.
If it is argued that [the cause] is being established— no, for that too is established from that very [same source].
Once it has been established that specific actions produce specific conjunctions and disjunctions,
[it follows that] specific conjunctions and disjunctions...
Because it is established by the facts that [the effects] are produced by specific actions;
for if those [effects] were not produced by specific actions, it would be impossible for specific actions to be their producers. That sūtra...
This [sūtra] establishes that action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction;
however, regarding the fact that conjunctions and disjunctions are the effects of action,
it is not established even for that [action], because conjunctions and disjunctions [are not yet proven].
Because it is impossible for an action to be the producer of that which is produced by an action;

and because both the repetition of words and the repetition of the meanings of words constitute defects; and because conjunctions and disjunctions, even though produced by action, [do not themselves produce action].
And because it establishes that action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. Of action...

If it is argued that this [sūtra], although intended to establish [manas] as the cause of conjunction and disjunction, is explained instead as being concerned with the fact that conjunctions and disjunctions are effects of action because it is a mere repetition— [we reply: no.
Nevertheless, since the fault of redundancy remains in that state,
even if that [subsequent] sūtra were intended to establish that action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction, it would still be redundant with respect to the preceding sūtra.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to explain [the previous sūtra] as being solely intent on [showing that] conjunctions and disjunctions are produced by action;
for if the previous sūtra were intended to convey both meanings, [it would be redundant].

If it is argued that "the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) exists"—[we reply] no, because that is not considered a fault in the Sūtras. [The Sūtra states: "Conjunctions and disjunctions are the effects of actions."

[The soul is] not [the agent], because it is distinct from the substances. (1.1.20)
"Because of its exclusion" means because it is distinct from substance, quality, and absence; and thus,
action is not the producer of substance.

"Because it is an existence (bhāva) devoid of substantiality (dravyatva) and quality-ness (guṇatva), like a universal (sāmānya). Nor is "the absence of possessing a universal" a limiting condition (upādhi) here, because it fails to pervade the probandum (sādhya) in the case of space and so forth. Nor [is it a condition] by virtue of possessing a universal.
[The reason] suffers from the fallacy of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*), because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space (*gagana*) and so forth.
Alternatively, action (*karman*) is not the cause of substance (*dravya*), because of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); for even in the absence of that [action], a substance arises.
Just as when a cloth is destroyed due to the disjunction of its constituent threads,
another cloth arises from the persisting conjunctions at that time, so it was in the preceding moment.
Due to the absence of action (*karman*), that [conjunction] does not possess the capacity to produce the cloth.

And when, through the conjunction of a thread already conjoined with another thread with yet another thread, a second thread is produced; and immediately thereafter, through the conjunction of that [second] thread with the first thread, a conjunction of the threads occurs; and immediately thereafter, the two-threaded dyad (*dvitantuka*) is produced—at that time, there is no action in the moment preceding the two-threaded dyad, because the two threads are devoid of motion.
Furthermore, the action of the [first] thread [ceases] through its conjunction with the substance of the thread.

Because the constituent parts are destroyed at the very moment the thread is produced, there is an absence of action [in those parts]; nevertheless, since the substance is still produced, action is not the cause of a substance.
Alternatively, action is not the cause of a substance, because of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): even when [action] exists...
Because a two-thread substance is not produced from two threads situated in distant locations; and because, even when that [conjunction] exists,
a two-thread substance is not produced during the moment prior to the conjunction.

If it is argued that action is required for the commencement of the conjunction produced by itself— no, because once the substance is established through conjunction alone, there is no evidence for action being its cause.
Because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) by their being producers of conjunction;
otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that even impulsion (*nodana*) and other factors which produce action would be causes of substance.
Alternatively, *vyatireka* (distinction) is that by which action is distinguished—that is, differentiated—from substance and the other categories; therefore, action is not the cause of substance.
And thus, the subject under dispute—action—is not the cause of substance.
Because it is an object (*karmatvāt*), like the object that is a jar (*ghaṭakarmavat*).

Alternatively, "distinction" (*vyatireka*) refers to that by which a substance is distinguished—that is, differentiated—from the mind and so forth; [it is] substantiality (*dravyatva*). [It is not] action (*karma*) because of that [substantiality].

It is not the substantial cause (*dravyakāraṇa*). Thus, that which is under dispute is not produced by action (*karmajanya*), because it possesses the nature of a substance (*dravyatva*), like space (*gagana*).
As for the explanation given by the teacher Ātreya—that action is not...

Because it is the cause of the cognition of a substance qualified by duality and so forth.
If it is argued that things in a state of perishing cannot be non-inherent causes— no, because [the cause must be] proximate.
Because there would be a contradiction in denying the status of non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) to that whose capacity has been ascertained by itself,
and because the definition of a non-inherent cause would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
Now, to dispel the doubt as to why the first action might not be common to all subsequent actions, the Sūtra states:
"Not so, because of the difference in their qualities" (1.1.21).
Action possesses a dissimilarity from quality, namely the absence of being a quality; therefore,
action is not the cause of action, and likewise, action is not the non-inherent cause of action.

or alternatively, it is because of its heterogeneity from quality,
meaning it is heterogeneous from those qualities— gravity, fluidity, momentum, and conjunction— which serve as the non-inherent causes of action.

And action is not the non-inherent cause of action,
because it is devoid of gravity, fluidity, momentum, and conjunction, like a jar.
Initial falling is the non-inherent cause of falling.

If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) based on the following: "Falling has gravity as its non-inherent cause, because—while being distinct from the first instance of falling—it is produced by that which has gravity as its inherent cause, just like the gravity of a composite whole," we say: no.

In the first inference, because the counter-position (pratipakṣa) is vitiated by the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), since the subject (*dharmin*) is specifically the action distinct from the initial falling; and because it is characterized by the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), namely "non-action-ness" (*akarmatva*). Furthermore, what is this "initial falling-ness"?

[Is it] the falling that produces falling, or something else? Not the first, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Not the second, because it would be a mere tautology (*punarukti*).
By this [same reasoning], the initial motion (*ādyasyandana*) is that which produces motion.

The counter-argument— that because there is a difference between the substance and the flow, [the flow] must be produced by a non-inherent cause consisting of fluidity, just like the fluidity of its constituent parts— is refuted.
Therefore, karma is not the common cause of karmas;
and this sūtra is indeed not to be commenced.
Because this has already been covered by the statement, "Action is not something to be accomplished by action" (1.1.10),
where the state of being accomplished by action was negated;
here, however, the state of having multiple actions as its cause is negated.

If [it is argued that]—no, because by the very negation of karma being the cause of karma, the negation of its being the cause of multiple karmas is not established, since it is untenable for something to be the producer of karma. In this regard, it is merely a proposition; it is not [proven].
If it is argued that [the term "cause"] is not redundant because it is being designated as a cause, we say no;
for in this context, there is no proposition stating "not by means of actions. In that case, what is negated is the causality of an action by way of its being an action.

If it is argued that this is because of a difference in property (*guṇavaidharmya*), we say no; for in that case, "being an object" (*karmatva*) was not stated as the reason (*hetu*). If it is argued that "being an object" is intended there as the reason, we say no, because even "being an object" [is not established].

Because there is no excess [of properties] apart from the dissimilarity of qualities (*guṇavaidharmya*). What is intended here as the reason is the specific dissimilarity of qualities that constitutes action (*karmatva*). If it is argued that there is a dissimilarity of qualities here distinct from that—no.
Because if one intends to state that merely the difference in quality (*guṇavaidharmya*) is the cause there,
then the futility of composing this sūtra remains as it was, since [the argument] would apply to all cases; and in that case, regarding the fact that action does not produce action—

If it is argued that perception is intended as the means of valid cognition here, whereas inference is intended there— no, because by perception one does not experience that an action is not a producer of another action.

If it is argued that the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) was intended [to be stated first], and that a subverting inference (*bādhaka-anumāna*) is now being set forth here— [we reply: no,
because the absence of a proving means of knowledge is already established simply by the statement of the subverting argument.
Because it is logically untenable for that which is being established to simultaneously act as its own sublater. || 21 ||
Now begins the section on the generality of the effect (*kāryasāmānyaprakaraṇam*).
The effect of substances is a substance; this is the commonality. (1.1.22)
It does not mean that there is one undifferentiated universal; rather,
it means that whatever substance is produced by certain substances, that [substance] is their single effect— for example, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
[The cause] of two atoms, space, time, and the Lord; and the triad [of atoms],
as well as three dyads, space, time, and the Lord, and so forth—
this is said when one intends to refer to the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substances.
Then, by resorting to the grammatical analysis (vigraha) as "in a substance" and "substances," some substance is the effect of two substances,
such as a dyad (dvyaṇuka) from two atoms;
some [substance] is the effect of many substances, such as...

"From three dyads (dvyaṇuka), a triad (tryaṇuka) [is produced]. This is untenable; for in that context, the common property (sādharmya) of substances being the originators of substances is being established, whereas here—
If it is argued that the fact that two substances, or many substances, initiate another substance is being established [by this sūtra]— no,
because the capacity of two or many to initiate [another substance] is already established by that very [sūtra].
Because the meaning has already been conveyed; for even there, the analysis (vigraha) "in a substance, substances" is possible, and because it would result in redundancy.
If it is argued that there is no such analysis there—no, [that is not correct].
In that case, for those who rely on such a formal debate (vigraha),
the commencement of this sūtra would be rendered powerless once the purpose of this sūtra has been established; [this applies] to both two [parties] and many.
Furthermore, since the status of being a substance-initiator is established by this very [definition] which explains that status, the futility of the preceding sūtra is unavoidable.
Therefore, the Sūtra will be explained otherwise: the commonality (*sāmānya*) of substances is their similarity (*sādharmya*) as effect-substances (*kāryadravya*). Likewise...
A dyad resides in two atoms, and a triad resides in three dyads, because the very nature of their property is that of being dependent [upon them].
Nor is the meaning already established by the preceding sūtra, because that [sūtra] does not establish that produced substances possess common characteristics. Of substances...
