From the demonstration that [substance] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of [other] substances, it follows as a matter of fact that a product-substance possesses the property of being based on multiple substances,
precisely because it initiates an effect that is inherent within itself.

If it is argued that this is because [the definition] is the characteristic of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), we say no; for by that [definition], the status of being an inherent cause of substance (*dravya*) is not established, since only the status of being a cause of substance in general is established. Not so.
And by this [sūtra], while demonstrating that effect-substances are produced from multiple inherent causes,
he demonstrates that substances are the causes of substances— therefore, [the category is] "substances."
The statement "they originate another substance" (VS 1.1.8) has its purpose already explained by this [sūtra],
because through it the fact that substances are the inherent causes of substances is established, [and thus] regarding effect-substances...
Because it establishes the state of having common properties. || 22 ||
Likewise, the qualities [are not perceived]. 1-1-23.

Just as a substance such as a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is a common effect of substances such as two atoms, space, time, and the Lord, so too are the qualities such as color (rūpa) belonging to a dyad and the like.
The meaning is that the effect is common to substances such as dyads (dvyaṇuka), space, time, and the Lord (Īśvara).
However, the teacher Ātreya [states]:
Because it is impossible for the color and other qualities of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) to be the effects of a single substance such as a dyad,
and because duality and the rest are the effects of multiple substances—
as already established by the very statement that "duality and the subsequent numbers [are qualities of substances]."

Thinking that this sūtra is fruitless because its meaning has already been understood, they have neglected it. That is incorrect, because it serves as a supporting proof for the objects such as form (rūpa) and so forth. || 23 ||
And numbers beginning with duality, as well as separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. (1.1.24)
The term "effect" (*kārya*) and "universal" (*sāmānya*) carry over from the previous context. Numbers such as duality (*dvitva*), separations such as dual separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*),
and all conjunctions and disjunctions belong to substances [in the case of multiple substances].
The universal is the effect of its inherent causes; for instance,
the duality of a jar and a cloth is the effect of the jar and the cloth,
and the triad of a jar, a cloth, and a pillar is the effect of the jar, the cloth, and the pillar.

The effect [is as follows]: the separateness of a jar and a cloth is the effect of the jar and the cloth; and the separateness of a jar, a cloth, and a pillar is the effect of the jar, the cloth, and the pillar. [Likewise for] conjunction and disjunction.
And the meaning of the sūtra is that the function belongs only to each pair of these two; this, however, is untenable,
because the purpose of this sūtra has already been covered by the sūtra "guṇaḥ" [1.1.18].

If it is argued that the state of being produced by multiple inherent causes (anekasamavāyikāraṇajanyatva) is what is being established here— [we reply] no, because this has already been covered by the previous [argument], since space, time, and God would also [otherwise] be inherent causes.
This is because color and the other qualities are also produced by multiple inherent causes; and this is already established by the previous sūtra: "Qualities [produce] another quality" (NS 1.1.9).
And because the meaning has already been understood,
this [sūtra] should therefore be explained otherwise:
just as being an effect-substance is a common property (sādharmya) of substances, so too are the qualities of triad-ness and the rest.
Number, separateness, and so forth [are also common properties].
Just as a substance such as a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is a common property of two substances, so too are duality, dual separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. And it is not thus [that they are excluded].
Since the meaning has already been established by the sūtra "And qualities [reside] in other qualities" (1.1.9) and so forth,
this entire [argument] is untenable, because it fails to demonstrate that duality and the like are properties common to multiple substances.

If it is argued that [number] does not exist because numbers distinct from jars and the like are non-existent, and because even in the case of a quality (guṇa) it is not an effect, or even if it were an effect,
its cause cannot be specified— [we reply]: no, for oneness has already been [established].
Because [numbers] are established through linguistic derivation; and because duality and so forth are established by perception as "two," "three," and so on;
for in the perception "two jars" and the like, [duality] resides in the jar and other such objects.
Because duality and so forth are experienced; and because of the inference: "This duality is distinct from this jar, because it is its qualifier, like color.
Nor is this [reason] unestablished, for just as one says "the white jar," one says "two jars."

This is because the perception of "two jars" and so forth is established for all people in the world. Furthermore, this duality is not devoid of being distinct from this jar, because it possesses this-ness (etattva).
That which is not thus is not so, just as a cloth is not [the subject under discussion]; such is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Because there is a counter-argument: since "being different from this jar" is unestablished anywhere,
its absence is likewise unestablished, resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Or, by that very same reasoning,

since duality is established as being distinct from insentient jars within the scope of valid cognition, the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) is sublated; for even if it were distinct from the jar, it would still possess the nature of a cloth (*paṭatva*).
For, just as with a pot, one also accepts non-difference with respect to a cloth. Nor is duality merely two onenesses;
this duality is distinct from those two onenesses.

Nor can there be a counter-argument based on a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), such as "this duality [is not composed of two unities] because it is a duality, like any other duality," since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.
Furthermore, the claim that "this duality consists of two unities because it is unity" does not constitute a valid counter-position (*satpratipakṣatā*) against the original argument.
Because a substance consisting of this oneness and duality is not established anywhere, the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Nor is this duality of the pot and the cloth identical with the oneness of this pot.
This constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*):
"That which is not of the nature of the oneness of this jar does not possess the duality of this [jar]," because there is a negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) regarding the oneness of a cloth.
Because, through the refutation [of your position], you have accepted that the duality of this pot and cloth consists in their being of one nature;
nor is it the case that this duality of the pot and cloth lacks the quality of being distinct from the unity of this pot and cloth, because it possesses that very nature.
It must be countered, because the conceptual construction is untenable. For instance,
is it being argued that the absence of that "distinctness" which has the oneness of pot and cloth as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is what is to be proven, or rather...
Is it that one entity is being established as distinct from the duality whose counter-correlates are the onenesses of the jar and the cloth; or rather,
are those two distinctnesses whose counter-correlates are the onenesses of the jar and the cloth [being established]?
Is it that the possession of those two absences is being proved?
Or is it that the pair of absences of the two distinctnesses—which have the oneness of the jar and the cloth as their counter-correlates—is being proved? Or what else?

The absence of the possession of those two distinctnesses, which have the oneness of the jar and the cloth as their counter-correlates (pratiyogin), is what is being proven. It is not the first [alternative],
because of the unestablished nature of the qualifier (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) due to the difference of the counter-correlates.
Because it is restricted to specific individuals, it is untenable for it to be anything other than the unity that has the unity of a jar and a cloth as its counter-correlate;
consequently, even the absence of such [a distinct unity] is unestablished. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
For it is impossible for there to be the absence of one of those two distinctnesses that have the oneness of the jar and the cloth as their counter-correlates,
since the difference between absences is necessarily determined by the difference between their counter-correlates. Not so.
The third [reason] is likewise [untenable], precisely because its qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
This is because the possession of that pair of absences which belong to those two distinctnesses whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are the oneness of a pot and a cloth is [unestablished].
Because it is unestablished anywhere;

for it is contradictory that there should be two absences of distinctness— one with respect to the distinctness of a pot and one with respect to the distinctness of a cloth— distinct from those [respective] counter-correlates.
Furthermore, even if the absence of difference from the oneness of the jar is established in the case of the jar's oneness,
the absence of difference from the oneness of the cloth remains unestablished.
Because the two absences of distinctness are sublated; and the same applies to the oneness of the jar. Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because it is contradictory;
for it proves the difference between the jar and the cloth—which is synonymous with the property of contradiction consisting in being the locus of the two absences of distinctness.
In the case of the oneness of a jar and a cloth, etc., there is no such thing,
because the state of being the locus of two absences— which are distinct from the oneness of the jar and the cloth—
is a contradictory property (*viruddhadharma*). This is so provided that [the reason] is not established without dependence [on further proof].

This is because the term itself would be contradictory; or, if it were not contradictory, it would constitute a different type of fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, the fault of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is simply impossible in the fourth alternative.
For the two absences—the absence of the pot-cloth identity and the absence of that [identity]—which reside in the pot-cloth identity, are well-known.
If it is argued that the substratum of these absences is not well-known, we say: no.
Because the inclusion of the pervading part (*vyāpakāṃśa*) is excessive for co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

It is not the fifth [alternative], because it would result in proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*). This is because there is no absence of the substratum-ness of the two [properties] distinct from the oneness of the jar and the cloth.
Because it lacks both the absence of duality— which is distinct from the oneness of the jar and the cloth—
and the state of being pervaded by that [absence]; otherwise,
if it were designated as the locus of the duality distinct from the oneness of the jar and the cloth...
Furthermore, if the jar and the cloth were identical, it would follow that there is an absence of both [the jar and the cloth] because they would be distinct from the singularity of the jar;
nor is this the case.
The absence of the dual substratum of the distinctness from the oneness of the jar and the cloth is the subject (pakṣa);
[the probandum is] the pair of absences consisting of the distinctness from the oneness of the jar and the cloth.

It should not be argued that [the reason] suffers from the fallacy of being counterbalanced (satpratipakṣatva) because it is eternal in the absence of its constituent parts; for, as in the case of the oneness of a jar and a cloth, the conclusion is reached even without such constituents.
Furthermore, since the two absences of duality— which are distinct from the oneness of the jar and the cloth—
result in the unavoidable presence of contradiction as previously demonstrated; moreover,
[this is so] by virtue of their possessing attributes contradictory to the oneness of the jar and the cloth.
Is the distinctness from the oneness of the pot and the cloth unapprehended anywhere?
Not the first, because it would involve an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*),
given that the distinctness from the oneness of the pot and the cloth has not been apprehended.

Because its non-existence is not established. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the existence of duality is established through the exclusion of the unity of the jar and the cloth, by virtue of their possessing contradictory properties consisting in their subsisting in two while residing in only one of the pair (the jar or the cloth).

Furthermore, the fact that duality resides in both [substances] is established by perception as "two," just as the fact that conjunction resides [in its relata] is established by perception as "conjoined."
Furthermore, because the properties of "subsisting in what is distinct from this jar" and "subsisting in what is distinct from this cloth" reside in the unity of this jar and this cloth,
and because their opposites— the duality of this jar and this cloth—
are established by perception. What [more is there to say]?
This duality is the locus of both [the property of] being this duality and [the property of] subsisting in something other than this jar;

it is like a duality other than this duality. Nor is this duality not the locus of both [the properties of] subsisting in something other than this jar and subsisting in something other than this cloth.

It should not be argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on the proposition: "This jar possesses color, because it is devoid of the properties of conjunction, disjunction, and separateness"; for this jar is the locus of qualities residing in it, precisely because it is devoid of the properties of conjunction, disjunction, and separateness.

Because it is a substance, like a cloth; for when this is established, the counter-argument regarding qualities is shown to be inconclusive. Furthermore, in the case of the statement "this duality is distinct from the oneness of this jar and cloth," [the same fault applies].
By the term "this duality," are only this jar and cloth intended as a unity, or is it something distinct from them? In the first case, there is a contradiction;
in the second, however, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Furthermore, because it is impossible for this [object] to be distinct from either the jar or the cloth;
since duality— which is established by perception as "two" and which is the subject (dharmin) under dispute regarding its distinction from those two— is denoted by the word "duality."

Is this intended to mean that the jar and the cloth are identical, or rather that they are distinct from one another? Otherwise, in the statement "the mountain possesses fire," would the property (dharma) be a mountain devoid of fire?

Or [is it] "possessing fire"? In the first case, there is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*); in the second, however, it can be said that there is a lack of proof for the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Now, one might object that the original inference is improper.
Because a distinction between two types—the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—is impossible;
and that impossibility arises because duality and so forth, being universals (*jāti*), are one and the same everywhere. Nor is there a transfer of duality and so forth into a universal.

Nor is it a subverting [reason], because that is not a refutation; and because, since duality, triad, and so forth occur in all substances, the relationship of pervader and pervaded is possible. Nor...

If duality, triplicity, and so forth were universals (*jāti*), the fact that they would have to reside in the same individual substratum (*tulyavyaktitva*) would be a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), precisely because [duality and triplicity] are admitted [to exist] in that way. Nor can it be argued that duality, triplicity,
and so forth are distinct from substance and quality like "cowness" (*gotva*), for they are not distinct from those two.

If [it is argued that it exists], no; because it is unestablished, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) proving its distinction from qualities (*guṇa*), and because its non-proving of qualities will be stated later. Nor also...
It might be argued that "duality and so forth are universals because, while being eternal, they reside in many [substances]";
however, this is unproven, since duality and so forth are not eternal.
Furthermore, because there is a lack of valid evidence, and because the proof for impermanence will be stated later,
the aforementioned inference is therefore established.
In this same way, triad-ness and so forth must also be established as distinct from unity; for there exists another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the number "one," namely: "This is a jar."
This [substance] is the locus of qualities residing therein which are not produced by conjunction or disjunction arising from sequential action,

because it possesses the nature of substance (*dravyatva*), like a cloth. This jar is [the locus of] those qualities not encompassed by the universals of conjunction-ness, disjunction-ness, or separateness-ness...
Because it is a substance, like a cloth. This jar is the locus of a number that does not reside in it, because it is a substance,
like a cloth.
This pot is the locus of a number residing in time,
because it is a substance, like time. Space is [the locus of] a quality residing in time that is devoid of conjunction and is not pervaded by the characteristic of separateness.

The inclusion of the term "devoid of the nature of conjunction" (*saṃyogatvarahita*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*) by means of [mere] conjunction; it is not, however,
for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established by means of disjunction (*vibhāga*), since that [fact] is admitted by both disputants.
Nor is it possible for a quality residing in time— which is not characterized by separateness and is devoid of conjunction— to exist [in a cloth],
because a part of a cloth cannot exist in the cloth itself. Not so.
And thus, since it is established as merely a plurality of numbers, duality and so forth are not established; for in the case of those things to be proven by the inference establishing plurality,
one must employ qualifiers such as "subsisting in many," "being the locus [of a universal]," and "not being the locus of the universal 'plurality'."
That which is the substratum of qualities residing in space— which is not characterized by the nature of separateness—
is a substance, because it possesses substantiality, like a jar. This jar is the substratum of the number residing in both space and the jar.

And because plurality is established by such [inferences] as "because it is a substance, like a cloth," and because duality is established by the means of knowledge that serves as the probans for the inferences proving plurality— [as in the case of the cognition] "this pillar..."

This pillar [is a substance], because it is the locus of qualities residing in space, a jar, and a cloth—which are not pervaded by the characteristic of separateness—since it possesses substantiality (dravyatva), like a jar; thus, the fourfold nature [of substance] is established.
This pillar...

The establishment of number is the substratum of the numbers residing in space, jars, and cloths. This pillar is the substratum of a quality that is devoid of both: (1) the state of residing in something other than this pillar, space, jar, and cloth; and (2) the distinctness (pṛthaktva) residing in space, jar, and cloth.

Because it is a substance (*dravyatva*), like a jar. This pillar is the locus of a number residing in the ether, the jar, and the cloth—[a number] devoid of subsistence in anything other than these [ether, jar, and cloth]—because it is a substance, like a jar; and so forth, by such arguments, the fourfold nature [of space] is established.
By this very same principle, the respective numbers of the subsequent [units] are established.
It is held that there is no number beyond the *parārdha* (the highest number).
As for the claim that Ātreya’s enumeration of numbers begins with duality and ends at the parārdha, that is untenable,
because even numbers such as the parārdha have already been established as proven by what was stated previously.
Furthermore, it is established by experience that one is a *parārdha*; otherwise,
since numbers such as the *parārdha* would be of an imperceptible nature,
the linguistic usage "one *parārdha*" would be untenable.
If you think that a number exceeding a parārdha cannot be established, that is not so;

for since the conventional usage of "eleven" and so forth is possible through the numbers one, ten, and so on alone, it would follow as an absurd consequence that the number eleven itself would vanish.
Parārdha is a certain number beyond which there is no further number;
since this is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its locus (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), any [claim to the contrary] would result in contradiction.
If you say this—no; for we do not take that which has its posterior limit thus established as the subject (*dharmin*), since it lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
[This applies to] "one decade" and so forth.

Furthermore, because numbers such as the thousand, which are established through a tenfold increase, possess the status of being subjects (dharmin), number is therefore truly infinite and does not terminate at the *parārdha*.
Furthermore, the status of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*) in duality (*dvitva*) and so forth is established by perception itself,
because the cognition and linguistic usage— "oneness is a number," "duality is a number"— are established for all people in the world. It exists.
And the linguistic usage of counting occurs in respect to oneness, duality, and so forth.
Its status as number (*saṃkhyātva*), however, is not established as being a universal (*jāti*), as that would be proven by the same logical principle as [the non-existence of] cowness (*gotva*).

Furthermore, [oneness] possesses a genus that is devoid of oneness, devoid of the occurrence of oneness, and devoid of the exclusion of manifoldness, because it possesses a genus, like a jar or like cowness; this is established by inference as well.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for its being a quality such as duality and so forth.
Because its measure is merely twoness;
the plurality of threads that produces the magnitude of a cloth is a quality, because it is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of magnitude, provided it is not itself a cloth.
Because it is inherent in the threads that produce the qualities of a cloth established in truth;
and because, while not being a cloth itself, it is inherent in the threads that produce magnitude— just like accumulation (pracaya), according to this inference.
[This is] because [number] is inferred to be a quality (guṇatva), like the plurality that produces magnitude.
Now, it might be argued: "Number is not a quality, because it is not distinct from those [entities] already accepted as qualities, just like a cloth; [and] the subject of dispute..."
Multiplicity is not a quality,
because it resides in the threads that produce magnitude while being devoid of the nature of dimension and conjunction,
like a cloth; [and] because it does not produce magnitude.

If it is argued that "multiplicity (bahutva), which possesses a number that generates magnitude, is not a quality because it inheres in many things other than separateness (pṛthaktva), like cowness (gotva)— and thus [the reason] is 'vitiated by a limiting condition' (sopādhitva) due to the absence of a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa)"— we say: no.

Because it cannot withstand critical analysis: when it is said that "it is not a quality," is it being argued that the absence of the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*) is the probandum, or the absence of the definition of a quality,
or the absence of possessing a genus that is devoid of both substantiality (*dravyatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*)?
Or [is it] the absence of being the ground for the application of the term "quality" (guṇa), or the absence of being a non-inherent cause devoid of the state of being an action (karmatva),
or simply the absence of being a non-inherent cause? It is not the first [alternative].

The first [alternative] is not tenable because the qualification is unestablished; for the Prābhākara, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, Vṛttikāra, and others, the quality-ness [of sound] is unproven, and thus its absence is likewise unestablished. Nor is it the second [alternative].

Because proving the absence of the definition of a quality as being excluded from number would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), while proving the absence of the definition of a quality as being devoid of exclusion from number would result in sublation (*bādhāt*); furthermore,
it would constitute proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*) regarding the absence of the definition of a quality.
Because of the absence of both the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and the nature of being an absence (*abhāvatva*);
[this refers] to the absence of the definition of a quality for those who do not admit the existence of qualities.

And because it is not accepted that [the subject] is pervaded by the absence of being a quality (*guṇatva*); for as long as being a quality is unestablished, its absence is unestablished, and thus its being pervaded by that [absence] is also unestablished. Nor is the third [alternative].

Because it is a different object; and because, by force of logic, the possession of a genus devoid of being a substance or an action is established through perception in the case of perceptible number. It is not [otherwise].

The fourth [reason] is [invalid] because it is subsumed by a different meaning already established previously, and because it proves what is already proven; for even by one who asserts that number is a quality, [the property of being a substance] resides in number.
This is because it is accepted that there is an absence of possessing a genus (jāti) that is devoid of substantiality, action-ness, and number-ness.

It is not the fifth [alternative], because, as before, it is swallowed by the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), and because it is vitiated by the condition (upādhi) of the absence of quality-ness (guṇatva). Nor is there any other [alternative].
[This is] as before, because it is a different matter;

for since the absence of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is also unestablished in the case of [the probandum] being established, it cannot logically function as a pervader of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*). Nor, when quality-ness is unestablished...

Since the absence of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is also unestablished, it must be stated that the probans (*upādhi*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), because this [probans] consists of the very same [property of] non-differentiated quality-ness. Of the property of being a quality...

Because this "number-ness" (saṃkhyātva) has as its only established meaning the mere absence of being the ground for the application of the word "quality," it constitutes a different point (arthāntara), even when used to prove the negation of quality.

This is because [the reason] lacks the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and because it is vitiated by a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*). Nor is numberhood (*saṃkhyātva*) pervaded by the probans; for numberhood is not the genus of quality (*guṇajāti*), since it subsists in numbers, just like knowability (*meyatva*), and so forth.

The opposing views have been refuted; for, since the meaning of the word "quality" cannot be established, the purpose of [proving] the mere absence of "number-ness" as a universal (jāti) has already been fulfilled.

Furthermore, because number lacks the property of being a quality (guṇatva), the proponent also does not suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) when proving that number is a quality; for we have already established the application of the term "quality" to number.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for the produced nature (*kāryatva*) of duality and so forth, as in the case of a jar; for even though the mere absence of duality residing in a jar and the like is established [by inference], the produced nature itself is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Otherwise, [the following would occur]:
Otherwise, it would follow that even jars and the like lack the status of being effects;
furthermore, this is established by inference: the multiplicity residing in a jar is an effect, because it is a quality of an effect, or because it is a multiple quality.
"Because it is a quality of a jar or a cloth, like conjunction. Nor does this [reason] possess the property of being over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpaka*),
because the quality of being an effect of a positive entity that is the oneness of a jar deviates from the absence of oneness [in the case of multiple jars].

If it is argued that the property of being a quality of an effect (*kāryaguṇatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the oneness of a jar is not [itself] an effect— since the oneness of a jar is established as being non-produced (*akāryatva*)— we say: no.
Oneness possesses a genus that resides in its effect and does not reside in anything other than that which lacks the occurrence of oneness and lacks the property of being a number,
because it is a number, like duality; thus, once the oneness of the effect is established,
there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the failure of the condition (upādhi) to pervade the probandum (sādhya).
Furthermore, the inference of the proponent is inconclusive.

Nor is there a lack of evidence for the fact that duality and so forth, which reside solely in eternal [entities], are effects; for such evidence is found precisely in the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*).
Because that [duality] is established;
for any proof of duality and so forth that resides solely in eternal [entities] serves as a proof that duality and so forth are effects.
Duality and so forth, which reside exclusively in eternal [substances], are effects because they possess the nature of a plurality, like the plurality of jars.
Nor is it the case that duality and so forth, which subsist only in eternal [substances], are not effects.

Because it possesses the number residing only in eternal substances, like the oneness of space; thus, there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa). Time is the substratum of those effect-qualities residing in something other than these [eternal substances], which are devoid of the nature of conjunction, disjunction, and separateness that do not reside in non-eternal things.

If it is argued that [the probandum] is established by the inference "because it is an eternal substance, like the self," this is not so, because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the effect "number" which is devoid of subsistence in impermanent things. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (arthāntaratā).
Because the quality of time residing in time— which is devoid of conjunctionness, disjunctionness, and separateness—
is characterized by multiple numbers residing in time;
[and because it is] that which resides in time other than non-time, being devoid of impermanent occurrence and devoid of conjunctionness, disjunctionness, and separateness.
If you think that a quality (guṇa) is devoid of plurality, conjunction, disjunction, and separateness because it is a quality of time, like the duality residing in time;

And since its possession of a manifold number has been established, time is not the locus of those effect-qualities residing in this [time] which are devoid of inherence in the impermanent, and devoid of the states of conjunction, disjunction, and separateness; for it is other than space— which is devoid of the nature of self— and is corporeal, like color.
There is the state of being counterbalanced (satpratipakṣatva), because the counter-reason possesses a limiting condition (upādhi) by virtue of its dependence on [the property of] being a cause.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for the non-eternality of duality and so forth.

For that [number] is established by the very proof of its being an effect; and regarding its being an effect, there is inference. Nor is there any impossibility of duality and so forth being causes, because of substances.

This is because [number] is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), while unity and so forth are non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) and so forth are instrumental causes (nimittakāraṇa). Nor is there a lack of evidence for this here.

This is because the fact that substances and so forth produce duality and the like is established by perception; and also because of the following inference: "The multiple number is produced by unity, because it is a product-number, like the unity of a jar. Not [so].

Furthermore, plurality is not produced by unity because it resides in many things, like conjunction and disjunction; thus, there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva). [Thesis: An atom is the substratum of qualities residing in magnitude that is produced by unity and devoid of the nature of conjunction, disjunction, and separateness.

Since it is established by the reason "because of being a substance" that even the number residing in a great atom is the subject (dharmin), there is sublation by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*) regarding any number other than that which is multiple.
Because there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) with respect to that very same subject (dharmin); nor is there the fallacy of proving something already established (arthāntaratā),
since [the property] resides in a great atom that is devoid of both conjunction-ness and separateness-ness.
Because it is characterized by the number one residing in a large atom,
it is a quality residing in a large atom, produced by oneness devoid of conjunctionness, disjunctionness, and separateness.

This is also because of the inference: "It is devoid of [the qualities of] conjunction, disjunction, and separateness residing in a great atom, because it is a quality of a great atom," like the duality residing in a great atom. Furthermore, in such a case, there is no possibility of a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).
And it has been stated that for the opponent, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The proof for the fact that the duality of a pot and a cloth, and so forth, is produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is as follows: the duality of a pot and a cloth...

The duality of the jar and the cloth is produced by a cognition that has the oneness of the jar and the cloth as its object, because it is an effect, like a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). The proof for its being produced by God’s enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is as follows: the duality of the jar and the cloth...
"The [notion of] oneness regarding a jar and a cloth is produced by the Lord’s [apekṣā-]buddhi,
because it is an effect," and so forth. Nor is there an impossibility of an example here,
for the Lord’s cognition regarding the oneness of a jar and a cloth is indeed the producer of an effect.

Because it possesses the nature of being an intellect (*buddhitva*), like our own intellect; thus the illustrative example is established. Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the intellect of the Absolute (*atyantabuddhi*), for that too is the producer of destruction (*pradhvaṃsajanaka*). Nor...
Because the property of being the object of the identity between a jar and a cloth is unestablished, there is here the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

[For instance, in the argument: "The identity between a jar and a cloth, and so forth, is the object of God's cognition because it is cognizable (*meyatva*)," [the locus of the reason is] God's cognition.

Because the establishment of the cognition of the oneness of the jar and the cloth [is achieved]; nor is there a failure to establish the example of the jar here, since that is established by the inference: "because it is a cognition, [it must have an object]," referring to the cognition of the Lord (Īśvara).
Furthermore, since the fact that [duality] is produced by something and has something as its object is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject itself;
for if duality and so forth were produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) belonging to us [ordinary beings],...

The proof is as follows: "I am one who possesses a direct perception whose object is the oneness of a jar and a cloth that generates the duality of the jar and the cloth, because I am a self, like God," and so forth. It is not [the case that this is invalid].
And "being the Lord of Cātra" is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),

for it serves as a qualification that excludes from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) the nature of being a Lord— which consists of being the creator of the earth and so forth, possessing eternal knowledge, and so on.
Because it is other than the subject; and because the final particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), unity, and so forth residing in God are not identical with God, since He is distinct from them—
just as one who possesses the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the unity of a jar and a cloth, which is the cause of the duality of that jar and cloth, is other than those [entities].
[The reason "because it is an object of cognition" (meyatvāt) is] distinct [from the probandum], like a jar and a cloth; for, since this is established,

the reason is not a pseudo-upādhi because it does not pervade the probandum in that which possesses the direct perception whose object is the singularity of both the jar and the cloth— the very thing that generates the duality of the jar and the cloth.

Nor can it be argued that this [reason] is countered by a valid counter-reason (*satpratipakṣa*) on the grounds of its being the Lord, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases where the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) breaks the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is it the case that "I am not..."

There is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on the following inference: "The one who possesses the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the oneness of the jar and the cloth—which is the cause of the duality of the jar and the cloth—is devoid of any conscious being other than myself, just like the jar," because [the subject] is qualified by non-selfhood (*anātmatva*).
Furthermore, my direct perception has as its object the oneness of the jar and the cloth.
It produces non-unity, because it is a direct perception whose object is the oneness of a jar and a cloth,
just like the direct perception of the Lord (Īśvara). Nor is this...
There is a deviation [in the rule] regarding the direct perception whose object is the oneness of a jar and a cloth in a state of perishing, because that [perception] also produces duality;
furthermore, duality of the jar and cloth would be untenable in the moment immediately following it.

For [the destruction of the pot and cloth] is established through the very destruction of the pot and cloth themselves. Nor is my direct perception (sākṣātkāra) having the oneness of the pot and cloth as its object the producer of their destruction, because it is my direct perception.

The argument "like the direct perception of another [object]" is countered by an opposing reason (*satpratipakṣatva*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a direct perception residing in this [subject] which has as its object the singularity of a jar and a cloth that produce the duality established by the aforementioned inference. This [applies to] the duality of this jar and cloth...

The proof for [the fact that] this [perception of mine] is produced by a direct perception whose object is the oneness of this jar and cloth is as follows: "I possess a direct perception whose object is the oneness of this jar and cloth which generates the duality of these two,
because it is a direct perception of the duality of these two that is not produced by yogic power."
"Like that of God. Nor is the qualification "not produced by the dharma of yoga" redundant,
for [this applies] to one who lacks the direct perception whose object is the oneness of this jar and this cloth, which is the generator of this [specific] duality.

This is because the phrase "like the direct realization of that duality" is intended to avoid the fallacy [of over-extension] regarding those who have been liberated for a long time and those who will be liberated in the future.

Nor is it the case that "I do not possess a direct perception whose object is the oneness of this jar and cloth which generates this duality, because I possess duality, like a person who is currently agreed upon," and so forth.

There is counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*) [in the argument for God], because it is established by the following proof: "This Lord is other than one who possesses a direct perception whose object is the duality produced by this [Lord] and the oneness of this jar and cloth, because he is knowable (*meyatva*), like a jar."

Because there is a deviation [of the reason] in that which is a conscious entity distinct from God, yet is a locus of suffering— such as one possessing a direct perception whose object is the oneness of this jar and cloth, which generates the duality of these two;
for this [perception] has as its object the oneness of this jar and cloth.
This cognition is the producer of this duality,
because it is a cognition devoid of being the effect of anything other than this [duality],
like the cognition of the Lord (Īśvara). Nor is it the case that this [cognition] is not the producer of this duality.
There is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on the reasoning "because it is a cognition, like that which is currently admitted," and so forth;
[this applies] to the direct perception residing in that [object], which is the producer of this duality established by the aforementioned inference.

Because of deviation [from the rule]. Nor can there be a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) based on the claim that "this duality is not produced by a direct perception whose object is the unity of this jar and cloth, because it is a duality, like any other duality," for such an argument is itself deviant.
Because it is pervaded by the absence of the pervader of the first inference; nor is there a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣa*) by implication,
since [the reason] does not exist without the absence of the probandum of the first inference.

Because it is impossible to define the non-termination of the second inference as something to be proven; this cognition, which has the oneness of the jar and the cloth as its object, is the generator of duality.
This is because it is established that [the subject] is devoid of being a cognition whose object is something other than this,
and because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of duality produced by this cognition.

This is so because, while dualities residing in those [two objects]— distinct from the duality produced by the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) which has as its object the unity of this jar and cloth— are produced by an enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) residing in persons such as ourselves.

The proof [is as follows]: [Duality] is the object of a direct perception produced by a direct perception whose object is the unity residing in me, which is distinct from duality produced by the merit (*dharma*) born of yoga that belongs to us and others, and which is not produced by a direct perception whose object is unity produced by the merit born of yoga;
like the duality produced by a direct perception whose object is the unity of a jar and a cloth.
Alternatively, the generality of duality resides in that which is produced by a cognition other than [the cognition of] unity.

Because it is not excluded from duality, like existence (*sattā*). Nor is "subsisting in duality" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, because this [condition] is merely "other than the subject" (*pakṣetara*), since its specific [instance] is unestablished and thus lacks any exclusion from the nature of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Because those that do not subsist [in two] are excluded by the very mention of "subsisting in two," and because those that subsist in two only—
provided they are distinct from the universal of duality— are equivalent to the subject of the thesis.
And because the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*) is the subject (*pakṣa*),
there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*),
since existence (*sattā*) resides in the cognition of a substance qualified by unity produced by the cognition of unity.

Nor is it the case that its purpose is fulfilled merely by its being produced from the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) of one, two, or so on; for it is not unestablished that all instances of duality are produced from enumerative cognition.

It must be stated that this is established by the following inference: "The disputed dualities are produced by cognitions whose objects are two unities, because they are dualities, like a single unity. The same applies to triads and so forth.
Furthermore, duality and so forth are produced by cognitions whose object is unity,
because they are multiple numbers, like the number two; or alternatively,
all instances of duality and so forth are produced by cognitions whose object is unity.

Because it does not pervade that which is to be established— the non-existence by destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) produced by the cognition of oneness— and because it also does not pervade the [cognition] to be established in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of oneness.
If it is argued that the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced by the cognition of a substance qualified by unity, and not by the cognition of unity itself— this is not so;
for even the cognition of a substance qualified by unity has unity as its object, and is therefore a cognition of unity.

Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in the case of a jar and so forth, because even that [jar] is produced by the knowledge of God, which has singularity as its object. Nor is the absence of the property of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*) a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in this case.

Because [the probans] is not pervaded by the property to be proven (sādhyāvyāpakatva) in the case of the oneness of a jar and so forth, which are produced by the cognition of the Lord whose object is oneness; for instance, "duality and so forth are not produced by the cognition of oneness, because they possess the nature of number (saṃkhyātva), like oneness."

If it is argued that this is not so— no, because if the oneness residing in a jar or the like were taken as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the oneness residing in the jar;
and because that [oneness in the jar] deviates from the oneness residing in God.
If it is argued that [the oneness] residing in the jar and so forth is equivalent to the subject (pakṣa) because it is produced by a cognition whose object is the oneness residing in God,
and because God is unestablished— [we reply: no, because of the Blessed One.
Because [the number] has been established as belonging to the Omniscient One; because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*) by virtue of not being an effect;
and in the case of duality and so forth produced by the cognition of unity previously explained.
And because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*):
or else, this jar is the locus of a duality that is devoid of the property of residing in this [jar] and is not produced by a cognition whose object is the oneness of this jar and that cloth.
Because it is the locus of duality, like a cloth. Or alternatively:

this pot is the locus of a duality that is devoid of being resident in a pot produced by a cognition whose object is not the oneness of the pot and the cloth, because it is the locus of touch, like a cloth, and so forth. Or again, I [am... (Note: The text appears to be a fragment of a formal Nyāya inference (*prayoga*). The argument establishes the existence of duality (*dvitva*) in a specific subject—here, a pot—by distinguishing it from a duality that would arise from a conceptual error regarding the identity of the pot and a cloth.)
[The self] possesses the cognition of a unity that lacks the property of residing in the same locus as the non-producer of duality, because it is a self, like any other [self].
Or alternatively: I possess the cognition of a unity that lacks the property of residing in the same locus as the non-producer of this duality.

Because it is a self, like another self; or else, this direct perception whose object is the oneness of the jar and the cloth is the ultimate cause of their duality, because it is a unity; for that which is not so is not thus.

Thus it is, as in the case of "the sky. Nor is the failure to define the ultimate cause of this duality a fault here; for what is intended is the causality of this duality, excluding that which coexists with the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the producer of this very duality.
Regarding the state of not being a cause in a single moment:
this refers to the non-causality of that which has arisen in the immediately preceding moment, as well as the non-causality of momentary causality within momentary causality itself.
Because this [duality] has as its ultimate cause that which arose in the moment immediately preceding it, distinct from the [prior] moment;
this duality is produced by that which arose in the moment immediately preceding it.
This is because the probandum is established— as in the case of a cloth produced at the very moment of its production—
and because the final cause of this duality is admitted by both disputants.

Nor is this direct perception of the identity between the jar and the cloth not the ultimate cause of their non-duality, because it is a direct perception, like any other admitted instance; thus, there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva).
"I am one who possesses the direct realization devoid of being terminated by the final cause of this duality, because I am the Self,
like any other Self"—
this [argument] fails because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the direct realization of the final cause of this duality.
Furthermore, the absence of being a direct realization (*sākṣātkāratvābhāva*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here,

because it lacks pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) in the instance where there is deviation from the counter-reason (*pratipakṣahetu*); and [it also possesses] the property of not pervading the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpakatva*), and so forth.

This is because there is no certainty regarding the absence of direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*) of the final cause of this duality. Nor is there any impossibility of a cause for the destruction of duality and the like.
Because of the possibility of both the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the destruction of its substrate,
as well as the destruction of the direct perception whose object is the unity that produces this duality.
This [momentary existence] is the ultimate cause for the destruction of this duality, because it possesses that very nature; for whatever is not thus is not so, like space, and so forth.
Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here, precisely because of what was stated previously.

Nor can it be argued that this destruction of the direct perception whose object is oneness is not the final cause of the destruction of this duality because it is a destruction; for such an argument would be subject to a counter-argument (satpratipakṣa).

"I am one who possesses the destruction of the final cause of the destruction of this duality, yet is devoid of the oneness residing in me and devoid of the direct realization of oneness," because of being a self, like any other self; [this argument is] established,
since there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the destruction of the final cause of the destruction of this duality.
Furthermore, the absence of perishability (*vināśatvābhāva*) in the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) cannot be the limiting condition (*upādhi*),
because its pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is broken in instances where there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the counter-reason (*pratipakṣahetu*).
And because there is no certainty regarding its being a pervader of the probandum;
for there is no certainty that this duality-ness and the cause of destruction lack the absence of destruction.
The direct perception of the destruction of the sensory contact with this skin-surface is the proof for its being the producer of the destruction of this duality.
[This is established by the inference: "I am one who possesses the destruction of the direct perception of being the producer of the destruction of this duality."
"Because it is a self [ātmatva], like another instance"— this is the proof for the fact that the destruction of one duality (dvitva) is caused by the destruction of the cause of that duality.
This is the nature of duality.

It is destructible by the destruction of its efficient cause and the destruction of its substance, because it is a duality, like the duality of atoms produced by God’s relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Nor is the example deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*), because it is admitted by all that the duality of atoms produced by the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) dependent on God is destroyed by the destruction of its efficient cause, which is the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

The duality of an atom, produced by a cognition dependent on a corresponding perceiver, is destroyed by the destruction of its cause of duality, because it is a duality, like a duality that is destroyed by the destruction of its substratum; this follows from such inference. It is not [the case that it is destroyed otherwise].
Furthermore, the destruction of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is impossible here, because both the atom and its unity are indestructible;
this is unlike the case of jars, cloths, duality, and so forth, which are destroyed by the destruction of their substrates.
Even regarding the fact that [the number] is destructible by the destruction of its cause, namely duality and so forth, this very [argument] is the proof.
Now, an objection is raised: "But the distinction between duality, trinity, and so on is untenable."
Because a distinction in causes is impossible; for it is also not tenable that duality has two inherent causes and triality has three,
since [the substrata] do not exist as "two" prior to the production of duality and triality.

Because three-ness is impossible [in that context], it cannot be the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) for duality; nor is it tenable to say that the non-inherent causes of three-ness are other than the unities (ekatva).
Because of the aforementioned fault, and because duality and so forth cannot exist in unity and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the cognition of two unities is the cause of duality,
nor that the cognition of three unities is the cause of triadness.

"It is logical [to say] 'because of the previously mentioned fault'—that is incorrect, because the alternative possibilities (vikalpa) are untenable. Does it follow here that there is an absence of difference due to the absence of a difference in causes, or is it so inferred? Not the first."
Because of the laxity of the root [reason]; for even if [the number] were produced by causes that do not produce duality, it would still possess the distinction of duality within eternal things,
precisely because it is produced by causes that do not produce duality.
If it is argued that this would result in the absence of being an effect distinct from duality— [we reply] no,
because it is accepted that duality and the like are produced by causes that do not produce duality.

This is because the jar, cloth, pillar, and the triad [of these] are also causes for the non-producer of the duality of the jar and cloth, as well as for the unity residing in the pillar and the cognitions directed toward them.
By virtue of not being the non-produced, non-producer, cause, or non-producer of the triad consisting of pot, cloth, and pillar, and by virtue of being the duality of pot and cloth,
there is an absence of being an effect produced by that which produces the triad of pot, cloth, and pillar, and so forth.
If it is argued that [the universal] has been established [as the cause], we say no; for even when there is duality between a jar and a cloth,
our cognition— which does not have as its object the singularity residing in a pillar (which is incapable of producing a triad consisting of the jar, the cloth, and the pillar)—
is nonetheless a cause [of that duality].

If it is argued that, because it is not produced by causes other than those that produce a triad residing in two atoms and a substance distinct from them, it follows that there is an absence of non-differentiation in the effect from the triad residing in two atoms and a substance distinct from them— [we reply: no, for this is also the case with the duality of atoms.

Because it is accepted that the cause [of the cognition of duality] is the Supreme Lord’s cognition, which has as its object the unity residing in two atoms— rather than the unity residing in something other than those two atoms— and because the Lord’s knowledge has everything as its object.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is possible because its object is oneness residing in something distinct from two atoms— no, for it is accepted that in the case of God, there is knowledge of all objects and knowledge of all things in all their states.
Nor does this entail the consequence of the destruction of God's omniscience, because the knowledge of all objects is indeed admitted;
even though there is the admission of knowledge whose objects are all things and all subjects.
Because omniscience is established. Nor is it a fault that a single cognition having all things as its object would result in non-existence, for that is precisely what is accepted. Not so.
If the Lord’s enumerative cognition were eternal, it would follow that the duality of atoms would arise at all times; however, this is precisely what is accepted.
Furthermore, the Lord’s enumerative cognition is not eternal. Nor is this the case with respect to the Lord.

The consequence of [His] knowledge being non-eternal is not a fault, because it is accepted [by us]. Nor does this contradict the admission of eternal knowledge in the case of Īśvara, for we do not admit that His knowledge is eternal. Not...
Furthermore, there is no evidence for such a relational cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*);

for it is established by the following inference: "The object of this direct perception is the object of a singularity that is distinct from the singularity of these two atoms, which is devoid of being the object of the singularity of this second atom while being the object of the singularity of this [first] atom, and is devoid of being the object of any singularity other than the dual-singularity of these two atoms, because it is an object of knowledge (*meyatvāt*), like a jar. Nor is it the case that...
Because of the absence of causes such as a body, there is no production of knowledge of effects in the Supreme Lord; this is because [the existence] of a body and so forth is not admitted. And thus—
The Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Purāṇas describe the Blessed One— the beloved of Umā, the moon-crested, the three-eyed— as the Supreme Lord.

Nor is there an impossibility of the Supreme Lord possessing the conceptual cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that produces duality— which in turn produces the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)— on the grounds that memory and so forth (or creation and so forth) are impossible at the beginning of memory (or creation), because a body and such do not exist for Him.

If it is asked: "Since a body existing within this particular cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is impossible, what is the destination after the dissolution of all cosmic eggs?"—the answer is: no, because at that time the production of duality in atoms is not admitted, [and thus] the dimension of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) at the beginning of creation [cannot arise].
Furthermore, this is because it is accepted that [the number] two is produced by the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) of the Supreme Lord existing prior to the dissolution.
Nor should it be argued that it is impossible for the "two-ness" existing prior to the dissolution to persist as long as the world endures.

Because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. Nor should it be argued that this duality perishes more rapidly than other dualities, like any duality other than [the one under discussion], for even the opponent [would have to admit this].

For one who maintains that the duality of atoms is produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), it must be admitted that even the duality existing prior to the dissolution of the world persists until the beginning of the next creation.
Because the example of the atom lacks the property to be proven; for the opponent also accepts that even the duality of a pot, a cloth, and so forth,
persists as long as its substratum exists, and this applies equally to the duality of an atom.
Furthermore, even though it is produced by a cognition that takes all objects as its permanent content,
it is accepted that [the duality] is produced by a conjunction that initiates a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) which does not reside in anything other than two atoms;
otherwise, that duality would have arisen even prior [to the formation of the dyad], since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) would already be present.
And this being the case, there is no undesirable consequence of the non-arising of triadic number residing in atoms that do not initiate [a composite],
because such is indeed accepted; for [triadic number] resides in the duality residing in atoms that do not initiate [a composite].

Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); because there is an absence of any effect such as the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka-parimāṇa*) and so forth. And this has been explained by us at length in the *Kiraṇāvalīdarpaṇaka*, titled *Haraprasāda*.
Or, let it be that in the case of the duality of two atoms,

the cause of the production of the cognition of the unity of the two atoms is not based on the unities residing in entities other than those two atoms which produce the triad distinct from those two atoms; nor is there [any such requirement] here.

There is an absence of valid cognition [proving such a thing]. This oneness of this atom is the object of a direct perception belonging to us and others, which is devoid of being the non-object of the oneness of a second atom that is not the object of the oneness of this atom, and which is devoid of being the object of an oneness distinct from the onenesses of these two atoms, because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*).
This is because of the inference "like a jar. Nor should it be argued that for people like us,
there is an impossibility of the knowledge that produces the duality which, in turn, generates the dimension of a binary atomic compound (dvyaṇuka) other than at the time of creation,
on the grounds that we lack bodies at that time.
Because for people such as ourselves,
at that time, there is the production of bodies existing within this brahmāṇḍa; and not [for those] such as ourselves...
The direct perception of the unity residing in atoms is not impossible,
as it is possible through the power of dharma produced by yoga.
Therefore, [this applies] to all dualities and so forth.
Because there is the occurrence of causes that produce other dualities, there is no resulting state of being an effect [of duality] by means of triads and so forth;
nor is there [such a result] from the second [alternative], because it is sublated.
Because the distinction between duality, triality, and so forth is established by perception, whereas the non-difference of their causes is unestablished according to the manner already stated;
[this applies] to duality, triality, and the rest.
And because there exists a distinction among causes, such as the prior non-existence of duality and so forth;
nor is it the case that first there is a cognition of the universal "oneness," and immediately thereafter a cognition of multiple things qualified by oneness.

If it is argued that immediately after that there is the cognition of the generality "duality," and immediately after that there is the cognition of the substance qualified by the quality of duality— just like the cognition "the pot is white"— we say no.

If the subject (*dharmin*) consists of cognitions of substances qualified by singularities produced at moments other than the one immediately preceding the production of duality, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
[This is so] because the cognition of a substance qualified by a singularity produced at the moment immediately preceding duality [is indeed admitted].
Furthermore, because the substratum is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*),
since you do not accept such a thing;
or, if you were to accept it, then there would be two substances.
Because it would follow that knowledge could not arise;
for at the very moment when duality arises through the cognition of a substance qualified by unity,
the "reckoning-cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*) desired by you would be destroyed.
Or rather, at the moment of the cognition of the generality of duality, duality is destroyed by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Therefore, an enumerative cognition distinct from the cognition of a substance qualified by the quality of unity is entirely without proof; thus, [the object] is struck by the substance qualified by unity.
[The cognition of a substance] is indeed conceptual, for it is the "relative cognition" (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Alternatively, let the relative cognition be a non-conceptual cognition whose object is the generality of oneness (*ekatvasāmānya*) and multiple instances of oneness. And the proof for that is this very cognition of a substance qualified by oneness, namely: "This is one," "This is one."
But there is no after-cognition (anuvyavasāya).

Because at the moment of the production of duality, there is no production of the cognition of the substance qualified by that [duality] and unity; therefore, the production of the after-cognition occurs only in the moment immediately following the production of duality, since at that time there is no production of the cognition of the generality (sāmānya) of duality.

Furthermore, at the moment immediately following the production of duality, when the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) arises, there is no production of the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*), because the simultaneous arising of two cognitions is not admitted.

And in the moment immediately following that, when the cognition of the generality "duality" (dvitvasāmānya) arises, there is no arising of the cognition of a substance qualified by duality— which occurs subsequent to it—

because [the substance] has already been apprehended in the moment of the cognition of duality by the cognition of a substance qualified by the singularities produced in that moment of duality, during the moment of reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).

Because of the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); and because, through the destruction of the enumerative cognition at the moment of the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*), the duality itself is destroyed;
nor [is it destroyed] at the moment of the production of the duality.
Because when the cognition of a substance qualified by oneness arises, at that moment of the cognition of the generality of duality, the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed;
and by the destruction of the enumerative cognition, [the quality of duality is destroyed] at the moment of the cognition of the quality of duality.

The doubt that "the non-arising of the cognition of the substance due to the destruction of duality is equally [the case] for you as well" is addressed by us at the very moment immediately following the cognition of the generality of duality.
Because it accepts a cognition qualified by duality;
for the indeterminate cognition of the universal has duality as its objective quality.
Because it is logically consistent for [the cognition] to have the knowledge of qualifiers as its object;
therefore, indeterminate perception has as its object multiple individualities accompanied by the generality of oneness.

Therefore, the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) occurs immediately after the cognition of the generality of non-duality, and not after the cognition of multiple singularities qualified by the generality of multiplicity, because there is no evidence for the latter.
For the [cognition of] duality and so forth is established from a non-conceptual [perception] itself, which has as its object the unity of each individual within the generality of consciousness.
Nor is a non-conceptual perception that has the unity of many individuals as its object the producer of that duality, because it is non-conceptual.
Or rather, it should be stated that it is like something already apprehended;

for, according to the logic previously established, it lacks the status of being the objective support for both multiplicity and unity, it possesses a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and it does not produce duality. Therefore...
The cognition of a quality as qualified by the generality of duality is also refuted immediately following the cognition of the generality of duality,
due to a lack of valid evidence. Nor is there such a thing as the cognition "two substances."
It should be stated: "The cognition of a qualified object is produced by the cognition of its qualifier, because it is a cognition of a qualified object, like the cognition of the number three.

This is not so, because [if one were to argue against this], there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*) regarding non-conceptual cognition and the cognition of universals.
Because that [cognition] also has duality as its twofold objective support;
for the rule that the universal and the individual have a single objective support is established for both disputants,
even though it remains unproven that the cognition of the generality of duality has duality itself as its objective support.
Therefore, because it is impossible to avoid [the consequence of] a different object,
the means of proof— the cognition of the generality of duality— is fulfilled merely by having duality as its objective support.
Because there is no finality in the cognition qualified by the generality of duality;
for in the case of "two substances," the generality of duality is not itself further qualified by another duality.

If it is argued that because the non-conceptual cognition of the generality of duality has a "distinguished" duality as its object, the existence of a cognition of a duality distinct from that [generality] is established— [we reply: no.
Is the qualification of that substance by the effect [duality]— that is, by that which possesses duality as qualified by the generality of duality— or is it the generality of duality itself,
or its state of being qualified? Or what else?
"Is it 'duality qualified by the qualification of being characterized by the generality of duality'?
Not the first [alternative], because even the non-conceptual cognition of the generality of duality has as its object the duality residing in a substrate qualified by duality.

Furthermore, the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*) remain as before. Nor can the second or third [alternatives] be maintained,
because it is impossible for two-ness (*dvitva*)— which resides in two-ness itself and is qualified by the universal of two-ness— to function as a qualifier of a substance.

Or, even if it were possible, it is not accepted; nor is the fourth [alternative], because it is refuted by the same defects as previously analyzed through the same alternatives. Therefore, the [view] of the ancient teachers is untenable.
As for us, however:
The first [cognition] is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka), having as its object the universal of oneness, the quality of oneness, and the substance.
Immediately following that is the cognition of a substance qualified by multiple instances of oneness as qualified by the universal of oneness; this is the "reckoning-cognition" (apekṣābuddhi).

Immediately thereafter, following the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there arises a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception having as its objects the two universals of duality,

the quality [of duality], and the substance; and immediately thereafter, due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition, follows the destruction of the duality, [resulting in] the quality of duality as qualified by the universal of duality.
The process is as follows: there is a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) in the form "two substances," which has as its object a substance qualified by the quality of duality (*dvitva*).
Or alternatively:

First, there is non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) whose object is the universal of plurality, the many individual unities, and the substance; immediately following that is the [conceptual] cognition of relative number (*apekṣābuddhi*), which has as its object a substance qualified by the quality of unity as characterized by the universal of unity, and [the universal of unity] as characterized by the quality of unity.
The conceptual [cognition] has as its objects duality and the two things; immediately after that,

there arises a non-conceptual [cognition] which has as its objects the generality of duality, the quality of duality, and the two substances, and which destroys the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Immediately thereafter, due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the destruction of duality; then, the determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) "two substances" arises, which has as its object two substances qualified by the quality of duality—which itself is qualified by the universal of duality—and by the generic property of being a quality (*guṇatva*). This is the process.

Regarding the non-conceptual nature of the cognition whose object is the generality of duality and so forth, conceptual cognition alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Conceptual cognition alone is the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). Now, [one might ask] regarding the cognition "two substances": [The opponent objects: But how can there be a non-conceptual cognition of two substances? For it is impossible for a non-conceptual cognition to have as its object a substance qualified by number, since a substance is not perceived without the perception of its qualifiers such as number. Furthermore, the qualifier cannot be grasped without the cognition of the qualified, nor can the qualified be grasped without the cognition of the qualifier; thus, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Moreover, the cognition of the qualifier must necessarily be preceded by the recollection of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, and that recollection must be preceded by the experience of that relationship; therefore, the cognition of the qualifier is not possible without the prior experience of the relationship. Consequently, the cognition of two substances is indeed conceptual. And since conceptual cognition is not a means of valid knowledge, how could there be a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)? Thus, the existence of the means of valid knowledge and the subsequent reflective awareness would be undermined. [The author replies: This is not so. Even if the qualifier is not previously experienced, the cognition of the qualifier arises through the very act of perceiving the qualified, just as in the case of the cognition of a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), where the cognition of the qualifier "blue" arises simultaneously with the cognition of the qualified "lotus. Therefore, the cognition of two substances is indeed non-conceptual. And since it is non-conceptual, it is a means of valid knowledge, and from it, the subsequent reflective awareness arises. Thus, there is no contradiction with the established doctrine. Furthermore, even if the cognition of two substances were conceptual, it would still be a means of valid knowledge, because conceptual cognition is a means of valid knowledge when it apprehends an object not previously known. Since the qualifier "duality" has not been previously known, its cognition is a means of valid knowledge. And since it is a means of valid knowledge, the subsequent reflective awareness is also established. Therefore, there is no fault. Thus, the cognition of two substances is both a means of valid knowledge and a subsequent reflective awareness. This concludes the section on the proof of the existence of the means of valid knowledge and the subsequent reflective awareness.
Duality is that which is qualified by the generality of duality;
and it is untenable to claim that the object is a substance qualified by duality at the moment of the cognition "two substances."
