Because duality does not exist [at that time] and because perception has only the present as its object; and if qualified cognition were to have as its objects the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, then—
The cognition "the sandalwood is fragrant" would not occur, because the eye does not apprehend fragrance and the nose does not apprehend the sandalwood.
Because it is untenable for [the sentence] to produce knowledge;
nor is a qualifier-qualified relationship possible as a positive entity distinct from the word-meanings, since such a thing is not admitted.
Nor is this [conjunction] simply inherence (samavāya), because, being beyond the senses,
it cannot be the object of a direct perception produced by the eye; nor is this [conjunction] simply an existent entity (bhāva).
This is logical because it is defined by its specific counter-correlate; otherwise,

there would be the undesirable consequence of no distinction between "this is one" and "these are two," since both would merely be the exclusion [of others] from the substratum where the absolute absence of the qualifier resides.
Udayana and others maintain that [the universal] is the object of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*).
That too is not tenable, because the conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are untenable.
[Consider] the absolute absence of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇātyantābhāva*):...
Is it the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of a single individual instance of the locus of the absolute absence of the qualifier,
or rather, is it that which has as its counter-correlates all individual instances of the locus of the absolute absence of the qualifier?

Is it a single mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), or rather all mutual absences whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are all individual instances that serve as the loci of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of their respective qualifiers? Or what?
Is it the absolute absence of the absolute absence of the qualifier,
or the absolute absence of the substratum-ness of the absolute absence of the qualifier,
or the absolute absence of the qualified?

Not the first [alternative], because it would entail the consequence of there being no distinction between "this" and "that," since even color (rūpa) is the locus of the absolute non-existence of this duality.
Not the second [alternative],
because it is impossible for there to be a single mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) having multiple counter-correlates,
and because of the fault that will be stated later.
Not the third [alternative],
because it is impossible to cognize the absences of that duality so long as all the individual instances— which are the loci of the absolute absence of that duality— are not themselves cognized.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) of supersensible individuals— which serve as the loci of the absolute absence of duality— to fall within the range of direct perception;
moreover, there would be the appearance of an infinite number of such mutual absences.
Furthermore, because the cognition of a counter-correlative is impossible [at that time]:
for that [cognition of the absence] does not arise at the moment of the cognition of the generality of duality,
nor at the moment of the cognition of the quality of duality, since simultaneous cognitions are untenable.

Nor [does it occur] at the second moment of its arising; for according to our view, this is so whether one adopts the position that the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is conceptual (*savikalpa*),
or the position that it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), in which case [the destruction occurs] by means of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous production [of cognitions] through the cognition of a substance qualified by oneness; and according to the system of Udayana and others,
[the object] would have perished at the time of the cognition of the universal.
Because it is logically untenable for the cognition of the counter-correlate (pratiyogijñāna) to produce the cognition of a substance qualified by duality at a time subsequent to itself;
nor [is it tenable] at the moment immediately following the cognition of the quality of duality.
Because there would be the undesirable consequence of [the cognition] arising through a cognition qualified by duality;
for, since they arise simultaneously, there is no distinction between the two objects of apprehension (ālambana) regarding their specificities as cause or non-cause.
Therefore, [the third option is rejected] because it would entail the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) of duality;
nor is the fourth [option valid],
because [it would involve] the absolute non-existence of the absolute non-existence of the qualifier.

For if [the two substances] were not distinct from the nature of their qualifiers, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition "two substances" would have duality as its object; whereas if they were distinct,
as in the previous case, the cognition of the counter-correlate would be impossible.
Because the apprehension of that [duality] would be impossible; for from that very [apprehension], if the cognition "two" were to arise, it would follow that duality itself is not established.
[Objection: Duality is established through the cognition of that quality of duality as qualified by the universal of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*).
If it is argued that [the number two is established] by means of that [non-conceptual cognition], no; for that has already been refuted.

If it is argued that the establishment of the number two arises from a non-conceptual cognition of duality, no; for in the absence of a conceptual cognition of duality, a non-conceptual cognition of duality cannot be established.
Because that [non-existence] is inferable through conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*),
and because if duality itself is not established, its absolute non-existence and so forth are likewise not established; nor is it the fifth [alternative].

For that very reason, it is not the sixth [alternative] either; for otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognitions "these two are separate," "these two are conjoined," and "these two are disjoined" would be indistinguishable from one another.
Because there is no distinction between the substratum (the qualified object) and the absolute non-existence of that substratum, both of which serve as the objective supports [of cognition].

Therefore, [the opponent argues] that if duality were destroyed by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the cognition "two substances" would lack a proper object. That is incorrect. Two...
Regarding the cognition "in the substance," since the cognition has as its object a substance qualified by duality,
even at the time of the cognition "two substances," the moment of duality has already perished and thus constitutes the object.

If it is argued: "No, because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka). This duality is not the object of this direct perception, because it lacks [the property of] being present at this time, like a future jar"—we say: No.

Because duality itself would be unestablished if it were the object of that respective direct perception, since its substratum would be unestablished; and because if it were the object of this direct perception, the proof of its absence would be contradicted. What [more is there to say]?
This is because, if the state of being an object of direct realization is unestablished anywhere, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*);
whereas if it is established, then by this very same reasoning, this [fallacy] applies.

This is because it is unestablished that duality is the object of this direct perception, as such a claim would be contradicted; furthermore, it is unavoidable that [the following inference] would apply: "This object of direct perception is another substance, because it possesses substantiality (dravyatva), like a future jar," and because [your reason] is unestablished (asiddha).

In our view, at the moment of the determinate cognition whose object is a substance qualified by the quality of duality, there exists an indeterminate cognition whose objects are the generality of duality and the quality of duality.

Because of the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), and because in the immediately subsequent moment the duality (dvitva) is destroyed by the destruction of that enumerative cognition, there arises the cognition: "two substances."

If it is argued that [the cognition in question] has as its object the qualifier alone because there is no sublation and because it is a qualified cognition— just like the cognition "fragrant sandalwood"— we say: no, for this would involve a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of inferential cognitions and the like.
Furthermore, under the view that it has only the qualificandum as its object,
there would be the undesirable consequence of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*). [This is so] when "being perceptible" is used as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*).
Because the example lacks the property to be proven; for even the cognition "fragrant sandalwood" apprehends a substance qualified by fragrance.
And because a substance characterized by fragrance is apprehended by the sense of smell alone,
and because both the sense of smell and the sense of taste are perceivers of substances,
as established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Because it is understood that the cognition of a substance qualified by odor is produced by the sense of smell,
and likewise [the cognition] of a substance qualified by taste.

Because it is understood that [the cognition] is produced by taste; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even the eyes and the sense of touch would not perceive substances,
since they [would function] together with the olfactory-produced knowledge of fragrance.
Or [it is so] because of the perception of a substance qualified by fragrance.

Nor does it follow that smell, in this way, would also be perceivable by the eye or the sense of touch, for that is accepted [as the case]. Nor, in this way, [does it follow] even for those who are deficient in their sense of smell...
There would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing a substance qualified by fragrance,
because it is admitted that the cognition of fragrance produced by the olfactory organ also serves as a cooperative cause. Likewise,
[this would apply] to the visual and tactile organs when assisted by the knowledge of taste produced by the gustatory organ.
Because it results from the cognition of a substance qualified by its taste; because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*);
and because the cognition "the sandalwood is fragrant" is inferential (*anumāna*). [The inference is as follows:
This sandalwood possesses this fragrance, because it is of this nature; for whatever is not thus is not so, just like...

Or, by employing a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) such as "this is a jar," there is the fault of having a well-known qualification (*prasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because this fragrance is established through direct olfactory perception.
Nor is it the case that, even though this fragrance is well known...

Because the state of possessing that [quality] is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), since it is not admitted that what is determined by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is its pervader (*vyāpaka*). This is also the case for the inference: "This fragrance is based on something, because it is a quality, like color," and so forth.

Because it is well-established: what is established by experience as a distinctness (*viśiṣṭatā*) that is distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is simply a particular state of being (*bhāvaviśeṣa*), like knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth.
Duality, when accompanied by another unitary oneness (*ekatva*), generates triad-ness (*tritva*); triad-ness, when accompanied by another unitary oneness...
And [the argument] that "it produces four" would not apply to the case of producing duality, and so forth— if this is objected, know that it is because there is no proving evidence.
For duality and the rest produce multiple numbers because they possess the nature of number (*saṃkhyātva*), just like unity (*ekatva*).

If you say this, it is not so; for there is a deviation [in the rule] when, at a stage where no further unification has occurred, duality and the like have perished without having produced triadness and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a deviation in the case of duality and the like that have been destroyed by the destruction of their substratum, according to your own view.

Furthermore, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of the number *parārdha* (the highest number). Moreover, if those [numbers] were also taken as the subject (*dharmin*), there would be a contradiction. And because there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*): "Duality and so forth do not produce multiple numbers, because they are multiple numbers, like duality and so forth that have perished due to the destruction of their substratum."
Furthermore, [the property of] being three and so forth is not produced by multiple numbers, because it is a number, just like oneness; this follows from inference as well.
Moreover, regarding the causality of multiple numbers—

Does this mean being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of multiple numbers, or being the cause of multiple numbers? Not the first, because it is subject to the same logical flaw (*upādhi*) as unity. Nor the second, because it is subject to the same logical flaw as the nature of multiple qualities (*guṇa*). [This applies] to triads and so forth.
Furthermore, if duality and so forth were produced [by this], it would entail the consequence that they have fixed causes:

for the dual cognition of a jar and a cloth, the respective unitary cognitions of the jar and the cloth would be the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); and for the dual cognition of a jar, a cloth, and a pillar, the respective unitary cognitions of the jar, the cloth, and the pillar would be the enumerative cognition.
Alternatively, the cognition of the duality of a jar and a cloth, or the unity of a pillar,
is [an instance of] relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) because it exceeds the [cognition of] the quartet consisting of the jar, the cloth, the pillar, and the wall;
whereas the cognition of the unity in the jar, the cloth, the pillar, and the wall is itself relative cognition.
[This refers to] either the cognition of the jar, cloth, pillar as three, and the wall as one, or the cognition of the jar, cloth as two, and the pillar and wall as two.
Nor is there a restriction regarding their causes, because distinct universals (jāti) are admitted for "three-ness" and so forth; otherwise [the confusion would be unavoidable].
Because it would entail the abolition of numerical conventions such as "ten," "five," and "fifteen. In that case,
due to the absence of contact with the previously perceived singularity, the eye, and so forth, there would be a single [cognition] whose object is the entirety of singularity.
The cognition "one hundred has arisen" arises as an uncontradicted knowledge;
therein, the relational cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) consists of the cognition of the number ninety together with the internal cognition of unity.
Furthermore, there is another latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the final unity, which has all [the preceding units] as its object.
Or rather, it is recollection, because no other possibility exists.

However, it is not tenable to claim that the number "hundred" arises from both the experience of the final unit and the recollection of the preceding units produced immediately thereafter, because [the number is not produced] by the recollection of the preceding units.
At the moment of the arising of the number one hundred, due to the destruction of the experience of the final unity by the experience of that final unity,
and through the destruction of the experience of the final unity at the moment of the cognition of the generality of "one-hundredness."
Because, upon the destruction of the hundred [units], there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition "one hundred" could not arise in the immediately subsequent moment;

for [the cognition] must have as its object all the units through the combination of the latent impression produced by the absence of the previous units and the sense-organ in contact with the final unit.
If it is argued that a cognition consisting of both perception and recollection arises as one hundred in number— no, for when there is the ascertainment of its being a perception,

its lack of being a recollection is inferred precisely by virtue of its being a perception; and when there is the ascertainment of its being a recollection, [its lack of being a perception is inferred] precisely by virtue of its being a recollection.
This is because of the inference from the absence of the state of being an apprehension.

Immediately after the experience of the final singularity, there arises a direct mental cognition in the form of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is all singularities without exception.
The teachers of the Ātreya school maintain that [the cognition] produces the number one hundred;
however, that is not so, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a cognition,
and because the number one hundred is established through the manner already described.
And because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects, the cognition of the number "hundred" with respect to a jar and such is indeed visual.
Nor should it be argued: "How can the cognition of the number 'hundred' be produced by the eye, given the absence of sensory contact with all the individual substrata of that hundred?"
Since it is possible for [the number] to be apprehended from that very same [object] by means of the contact with a single substratum, just as [a universal] is;
and because the experience of "a hundred" cannot be denied;
and likewise for numbers such as "parārdha" and so forth.

Now, it is not tenable that separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is a property of many things, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for separateness. If it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*)—in the form of the cognition "separate"—is the means of valid cognition, we say no;
for that [perception] has mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its objective support. Separateness itself must first be defined.
If it is argued: "This [is] distinct from that" involves the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) because it refers to a limit (*avadhi*);

however, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not determined by a limit, for otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence of using the ablative even in cases such as "this is not that. [Response: No; for in expressions such as "this is other than that" or "this is different from that," mutual non-existence is indeed determined by a limit.
If it is argued that words such as "different" (*anyabhinnādi*) also denote only separateness (*pṛthaktva*), we say no;

for even in the absence of separateness, expressions such as "taste is different from color" (*rūpād raso bhinnaḥ*) or "it is other" (*anya*) are employed. [As explained by Prasāda and others: the use of words like "different" occurs through the superimposition (*āropa*) of separateness upon taste and so forth.

If it is argued: "No, because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka). If it is argued that 'separateness (pṛthaktva) does not reside in a quality because it is a quality, like color'—this is the subverting evidence—[we reply: No, because the quality-status of separateness is unestablished.
Regarding words such as 'other' (anya) and so on, if they were coextensive with mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), [then] in cases such as 'this is other than that'..."

If it is argued that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would not apply [to "this"], because it lacks a defining limit (*avadhi*), we say: no, for that too is defined by a limit. If it is then argued that the undesirable consequence of the ablative would follow even in the expression "this is not that" (*nāyam ayam*), we say: no, because in this case [the distinction] exists...

This is because the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is not intended to be expressed. If it is argued that if the status of being a limit were intended to be expressed, the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) would necessarily follow—[we reply] no; for the cognition of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is established by the mere expression "this is not this."
Because it is possible to intend the limit [of an action] as being purposeless;

if it is argued that "if there is an intention to express the limit, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) would not occur even when words such as *pṛthak* are used," [we reply]: no, as in the case of "the jar exists" (*sattvaṃ ghaṭaḥ*).
Because we observe such usage as "separate from" (*pṛthak*), and because separateness (*pṛthaktva*) itself lacks the property of being defined by a limit (*avadhi*),

and because there is no evidence that jars and the like are defined by limits— [if it is argued] that the ablative case in the expression "the jar is separate from the cloth" (*paṭāt ghaṭaḥ pṛthak*) is itself the proof for its status as a limit— we say: no, for that [ablative]...

Because the status of having "pṛthak," "anya," "bhinna," and so forth as qualifying adjuncts is obtained, it is possible for [the ablative] to arise in reference to the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Nor does this entail the undesired consequence of using the fifth case (*pañcamī*) even in an expression such as "a jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*),
since the status of being the counter-correlate of mutual absence is indeed possible there.

If it is argued that this [usage] is also applicable to me because there is no other word such as *pṛthak* (*separate*) or *anya* (*other*) as a subordinate term (*upapada*), and because [the usage] has been established by Pāṇini, Śākaṭāyana, and others, and because it is not mentioned [as a separate category], and because it possesses the characteristics of either *anyatara* or *itarat*, and because it is an indicator synonymous with the word *anya*— then [we reply]: in that case, the ablative case would also undesirably follow in the expression "The pot is not the cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*).
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of not employing the word *itara* (other). For that [word *anya*] is also a synonym for the word *anya*.

If it is argued that the word *itara* denotes what is similar to that [object], and thus is not a synonym for the word *anya*, we say no, because there is no evidence for this. The very fact that the word *itara* is not employed in such cases is itself the proof.
If it is argued: "No, because when that [word] is not joined with another word, the meaning of the fifth case (ablative) would be already established";

or if it is argued: "In the case of being an *upapada*-case, the fifth case would be redundant"—we say: no, for it possesses meaning as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

If it is argued that *avadhitva* (the state of being a limit) is postulated because postulating [it as the cause] for the employment of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) by words such as *pṛthak*, *anya*, and *bhinna* would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)— we say no;
for since the fifth case is justified by the power of the established *upapada* itself, the postulation of *avadhitva* is indeed [unnecessary].

Because it is more significant; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the dissolution of all case-endings used with prepositions (*upapada*). Since even in that case, it is not possible to assume a different meaning—just as in the case of [the word] *avadhi*—one must necessarily accept that this [word *anyatra*] functions as a case-ending used with a preposition (*upapadavibhakti*). Otherwise, [the rule] "in the sense of 'other than,' *ārāt*, 'different from,' *itarat*, *ṛte*" [would be contradicted].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of not commencing the discussion of the sūtras;

for since the ablative case is prescribed precisely when there is a limit (avadhi), the ablative would also apply in cases such as "the cloth is other than the pot," because the nature of being a limit (avadhitva) cannot be defined [in such instances].

If it is argued that being a delimiting factor (*avadhitva*) is simply being a defining relatum (*nirūpakatva*), we say no; for then the ablative case would undesirably follow even in the expression "the pot is not the cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), since the cloth and so forth are also defining relata of the mutual absence residing in the pot, provided they lack the status of being counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of that mutual absence.
If it is argued that being the locus of determination (*nirūpakatva*) is itself the nature of the limit (*avadhitva*), we say no; for such a thing is impossible.

For any given entity, how could it be so? Since it is impossible for it to be devoid of that [limit], because it is distinct from something else by virtue of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), as in the case of "the cloth is separate from the jar," and so forth.
Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that the ablative case (pañcamī) could not arise;

for since jars and other such objects function as the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) of mutual non-existence, it is impossible for them to be devoid of that [non-existence]. Separateness (pṛthaktva), on the other hand, consists in being the determiner (nirūpakatva) or the limit (avadhitva).

If you say this, it is not so, because that [distinction] is also unestablished. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the ablative case even in the case of "cloth" and so forth, since cloth and the like do not establish a distinction [from themselves].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the ablative case would not arise even in the expression "the pot is distinct from the cloth."
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the ablative case would not arise in expressions such as "this is distinct from that" (*ayam asmāt paraḥ*).

Moreover, since that which defines separateness has not been established, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence: the definition of the limit (*avadhi*) by means of separateness, and the definition of separateness by means of the limit.

If it is argued that "being the specifier of a quality" constitutes being the limit (*avadhitva*), we say no; for then the ablative case would undesirably follow even in the expression "the jar is not the cloth," since the jar and so forth also specify qualities such as distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and priority (*paratva*). This would also apply in cases such as "Being (*sattā*) is higher than jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*)."

Furthermore, it would follow that the ablative case (pañcamī) could not arise. If you argue that being an "ablative" (apādānatva) is simply being a "limit" (avadhitva), we say no, because that too cannot be defined.
Moreover, if one accepts that the limit resides in the cloth and so forth, then [the same would apply to] mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).

Because it is defined by a limit (*avadhi*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is defined by a limit such as a cloth; and if one accepts that the cloth and so forth possess the status of being a limit,
then the same applies to separateness (*pṛthaktva*) as well.
Because it is impossible for cloth and the like to be defined by a limit (*avadhi*), since they lack the status of being a limit;
if it is argued that distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is defined by a limit residing in the cloth and so forth, whereas mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not—[we reply: no.
This is because the properties of residing in a cloth or similar object, being a limit (*avadhi*), and being definable (*nirūpyatva*) are likewise devoid of any proof.

By this, the following inference is also refuted: "Distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) differs from mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); it is either a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a quality (*guṇa*), because it is definable by a limit, like priority (*paratva*)."

Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because it is separateness; whatever is not so is not so, as for example, a jar. The separateness of a jar is the mutual non-existence of a jar, because it is mutual non-existence; whatever is not so is not so, as for example, a jar.
The mutual non-existence of a jar is distinct from a cloth, because it is the mutual non-existence of a jar;
for that which is not so is not thus, like a jar— and so forth— this is a negative-only (vyatirekin) inference, since the distinctness of mutual non-existence and the like are well-established.
Furthermore, because the state of being an absence of what is distinct from that is also well-established.

Therefore, [you claim] that separateness does not exist due to a lack of evidence; this is incorrect, as it cannot withstand critical analysis. For instance, regarding the lack of evidence for separateness—what exactly is meant by this?

Or [is it] in the sense of being distinct from mutual non-existence? Not the first, because there exists the very perception that "the jar is distinct from the cloth" and so forth. Not the second, because the distinctness of the cloth is not the mutual non-existence of the cloth, since it is [simply] distinctness.

Because [the reason] exists in the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of a pot and so forth. Nor is the distinctness of a cloth the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the cloth, because it is the distinctness of the cloth. There is no counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) such as "whatever is not thus is not thus, like a pot," on account of its being devoid of qualities (*aguṇavattva*).

Because it possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhitvāt*). Nor does this [condition] pervade the probans (*sādhanavyāpakatva*), because the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of a jar, being unique (*asādhāraṇa*), proves the absence of quality (*guṇābhāva*);
for color and so forth are excluded from action and so forth, just as qualities are excluded from action and so forth. Nor is this...

The property of being "other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) is also not a valid reason, because it is excluded even from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as color and so forth, which are devoid of the mutual absence of a cloth; nor does it possess pervasion by the probandum (sādhyavyāpakatva),
since there is a certainty that the state of being the mutual absence of a cloth is pervaded by the absence of being a quality (guṇatvābhāva).

Because it is ascertained that the absence of being a quality (guṇatvābhāva) is a pervader of the state of being the mutual absence of a cloth (paṭānyonyābhāvatva), [the following inference holds]: "A cloth is the counter-positive of a mutual absence distinct from the separateness of a cloth (paṭapṛthaktva), because it is knowable (meyatva), like a cloth. This is established even by the fact that the cloth, as a similar instance (sapakṣa), possesses the mutual absence of another cloth.

Furthermore, because distinctness from the cloth (*paṭapṛthaktva*) is unique [to that cloth] due to its exclusion [from others]. Moreover, if by the term "distinctness from the cloth" you mean the object of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the cloth, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). And if you intend to refer to a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for you.

If it is argued that even if [the property] is established, there is no sublation by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), and therefore the pure [entity] possesses the status of a locus because it is perceived separately— [we reply: no.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction in taking even the color and other qualities residing in a jar— which are in contact with the sense organs and are objects of separate cognition— as the subject [of the proposition], because [the reason] would be unestablished;
for apart from the jar and its resident color and so forth, there is no such thing as "a cloth is separate from the jar."
If it is argued that the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) belongs to the object of cognition— no, for in your view,

it is precisely the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the cloth, which is distinct from the jar and the color and other qualities residing in it, that is the object of the cognition "the jar is distinct from the cloth," whereas in our view [it is not].

Furthermore, because a cloth that is in contact with the sense organ is the object of the cognition "a jar is distinct from a cloth" due to its being the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) [of the jar] in relation to the cloth; and since that [cloth] is the locus (*dharmin*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
This is because the jar and the color and so forth residing in it are distinct from the mutual absence of the cloth.

Furthermore, if that which is the object of the cognition "the jar is distinct from the cloth" were the subject (*dharmin*), it would be sublated; moreover, for you, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
If it is argued that the subject is that which is denoted by the word "distinct" (*pṛthak*)—no, because by the word "distinct"...

If it is argued that because a word denoting a substance qualified by separateness denotes both the separateness and the substance, and since the status of being the locus (*dharmitva*) is precluded for those two, the status of being the locus must belong to that which is denoted by the word "separateness"— we say no.
For in your view, it is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) alone that is denoted by the word "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*); whereas in our view,
mutual non-existence, like a particular quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), is also denotable by the term "separateness."

This is because we accept that the word *pṛthaktva* (separateness) has multiple meanings; and if that [word] were the subject (*dharmin*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). If it is argued that the subject is that which is denoted by the word *pṛthak* as distinct from mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)—we say no, because there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) in proving that such a thing is mutual absence itself.

In the case of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of two cloths, there is no "separateness of cloth" (*paṭapṛthaktva*), because it is an absence (*abhāvatvāt*), just like [other] well-established absences; this is also because of the following negation:
"The mutual absence of two cloths is not the separateness of cloth, because it is a mutual absence of cloth."

If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), such as "that which is thus is not thus, like a jar," we say no; for this [inference] is contradicted by a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*).
This is because the specific property of the reason, namely "non-existence" (*abhāvatva*), is pervaded by the absence of the probandum.

Because it is contradictory to the probandum (*sādhyaviruddha*). For, just as the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣyāsiddha*) is a flaw, so too is the contradictory (*viruddha*) a flaw. Furthermore, if a contradiction with the qualified (*viśeṣya*) were not considered a flaw, it would follow that other types of contradictions would likewise not be flaws, since the underlying logic is the same.

"A pot is the counter-positive of a mutual absence distinct from the separateness of the cloth, because it is an object of cognition, like the cloth"—this argument fails because once it is established that the mutual absence of the cloth is distinct from the separateness of the cloth, the reason becomes contradictory, as the mutual absence of the cloth is already included within that [distinction]. Furthermore, if by the term "separateness of the cloth" one intends the mutual absence of the cloth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If one intends a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), there is sublation (*bādha*). And if one intends the meaning of the word "separateness" as established by its distinct perception, there is the aforementioned defect.

By this, the two negative-only (*vyatirekin*) inferences—"distinctness is mutual non-existence because it is distinctness," and "mutual non-existence is distinctness because it is mutual non-existence"—are refuted.

If you argue that even in your own inference—"the distinctness of a cloth is not the mutual non-existence of the cloth," and so forth—the fallacies of unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and others would arise, whether the word "distinctness" intends mutual non-existence or intends a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), we reply: no, for [we do not intend] a specific quality by us...

Furthermore, by the logic to be stated hereafter, the cloth and so forth are the substrata of an entity that lacks subsistence in a cloth distinct from the separateness of the cloth, because they possess substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a jar; thus, through such arguments, the positive nature (*bhāvatva*) of the separateness of the cloth is established.
Nor is it the third [alternative]: "This jar is either the substratum of a quality that lacks subsistence in a jar distinct from its separateness, or..."

"Or, [this] is the locus of qualities that are distinct from the distinctness [of the cloth] and lack inherence in it; or, it is the locus of qualities that are distinct from the distinctness of the cloth and lack inherence in it,
because it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and the nature of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), like a cloth," and so forth.
Furthermore, because the quality of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is established through inference based on the distinctness of cloth and so forth,
and because the quality of distinctness is thus proven;

likewise, earth is the substratum of qualities other than color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Because it is a substance, like the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, when taking earth as the subject (*pakṣa*) while excluding its being a substance, a qualification other than "being a substance" need not be employed at all, because neither the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) nor the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) are possible through the property of being a substance. Nor is "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here.

Because it would entail the fallacy of the probandum's pervasion being absent in space (*ākāśa*), since there exists in that [space] oiliness (*sneha*) distinct from color and so forth. Nor is "non-earthness" (*apṛthivītva*) a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it is merely the exclusion of the subject (*pakṣetaratva*). Furthermore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of this [adjunct] in respect to time and so forth, because those...

Furthermore, because its distinctness is unestablished, it is equivalent to the subject (*pakṣatulya*). Nor is there a possibility of a counter-argument here, because [the reason] is overqualified by "substancehood" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Water is the locus of qualities other than color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and momentum, just like the self (*ātman*).
Fire (tejas) is the substratum of qualities other than color, touch, number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity,
and mental impression, because it possesses the nature of a quality, like the self (ātman). However, if fire devoid of taste is taken as the subject of the proposition:
The qualification "other than fluidity" need not be included at all.

Air is the substratum of qualities other than touch, number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and impression, because it possesses the nature of a quality, like the self (*ātman*). Nor is there a deviation from the probandum here due to odor, [since] in air...

Because the absence of odor is established by [the presence of] "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth, the qualification "distinct from odor" is introduced in order to exclude that [possibility]. Space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum of qualities other than sound, number, dimension, conjunction, and disjunction.

Because it is a substance (*dravyatvāt*), like the self (*ātmavat*). Space and time (*dikkālau*) are substrata of qualities other than number, dimension, conjunction, and disjunction, because they are substances, like the self. The self (*ātmā*).

The substratum of qualities other than cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), number, dimension, conjunction, and disjunction is a substance, because it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), like water. Nor is "possessing touch" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, because its pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is broken in the case of space (*ākāśa*). [This applies to] non-substances...

Even for those possessing qualities (*guṇin*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*) does not follow from that [reason], nor does causality (*kāryatva*); for that very reason, there is a failure of the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*). [This applies to] the mind (*manas*) as well.

It [the soul] is the substratum of number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*), because it is a substance, like a jar. Nor is "possessing qualities that are qualifiers" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, because it is present in everything other than the subject (*pakṣetaratva*). This is because of the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
Because there is no specific feature to be excluded; for non-substances are already excluded by their very nature as qualities (*guṇatva*),
and because the mind (*manas*) and space-time (*dikkāla*) are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*) in the proving inference.
Because that [existence] is established from those very [premises] by means of employing the qualification "residing in two";

for example: "Space is the substratum of qualities residing in two that are distinct from sound, number, and so forth, because it is a substance, like a jar," and likewise, "because it is the substratum of qualities residing in two that are distinct from direction, time, number, and so forth."
Because of its existence.

[Objection: Let there be "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), but "dual separateness" (*dvipṛthaktva*) is not established, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Reply: The perception "two things are separate" is the means of valid cognition.
If you say this, it is not so; for that [cognition] is accounted for by the very unity and separateness conjoined with duality.

Otherwise, there would result the occurrence of "two-ness of posteriority," "two-ness of whiteness," "two-ness of sweetness," and so forth, because of such perceptions as "two posteriorities," "two whites," and "two sweets."

This is because [the fault] is unavoidable. Nor can it be argued that one should accept a dual purpose (dviparatva) for the word, lest there arise the contingency of the co-inherence (*samāveśa*) of the universals (*jāti*) of priority, posteriority, and so forth in that very same thing—on the grounds that one [instance] is merely "slightly prior" while the other is "furthermore prior. This must be stated.

This is because it would have to be admitted that the two [qualities]—slight priority (*īṣatparatva*) and extreme priority (*parataratva*)—which respectively reside in one and the same substratum of priority, actually reside in two distinct [substrata].

Consequently, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the co-inherence (*samāveśa*) of the genus of slight priority, the genus of posteriority (*aparatva*), and so forth, in that very same [single] locus.
Therefore, it must be stated that one [quality] is slight priority and the other is extreme priority.
This is because it is accepted that there are two types of "remoteness" (paratva), each residing in a single instance of remoteness and depending on another instance of remoteness,
and both residing in that which possesses two instances of remoteness; furthermore, the commingling of universals (jātisaṃkara) is not a defect.
Nor should it be argued that "let there not be duality and so forth," because it is untenable for a single separateness (ekapṛthaktva) to possess the same attributes as multiple substances;
thus [it was stated] by the author of the Sūtras.

And [it is argued] because separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is established as having the property of belonging to both multiple substances and non-multiple substances; that is incorrect, because multiple instances of separateness and so forth are established through inference. And thus, this jar...
That which is the substratum of qualities residing in this [entity] is devoid of conjunction-ness, disjunction-ness, and number-ness,
because it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a cloth.
This pot is the substratum of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) not residing in this [entity], because it possesses substantiality, like time.
Nor is "being time" (kālatva) an adventitious condition (upādhi) here;

for it is established that "time is not resident in time, because it is a substance, like a cloth," since the pervasion of the probandum is broken in the case of time which possesses temporal distinctness (kālapṛthaktva).
Nor is "temporality" (kālatva) an adventitious condition (upādhi) here, because it is "otherness from the subject" (pakṣetaratva).

Furthermore, number-ness (saṃkhyātva) is distinct from the sub-class of quality-ness (guṇatvāvāntarajāti) that resides in time alone as well as in both time and non-time, because it is knowable (meyatvāt), like a cloth; and this is established by the existence of both unity and plurality of separateness (pṛthaktva). Nor is it thus...

The non-establishment of duality and distinctness [is avoided] by adding the qualification "devoid of subsistence in many" to the very probanda already stated; for by that, their establishment is achieved. This pot is the locus of qualities subsisting in exactly two [substances], excluding the nature of conjunction, the nature of disjunction, and the nature of number residing in it.
Because it is a substance, like a jar; by such arguments, the existence of separateness beyond triadic separateness is established.
Nor is there a failure to establish [the categories of] separateness and so forth, precisely within the aforementioned probanda.

Because that [separateness] is established by employing a qualification that excludes existence in many; for separateness is not established by such arguments as: "This jar is the locus of a quality that exists in three [substances], is devoid of the state of being a number residing therein, and is devoid of existence in many, because it is a substance, like a cloth. Nor is it...

The example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*). This is because properties such as "residing in something other than this pot" or "residing in a pillar or a wall," which are devoid of residing in this very pot, exist even in a cloth. Nor can the case of "being two others" (*dviparatva*) and so forth serve as a counter-example (*pratibandī*), because there is no evidence for it; [the term] "two others" (*dvau parau*) [refers to two distinct entities].
Because direct perception is established otherwise by means of co-occurrence with duality and singularity; [for example]:
"This jar is the locus of that which resides in another, because it is a locus of priority."
In the argument beginning with "like a cloth" and so forth,

the qualifiers such as "ornaments" and the like are unestablished (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*), and [the probans] is also unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). This is because, when "remoteness" (*paratva*) is unestablished, the property of being the locus of remoteness residing in that [cloth] is likewise unestablished.
And for the Vaiśeṣikas,
[the reason] is unestablished as being pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*), because in a cloth there is an absence of "remoteness" (*paratva*) and so forth residing in that [cloth].

Because the property of being the locus of "remoteness" (paratva) is not pervaded by that which is the locus of a remoteness residing in something other than this; or, if such pervasion were to exist, it would follow that "remoteness" residing in something other than this would unavoidably reside in a cloth. Furthermore, to prove that would entail an abandonment of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) and would be contradicted by evidence (bādha).
For one who accepts the absence of pervasion (vyāpti), this results from accepting a valid means of knowledge that establishes existence; furthermore,
even when establishing "remoteness" as residing in a jar, the faults of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) and sublation (bādha) remain as they were.

Because [the reasons] such as "because of being directed toward subsistence" and "because of not being excluded" are unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*) for the *Bhūṣaṇa* and other [texts],
and because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), since non-existence lacks the property of being directed toward subsistence in many [things].

Because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "the exclusion of otherness" by "subsisting in what does not reside in this [object]," or because if such pervasion existed, the presence of multiple instances of otherness would be unavoidable; and furthermore, in proving that,
[there would be] the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor does the impossibility of a cause constitute a subverting argument against distinctness,
because in the case of the single distinctness residing in a jar and so forth, the jar and so forth serve as the inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa),
and the cognition whose object is the single distinctness of the jar and the cloth serves as the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Furthermore, in the case of the pot, the cloth, the pillar, and their respective distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), the cognitions whose objects are the pot, the cloth, the pillar, and their distinctness have as their causes the inherent (*samavāyi*), non-inherent (*asamavāyi*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes;
and because God, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth serve as instrumental causes everywhere. Nor is there [any contradiction] here...
If it is argued that there is no proof [for conjunction] because it is established by the same logic as number, we say:

no, for there is no lack of proof regarding conjunction; rather, there is the perception that "these two are conjoined. Nor is this perception otherwise explained as being due to the production of objects in contiguous locations.
Because it is impossible to define the production of parts in contiguous locations as anything other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Nor is it logical to claim that the absence of disjunction (*vibhāga*) alone is the object of the cognition of "conjoined," [for then one could argue]:
"The conjunctions of a jar and a cloth are the absence of the disjunction of the jar and the cloth, because they possess the nature of conjunction."

Like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). The absence of disjunction (*vibhāga*) is not conjunction, because it is an absence (*abhāva*), like the absence of a jar; for it is thus refuted by such arguments. Furthermore, even when color, taste, and so forth are present, the cognition of "conjoined" does not arise in the absence of disjunction. [Therefore, disjunction is not merely the destruction of conjunction. Disjunction is the destruction of conjunction.

If it is argued that [the cognition] has "conjunction" as its objective support— no; for even when the prior disjunction has perished, the cognition of conjunction does not arise as long as there exists another part [of the object], until the destruction of the produced disjunctions [is complete].

If it is argued that [the notion of conjunction] has as its object a real conjunction as a causal condition (*saṃyuktapratyayālambana*), we say no; for even in those who lack the experience of the actual separation of a jar and a cloth as they arise, the cognition "these two are conjoined" occurs with respect to the jar and the cloth, even though the destruction of the [prior] separation is absent.
And because there is the cognition of conjunction in such cases as "the cloth has just arisen," in that instance,
due to the absence of a cause, disjunction prior to conjunction is untenable;
for disjunction is impossible for that which has not yet arisen.

[This is] because of the impossibility of [the drum and the space, or the drum and the drumstick] being the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) respectively, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that sounds such as those of a drum could not arise.

Now, what is the proof for disjunction (*vibhāga*)? If it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the proof in the form of the cognition "it is separated"—no, for that [cognition] has the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*) as its objective basis. And this is not the case even in the perception of a thread.
There would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of separation [arising] even there, because the absence of conjunction is not perceived;
or, if it were perceived, one would have to admit that the cognition of separation [arises] from that as well;
for the destruction of conjunction is not the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the cognition of the separation of a cloth. And it is not thus.

If [the conjunction were destroyed] by the destruction of the jar, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition that "the jar and the cloth are disjoined" when the conjunction between the jar and the cloth is destroyed; for the jar, which is the objective basis of that cognition, would no longer exist.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition that "the jar and the cloth are [mere] destructions and conjunctions."

If it is argued that even in the cognition of a jar and a cloth, the destruction of their conjunction is also cognized— then one should be satisfied that it is likewise cognized in the case of disjunction as well,
since disjunction resides in both [relata]. As for the non-cognition of the absence of the jar...
If it is argued that this is not so—no, because the destruction of conjunction also resides in both [relata].

This is because destruction occupies the same location as its counter-positive (pratiyogin), and the counter-positive, which is the conjunction, resides in both. Furthermore, there is the cognition "separated" regarding this [destruction].

If it is argued that [separateness] is established because the word "vibhu" (all-pervading) is used [for space], and its establishment follows from that usage—[we reply: no, for that [usage] is adequately explained as being merely the cognition of the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyogadhvaṃsa*). This being the case, the cognition of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is also established, as in the expression "separate."
If it is argued that the conventional usage [of "separate"] is established simply through the cognition of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), then what follows?

[The distinction] is established through the inference of separateness (*pṛthaktva*). If it is argued that inference is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding disjunction (*vibhāga*), we say no, because that [disjunction] cannot be defined.

The sound produced immediately after the splitting of the bamboo slivers is generated by a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because it is a positive effect (*bhāvakārya*) and because it is a quality of an effect (*kāryaguṇa*); [this is] not set aside by the alternative explanation that it arises from the contact between the bamboo slivers and space (*vaṃśadalākāśasaṃyoga*). This...

If it is argued that "sound does not have conjunction as its non-inherent cause, because it is produced by conjunction, like a sound produced from another sound"— this is not so, because [the reason] is stated while taking the audible sound as the subject (*dharmin*). If it is argued that "that [audible sound] is indeed the subject"— no, [it is not].
In the statement defining the division of the "doubtful" (*saṃśaya-lava*), [the reason] is not established for us;

for even if a sound produced by the conjunction of a drum and a stick were the subject (*dharmin*), there would be a contradiction. Furthermore, if a sound produced by the conjunction of sounds were the subject, there would be a lack of a substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

If it is argued that the sound produced by the splitting of bamboo slivers possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*) because we do not accept that such a sound is produced from the conjunction of sounds— [we reply: no,
for by the term "sound produced by the splitting of bamboo slivers," the separation (*vibhāga*) of the bamboo slivers is denoted.
This is because [the reason] is unestablished with respect to us (*āśrayāsiddha*):

for you do not accept the disjunction of bamboo-splits and sound; and even if one were to designate the action of the bamboo-splits as the subject, it would be unestablished for both parties, since you do not accept that sound is produced.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of the destruction of the conjunction of bamboo slivers, the substratum is unestablished;
for you, who maintain that sound is produced by disjunction, do not accept the destruction of the conjunction of bamboo slivers as a cause of sound.

If it is argued that the final sound in the series of sounds heard immediately after the splitting of the bamboo slivers possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*)— no, for it is also possible to hear the final sound in the series of sounds produced by conjunction immediately after the splitting of the bamboo slivers.

Because there is a contradiction [with perception] if the subject (*dharmin*) is the first sound of that series; and because there is a contradiction if the subject is the first sound of the series of sounds heard immediately after the splitting of bamboo sections, which is not produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Because, for us, [the reason] suffers from the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*),

and because, for us, the property of being produced by conjunction (*saṃyogajanyatva*) lacks the status of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*); for we accept that it is produced by the conjunction of the space within the bamboo-splitting tool and the bamboo-split.
If it is argued that the reason is "not being produced by a conjunction [of parts] possessing a cause-sign" (*nimitta-saṃyoga*), we say no, because that too is unestablished (*asiddha*).

This is because one accepts that even the conjunction of a self possessing effort with the segments of a bamboo stalk, as well as the conjunction of a self possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) with the segments of a bamboo stalk, and so forth, are causes of sound. [Furthermore, the reason would fail if defined as] "not being produced by a conjunction residing solely in corporeal things."
If it is argued that there is a cause—this too is unproven;

for if one does not admit that the conjunction of air, which arises as the efficient cause of the sound from a split bamboo stalk, is itself the efficient cause of the initial series [of sounds], it would follow that the series of sounds would never cease. And even if that were admitted, [the series would still cease] due to the exhaustion of the momentum (*vega*).

Because when the wind ceases and no other sound begins, it is possible for the series of sounds to terminate; furthermore, this [argument] is vitiated by a "limiting condition" (*upādhi*), namely the absence of being a sound produced by a sound.
By this same reasoning, one might argue: "This sound is not produced by the conjunction of the bamboo-splits and space, because it is a sound."
Arguments such as "like the word 'anya'" and so forth are refuted;
furthermore, this conjunction between the bamboo split and space— which produces the sound resulting from the impact of the bamboo split—
is not the generator of this [specific] sound, because it is a conjunction, just like the conjunction between the bamboo split and space that produces a different sound.
If it is argued that this is like the conjunction with another [sound]—we say no; for by the term "this sound," there is an intention to refer to the sound being currently heard.
This remains true even when there is an intention to refer to a sound not produced from a [prior] sound.

This is because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*), since even sounds produced by the contact of a drum and a stick are not produced from the contact between the bamboo slivers and space. Furthermore, if one intends to specify "a sound not produced from sound or conjunction," the qualification would be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvāt*), given that a sound produced from another sound is itself unestablished.

Because the absence of being its producer is unestablished, and because there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the case where one intends to speak of the initial sound in the series of sounds heard after the splitting of bamboo slats;
[this applies] immediately after the splitting of the bamboo slats.
The sound heard from the conjunction of a drumstick and a drum is not caused by the conjunction of the bamboo split and space;
for this is evident immediately after the splitting of the bamboo.

Furthermore, because the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*)— since there is no desire to express a sound that is not produced by the conjunction with a non-sound from the continuum of sounds being heard— and since such a sound is likewise unestablished for him [the opponent], therefore, there is no disjunction (*vibhāga*).
That is incorrect, because there exists an inference that establishes [the existence of] disjunction (*vibhāga*). For instance,

earth is the substratum of qualities devoid of the nature of substance (*dravyatva*) and devoid of the natures of color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, priority, posteriority, gravity, momentum, and conjunction.

Because it possesses the nature of earth and the nature of substance, like earth which is the substratum of the nature of substance. Nor is there a difference in meaning here due to [the presence of] moisture, sound, cognition, and so forth, because its distinction from moisture, sound, cognition, and the like is established precisely by its being restricted to earth. Not...
Furthermore, even if a quality devoid of multiplicity and so forth were established, the exclusion [of such qualities] from the category of *vibhāga* (division) would still not be proven;
for the definition of *vibhāga* is simply the state of being a quality that is devoid of the twenty-three [qualities] beginning with color (*rūpa*).
Nor is there a failure to exclude it by this [definition], since through it one establishes its being devoid of stickiness (*sneha*), soundness (*śabda*), and so on.

By this [definition], even though the absence of oiliness (*snehatva*) and so forth is not established [in general], it is established in those cases where there is an absence of oiliness and so forth;

for that alone is the meaning of the term "division" (*vibhāga*), and because that which is devoid of oiliness and so forth possesses that characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). And that [characteristic] is also known through other means of valid cognition (*māna*).

Since there is no sublation by means of [the absence of] affection and so forth— which would otherwise establish the existence of a desired entity— the very inference under discussion establishes the qualities as being devoid of the twenty-three universal classes such as *rūpatva* (color-ness) and so on. Furthermore, "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here, because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of the self (*ātman*).

Nor is "selfhood" (ātmatva) a limiting adjunct (upādhi), because it does not pervade the probandum (sādhya) in the case of space (gagana). Nor is "omnipresence" (sarvagatatva) a limiting adjunct, because it does not pervade the probandum in the case of water.
Nor is "non-earthness" (apṛthivītva) a limiting adjunct, [because it does not pervade the probandum] in the case of earth which possesses substantiality (dravyatva).

Because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is "being distinct from substance-ness and earth-ness" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it is merely "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) due to the lack of intent to exclude [the probandum].

Nor does this [reason] possess a counter-balanced opponent (satpratipakṣatva), because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases where the absence of other-limited adjuncts (upādhi) is not a non-pervader of the probandum (sādhya), and because the absence of the "other-limited adjunct" that is the subject's own other (pakṣetara-upādhi) is over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa).
Or, because other counter-arguments would possess a limiting condition (*upādhi*) by virtue of being substantial entities; for example:

"Water, when devoid of natural fluidity, is the substratum of qualities such as color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, priority, posteriority, gravity, viscidity, momentum, conjunction, and disjunction, because it is water."
[It is] like that which is currently perceived, because it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a jar.
Nor [is there a lack of proof], because those things which establish the existence of water devoid of natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) are established by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Not...

Furthermore, "the absence of water" (*anudakatva*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here, because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) in that which possesses innate fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatvavat*); and because other possible limiting adjuncts have been refuted by the reasoning previously stated. Fire...
Air is the substratum of qualities devoid of color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and impression, because it possesses fluidity, like the self.
Air is the substratum of qualities devoid of color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, priority, posteriority, impression, and conjunction.
Because it is a substance, like the self. Space is the substratum of qualities excluding sound, number, dimension, separateness, and conjunction;
because it is a substance, like the self.
Nor is there any deviation [of the reason] in the case of space and time by such [examples],
because those two also, being considered as possessing divisions established in the form of water,
are equal to the subject (*pakṣa*). Space and Time.

It is the substratum of qualities devoid of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and the universal "quality-ness," because it is a substance, like the self. The self is the substratum of qualities devoid of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and the universal "quality-ness."

Because it is a substance, like a jar. The mind is the substratum of qualities devoid of remoteness, proximity, velocity, number, dimension, separateness, and conjunction, because it is a substance, like a jar. This jar...
This [ether] is the locus of a quality produced by action that lacks conjunction residing in it,
because it is a substance, like a pot.
Ether is the locus of a quality produced by action that lacks conjunction residing in ether.
Because it is a substance, like a jar;

nor is there any possibility of an *upādhi* here, for the very reason stated previously. This action produces a quality residing in two substrata that is devoid of the nature of conjunction produced by that [action], because it is an action.

It is like any other action (*karma*). Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this case regarding the action upon a substance (*dravyakarma*), because [that] is admitted. [The subject] is either different from the dual-locus quality produced by an action devoid of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*), or it is different from the dual-locus quality produced by this action devoid of the nature of conjunction, because it possesses the nature of conjunction.

Nor is there here the possibility of a counter-instance based on an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), as [the property to be proven] is present alone. Alternatively, one should formulate the argument as follows: "Time is the substratum of qualities distinct from color, touch, smell, viscidity, fluidity, gravity, priority, posteriority, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), number, dimension, separateness, conjunction residing in time, and disjunction;
because it is a substance, like a jar."

Nor is there any other meaning here. It should not be argued that [the reason] suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) because "odor" as a quality devoid of the twenty types [of odors] is not established in jars and the like, nor that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
This is because a quality qualified by the absence of the nature of conjunction residing in time— which resides in twenty-two things such as form—
is established precisely by the absence of the nature of conjunction residing in jars and the like;
for [such a quality] is precluded by the non-existence of [conjunction] residing in time.

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*)— because a quality devoid of the twenty-three universals such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth is not established in things like jars— and that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

This is because a quality qualified by the absence of conjunction residing in twenty-two categories such as "color-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth— namely, a conjunction residing in a jar and the like— is well-established in relation to jars and other such objects.
Nor, in this way, is earth devoid of fluidity.

There would follow the undesirable consequence that qualities distinct from [the specific qualities] beginning with color (rūpa) and ending with disjunction (vibhāga) are established, by means of such arguments as: "It is the substratum of qualities devoid of color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, priority, posteriority, gravity, momentum, conjunction, and disjunction, because it is a substance, like the self."

This is because of the absence of any corroborating evidence (*anukūlakarma*). It should not be argued that if that [evidence] is unestablished, then disjunction (*vibhāga*) and so forth are also unestablished;

for such a claim would involve a blatant contradiction (*vyāghāta*), since it is impossible for something devoid of the nature of color (*rūpatva*) and so forth to be devoid of the nature of disjunction (*vibhāgatva*), and likewise for something devoid of the nature of disjunction.

Because it is impossible for there to be an absence of "color-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth; for the state of being a quality devoid of color-ness and the like constitutes the definition of disjunction, and it is that which establishes the universal (jāti) of "disjunction-ness" (vibhāgatva).
[Objection: If that is the case, then disjunction itself would not be established, because those means of proving it—

[The opponent argues: "Because [separateness] is established as something distinct [from other qualities], since it is possible for the definition of separateness to be 'the state of being a quality devoid of color-ness (rūpatva) and so forth,' and because it serves to establish the universal (jāti) of separateness. This is not correct, because [separateness] is devoid of color-ness and so forth...

If the definition of quality (*guṇatva*) were simply "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), then disjunction (*vibhāga*) would be included within separateness itself. Furthermore, if the definition of quality were "being perceivable by a single external sense-organ while lacking [the property of] number," then [the definition would over-apply to] dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth as well.
Because it is included within number;

and because, if "the state of being a quality devoid of being perceptible by a tactile organ" were the definition of sound, then cognition and the rest would also be included within sound; [likewise] regarding "the state of being a quality devoid of the nature of color."
Furthermore, if the definition of taste were applied to smell and the other [qualities], then smell and so forth would also be included within taste;
and if the definition of quality were applied to color, then taste and the others would also be included within color.

If it is then argued that the number of qualities would consequently not be twenty-four—[we reply]: no, for under such a view where distinctness and so forth constitute the definitions, we do not admit that the qualities are twenty-four based on their substrata being twenty or more.
Furthermore, on the view that distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and so forth are characterized by the exclusion of disjunction (*vibhāga*) and the like, the number twenty-four would be unavoidable. || 24 ||

But surely action (*karman*) is also common to many inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because the action of a cloth inheres in the parts of that cloth and their own parts; otherwise, when they move, there would be no production of conjunction with a subsequent location. This is also the case therein.
To dispel the doubt that "if action were to be postulated [as a quality of the whole], it would lead to the fallacy of an infinite regress," the Sūtra states:
"Because of non-inherence, action as an effect does not exist. (1.1.25)

In the phrase "due to non-inherence," the word "in many" is to be understood as the ellipsis. First of all, perception is not a means of valid cognition for the fact that the action of a cloth resides in many [substances], because such is not experienced.
Nor is there inference [for this], such as: "the action of a cloth is inherent in something other than the cloth, because it is an action."

This is because [the arguments] such as "like the action of a jar" are sublated by perception; for in the perception "the cloth moves," the action of the cloth is cognized as residing in the cloth alone.
Otherwise, [one might argue]: "The color of the cloth must reside in something other than the cloth, because it is a color."
Otherwise, it would follow [absurdly] that [the pot] would possess the form [of the cloth], and so forth.

Nor is there any impossibility of the conjunction with a subsequent location for the parts of the cloth and so on, since this is established by the very motion of those parts of the cloth. And it does not entail the assumption of an infinite number of motions.

Because it is established by direct perception; and because there is no fault in postulating [motion] on the strength of its conjunction with a subsequent location, which is otherwise established. If it is argued that "action is not produced by multiple inherent causes, because it does not inhere in multiple [substances]," this would be a case of the reason being non-different from the probandum—[we reply: no.

Is "being non-distinct from the probandum" (sādhyāviśiṣṭatva) identity with the probandum? No, because it exists even in universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which lack that [identity]. Nor is it the second [alternative], because the absence of residing in multiple substrata is established by perception. [This applies] to the nature of inherence (*samavāyatva*).

Because it is established by perception that [inherence] resides in many; for, given that it is inherence, the meaning of the term "residing in many" is "being inherent in many. And this is not [the case] in this sūtra.

The absence of being produced by multiple inherent causes is inferred from the absence of inherence in multiple [substances]. However, being produced by multiple inherent causes has as its constituent element the state of inhering in multiple [substances]. And that...
It is established that [the reason] is devoid of proof and contradicted by perception; therefore,
there is no room for the fault of being non-different from the probandum.
If it is argued that this has already been explained by the sutra defining action as "subsisting in a single substance" (*ekadravyam*), we say no;
for that [sutra] is intended to establish a definition characterized by such qualities as subsisting in a single substance as proven by the sutra itself. In this [context]:
And because there is no contradiction even in the breaking of the sūtra, as its meaning is already established by the proof that [the universal] resides in a single substance. || 25 ||
Substance is the basis of conjunctions. 1-1-26.

The term "saṃyogāḥ" refers to conjunctions (saṃyoga) and collections of conjunctions (saṃyoga). Their effect is substance (dravya), which is their commonality (sāmānya). Thus, some substance is the effect of two conjunctions, such as a three-threaded fabric; some is the effect of many, such as a cloth (paṭa).
Furthermore, since a dyad (dvitantuka) and so forth is produced by many conjunctions alone, there is no single effect common to two conjunctions nor even to multiple conjunctions.
However, the teacher Ātreya maintains that:
Furthermore, they say this: a two-threaded [fabric] is produced from two threads;
and a three-threaded [fabric] from two other two-threaded threads—thus, the three-threaded [fabric] is produced by a single conjunction alone. Likewise, when [the threads] are stretched out...
