First, a fragmentary cloth is begun by means of a thread that has entered into the interval between two threads; subsequently, another fragmentary cloth is produced by means of that other thread, and in this sequence, the cloth is generated. Thus, the cloth—
Since a substance is also initiated by a single conjunction alone,
the sūtra stating that "a substance [consists] of many conjunctions" is indeed untenable as it stands.

This should be explained by means of figurative usage (*upacāra*), since even the conjunctions that initiate a fragmentary cloth— consisting of the parts of a cloth and their own parts, as well as the causes of those causes and so forth— are metaphorically designated as "causes" merely on account of their prior existence.
That is untenable, because a triad (tryaṇuka) is produced by multiple conjunctions based on dyads (dvyaṇuka).
A single substance is initiated by two triads; it is not the case that a triad is formed by another dyad. Thus, even a triad [is produced] by means of a single conjunction alone.

If it is argued that [the large dimension] is produced [from the parts], we say no; for if a triad (tryaṇuka) were produced from two [atoms], it would follow that it lacks largeness, because the plurality of causes, their own largeness, and their accumulation are impossible [in that case]. And as for the cloth—

Because a fragmentary cloth lacks the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Thus, a fragmentary cloth is not the inherent cause of a cloth, because it is not made of threads (*atantutvāt*), like a pot.
Nor is this [argument] sublated by perception, for there is a cloth produced from fragmentary cloths.

This is because such a thing is never experienced. Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] in the case of two small pieces of cloth that together constitute a larger cloth, for those two cases are equivalent to the subject under discussion (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that a cloth is produced from two small pieces of cloth based on direct perception alone.
It cannot be said that two pieces of cloth are the originators of a single cloth,
because there is no such experience; or even if such an experience were to exist, it would lack validity,
since a cloth is established as arising from threads alone.

Nor is the absence of a torn cloth (*khaṇḍapaṭa*) a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, because it is "other-than-the-subject" (*pakṣetara*) due to the lack of intent to exclude it; for that torn cloth also lacks the capacity to originate a [whole] cloth.
Nor is the absence of either being a torn cloth or [the other property] a limiting condition, because [it applies to] the subject...
Because the state of being one or another fragmentary cloth lacks any distinctness from the fragments of thread and the fragmentary cloth;
because that absence [of distinctness] consists in the very nature of not being distinct from the fragments of thread and the fragmentary cloth;
and because that which is distinct from the fragmentary cloth is excluded solely from the subject (pakṣa).

Because it does not exclude the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Just like that which does not exclude the counter-example, even that which possesses the qualification "not being the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) is likewise [inconclusive], because it too is the state of being other than the subject. Otherwise, there would be no inference of fire from smoke on the basis of the absence of "being either the fire-bearing mountain or something else."

Because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor can this [reason] be countered by a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) such as "being either a thread or a cloth," because that too possesses the limiting condition of "being a thread. This fragmentary cloth is not the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of this cloth.

Because it is a fragmentary cloth (*khaṇḍapaṭa*). Furthermore, from the inference: "This other fragmentary cloth has conjunction as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it is a cloth, like any other cloth. Therefore, it is the threads themselves, accompanied by conjunction, that originate the cloth; thus, conjunctions possess the effect that is the cloth.
Regarding the term "universal": where threads are conjoined simultaneously, they originate a triad-thread substance, or a four-thread, five-thread, or even greater substance,
just as two opposing actions do.

[It is] conjunction. In that case as well, whether it be two conjunctions or multiple conjunctions, they possess the capacity to originate a substance because no distinction [in their causal efficacy] is perceived; otherwise, even the property of being produced by the action of both [substances] would be undermined for conjunction itself.
If it is argued that simultaneous conjunction does not occur— no, for the same applies to actions as well.
If it is argued that in that case there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for "two [actions] have moved simultaneously"— no,
because the direct perception that "the threads are conjoined simultaneously" is equally valid.
Because the absence of sublation is common to both cases,
it is therefore established that two conjunctions and multiple conjunctions originate a substance; thus the aphorism is justified.

"Substance [is that which arises] from conjunctions" (VS 1.1.26). Do the initial threads produce the cloth by first producing the intermediate cloths, or without producing them at all? Not the first, because it would entail that corporeal entities occupy the same location. Not the second, either.

If it is argued that [the existence of ether] is established because it is a cause for the perception of a piece of cloth, and because there is a rule that conjunction with a homogeneous substance is a necessary condition for the production of a new substance— [we reply: no, because for corporeal things, it is impossible for two such things to occupy the same location.

Because in some cases it is impossible to establish that which is already established as a substance; and because, given the definition of the probans (*āpādaka*), if the probandum (*āpādya*) is not established, there can be no apprehension of the connection between the probans and the probandum, resulting in a failure of the root [of the argument]. Furthermore, by us, [the existence of] corporeal things such as torn cloths and the like—

And because [the existence of multiple things] in the same location is accepted. If it is argued that this would then entail that jars, cloths, and so forth must also occupy the same location—the answer is no; for while parts such as fragments of cloth and whole cloths may occupy the same location, jars, cloths, and so forth do not.

Because [the property] is not pervaded by being in the same location; because for you, the state of being in the same location as a fragmentary cloth (*khaṇḍapaṭa*) and so forth is unestablished; and because we accept that jars, cloths, and so forth occupy the same location, such as on this very floor. On this very floor, jars, cloths, and so forth...
If it is argued that there is the destruction of a cloth and so forth on the ground delimited by a jar—
no, for this is precisely what we accept; since there is no difference between the ground containing a jar and the ground containing a cloth and so forth,
because the ground is one throughout the world, as far as the ground extends...

If it is argued that the destruction of the cloth and so forth occurs only within the limits of the jar—no, for this is precisely what we accept. It is possible for the entire floor delimited by the jar to be possessed of the cloth and so forth, precisely because the floor itself is a locus of absence. In whichever part of the floor the jar resides, in that very same part [the cloth may exist].

If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence [of finding] a cloth and so forth [wherever there is a pot], we say: no, because this is precisely what is accepted. If it is argued that since a cloth and so forth occupy the very same parts of the ground, such as a house, where a pot occupies only itself, then it would follow that a cloth of the same dimension as that pot must also be present there—we say: no, because in that case...

Even though cloth and other objects do not coexist within a cognition of a jar and so forth, the contradiction between corporeality and occupying the same location remains as it was, because jars, cloths, and so on do indeed coexist in a place such as the floor.
Furthermore, because the parts of a cloth and their own parts, and so forth, occupy the same space as that which possesses a dimension suitable for the occupation by the jar alone;
and because, regarding the conjunction of corporeal entities, even though it resides in each [relatum] individually, it is nonetheless inherent in one [substratum].

If it is argued that [the two] are contradictory—no; for what is "subsisting in one" (*ekasamavetatva*)? Is it subsistence by means of a single inherence (*samavāya*), or, given the position of inherence, is it the state of having a single substratum (*ekāśritatva*)? Not the first, because even multiple parts possess inherence with a single whole (*avayavin*). Nor the second, because...
This is because things possessing inherence, such as jars and cloths, are dependent upon a single ground.

If it is argued that there is no inherence of jars and the like in the earth—no, for since inherence is one, that [inherence] exists there as well. [As we see] branches in a tree, threads in a cloth, and [cows] in a cow...

Because [the color] inheres in the two horns. If it is argued that branches and so forth do not inhere in trees and the like—no; for when there is inherence in something, the state of being supported by it is precisely what constitutes inherence in it.
Trees and the like are supported by their branches and so forth, but the branches and so forth are not.

If it is argued that [the relationship] exists in trees and so forth—no, because there is direct perception [of such relationships], namely: "branches in a tree," "threads in a cloth," and "horns on a cow. If it is argued that this involves mutual dependence—namely, "a tree in the branches" and "branches in the tree"—no.
Because mutual dependence is not a defect when there is no obstruction to production or manifestation;
or, let it be that threads are the originators of a fragmentary cloth, even so, it is not [the case that...].

There would follow the consequence of multiple corporeal entities occupying the same location; for, upon the destruction of the constituent conjunctions through the disjunction produced by the action arising from impact and pressure, the prior [state] ceases, and then, through the conjunctions of the threads produced by a newly arisen action, the cloth is originated. Not so.
Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for such a conceptualization;

for there is no proof for it other than the fact that it is impossible for corporeal objects to occupy the same location. Or, let it be that [the threads] possess the capacity to initiate the cloth precisely because a fragmentary cloth was not previously produced; otherwise, [it would not].

Even in your own view, it would follow that the conjunction of a thread with a fragmentary cloth—which is the initiator of a cloth—would itself initiate another substance; by that, there would follow the consequence of corporeal things occupying the same location. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, since [it is observed] among corporeal things...
Because the impossibility of occupying the same location is itself the proof in this case:

those threads that produce a cloth distinct from the final thread do not possess an effect-substance in the immediately preceding moment, because they are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of this cloth.
And because of the inference "like the final thread.

Nor is there a contradiction with the perception of a fragmentary cloth (*khaṇḍapaṭa*), for that [perception] has existence as its object. Nor does conjunction possess the status of an independent cause in the non-production of a substance.
Because the conjunctions that initiate a substance— other than the final conjunction of the threads— are dependent [on other factors],
as stated in the aphorism: "It is likewise from those that are dependent and from those that are independent."
Alternatively, since the conjunction [of threads] is demonstrated to be both dependent and independent at the commencement of a substance,
and because the partial cloth would not arise [if it were dependent], and because the cloth would perish upon the dependence on the final thread, [the cloth cannot be the object of the cognition].
If it is argued that "something [distinct] would be perceived"— no, because a cloth is produced from the conjunctions of threads already situated [in their respective positions].
Others, however, hold that if the threads, having first produced fragmentary cloths, then produce the [final] cloth...
"In that case, because the initial thread is removed, the entire causal series initiated by it—including the cloth—would have perished, and thus nothing at all would be perceived.
This is what they state as the refutation of the theory of the produced initiating the producer (*ārabhyārambhaka-vāda*). That is incorrect.
Even when the series of effects initiated by the first thread is destroyed,
the series of effects initiated by the second and subsequent threads is not destroyed; furthermore, from the persisting conjunctions, another cloth arises.

Others, however, say that because the relationship of being produced and producer is established by direct perception in the case of a granary and so forth, it must likewise be accepted in the case of cloth and other things.
That too is not tenable, because the relationship of being produced and producer in the case of a granary and so forth...
Because it is not contradicted by perception and because it would contradict the reasoning stated previously.
Therefore, it is established that the threads themselves, when conjoined with one another, originate the cloth; thus, conjunctions possess the general property of being the cause of substances.
"Now, this is untenable, because there are no composite wholes (avayavin) such as cloth that exist apart from the threads," so say the Buddhists (Saugatas).
That is incorrect; for there are composite wholes such as cloth, as evidenced by the cognition, "This is a cloth."

[Because it is established by direct perception. Nor is it logical that the threads and so forth alone are the objective support (*ālambana*) here; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a direct perception of "cloth" even when the threads and so forth are not joined to one another. Threads that are not conjoined with one another are not cloth.
If it is argued that [the cloth] is thus an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣālambana*), we say no;

for in the absence of the activity of the weaver, the shuttle, and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a cognition such as "this is a cloth" arising with respect to the threads and other components, even when they are merely conjoined in some manner.

If it is argued that threads and other materials, when conjoined with one another and devoid of the activity of the weaver, the loom, and so forth, are the objective basis for the cognition "this is a cloth"— [we reply: no, because even in the absence of the activity of the weaver, the loom, and so forth, [the cloth would still exist].

If it is argued that the threads themselves, possessing specific configurations (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), are the objective basis (*ālambana*) for cognitions such as "this is a cloth," we say no; for if by the term "specific configuration" one intends the composite whole (*avayavin*), then the composite whole is thereby established.
Furthermore, if one intends to speak of the conjunction of the threads and so forth, the previously mentioned fault remains;

for it is the threads and so forth, accompanied by such a conjunction, that originate the cloth and other effects, and it is the threads and so forth, accompanied by such a conjunction, [that produce] the cloth.

If it is argued that [the universal] is the objective support (*ālambana*) for such cognitions as "this is a cloth," we say no; for it is impossible to define anything other than the capacity to produce a cloth and so forth. Furthermore, if the capacity to produce a cloth were the objective support for the cognition "this is a cloth," then the existence of the composite whole (*avayavin*) such as the cloth would be established.

Furthermore, there is the cognition of a whole (*avayavin*) in the form "this is a spherical lump of gold," which is devoid of specific configurations of parts such as lines and sub-lines that could be perceived; moreover, the Buddhists do not even admit the existence of specific parts such as threads.
If it is argued that by the word "threads" (*tantu*) and so forth, a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is intended—no;

for if the word "atom" is used to denote the material cause of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), since those [atoms] are unestablished, it is impossible to claim that the cognition of cloth and the like is otherwise accounted for by them. [It must arise] from the dyad itself.

For when that [the triad] is established, the composite whole consisting of the dyad is established; and when the dyad is not established, its composite whole is also not established. Furthermore, when the dyad is established through the triad (trasareṇu), and when the parts of the triad are designated, [it follows that] they are not established by those [dyads].

Because it is impossible to state that the cognition of cloth and so forth is established [without parts], since that [cognition] is established only in the case of the *trasareṇu* (the mote of dust),
it follows that the *trasareṇu* itself is established as a composite whole (*avayavin*).

Furthermore, since dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and their parts are beyond the senses of persons such as ourselves, it would be untenable for them to be the objects of the cognitions of pots and other things that are perceptible to us.

If it is argued that atoms, having arisen with the capacity to be perceived by those beyond our senses (such as us), will become the objects of our sensory cognitions of cloth and the like— no, [this is not so].

Because atoms that possess the property of arising— which would be perceptible by the senses of people like us— are unestablished, it is impossible to establish the cognition of cloth and so forth as being otherwise accounted for by means of them.

If it is argued that since those very parts are established as having composite wholes when designated as "trasareṇus," they alone are partless atoms (*paramāṇu*)— we say no, because this will be refuted later;
for we do not admit a collection that is distinct from its constituent members, or if such a distinction were admitted, [it would lead to further difficulties].

If it is asked, "Once that whole (*avayavin*) is established, what is the referent of the word 'collection' (*samūha*) in cases such as an army or a forest?"— if you reply, "It is simply the superimposed whole; that very thing is the referent of the word 'collection' for us as well"—
we say no, because [you do not admit] a whole anywhere at all.
For the superimposition of that [whole] is itself untenable, as it has been refuted by those who have not yet reached a conclusion [on this matter].

If it is argued that the collection is delimited by a single part—no, for if a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, a single part is impossible. And as for mere atoms, [the cloth] would reside in the atoms.
Because this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of such cognitions as [the perception of] "this" and so forth.

If it is argued that the atoms joined together serve as the objective basis (ālambana) for the cognition of a cloth and the like— [we reply that] since the conjunction of atoms is not established as a real entity, it is impossible to justify the cognition of a cloth and the like through that [conjunction].
Furthermore, since that [conjunction] is established as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the composite whole—the dyad—is thereby established;
moreover, you do not admit a conjunction that is distinct from its conjuncts. If it is argued that "it is a qualified production," we say no.
Because it is impossible to define it [as such], and because the production of atoms is impossible.

These atoms are not the objective support (ālambana) for the cognition of this cloth, because they are atoms, like other atoms. The cognition "this is a cloth" does not have these atoms as its object.
Because it is a direct cognition residing in ourselves, like any other direct cognition residing in ourselves. These atoms are not a cloth, because they are atoms, like other atoms.
This [cloth] is not a collection of those atoms.
And because of the refutation [of the opponent's position] by means of such arguments as "because it is a cloth, like any other cloth," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is a fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) because the existence of the cloth and so on is not established, we say no;
for the cloth is established for both disputants. It is only its being distinct from the nature of an atom (*paramāṇu*) that is in question.

Because of the dispute, and because of [the cloth's] grossness and unity, it is established that the cloth is distinct from subtle and multiple atoms. If it is argued that the grossness and unity of the cloth are unestablished—[we reply: no, for "the cloth is gross" and "the cloth is one."

This is because [the existence of parts] is established by such direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is this [perception] invalid, as there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), since there is an absence of such perceptions as "the cloth is not thick" or "the cloth is not one," and because inference (*anumāna*) is impossible. For that which subsists in many [parts]...
That [universal] is manifold, like mango fruits contained in different vessels.

If it is argued that its existence in many substrates and its being a whole (avayavin) constitute a sublation [of its being a universal]—no, for there is deviation in the case of genus (jāti), inherence (samavāya), and non-existence (abhāva). These are equivalent to the counter-example (vipakṣa).

If it is argued: "No, for its status as the subject (dharmin) is established by such [inferences] as 'this atom is the locus of a single [quality], because it is an object of cognition (meyatva), like any other thing'; and thus, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends it as the subject [of the original inference]. As for its being another subject..."
Because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding its occurrence in multiple instances in that very same [locus];

and because if the parts were established, there would be a lack of proof for the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*); or, if they were established, there would be a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). By the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject...
Furthermore, since the whole (avayavin) is established as being a single entity, its subsistence in many [parts] is unproven for you;
for one who accepts the existence of a whole cannot possibly accept that it subsists in many [parts].
If it is argued that "whatever is superposed with contradictory properties is manifold, like fire and snow;
and since the whole (avayavin) is thus superposed with contradictory properties, this constitutes a sublation of its unity"— we say no,
because of the faults already mentioned previously, and because the superposition of contradictory properties is unestablished.

If it is argued that shaking and non-shaking are contradictory properties—no, for shaking and non-shaking cannot exist simultaneously in one and the same thing; and for those who maintain the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), shaking and non-shaking cannot even occur successively in one and the same thing. This is also the case for those who maintain the doctrine of stability (*sthiravādin*).
Because shaking and non-shaking are not contradictory in succession; for it is well known that while one part moves,
another part remains motionless, such that shaking and non-shaking are established simultaneously.
If it is argued that this is not so—[we reply: no, because when a part moves, the movement of the whole must necessarily be admitted;
for when the hand moves, the movement of the body is not perceived, and because the cause of the hand’s movement, such as a weak effort, does not produce the movement of the body.

If it is argued that passion (*rāga*) and its absence (*arāga*) are contradictory properties—no; for do you intend by "passion" and "its absence" the presence and absence of the state of being colored, or the conjunction with the substance of color? It is not the first, because the presence and absence of the property of being colored are not established in a single composite whole (*avayavin*). Nor...

The second [objection] is that, since conjunction is a pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), it is impossible for the conjunction of a substance with passion and the absence thereof to exist simultaneously in one and the same place. This is not so;
for conjunction and the like are pervasive occurrences because they are qualities, just like color (*rūpa*), and so forth.
Because conjunction and the like are established as being pervasively present [in their substrata].

If it is asked, "How then is there the conventional usage that 'a cloth which is half-red is both red and not red'?"—the answer is: by virtue of the absence of the conjunction with the coloring substance in those parts where it does not reside.

If it is argued that because the conjunction of the coloring substance with the cloth is all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), it would follow that even when a part is covered, there would be the cognition "the cloth is red"— we say no, because the coloring substance is not perceived due to its being covered.

Because even the conjunction inherent in that [object] is not perceived; for when a conjunction is perceived, it is the cause for the perception of the two conjoined things, as the nature of this causal relationship is determined through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). And if there were no exclusion...
Because the conjunction of the substance of passion and its absence have been cognized in one and the same locus,

a contradictory property is not established. Thus, [the argument] "this [person] is absolutely devoid of the conjunction with this passion, because he is cognizable, like another person" is not valid.
This [perception] does not constitute a sublation of the perception that apprehends the conjunction with passion,

because this conjunction with passion lacks the status of being the absence of an absolute non-existence of the conjunction of that substance of passion, which was to be established by the preceding inference.
Because the absence of an absence is not distinct from its presence;

and even if it does not apprehend the absence of the previously stated probandum, it nevertheless does not apprehend the contact with this substance that is red, which is contradictory to it. Therefore, this constitutes a sublation (*bādhaka*).
If it is argued that in the case of "Fire is hot because it is a substance," perception itself is the apprehender of heat—
no, for the conjunction of that [fire] with a colored substance is not established as being contradictory to the absolute non-existence of that [heat], since fire is hot...
Because, in such cases, the perception that grasps heat serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*).

If it is argued that, in that case, [the inference] "fire is hot" and so forth would be sublated by inference—[we reply: no, because this [inference] is sublated by the perception that "this fire is not hot" and so forth. If so, then the present inference as well...

If it is argued that this [conclusion]— that "this [cloth] does not possess the absolute absence of the conjunction with the coloring substance"— should be considered sublated by perception, we say no; for one who accepts both the conjunction of the coloring substance and its absolute absence in the cloth.

If it is argued that this is not so because such [simultaneous] perception and so forth are not admitted, but rather— on the contrary— that the experience "the cloth is red and not red" is accepted, and that from this there is an inference of the absolute absence of that [redness] due to its conjunction with a substance possessing color— [we reply: no, because the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvāt*).

On the view that conjunction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), since the absolute absence of the conjunction of this substance with passion exists everywhere, the absolute absence of that [absolute absence] would also exist everywhere; consequently, such an absolute absence is not established anywhere at all.

If it is argued that this [subject] is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogin*) of the absolute absence of conjunction with a substance possessing passion, because it possesses an absolute absence that is co-locational (*samānādhikaraṇa*), just like the absolute absence of color—[we reply: no, because that would be contradicted (*bādha*).
For there is also an absolute absence of the absolute absence of conjunction with a substance possessing passion.
Because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*), as it is co-located with its own counter-positive (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇatvāt*).
[The opponent argues: "Knowledge and so forth are co-located with the absolute non-existence of color (*rūpātyantābhāva-pratiyogika*), because they are co-located with knowledge itself.
[We reply: It is not the case that [the property] is being proven merely by the absence of co-location with its counter-positive.

If this is expressed by its own term as the absolute absence of conjunction with this colored substance, there is the fallacy of deviation residing in the absolute absence of color which is co-located with the conjunction of this colored substance—the counter-correlate of that [absolute absence].
And if it is expressed as the absolute absence of color, there is the previously mentioned fault; and as for anything else...

Because the meaning of the word "own" (sva) cannot be determined; because there is deviation even in the case of the absolute absence of a jar and the like in what is itself doubtful; and because one simultaneously accepts both the jar and its absolute absence on the same spot of ground—[as in the thought]: "This jar is here on the ground..."
Because one experiences the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar that is restricted to the ground as being on that very ground;
[this is so] because of the absence of co-occurrence (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) with the conjunction of this substance and redness.

This is because the very absence of the non-existence of this [probandum] constitutes the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor does this [condition] possess the character of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*),
because it is excluded from the counter-instances (*vipakṣa*), such as the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of this [subject].
Furthermore, because it constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) by virtue of being the absence of the conjunction of this substance of passion,
it is contradictory [to say] that "because of the conjunction of this substance of passion, there is an absence of the conjunction of this substance of passion."

If it is argued that the definition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is "the state of being a non-existence devoid of co-occurrence with its own counter-positive," we say no; for the definition of absolute non-existence is simply "the state of being a non-existence residing in its own counter-positive," independent of any other counter-positive.
And because there is no contradiction in such a proof, it remains so; nevertheless, it is contradictory for non-existence to be co-locus with its counter-positive,
since the very nature of non-existence consists precisely in being devoid of co-location with its counter-positive.
If you say this, it is not so;
for the definition of non-existence (*abhāva*) is the state of being devoid of a definition that is independent of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
Otherwise, even mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and the like would fail to obtain the status of non-existence.
If it is argued that there is the imposition of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa) due to being covered and not being covered—[we reply:

no, because even when half is covered, the whole (avayavin) remains covered, and thus the property of "not being covered" is absent. By this, the claim that there is the imposition of contradictory properties due to being perceived and not being perceived is also refuted.
Furthermore, because grasping and non-grasping are properties of the self (ātman), it is impossible for them to be properties of the whole (avayavin).

If you argue that if the whole does not undergo motion or obstruction even when its parts do, then it would follow that they are inseparably established (ayutasiddhi)—we say no; for what is this "inseparable establishment"? Is it distinctness?
Or [the definition of disjunction] is separation; or it is a relation residing in the motion of moving parts;
or it is the state of being established on separate substrata; or it is the possession of separate motions;
or it is the state of not being dependent upon that [substratum]. Not the first, because it is accepted [by us]. Not the second, because...

Because of the loosening of the root; for even when there is movement of the parts, if there is no movement [of the whole], there is an absence of disjunction of the parts from the form and other qualities of the parts. It is not the third [alternative], because that is desired [by us] and because there is no difference between the consequence to be established and the reason establishing it. It is not the fourth, because...
It is not the fifth [alternative], because it is already accepted as such due to the aforementioned laxity of the root [of the argument].

It is not the sixth [alternative] either, because for Vāgbhaṭa and others, [the quality of] "whiteness" and so on resides in something other than the thread that serves as its substrate, namely in the cloth.

Because it would entail proving what is already accepted: the mutual distinctness of the threads and the cloth follows from their possessing motion, and because, as before, the root argument is undermined. It is not the seventh [alternative], precisely because the root argument is undermined when there is movement of the parts.

[This is] because the form and other qualities of the parts are dependent upon the parts. If it is argued: "If the whole does not move even when the parts move, then there would be no separation from its previous location due to the absence of a cause," we say: No.
For that [separation] is established simply through the disjunction from the previous location of the part produced by the action of the part itself.

Does the whole (avayavin) reside in its parts in its entirety, or by way of a single portion? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that the whole is absent from the second part and so forth; for the first whole...

Because it would entail the consequence of separation; for the whole would be fully completed within its very first part. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because one does not admit that the whole exists in each individual part as distinct from the other parts. Or, if such admission were made, [the following would occur]:

If it is argued that [the definition is flawed] because one would have to follow further constituent parts in order to exclude the possibility of total pervasion (*sarvatva*), leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), we say no; for we accept that the whole (*avayavin*) exists in its constituent parts (*avayava*) in its entirety (*kārtsnyena*).
Nor does this imply the consequence that the whole would not be perceived in other constituent parts.

Even in that case, because the whole (avayavin) exists [in its entirety], if it were argued: "Whatever exists in its entirety in one place does not exist elsewhere, just as color [does not exist elsewhere]," we say: no, because the qualification "in its entirety" would be redundant; for [the whole] exists in many pillars by way of its parts.
If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "entirety" (*kārtsnya*) is for the purpose of excluding the present bamboo-staff and so forth— no,
because the entire bamboo-staff exists right at each pillar.
If it is further argued that, such being the case, there would be no bamboo-staff when another pillar is encountered— no, for even there...

If it is argued that this is the subverting argument here—namely, that because a thing exists as a whole (*kārtsnya*) in one place, it does not exist elsewhere—the answer is no; for even here, the inclusion of the term "as a whole" serves no purpose. [It would be sufficient to say] "for the sake of excluding conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth."

If it is argued that [the term] "entirety" (kṛtsna) is included [in the definition], we say no; for even in the case of conjunction and so forth, the [quality] resides in its entirety within the substratum of perception. This is because it is impossible to define an "entirety" that is distinct from the thing's own nature (svarūpa). The same applies to the claim that [a quality] "subsists by way of a part" (ekadeśena).
And because it is impossible to provide a definitive definition:
when it is said that "the beam exists in the pillars by means of one part," is it intended to mean that wherever the beam exists, it also exists in its constituent parts? Or rather...
"It does not reside in its parts"— this cannot be the first [position], because if the whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted,
then the bamboo and its parts would be impossible. Nor can it be the second, for by that very same reasoning, the perception that "the bamboo resides in the pillars" would be contradicted.
If it is argued that atoms are intended by such terms as "bamboo" or "its parts," we say no;

for since they lack spatial extension (ekadeśa), it is impossible for them to exist [in a whole] by way of occupying a single part. Let this alone suffice as the subverting argument: that which exists in one place cannot exist elsewhere.

If [you say] no—[we reply]: it is not so; for the reason "because it exists in this particular part" (etadavayavavṛttitvāt) would be unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) regarding the whole (*avayavin*), since it is already established that the whole does not exist in another part, like something residing exclusively in that [specific] part alone. Or, if [the whole] were established [as existing there], [the reason would be contradictory].

Because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*). For when it is established by the inference, "This [entity] possesses this [property], because it is cognizable, like anything else," that multiple occurrence resides in the substratum; thus, it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum. By this, [the argument] "whatever exists is partless, just as... [is refuted].
Form [is not a substance], because a partless entity— another term for which is "being without parts"—
is unestablished, since that which possesses parts lacks the state of being a whole. Whatever exists is not a substratum for a produced substance.

If it is argued that, just as with form, the existence of atoms constitutes a subverting argument against the "whole" (avayavin)—we say no; for as long as the substratum of the effect-substance is not established, the negation of its substratum remains unestablished. Or, if it were established, [the negation would apply] only to that very [substratum].
Because there is deviation from the reason "being an entity" (sattva).
If it is argued that "atoms are not substrata of substance" is what is being proved—
[we reply] no, because of the previously mentioned fault and because it would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenet (apasiddhānta) regarding the substratum of substance.

In some cases, even if [the subject] is not established, there is either the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) or a lack of proof (*asiddhi*); for in that very case, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, if the atom (*paramāṇu*) is not established, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

And if its existence is established by taking the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) as its locus, it is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*).
If it is argued that "atoms do not initiate substances" is what is being proven— no,

because of the previously mentioned fault and because of contradicting your own tenets; for you have already accepted that preceding atoms produce each subsequent atom, and thus [the proposition] would entail proving that they do not initiate effect-substances.

Furthermore, this follows from the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), because according to your own view, even the subsequent atoms are effects. "That which is a sense organ does not apprehend a substance, as in the case of the olfactory and gustatory organs; and the visual and tactile organs are indeed sense organs"—this constitutes a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*).

If it is argued [that the reason is valid], no; because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*). For even the olfactory and gustatory organs have as their substrata (*adhikaraṇa*) odors and tastes, since they grasp qualities such as those of sandalwood. If it is argued that the mind (*manas*) is the example—no;
Because that [example] also lacks the probandum, since it too possesses the grasping of a self.

If it is argued that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is the example—no, because the example lacks the probandum. The auditory organ is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is a substance (*dravyatva*).

If it is argued that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is indeed a substance-grasper because, like a jar, it generates an inference whose object is the self (*ātman*), and that the auditory organ serves as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) because, like the logical reason (*hetu*), it generates an inference regarding its own substratum (*dharmin*)— then [we reply that] the capacity to generate a direct perception of a substance...
If it is argued that the capacity to apprehend substances does not exist in the auditory organ at all— [we reply: no, for according to the view that space,

like direction and time, is a real entity (sat) and a producer of effects, the auditory organ also possesses the capacity to apprehend substances, since it generates the direct perception of substances such as jars.

Because space and time are apprehended by all the sense organs; because even if space and time were not perceptible, there would be a sublation of the proof for the specific probandum under discussion; and because, in our view, the eyes and the sense of touch apprehend composite wholes such as jars, whereas in your view [they do not].

And [this is so] because [the cognition] grasps a collection of atoms. If it is argued that the Buddhists do not admit the existence of atoms distinct from color, taste, smell, and touch—[we reply: no, for the grasping of a substance is never unperceived.

Because the proof of its non-existence suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason with respect to that very sense-organ when it perceives [an object], if it perceives that [object] elsewhere,
how can the status of being a perceiver of a substance be established merely by its being a perceiver of parts?

Or [is it] by virtue of being the grasper of substances such as space? Not the first, because the existence of the whole (avayavin) would be established. Not the second, because even in the absence of a whole, the inference of space and so forth would be possible through the operation of the force of those very examples.

Being an effect does not reside in substance, because it resides in effects [such as qualities]. If it is argued that it is like "being an effect" which resides in form (rūpa)—no, for if the residence in substance is unestablished in some cases, the qualification is unestablished; whereas if it is established...

Its establishment [as a whole] occurs by virtue of its subsisting in the parts, or else [the ether] is not [established] by virtue of subsisting in the ether, because the whole itself is not yet established. It is not the second case; for if the whole is unestablished, there can be no possibility of an inference proceeding on the strength of an example, since the ether and so forth are themselves unestablished.
Therefore, since there is no sublation, it is established that the perception "this is a jar" is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the whole (*avayavin*). || 26 ||
The form of forms. 1.1.27.
Regarding color and colored objects—[that is, colored objects]—the color belonging to the whole is the common effect of those [colors] residing in the parts.
This is also an illustrative indication for taste and the other [sensory qualities]. Therefore, of those residing in the parts...

The meaning of the sūtra is that the color, taste, smell, touch, oneness, separateness, largeness, length, heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity belonging to the atoms (the causes) and the color, taste, smell, touch, oneness, separateness, largeness, length, heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity belonging to the whole (the effect) constitute a common effect.
This sūtra as well has little purpose, because its meaning is already established by the rule: "Qualities, moreover, initiate another quality" (1.1.9). || 27 ||
Throwing upward results from gravity, effort, and conjunction. (1.1.28)
When Devadatta, through effort, throws upward a heavy object such as a stone with his hand and so forth, then, in that act of throwing upward, there is [an action] residing in the stone and so forth.

Gravity is a cause, because upward throwing is impossible for air and other substances that lack gravity. Likewise, the effort of Devadatta [is a cause], because in its absence upward throwing is impossible. And likewise...

The conjunction of Devadatta’s hand with a stone and so forth, which possesses gravity and serves as its substratum, [is the cause], because upward motion does not arise even in the absence of that [conjunction].
Therefore, having set aside gravity, effort, and conjunction, the first instance of upward motion and so forth [arises from volition alone].

In that case, the effect is the same for upward throwing. However, since a second or subsequent upward throw is produced by being generated from the first upward throw as well, gravity, effort, conjunction, and velocity have a common effect. || 28 ||
Conjunctions and disjunctions are the effects of actions. (1.1.29)
The term "action" (kārya) is understood to mean "common" (sāmānya). However, this sūtra is untenable as it stands,
because multiple actions lack the capacity to produce conjunction and disjunction [simultaneously], or because [the definition] would apply to the action of only one of two [interacting bodies].

Conjunction and disjunction are produced; for example, conjunction and disjunction [of a post] are produced by the action of a hawk. Or, conjunction and disjunction are produced by the actions of both; for example, conjunction and disjunction between two wrestlers are produced by the actions of both wrestlers. And as in the case of...

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that conjunctions and disjunctions of rams occur through the actions of the rams, because perception, inference, and scripture are inapplicable, and no other means of valid cognition is admitted. This is especially so in cases where many objects are simultaneously conjoined with one another.
If it is argued that the conjunction and disjunction of many actions therein have a common effect and are thus perceived— no,
because in that case, conjunction and disjunction residing in more than one [substance] are impossible.
Furthermore, because conjunction and disjunction reside in two measures (*dvimātra*),
and since conjunctions and disjunctions residing in two measures are produced by the actions of both [the drum and the air],
it is impossible for them to be produced by many actions; for there cannot be many [simultaneous] producers of conjunction.

Because it is impossible for [an action] to produce disjunction, and because it is impossible for those things that produce disjunction to produce conjunction; therefore, conjunction produced by the actions of both is a common effect of actions,
as is disjunction produced by the actions of both.
The function is the same. || 29 ||

Now, it might be argued that conjunction or disjunction is a common effect of many actions. However, it should not be said that conjunction and disjunction are the common effects of actions, because [this would apply to] second and subsequent actions.
To resolve the objection that [the first action] is produced by a prior action, the Sūtra states:
"Among substances and actions, when there is a commonality of causes, action is said to be the cause of action."

The "commonality of causes" (*kāraṇasāmānya*) refers to that section in which it is established; therein it was stated that "action does not produce action," because of its dissimilarity to qualities, as in the sūtra: "Action does not arise from actions, because of their dissimilarity to qualities" (NS 1.1.21).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the Sūtra": this Sūtra as well is indeed not to be commenced, because its meaning is already established by these two [Sūtras]: "Action is not to be accomplished by action" (1.1.10) and "Because of the difference in nature from qualities, there is no action of actions" (1.1.21). That is the very same point.

If it is argued that the [Bhāṣya] is recorded for the purpose of removing doubts— no, for those two [the Sūtras] alone suffice to establish the removal of doubts; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of composing a commentary on the meaning of every single Sūtra merely for the sake of reminding one of the meanings of all other Sūtras.
If it is argued that "let it be so" in order to avoid other objections, we say no;
for such doubts are easily found everywhere, and because there would be a violation of the Sūtra's purpose if one were to repeatedly remind [the reader] of what has already been stated. || 30 ||
Thus ends the second daily lesson in the first chapter of the *Kaṇādasūtravārtika*, composed by the illustrious servant of Lord Hara, the supreme scholar, the master of Nyāya, Bhaṭṭa Vādīndra.
The third chapter (Āhnika),
from the beginning up to the section on the general nature of effects, establishes that atoms and other such entities serve as causes in the production of dyads and subsequent compounds.

That is untenable, because if atoms and the like were the initiators of dyads and so forth, it would follow that all dyads and the like would arise simultaneously; for there can be no delay for that which is capable [of acting]. Alternatively, if they were incapable, it would follow that dyads would never arise at all.

Because of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). To dispel the doubt that "the definition of existence (*sattva*) must be the capacity for causal efficiency," there are these two aphorisms:
"Due to the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect" (1.2.1).
But it is not the case that the absence of a cause follows from the absence of an effect. || 1-2-2 ||

Even though atoms and the like initiate dyads and so forth, they do not initiate them all at once, because of the absence of causes such as conjunction that must be depended upon. Nor is it the case that [the production] arises from such dependable causes as conjunction alone.
Atoms and the like do not possess causality with respect to the production of dyads and so forth,

because atoms and the like are established as the causes of dyads and so forth precisely by the means of valid cognition that apprehends their nature as subjects (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*). Let atoms and the like produce [their effects] all at once.
And thus, since all causal functions [cease] in the second moment, atoms and other such entities would result in non-existence due to the absence of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*); therefore,
the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established through the criterion of being capable of purposeful activity.

Because the meaning of the word "existence" (sattva) is not accepted [as the probans]; for the meaning of the word "existence" is either the universal "Being" (sattājāti) or the property of being an object of cognition (prameyatva). This very point has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "[But] the absence of the cause does not follow from the absence of the effect" (NS 4.1.20). As was previously stated:

In response to the inquiry— given the statements that "substance is not opposed to its effect" (NS 1.1.11) and "quality is [not opposed] in both ways" (NS 1.1.12)— as to how there can be the destruction of substances, qualities, and so forth, which are not opposed to their effects or causes, it was stated:
"From the absence of the cause comes the absence of the effect" (1-2-1).
Now, one might ask: why could the destruction of the effect itself not be the cause for the destruction of the substance and so forth?
To this it is said: "But from the absence of the effect does not follow the absence of the cause" (1-2-2). Or else:
In the first chapter,
substance, quality, and action are introduced; in the second chapter,
the generalities and particularities of action are explained, because of the absence of generalities and particularities [in action].

Thus, by this aphorism, the cognition of those two alone [is established] because they are real entities. In that case, there are no universals or particulars, due to the absence of a cause and the absence of an effect; for indeed, without a cause, [an effect cannot exist].
Something acquires its own nature because all things are dependent upon causes;
and the existence of anything is not possible without an effect, since the very definition of existence is the capacity to produce an effect.
Furthermore, because of the absence of cause and effect, inference regarding universals and particulars is impossible;
for there is also an absence of any other inferential mark (liṅga), and as for perception—
Because [the universal] and so forth are not established;
because conceptual cognitions such as "cow, cow" are either invalid or valid [depending on the view];
and because non-conceptual cognition, which has the universal as its object, is [the only true means of knowledge]. Furthermore...

The Buddhists maintain that [the self] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To refute this, two sūtras are stated: "From the absence of the cause comes the absence of the effect" (1.2.1), and "but not from the absence of the effect comes the absence of the cause" (1.2.2).
For it is the cause that, when ceasing, causes the effect to cease.
But the universal and the particular are not effects; therefore, how can the cessation of the universal and the particular be established through the non-cessation of the cause?

Furthermore, that which is devoid of a cause does not exist, just like a sky-lotus; and it is intended [by the proponent] that the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa) are devoid of a cause. Or rather, [is this the intended meaning]?
"That which is devoid of a cause is not born," as for example the sky;
and "the universal and the particular are devoid of a cause. [To this we reply: Not the first [alternative], because the universal and the particular have already been established.

Because it is unestablished due to the sublation by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Furthermore, when it is said "it does not exist," is it being proven that it is the counter-positive of a mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*) or the counter-positive of a destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*)?

Is it the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), the absence of being a producer (*janakatva*), the absence of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), or the state of being non-existent (*abhāvatva*)?
Not the first, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
This is because both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*),
since it is accepted that "a jar is not the universal and the particular.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, as it is vitiated by the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*).

Even if the destruction of both the universal and the particular were established, [the definition would fail] because their own nature would not be obtained; furthermore, there is a deviation in the case of space and so forth.
Nor is it the third [alternative], because it would result in proving what is already established, as in the case of a jar or "cowness."
Because it is accepted that there are no specific [causal capacities]. Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because the qualification "specific causal efficiency" (arthakriyā) would be redundant;
for by establishing the absence of agency—which is synonymous with being a producer—the point is already proven.

Because its purpose has been fulfilled. It is not the fifth [alternative], because since the universal and the particular do not produce anything else, their own nature is not negated. It is not the sixth, because...
Because the qualification is unestablished; because knowability (*prameyatva*) is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property;
and because there is a lack of proof for the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) when the specific universal is not cognized.

And because there is a contradiction regarding valid cognition (*pramiti*). Nor is it the seventh [alternative], because if the absence of an absence is considered to be a positive entity (*bhāva*), it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
This also applies to the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*).
Because it is the absence of its own absolute non-existence and so forth; and in the case of the view that it is distinct [from existence], what constitutes its nature as an absence?
Is it the state of being devoid of the six characteristics of substance and the rest?
Is it the intended meaning, or is it the nature of being a negation? Not the first,
because [this would lead to] proving that both the general and the particular are devoid of the characteristics of the general and the particular.
Because sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*vyāghāta*) would be unavoidable. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,

because since both the general and the particular are established as being positive entities (*bhāva*), it would contradict the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*).
Furthermore, by the term "universal" (sāmānya), is the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti) intended, or is it being distinct from them (tadvyatiriktatva)?
Not the first, because the locus (āśraya) would be unestablished for a positive entity (bhāva). And as for the term "particular" (viśeṣa)...
Is it intended that [the substance] resides in each one individually, residing in each one as something distinct from qualities and actions,
or residing in each one as something distinct from the absence of qualities and actions? Not the first, because [that would apply to] color and so forth as well.

The first [option] is not tenable because it contradicts the nature of the subject (*dharmin*). Nor is the second, because even if non-existences such as prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) were taken as the subject, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Nor is the third, because it would entail both contradiction and inconsistency.
Not the second [alternative], because it proves what is already established;
for it is accepted that both the universal and the particular are unproduced. Nor does the cause cease to exist upon the cessation of the effect.
Because even when smoke is excluded, fire is not necessarily excluded. Furthermore,
is it intended that whatever is devoid of an effect does not exist— such as a sky-lotus— or is it that whatever is devoid of an effect...

To say "that exists" involves a contradiction, because the meaning of the word "existence" (sattva) is precisely that which produces an effect. [If you argue this], it is not the first [alternative], due to the previously mentioned fault;
nor is it the last, because of the deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of final liberation (antya-mukti). As for the example...
And because it is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*); for even a sky-lotus exists and is a generator of conjunction and so forth,
since a lotus situated on a pond is perceived as being in contact with the sky.
Because the term "sky-lotus" lacks a referent;

because the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) will be refuted; and because the second alternative is not tenable, as we do not accept that the meaning of the word "existence" (*sattva*) is simply the capacity to produce an effect.

Because the meaning of the word "existence" (sattva) is either the universal of existence (sattājāti), or existence in the form of non-origination, or the state of being an object of cognition (prameyatva); and because there is no contradiction in that case.
And these two sūtras are for the purpose of characterizing existence as that which obstructs both the general and the particular objects; therefore, there is no other.
These [objections] are to be refuted as before, by means of specific refutations and so forth.
For example: Is the universal such as "cowness" omnipresent, or is it present only in individual bodies? In the first case, [it would follow that it exists] even in pillars and the like.

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving "cowness" and so forth even in what is not a cow. In the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence that for all produced individuals such as the Śābaleya cow, there would be no relation to "cowness" prior [to their production]. Previously...
In that case, because there is no connection between what was previously non-existent and the cow-individual produced there, [one might argue]: "Having come from another cow-individual,
it connects with the cow-individual produced there"— but this is not so.

Because a universal (jāti) is devoid of activity. If it is argued that "the nature of being a cow exists only where a cow is perceived, and not everywhere," we say no; for the object [cow] is possible in every instance of a cow-individual.
Therefore, since it is impossible for both [the universal] to be omnipresent and to reside in a single composite whole,
it is incorrect to say that there is no universal; as for its omnipresence,
if it were conjunction with all corporeal things, that is certainly not accepted.
Because conjunction is impossible due to its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), or because it must reside in everything; in that case,
the admission of the universal "cowness" (*gotvajāti*) would mean residing in all individual cows (*piṇḍa*), and not merely residing in some individuals.

Because the absence [of sound] in pillars and the like is established by perception, and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to prove its existence there. If it is argued that [sound] previously resided even in those [pillars], we say no; for [sound] was not present there previously either.
Just as in the case of form and so forth;
because it is possible for it to depend on a mass that has arisen therein,
whereas previously— before [the mass] had arisen— it was not present there.

How is it that there is dependence on the arisen aggregate (*piṇḍa*) in that case? It is not that those two arise simultaneously, because [the relationship] is established like a substance depending [on a substrate].
And how could that which has not yet arisen—either simultaneously with or after [the aggregate], yet exists at that time—[be dependent]?

If it is argued that [the universal] resides there as something dependent upon the produced individual—how so? Is this a question regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its being dependent, or a question regarding its cause?
It is not the first, because the very thesis [itself] serves as the proof. Nor is it the second.

In that case, since being dependent [on a substrate] consists in being produced, there is no dependence on a cause. By this, the objection— "How can there be a connection with a lump produced there for something that was not previously present there?"— is refuted, because of [the nature of] inherence (*samavāya*).
Because it is established by one or another means of valid cognition, such as direct perception or inference;
and because, being unproduced, it is independent of causes.
Furthermore, that which is non-existent is not produced, since its production is impossible.

If it is argued that the pervasion is established because [the universal] resides in a lump of matter produced therein—[we reply: no; for what is "cowness"? It is that which resides in a lump of matter possessing a dewlap and so forth, given that it does not arise after that [lump], but rather arises simultaneously with it.
Is the intended inference "because it was previously non-existent there," or rather, "if [the universal] were the cow-ness,
because it would be possible for it to exist through that [individual], then prior to its production, while it is as yet unproduced"?
In that case, there would be a contradiction regarding the object of action for something that does not exist;
for if it were to result in existingness, it would be contradicted by perception,
and if it were to result in simultaneous arising, [the same fault would apply].
Because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the beginninglessness of the genus (*jāti*).
If it is asked, "Where was this 'cowness' (*gotva*) supported prior to this individual [cow]?", we reply: "In another earlier individual cow. Previously...
If it is asked, "Supported by what?"—no; [it is supported] in another cow-body that has arisen prior to it;
thus the path is beginningless. If it is asked, "When at the dissolution all cow-bodies are destroyed everywhere, supported by what?"—[the answer is: at the dissolution of a single Brahmāṇḍa.
We say that [the atoms] reside within the masses of earth (gopiṇḍa) existing inside other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa).
If it is asked, "Upon what are they supported during the dissolution of all cosmic eggs?"—[the answer is] "Nowhere. If so, then how is there perception at that time?
If it is argued that "universal-ness" (jātitva) is untenable because the definition— "being eternal and inherent in many"— is absent [in the case of the universal 'existence'], we say no;
for at that time, [the universal 'existence'] possesses both eternality and the property of being inherent in many.

Because it is not accepted that [universals] have the characteristic of being a genus (jāti), and because even previously, the state of inhering in many [individuals] was established by virtue of their inhering in many [individuals] while being eternal— let this [objection] not occur.
In response to the inquiry as to what sublates the notions of generality and particularity,
the Sūtra states:
"Generality and particularity depend upon cognition" (1.2.3).

"Dependent on cognition" (buddhy-apekṣam) means that it depends upon cognition as a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). It also means that [categories] such as "universal" (sāmānya) and "particular" (viśeṣa) are likewise dependent on cognition. And thus, this...
The direct, inclusive cognition in the form of "cow" and so forth is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the universal (*sāmānya*). [The inference is:
"This atom possesses a state that resides exclusively in this [atom] alone, being distinct from qualities and actions."

The cognition that is direct perception, when it resides in the Supreme Lord and others, is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the particular (*viśeṣa*). If it is argued that the cognition which is direct perception is the result of valid knowledge (*pramiti*) and not the means of valid knowledge—[we reply: no, for here it is the very [cognition as] the result of valid knowledge [that is intended].

Because it is intended to be expressed as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The distinction between "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is merely a matter of conventional usage; however, even regarding the claim that "there is no such cognition," this very same [point] serves as the answer: the universal...
The term "particular" (viśeṣa), however, is dependent upon cognition; the conventional usage of "universal" (sāmānya) and "particular" is dependent upon cognition and is produced by cognition,
as established through the methods of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka).
This is because it is determined that [the cognition] is produced by the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of the intellect; otherwise,
even the cognition of a jar or the like would not be established from the linguistic usage of "jar" and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpikā buddhiḥ) having universals (sāmānya) and particulars (viśeṣa) as its objects is unestablished [for you], while conceptual cognition (savikalpikā) is your means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the answer to this is the same: the universal and the particular...
"Thus, it depends upon cognition" (1-2-3).
There exists, first of all, determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) whose objects are universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, such as "cow" and the like;
and that depends upon indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), because it is produced by it. For indeed...
Without a non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka) whose object is the qualifier and so forth, a conceptual cognition (savikalpaka) having a qualified object does not arise,
because a cognition of a qualified object is produced by the cognition of its qualifiers and so forth.

Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). When the sūtra states "the universal" and "the particular," it establishes the existence of the universal and the particular through inference (*anumāna*).

It is explained as follows: they state that the meaning of the sūtra is that the cognition "this is a universal" and "this is a particular" depends upon a cognition whose object is a logical mark (liṅga). First, [the cognition] "this is a cow" does not [arise with respect to the universal].
Perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object is a particular (*vyakti*) that exists elsewhere [in space].

If it is argued that, in that case, the cognition "this is a cow" would not occur with respect to another particular, we say: no; it is true that this cognition does indeed not arise with respect to another particular.
In that case, [it cannot be so] because the cognition "cow" is distinct [in each instance].

If it is argued that the cognition "cow" arising with respect to another individual is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), we say no; for it is logically possible that such a cognition has a different individual as its objective support (*ālambana*).
If it is argued that the recurring cognition "cow, cow" is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the universal "cowness"—
no, because individual cognitions are mutually exclusive and thus lack recurrence.
Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of "cow-cognition-ness" as something experienced;
nor is there evidence for a recurring "cow-cognition-ness," because the occurrence of a recurring cognition has been refuted by the reasoning previously stated. Let it be so.
Or [it is established] from the recurring cognition "cow, cow"; otherwise, the establishment of cowness (*gotva*) would not occur,
because this is accounted for by the presence of the dewlap-ness (*sāsnātva*) and other such factors that establish the conventional usage of the term "cowness."
Nor does the negation of universals, based on the [specific] determiner,

entail the consequence of the total abolition of all universals, for that is what we accept. Or rather, let it be that the recurring cognition "cow, cow" has as its recurring objective support the exclusion of non-cows.

Nor is it inference, because no probans (liṅga) pervaded by "cowness" (gotva) and so forth is perceived. If it is argued that "possessing a dewlap" (sāsnādimattva) is the probans—no, for as long as "cowness" is not established, its being pervaded by that [dewlap] cannot be known. By this [same reasoning],...

The argument that the linguistic usage of "cow" (*govyavahāra*) is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has been refuted. If it is argued that the linguistic usage of "cow" is being proven to be based on the cognition of the object to be designated (*vyavahartavyajñānanibandhana*), we say no; for by implication, the property of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would already be established.

Because it would result in proving what is already established by means of the cognition of an individual cow. If it is argued that the point being proven is that [the cognition] is based on a cognition distinct from the cognition of an individual cow—
no, for even the cognition of an individual cow [is based on such a distinction].

Since the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) remains as it was— because [the cognition] has as its object the form (*rūpa*) and other qualities residing in that [cow] which are distinct from the individual cow (*govyakti*)—
[the definition] must be "based on a cognition distinct from both the individual cow and its properties."
If it is argued that [the universal] is established [by perception], we say no;

for the establishment of the universal "cowness" and so forth as a property of that [individual] would be a different matter (an *arthāntara*), since the cognition of the individual cow has as its object the earth and other constituent parts of the individual instance of cowness— which is in sensory contact with the senses— distinct from both the individual cow and its properties.
"And because [the argument] remains in the state of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

This is incorrect; for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) such as "this is a cow" proves the universal (*jāti*) of cowness (*gotva*) and so forth. To explain: just as this [perception] "this is white" [proves whiteness].

Just as the direct perception "this" and so forth takes white and other qualities as its objects by way of being qualifiers of that which stands before one, so too does the direct perception "this is a cow" and so forth [take them as objects] by way of being qualifiers of that which stands before one.

This also applies to [universals] such as "cowness" (gotva). If the cognition were based on the individual alone, it would be merely "this," and not "this is a cow. Otherwise, even qualities such as whiteness could not be established as qualifiers of the individual.
Even something like whiteness that is distinct from the object standing before one is not admitted [as a real entity].
If it is argued that in cases such as "this is white," the exclusion of non-whiteness (*aśuklādivyāvṛtti*) itself is the qualifier— no, for [the category of] whiteness...

If it is argued that, just as in the case of inference, the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) is the qualifier here because the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is established through its being a qualifier—[we reply:
no, because exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) cannot be defined; for [it would have to be] mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
If it is argued that [the definition] is "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), [we reply: no, because non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be defined;
for when there is an absence of a positive universal (*bhāvarūpajāti*) lacking the six characteristics such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, that characteristic [of exclusion] is impossible.

Because it is impossible for that [universal] to be devoid of them; because it is all the more possible for a universal in the form of a non-existence (abhāva) to subsist [in its loci]; and because if one accepts a universal in the form of an existence (bhāva), the universal is thereby established. [For a non-existence is the negation of an existence.]

If you say this—no, because negation-ness (*niṣedhatva*) cannot be defined; and because even when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the non-cow, is not known, its qualifier, cowness (*gotva*), appears as uncontradicted. Otherwise, [the same would apply to] the individual cow and so forth.

Because it would follow that [the cow-pile] is a negation. If you argue that the cow-pile is something distinct from the atoms—no, because it would then follow that even the atoms and so forth are negations. Furthermore, is there a single exclusion of each individual non-cow?

Cowness is either the exclusion of all non-cows, or [the exclusion of each individual non-cow]. It cannot be the first, because even though the exclusion of one particular non-cow exists in another non-cow as well, it would follow that the cognition "this is a cow" would arise with respect to that other non-cow too. Nor can it be the second.

The first [alternative] is not tenable because, since everything other than all individual cows is unestablished as being outside the scope of cognition, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from that is likewise unestablished. Nor is it the third,
because by virtue of being different from some particular cow-individual, even a *śābaleya* cow and others would consequently be non-cows.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of "cowness" (gotva) due to being devoid of the exclusion of that [non-cow].
