Nor is the fourth [option] valid, because as long as the cognition of all cows is absent, the cognition of a non-cow is impossible, and thus the exclusion of the non-cow [is likewise impossible].

Because it is impossible to comprehend [it otherwise], and because, if "cowness" (gotva) is not admitted, the individual cow (gopiṇḍa) cannot be defined; and if it is not admitted, what is it? Is it the universal "cowness," or the exclusion of non-cows (agovyāvṛtti)? Not the first.
Because [the definition] would be established through [prior] birth. Not the second [alternative], because of mutual dependence:
namely, that the establishment of a cow is qualified by the exclusion of non-cows.
Nor is the dewlap and so forth the qualifier in the case of "a cow is nothing but the dewlap and so forth."

Because there arises the cognition "this is a cow" even with respect to something lacking a dewlap and so forth; because [the cognition] arises from possessing a dewlap and so forth; and because there does not arise the cognition "this is a cow" with respect to a gavaya. And what is this "possessing a dewlap and so forth"? Is it the state of possessing this very dewlap?

Or [is it] the possession of a genus such as "having a dewlap"? Not the first, because it would follow that the cognition "this is a cow" would not arise with respect to another individual cow that lacks a particular dewlap. Nor the second.
Because the universal of "having a dewlap" itself is established;
let there be "having a dewlap," since the cognition "this has a dewlap" cannot be accounted for otherwise. But the universal of "cowness" is not [established].
If it is argued that [the universal] is established because the cognition "cow" is otherwise accounted for by the presence of a dewlap— no,
for that would constitute a defeat for the Buddhist (saugata). By him...
This is because the genus "possessing a dewlap" is also not admitted;
for we observe the cognition "this is a cow" even when the dewlap has been cut off in one case, yet we do not observe the cognition "this is a cow" in a gayal, even though it possesses a dewlap.
Because, by means of the dewlap, there is established a "cowness" (gotva) distinct from it,
since— as will be explained later—
one can infer a genus residing solely in that which possesses a dewlap.

Nor is it merely a particular configuration of parts that serves as the qualifier in the case of "cow," because such a configuration is excluded from gavayas and the like, yet is not common to all individual cows.
Furthermore, even that specific configuration of parts which is distinct from "cowness" (gotva) cannot be defined;
nor is it possible for a specific configuration of parts— which, being a specific conjunction of parts, resides in the parts themselves— to serve as a qualifier of the individual object (piṇḍa).
Furthermore, because this specific configuration of parts residing in one cow-individual cannot exist in another cow-individual,
it would follow that the cognition "this is a cow" could not arise with respect to the latter. This is because [the configuration] is not common [to all].
Furthermore, because the Buddhists do not accept that a universal (*jāti*) consists in a specific configuration of parts,
and because its exclusion [from other things] has already been refuted as before, and because there is a recurring cognition such as "cow, cow."
Because the nature of "cowness" is established; otherwise, it would be impossible for a cognition to be continuous with respect to an excluded object,
since continuity is possible only when the object of the cognition is a continuous entity.

Nor is the cognition of a recurring entity unestablished; for it is established by the conventional usage of recurring entities, such as "this is a cow," "this is a cow," and so forth. Otherwise, [it would be established] by the conventional usage of excluded entities.
If the cognition of an excluded object were established, then that excluded [object] would also be dissolved by the [positive] object;
nor is there the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya) in the establishment of a persisting object.
This is because it is not accepted that the cognition of a recurring entity has "genus" as its qualifier; furthermore,
in the argument that the existence of a recurring entity is established from the cognition of a recurring entity, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśrayatva).

If it is argued that the cow, as excluded from non-cows, is the objective basis for the recurring cognition "cow, cow"— we say no; for if the individual cow is not perceived as being grasped by the absence of cowness, then the individual cow cannot be perceived as being grasped by its exclusion [from non-cows].

Because it is impossible to cognize the exclusion of "cow" [as a distinct entity], and because the universal (jāti) is established through inference; for instance, this individual cow is an entity residing in this [individual] that is devoid of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in this [same individual].

[The inference is: "These [categories] are devoid of eternity because they are dependent on that [substance], and because they are objects of cognition (*meyatva*), like a jar. Nor is there here the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) with respect to inherence (*samavāya*), because that [inherence] is non-dependent (*anāśrita*).
Alternatively, if [the property] is dependent, it is because of its lack of a [separate] relation, or because it is devoid of inherence (*samavāya*),
due to the qualification by similarity. Furthermore,
there is no possibility of obstruction by a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here, because [the reason] is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*).
Or else: this cow possesses an eternal state residing in it that lacks an inherent cause, because it is knowable and because it is a substance, like the sky. Nor is there...

There is deviation [of the reason] in respect to genus (*jāti*) and so forth, because it is admitted [to exist] everywhere. Nor is "eternality" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for these two, because it is the "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*). [The inference:
"That which is other than the aforementioned probandum (i.e., that which is devoid of non-eternal things such as space) is knowable, because it is an object of cognition."
Furthermore, because the pervasion of the probandum would be destroyed once an impermanent thing— possessing the probandum under discussion— is established,
and because a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not a genuine defect; or else, [consider] a cow produced at this very moment.
"It possesses an absence residing in a cow that has long since perished and is devoid of the nature of inherence,
because it is the locus of an existent," and so forth.
Now, [an objection]:

If it is argued that because existence (*bhāvatva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the other six characteristics, as well as cognizability (*prameyatva*), are not established prior to the proof of the categories (*tattvajāti*), this constitutes the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*)— [we reply]: here, [the distinction is made] by saying "this is non-existence" and "this is existence."

Because the meaning of the word "existent" (bhāva) is that which possesses existence established by cognition; nor is there any deviation here in the case of jars and the like, since even there fluidity and so forth exist. Let it be granted that [the word] denotes merely the universal (jāti).
If it is asked how the establishment of "cowness" (gotva) occurs, understand that it is from perception itself, namely through such cognitions as "this is a cow" and "this is a cow.
However, Viṣṇumiśra [states]:
Furthermore,

this [subject] possesses the absence of the state of being non-resident in that which possesses a dewlap, possesses a dewlap resident in that [same subject], possesses the state of being excluded from that [same subject], and possesses the absence of residing in that which possesses a dewlap resident in that [same subject],
while being devoid of impermanence resident in that [same subject], because it is knowable (*meyatvāt*).

They say that "like a jar" is the proof for [the existence of] cowness (*gotva*). That is not so; for since the purpose is fulfilled by the establishment of a genus (*jāti*) common to both the dewlap and the cow-particulars, it does not prove cowness. This...

If it is argued that "the [subject] possesses a non-eternality residing in this [locus], because it is an existent (bhāva), like a jar"— wherein "possessing a dewlap distinct from that of a *gavaya*," "devoid of the state of being an absence residing in this [locus]," "devoid of the exclusion of that which possesses a dewlap distinct from that of a *gavaya* residing in this [locus]," and "devoid of occurrence in that which is not pervaded by the state of possessing a dewlap distinct from that of a *gavaya* residing in this [locus]"— then [we reply]: no,
for this [inference] establishes a genus (*jāti*) that excludes even a lump of flesh with a severed dewlap.
Because it does not establish "cowness": the universal [in question] resides only in those possessing a dewlap that is distinct from the dewlap of a gavaya,
and it excludes a cow-individual whose dewlap has been cut off.

If it is argued that "cowness" (gotva) is established by this [perception], even in a lump of clay where the dewlap has been cut off— since the experience of cowness is established as being sublated there—
if you say that in that case there is no experience of cowness at all, we reply: no, for [there is the cognition] "this is a cow."
Because it is established through conventional usage;
this application of the term "cow" to [an animal] possessing a tail and so forth due to its similarity to a cow is secondary (gauṇa).

If it is argued that the term "fire" is applied to a young boy because of his similarity to fire—such as his tawny complexion (*paiṅgalya*) and so forth—it is not so; for there is no evidence for such usage in the primary sense.
Or, if such evidence does exist, then the establishment of "cowness" (*gotva*) may likewise result from this very inference. Thus...
The universals such as "buffalooness," "horseness," "clothness," and so forth, are to be inferred from existence (*sattva*).
Now, one might object: let the universal be established, but the particulars (*viśeṣas*) are not established.

Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that "eternal substances possess distinguishing attributes (*vyāvartaka-dharma*), because they are substances (*dravyatva*), like a jar"—this is not so, because the point is already established by [the property of] being a substance and so forth (*siddhasādhana*). No.

[The definition] "possessing properties that distinguish substances" is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*) by means of [the universal] earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth; therefore, the atoms of earth and the other elements are not [the subject].

If it is argued that the probandum is "possessing properties that differentiate [it] from earth and so forth," then color and other qualities produced by baking (pākaja-rūpādi) would constitute a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana), because those qualities do not exist in the earth that is an effect (kārya-pṛthivī).

If it is argued that "possessing the property of being a producer [of color] while not being an earth-atom" is what is being proved— no, for when a white earth-atom is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), [the reason would be contradictory, as it is] white...
If it is argued that a white earth-atom is established as a white earth-atom because it possesses whiteness— no,
for this would apply even when one takes as the subject a white earth-atom devoid of degrees of whiteness such as "whiter" or "whitest."
Because it would be proving what is already established [to prove] that an earth atom possesses a white form devoid of degrees of whiteness;

[the thesis would be]: "An earth atom possesses a white form devoid of the qualities of being whiter or whitest, and thus it possesses a property that causes [the appearance of] being whiter or whitest."
If it is argued that [the property] is being proven— no,

because there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established by means of such qualities as a slightly darker black color produced at a different time within that very same atom. At a single atom, due to the difference in time...
Because of the acceptance of color produced by ripening (*pākaja*) such as black and so forth; for instance, "this earth-atom,

which is currently devoid of degrees of whiteness (whiter or whitest) and possesses a white color," and "this earth-atom, which possesses a distinguishing property that differentiates it [from others]."

If it is argued that [the earth-atom] is being established [as distinct], we say no; for this would result in proving what is already established by means of specific qualities such as taste, smell, and touch. [The formal argument is:
"This earth-atom possesses a property that distinguishes it from other earth-atoms possessing similar qualities."

If it is argued that [the property] is yet to be proven (*sādhya*), we say no; for regarding the "similarity" (*samānatva*) of qualities, does it mean being of the same class (*sajātīyatva*) or the absence of being of a different class (*vijātīyatvābhāva*)? It cannot be the first, because that would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the white color and other qualities residing in this very [subject].
For even those [atoms] serve to distinguish the earthly atoms possessing black color and so forth from those belonging to the same class as white color and so forth.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because of such an earthly atom...
When "possessing upward motion" (utkṣepaṇavat) is the subject (dharmin),
[it refers] to such an earthly atom as well as one that lacks upward motion and so forth.

If the probans is intended to establish a differentiating property (*vyāvartakadharma*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of [properties] such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*).

This is because, when one seeks to prove that a specific earth-atom possesses a differentiating property, that very atom— though already endowed with properties such as upward throwing— is precisely what remains uncertain insofar as it might not possess such properties.
Because it would follow that there is a different object [of cognition] due to [the presence of] upward motion and so forth;
for such an earthly atom possesses upward motion, whereas another does not.
Furthermore, in establishing that such an earth-atom possesses a property that differentiates it [from others],

if its subjecthood (*dharmitva*) is based on having a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), and the possession of a differentiating property is proven by excluding what is devoid of dyads, then [the proof] would be by means of the dyad.
This is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Alternatively, if the subject (*dharmin*) is such an earth atom whose nature as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) has not yet been ascertained;
When the possession of a differentiating property is being proved for such an earth-atom whose nature as a dyad is not yet established,
then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), because [the property] exists in a dyad.

In this way, the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) of such an earth-atom is established, just like a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); and furthermore, the possession of a distinguishing property (*vyāvartakadharmavattva*) by such an earth-atom is also proven. Even then—

Just as throwing possesses [the property of being a motion], so too does such an earth-atom possess the status of being the subject (dharmin); and just as throwing and so forth do not belong to such a dyad,
so too such an earth-atom lacks the property that distinguishes it [from other atoms].

If it is being proven [that a substance possesses a specific property], then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of a binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) that possesses upward motion;

for this would consist in proving the possession of a distinguishing attribute in something that has not yet been ascertained as possessing such a nature, based on something else that is likewise unascertained as possessing such a nature.
[The argument] with "that which possesses upward motion" as the subject is a different matter [from the previous one].

Now, if it is being proved that a binary compound possessing upward motion (*utkṣepaṇavat-dvyaṇuka*) is the subject of such an earth-atom, and that such an earth-atom possesses a distinguishing property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) belonging to that which possesses upward motion, even then, just as in the case of a binary compound that has begun to produce a tertiary compound (*tryaṇuka*), [the same fault applies].

If it is being proved that such an earth-atom possesses the property of being a subject (*dharmin*) and possesses a differentiating property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) from an earth-atom that has not begun a triad (*tryaṇuka*) or a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*),

then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the triad or dyad begun by that [other] atom. This is because such a [differentiation] is not yet ascertained.

And in the proof that an earth-atom possesses a property that distinguishes it from other such earth-atoms— where [the subject] is an earth-atom not yet determined as possessing such a distinguishing property—
the possession by this earth-atom of a property that distinguishes it from other such earth-atoms is established by its being a constituent of this very dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

[If you say it] is being proved, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) residing in such past or future earth-atoms as are distinct from these [present ones]. Now, this...
It is argued that the atom (paramāṇu) is established as being devoid of a universal residing in it,

as not being the locus of a universal residing in it at present, as being devoid of possessing a universal that does not reside in qualities or actions residing in it at present, as being the substratum of qualities and actions at present, and as being the substratum of an absence of differentiators at present that resides in this current dyad (dvyaṇuka).
However, even that is not correct, because such a state of being a differentiator...

Is it the state of being an eliminator of such a kind, or the producer of the exclusion of such a kind, or the indicator of the exclusion of such a kind, or the generator of the direct perception of the exclusion of such a kind?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it results in proving what is already established by means of the color and other qualities residing in those atoms. As for the second, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Because exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is unproduced, that which produces it is not established.
Nor is the third [alternative] valid, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of [properties such as] knowability (*prameyatva*).
This...
[The opponent might argue: "An atom possesses such an exclusion (vyāvṛtti) because it is an object of cognition (prameya)," and so forth;
for [the property] of such an exclusion is established through inference.
Furthermore, [the argument] would result in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) by means of the color and other qualities residing in this very atom.
This atom is distinct from others because of its form and other qualities;
for that which is not so is not thus, just like a jar—this is also [established] by inference.
Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because it would result in proving what is already established by the form and other qualities residing in this [atom]. This is also true of those [qualities].
Because it produces the direct perception of its own specific atoms established in the yoginī,
and because in the case of a specific perception, there is the manifestation of the exclusion of that which possesses the absolute non-existence of the qualifier;
[this applies to] the color and other qualities of these atoms.
If it is argued that "these [atoms] do not exclude other such atoms because they possess such color and so forth,
just like the color and so forth of other such atoms"— we say no, because the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikala).
For it is admitted that even such a form belonging to one atom possesses the quality of differentiating itself from another atom of the same kind.

If it is argued: "The form and so forth of this atom do not differentiate [itself] from those of the same kind, because they are forms of that kind, just like the forms of that kind [of other atoms]"—this is not so.

Because that which possesses such form and so forth—which would serve as its differentiator—is unestablished, the absence of this [differentiator] is likewise unestablished; thus, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established with respect to the qualifier, since you [the opponent] do not accept the existence of form and the other qualities.
Because the exclusionary nature [of the property] is not denied:
"This atom possesses such an exclusionary property residing in it, which is devoid of the substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness found in this [other] substance."
If it is argued that [the property] is being proved— no,
for by means of the prior non-existence and destruction of those very qualities and actions residing solely in this [object],
the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) are unavoidable.

If it is argued that this atom is established as being devoid of substance, quality, and action residing therein, and as possessing a state that distinguishes it from such atoms— [we reply: no, because of the inherence of color and other qualities residing in this very atom.
Because either proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) is unavoidable;
for since inherence (*samavāya*) is unitary, it exists everywhere.
If it is argued that [inherence] does not serve to differentiate such atoms—[we reply: no.

Because this [universal] has fulfilled its purpose by establishing that the inherence of color and other qualities in this particular atom distinguishes it from such other atoms; for the [alleged] distinct object remains in its original state.
This is so even if there were no exclusion from such other atoms.
Furthermore, it is impossible for inherence (samavāya) itself to produce the direct perception of such an exclusion from other atoms.

If it is argued that the probandum must be qualified by being distinct from inherence— no, for that would lead to the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), namely, that [the subject] possesses color and so forth, since it is already distinct from inherence.

If it is argued that the state of being the substratum of form and so forth is also merely non-existence (*abhāva*), and is thus excluded by the mention of "existence" (*bhāva*)—we say no. For what is this "existence"? Is it the state of being a positive affirmation (*vidhitva*), or is it the state of possessing the six characteristics beginning with substance (*dravya*)? In the first case, even the possession of form and so forth [would be included].
The objection that "it is simply existence" cannot be avoided, as it results in the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratva*);

for even without the cognition of a counter-positive, there is a positive cognition (*vidhitvena pratyayāt*) such as "this possesses this color and so forth," which establishes its possession of that color and so forth. In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Because the qualification is unestablished, its definition is likewise unestablished;
consequently, even the property of being one or another of the six definitions such as substance is unestablished.
Furthermore, for those such as the Mīmāṃsakas, there is the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), since [the definition would apply to] the knowledge of potency and so forth.

This is because the inclusion of the terms "distinguishing" (*vyāvartaka*) and "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) would be redundant. By this, the following syllogisms and others are refuted: "Atoms, liberated selves, and [other such entities], being of the same genus, quality, and effect, possess inherent distinguishing properties (*vyāvartaka-dharma-samavāyin*), because they are substances, like a jar."

And because of contradiction; for it is impossible for those residing in each individual [atom] to be mutually exclusive, and it is untenable for those that are mutually exclusive to reside in each individual atom and so forth. And as for the word "mutually" (mithas)—

Because they are mutually expressive; and because it is impossible to define the mutual relationship between word and object as something that pervades atoms, jars, cloths, and so forth; for that which is itself excluded cannot logically serve as the excluder.

Because there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the color and other qualities of the atoms themselves, which have been made the subject of the argument; for even those [qualities] mutually differentiate the pot from its constituent atoms, and because there is also the fallacy of proving what is already established by means of the color and other qualities residing in the pot and so forth.

Because even atoms possess the state of being inherent substrates (samavāyin) by virtue of being the substrates for the inherence of color and other qualities residing in jars and the like; since inherence is a single entity, it is established that [atoms] must be substrates of distinguishing attributes. Nor is it the case that the color and other qualities of jars and the like have atoms as their substrates.
If it is argued that this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), we say no;
for since the purpose [of the argument] is fulfilled by establishing the absence of mutual exclusion, there would otherwise be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*).
As for the inference— that "the mind is excluded from other minds because it lacks a universal [in that regard], since it is a substance possessing inherence, like a jar"— that too is not tenable,
because it results in proving something else [an extraneous point], namely, the establishment of a subordinate genus called "mind-ness" (*manastva*) which excludes other minds.
If it is argued that by the phrase "excluded from other minds" (mano-antaravyāvṛtta), what is intended is the exclusion of all minds other than the mind under discussion (pakṣīkṛta-manas)—
we say no; for if that were the case, then [the reason] would reside in those minds other than the mind under discussion, which possess substantiality (dravyatva).

Because of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*). If it is argued that the qualification "being distinct from the mind under discussion" must be adopted as a property of the reason (*hetu*), we say no; for [the reason] would then be subject to a limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting in "not being the mind. Nor does this [qualification] constitute the fallacy of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratā*), because of the phrase "excluded from other minds."

Because it is excluded from all dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), which are pervaded by all atoms excluding the mind under consideration; and because it is the counter-instance (pratipakṣa) by virtue of being the mind itself. The mind is devoid of the state of having multiple mental modifications, because it is a substance that inheres in no universal (niḥsāmānya-samavāyi-dravyatvāt).

The argument "like a jar" is also not tenable. This is because it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in terms of being a jar. Furthermore, that [jar] is devoid of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*), both individually and collectively; it is devoid of universals (*sāmānya*); and it is inherent in the mind which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*).

If it is argued that, because inherence is one, it is being proved that [the universal] is the substratum of generality by virtue of its being the state of being both mind and non-mind— [we reply: no,
because this would result in proving what is already established, namely, the absence of prior non-existence, priority, and posteriority, as well as the momentum of action residing in the mind.
And because it has already been answered;
for even by establishing its existence as a positive entity, that [objection] is satisfied, and thus the other point remains in the same state.
As for the inference: "The subject under dispute [is not a substance], because it is a substance inhering in something else,"...
As for the example "like a jar," it results in proving what is already established because [the property to be proven] is already admitted in the case of dyads (*dyaṇuka*).
Furthermore, if space, time, direction, and the self were taken as the subjects (*dharmin*),
the qualification "distinct from action" would be redundant, since action is absent in them.

Because there is no [other] thing to be excluded; and because if the mind were the subject (*dharmin*), the argument would be vitiated by proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)—since the existence of the mind is already established by its being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)—and thus it would be swallowed up by a different point (*arthāntara*). Also, of the mind...

Furthermore, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because [the pot] is already established as the inherent substratum (*samavāyin*) of a pot that is distinct from quality, action, and generality;
for inherence is one, and thus it is the locus of the inherence residing in a pot that is distinct from quality, action, and generality.
If it is argued that what is being proved is the state of being the locus of an entity (*bhāva*) distinct from quality, action, and generality—[we reply: no.
Because the other entity remains in that same state, and because the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

This is because, in a jar, there is no existence or non-existence apart from qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and universals (*sāmānya*); since the parts of the jar do not reside in the jar itself, [the argument fails]. As for the claim that water and so forth reside in the jar, the jar—

If you say it is because of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then since atoms and so forth also exist in space and the like, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is unavoidable.
If you argue that although atoms and so forth are conjoined with space and the like, they are not dependent upon them— that is not so.

[The inference] "Space is the substratum of substances because it possesses substantiality" fails to establish [space as] the substratum of substances; for even if the property of being a substratum of corporeal things is not established, that [inference] would already have fulfilled its purpose, and thus it would be impossible to prevent the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara).

If it is argued that the probandum is "having a substratum distinct from substance, quality, action, and generality"— no, because this would result in proving what is already established by means of inherence (*samavāya*). If it is argued that inherence itself is without a substratum— no,
because its establishment occurs precisely through its residing in inherence.

Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) is established as being dependent through the inference of dependence based on its being a relation between eternal substances and so forth, this [inference] already fulfills its purpose; thus, it is impossible to avoid the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). [Therefore, inherence] must have a substratum distinct from substance, quality, action, generality, and inherence itself.
If it is argued that [the substratum] is being established— no, because that would result in proving what is already established by means of non-existence (*abhāva*).
If it is argued that what is being established is "that which has as its substratum something other than substance, quality, action, generality, and inherence"— no, for the Bhaṭṭa...
Against the Prābhākara, [the argument fails] because it would result in proving what is already established by means of capacity, cognizedness, number, similarity, and sequence.

Furthermore, if one were to employ a qualification distinct from that [consciousness], it would entail the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); since that [qualification] is unestablished,
"being distinct from that" is likewise unestablished for the Bhāṭṭas and others.

And because the qualification is unestablished for them as well; for even according to the Bhāṭṭas, there is no established existence of any entity distinct from substance, quality, action, generality, inherence, and potency.

Furthermore, since inherence is unestablished, its distinctness [from other categories] is also unestablished. Thus, it is being proven that "space is the substratum of an entity distinct from substance, quality, and genus. Consequently, the example is neither characterized by an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) nor is it deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
If it is argued that [the reason] is established because such an action alone exists in the case of a jar— no,

for there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a jar that has not yet produced an action or one that has already perished. Therefore, the reason must be qualified by the exclusion of those jars in which no action has been produced.

If [it is argued that] this is not so—[we reply: no, because it is overqualified by the property of being an object (*karmatva*). Nor is this [property] "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), because it is excluded even from the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*) such as unproduced actions or destroyed pots, and because the aforementioned fallacies, such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), remain as they were.

As for the inference: "Supreme magnitude (paramamahattva) is co-located with an entity that does not reside in anything other than [the category of] quality, because it is a magnitude, like the magnitude of a jar"— that too is incorrect, [because the reason is over-pervasive] due to [qualities such as] power (śakti), cognizedness (jñātatā), and so forth.
Because it would be proving what is already established for the Bhāṭṭas and others;
for even by establishing a subordinate genus under "substance-ness" residing in an unexcluded ether, [the point remains proven].
Because its purpose has been fulfilled, it is subsumed by another object, like a universal;
because it is inherent in that which is inherent in something other than a universal;
and because its exclusion from both the portion consisting of the gift and the portion consisting of inherence is established.

Furthermore, [the reason] is vitiated by a different meaning (arthāntara) because its purpose has already been fulfilled; and it is also subject to a limiting condition (sopādhitva) due to the absence of eternal dimension. Nor is this [reason] "other than the subject" (pakṣetaratā), since it applies even to the counter-example (vipakṣa), namely the dimension of atoms.
Because of exclusion; because there is a counter-argument due to the absence of limiting conditions (upādhi);
and because the previously mentioned qualification of the hundredfold probandum is itself afflicted by defects.
As for the inference as well—this...

"The atom is the inherent cause (samavāyin) of that which is distinct from the universal [of inherence] and possesses a universal residing therein, because it is an inherent cause and because it is a substance, like a jar"— this too is not correct, because it results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) by the case of space and so forth, since space is distinct from the universal [of inherence] and possesses a universal residing therein.
And because this atom is the substratum of the inherence residing therein, and because inherence is unitary,
it is being proved that it is a substratum distinct from the universal, like the universal residing therein.

If [it is argued that it is not so], no; for there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*) by means of space (*gagana*) and the like. This is because the Prābhākaras accept that [space] is devoid of universals (*sāmānya*) and is the substratum of all corporeal things (*sarvamūrtāśraya*), based on Praśastapāda’s statement: "Because it occupies the same location as all corporeal things."
Space and the rest are dependent on a substance, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and for other such reasons.

If it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is qualified by being distinct from space, time, direction, and self—no, for this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since [the property] is absent in those very things. This also applies to the case of being an entity (*bhāvatva*).

If it is argued that this is a qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*), we say no; for against the Prābhākara, this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of color and so forth, since in his view the color and other qualities of space (*gagana*) lack any universal (*niḥsāmānya*). [This is the point.]
Furthermore, because [the probans] is unestablished— just like the "universality residing in these atoms"—

and because the probandum, being distinct from that, would be unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); moreover, the qualification of the positive entity (*bhāva*) is redundant.

If it is argued that because Prabhākara accepts non-existence (abhāva), the qualification "existent" (bhāva) is not employed against him— this is not so, because it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) by means of the non-existence of existence.

Furthermore, because the universal residing in these atoms is not established for the Prābhākara, and because its distinctness from that which possesses the universal residing in these atoms is unproven for him;
[this applies] to the Bhāṭṭa as well.
And because the qualification is unestablished:
for one who accepts the non-difference of the property and the substratum, if it is not admitted that anything resides in an atom, then its absence must also not be admitted.

For one who accepts the non-difference of universals, forms, and so forth, that [reason] is likewise unestablished; moreover, the qualification is redundant. This is because for one who correctly maintains the non-difference of property and substratum, [the reason] would belong to that which possesses the universal residing therein.
Because that which is to be excluded [from the definition] is not admitted.
For even though every inference [is such that it is] a genus excluded from non-existence— which is distinct from existence-universal (sattāsāmānya) and inherence (samavāya)— because...

As for the argument "like the nature of being a cow" (*gotva*), that too is not valid, because it is subject to the same defects as those previously mentioned regarding the definition of existence (*bhāva*),
and because it is overqualified (*sopādhi*) by the property of being excluded from [the locus of] the probandum.
Nor is it the case that [the reason is absent] from the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), such as knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

It should not be argued that because the qualifier is non-excluded precisely by virtue of being excluded, there is no counter-example (vipakṣa) to be excluded, and thus this [reason] is merely "other than the subject" (pakṣetara);
for there exists a counter-example to be excluded, such as "being an entity" (bhāvatva) and so forth.
Furthermore, what is intended by "existence" (sattā)?
Is it a genus (jāti) devoid of exclusion (vyāvṛtti), or is it that which resides solely in substance, quality, and action? Not the first, because of contradiction. Nor...

The second [reason] is fallacious (*vyabhicāra*), because it applies to a genus (*jāti*) that lacks the quality of being excluded [from others]. If it is argued that "the genus is excluded because it is a genus," [we reply] no, because this would be fallacious with respect to "existence" (*bhāvatva*).
If it is argued that "existence is not a genus," [we reply] no, for by the same logic as that of "cowness" (*gotva*), that [existence]...

Because the existence of a universal (jāti) is established; for it is established that there exists a universal residing solely in positive entities (bhāva), by the inference: "A jar possesses a universal excluded from those entities that are excluded from the existence residing in jars, because it is a positive entity (bhāva), like a jar and so forth."

If it is argued that [the universal "existence"] is a universal because it is a genus residing only in substance, quality, and action—[we reply: no, for this would result in the example being devoid of the probans. This is because the universal "cowness" does not reside in substance, quality, or action; rather, it is a universal that does not reside in anything other than substance, quality, and action.

If it is argued that this is not so—[we reply] no, because [the reason] has a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the form of being an occurrence (*vṛttatva*). Nor is this [reason] "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), because properties such as existence (*bhāvatva*) are excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, because it is not excluded from the object [of the probandum], there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*).

"Because it is the substratum of an entity distinct from substance, quality, action, generality, and inherence, and because there is a lack of proof for it and the presence of refutations, the existence of *viśeṣa* (particularity) is not established. This is incorrect; [it is] time.
[The subject] is the substratum of inherence (samavāya) that is devoid of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction-ness, and disjunction-ness,

because it is a substance, like a jar; since such [an inference] exists, there is no proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) or proving something irrelevant (arthāntara) by means of inherence and absence.

Because those two [alternatives] are excluded by the term "substratum of inherence" (*samavāyādhāra*), nor is "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth a limiting condition (*upādhi*), since it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like. This concludes what was shown here as the establishment of the particulars (*viśeṣas*).
Without transgressing the established boundaries of the former Vaiśeṣika masters.
But when one accepts our own view— that even inherence and non-existence possess inherence as their substratum— then [the previous arguments] regarding inherence and [non-existence]...

Because it would be either a proven conclusion (*siddhasādhana*), a different meaning (*arthāntara*), or both; for otherwise, one might employ the following argument: "Time is the substratum of a positive entity (*bhāva*) that is devoid of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and the universal (*jāti*) of being [such], and is devoid of the inherence (*samavāya*) in a universal that is itself devoid of [those aforementioned qualities], because it is a substance (*dravya*), like a jar. And this is not [proven] by means of a jar, etc.

This would result either in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or in the fallacy of shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*), because the dependence of a jar and such things upon time has already been negated;
or, if it were not negated, the probandum would be qualified by the absence of substantiality (*dravyatva*). Nor, furthermore...
[The argument] that [the subject] is the substratum of number, the substratum of dimension, and so forth,

results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or constitutes a different point (*arthāntara*), because such properties are excluded by the qualification "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*), since [the subject] is an absence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, it is devoid of being the substratum of an entity.
Because there is no distinction from the probandum. Furthermore, there is no absence of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) in those things that are the substrata of number,

because being a substratum is established by experience in the case of separatenesses as in the case of separateness, in the case of farnesses as in the case of farness, and in the case of nearnesses as in the case of nearness— namely, in those things which are the substrata of number and so forth.
Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of [the existence of] capacity, being known, and so forth, for those too are established.
If it is argued that these are established for the Bhāṭṭas and others— no, because even for them they are not established without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that those [entities] are established for them through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and so forth—no, because they are observed to be accounted for otherwise; nor can there be another object [such as a universal] by means of capacity (*śakti*) and so forth, because such a view cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpa*). For instance, what...

This [argument] is rendered redundant by another point: namely, that [the object] is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) which lacks a specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), such as its capacity (*śakti*). Alternatively, it is [redundant] because of its capacity and so forth, which are well-known through another means of valid cognition that lacks a specific characteristic.

Is it that [the term "power"] signifies the state of having accomplished its purpose, or is it a distinct entity whose name is "power" and so forth because it is that which is established by this [inference]? Not the first,
because of the refutation of any means of valid cognition regarding such objects as power.
Not the second, because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*) for us, as [the object] is devoid of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

Not the third, because there is no dispute (*avivāda*); for by the will of a person, a convention (*saṃketa*) can be established for any word whatsoever regarding anything at all. [This applies even to] the Bhāṭṭas and others.

Alternatively, by including the qualification "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) in the probandum (*sādhya*), there is the exclusion of the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), because the Bhaṭṭas and others maintain that capacity (*śakti*) is not perceptible.
For even duration (*kāla*), destruction (*niṣṭhā*), number (*saṃkhyā*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and sequence (*krama*) are admitted by the Prābhākara to be non-perceptible;
the same is held by the Bhāṭṭa as well.
Since the experience of the fruit of knowledge is admitted to be grounded in the self, and since "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is not accepted,

it is impossible to state that those two [objections] constitute either a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or a shift in the subject matter (*arthāntara*). This is true even for the proponent of *jñātatā*.
By the Bhāṭṭa, who maintains that time and so forth are sense-faculties, [the cognition] residing therein is the "cognizedness" (jñātatā).
Since even for one who maintains that time is perceptible does not admit that [time] is directly perceived,

the term "in the probandum" (*sādhye*) is used in order to avoid the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), namely, the "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) residing in that [time] as asserted by the Bhāṭṭas.

Because it includes a qualification not produced by cognition, and because the aforementioned probandum—which is qualified by that which is not produced by cognition—is absent in a jar and so forth, there is a deviation from the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*); thus, the example is devoid of the probandum. The jar...

If it is argued that [the reason is invalid] because of "knowledge"— no, because the reason is qualified by "eternality," and because atoms and the like are adduced as examples, or because [the subject] is devoid of being produced by knowledge residing in time.

Because of the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇāt*); because such a probandum exists even in the case of a jar and so forth; because it does not prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) for the Bhāṭṭa; and because the mind (*manas*) is taken as the subject (*dharmin*).

And even in the Bhaṭṭa school, since that [cognition] is not itself perceived, the "knownness" (jñātatā) residing therein is also unperceived; thus, it is rejected on the grounds that it cannot serve as a qualifier for something unperceived. This is because it lacks the defining characteristics of knownness.

Or [the reason is fallacious] due to the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇāt*). Nor should it be argued that, since the establishment of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is not yet proven, its definition is unestablished, and therefore even that which lacks it remains unproven, resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*); for [it is already] cognized...
This is because "this-ness" (*jñātatā*) is established for both disputants by the force of experience;

therefore, the dispute concerns only whether it is the objecthood of cognition or something distinct from it. Furthermore, since number is excluded by its lack of the property of being a number (*saṃkhyātva*), and since similarity, if it were a universal (*jāti*), [would be subject to the same refutation].

Because it is refuted by its being devoid of the nature of a genus (*jāti*); because, even if it were "cowness" (*gotva*) consisting of a commonality of many parts, it is refuted by its being devoid of the characteristic of inherence (*samavāya*); because it could exist in time;
and because, if it were a distinct entity, it would be excluded as a qualifier of an existent (*bhāva*), or else it would simply be an existent itself.
Because, if that [time] were unitary in all respects, it would be qualified by the probandum as being distinct from similarity;

and if it were diverse, it would be qualified by the probandum as lacking the definition of similarity; and because sequence—whether produced by space or restricted to non-omnipresent things—is impossible in time, which is omnipresent.

Because of impossibility; for that which is produced by time and restricted to its effect is impossible in what is not an effect and at a time other than [its own]. Or, even if such were possible, in order to exclude it, the probandum is qualified by the absence of a sequence-characteristic, thereby distinguishing between similarity and sequence.

If it is argued that, since two distinct categories (*padārtha*) are not established, their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is unestablished, and thus the qualifier "devoid of duality" is an unestablished qualification— [we reply: no, for even if those two are not established as distinct categories, this [object] is similar.
Since it is established by experience that "this [cognition] possesses succession," once its definition is established, the absence of that [succession] is also established. In this very way,

there is a refutation of both the *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already proven) and the *arthāntara* (irrelevant matter) advanced by other non-Buddhist schools, which proceed by relying on categories of existence imagined within their own systems.

Alternatively: Time is the substratum of the absence of perception, which is devoid of being the locus of that which lacks multiple loci distinct from the unity and individuality residing in time, and which is devoid of being the locus of that which is produced by a cognition whose sole object is time;
because it is a substance, like a jar. Nor [is there a flaw here] against the Mīmāṃsaka...

[The objection that] it is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) regarding [the category of] "capacity" (*śakti*) and so forth, or a *arthāntara* (proving something irrelevant), is rejected because the *siddhasādhana* regarding the number "one" (*ekatva-saṃkhyā*) is excluded by its being distinct from [the mere property of] oneness;
[this is further supported] by [the presence of] multiple numbers, similarity, sequence, and cognitions residing in multiple loci.

Furthermore, because [the defects of] proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) are excluded by the fact that [the opponent's reason] is not produced by a cognition whose sole object is time; and because [the defects of] the possible-to-be-proven (*śakya-sādhya*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*) are excluded by its being perceptible (*pratyakṣa*),
the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that power (*śakti*) is not perceptible.
The qualification is inappropriate; for,
according to the Vaiśeṣika system, since all categories are perceptible, there is no non-perceptible thing to be excluded, and thus [the qualification] is redundant.
If [it is argued that it is not so], no; for [the argument] is fruitful precisely by avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) against the Mīmāṃsaka.

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*asiddhasādhanam*) or the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratvam*) on account of being the substratum of temporal succession, the substratum of the singular separateness residing in time, or the substratum of the magnitude residing in time.

Or rather, because they are excluded by the qualification of "existence" as being non-existent, that which is the absolute absence of the absolute absence of the unity residing in time must itself be the substratum of the unity residing in time.

Because the absolute absence of the absolute absence of the singularity of time-located [entities], and the absolute absence of the absolute absence of the magnitude of time-located [entities], have as their substratum the magnitude of time-located [entities].
[The subject] is the substratum of an entity that lacks inherence in anything other than [the categories of] perishability, singularity, separateness, magnitude, and being a substratum;

because it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), like a jar. Nor, in this case, is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of action (*karman*), nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), because of that [action].

Because it is impossible for that which depends solely on a corporeal substrate to exist in time; nor can it be something other than [the action] by way of potency (*śakti*) and so forth, since those [potencies] themselves are unestablished,
and consequently, the "action" as a distinct entity is also unestablished— or if they were established, [the same would apply to them].

Because it is excluded by being included within substance, etc., as that which is devoid of substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth. Alternatively: Time is the locus of the absence of that which is devoid of being an object residing in time, because it possesses substantiality, like a jar. Or else: Time...
"The substratum of non-existence is devoid of having time as its ultimate object and devoid of having multiple things as its ultimate objects,

because it is a substance, like a jar. Nor should it be argued that here, because the property of "having [time] as its object" is unestablished, the absence of that property is also unestablished, resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
This is because the universal (jāti) residing solely in substance, quality, and action is established for both disputants;

and because that [universal] alone serves as the basis for the application of words whose referents are already established. Nor [is it the case that] these [universals] lack the possession of sub-class universals such as substantiality (dravyatva), nor are they devoid of direction (dik) or space (ākāśa).

The condition (upādhi) consisting of "being an absence distinct [from the subject]" and so forth is [invalid] because it is merely "otherness from the subject" (pakṣetaratva) and because it does not pervade the probandum (sādhyavyāpaka); for, according to your own view,
[qualities] such as potency and cognizedness are possible even in qualities (guṇa) and other categories.
And because the qualification (*upādhi*) is not a defect;

nor is there a counter-balancing argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on being distinct from space and direction—excluding space and direction that lack the lower genus of substantiality (*dravyatvāvāntarajāti*). This is because [the reason] is qualified by non-substantiality (*adravyatva*). Thus...

When taking all eternal substances such as space (*dik*) and so forth as the subject of the thesis, [the probandum is] the state of being a locus for the absence of that which is devoid of the inherence (*samavāyitva*) in the respective universals (*jāti*) of quality-ness (*guṇatva*),

substance-ness (*dravyatva*), and the like residing therein; and when taking those respective universals of quality-ness, substance-ness, and so forth as the subject of the thesis, [the probandum is] the state of being a locus for the absence of that which is devoid of the inherence in those respective universals of quality-ness, substance-ness, and so forth.
It must be established that [the subject] possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*) alone.

Nor should it be argued that because the universal "substantiality" (*samavāyatva-jāti*) does not exist— since inherence (*samavāya*) is unitary— the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatā*), for even that which lacks such a universal remains unestablished.

Because the nature of inherence (*samavāyatva*), characterized as inherence itself, is established for both disputants; therefore, the existence of *viśeṣa* (particularity) in eternal substances is established by means of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), as well as by purely positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*). To illustrate this, time—

Time is the substratum of that which is devoid of the properties of being a quality (*guṇatva*), being a universal (*jātitva*), being a substance (*dravyatva*), and being inherence (*samavāyatva*), yet is not devoid of the property of being an absence residing in time, because it is an object of cognition (*meyatva*), like a jar.

Time is the substratum of that which is devoid of residing in more than one thing— excluding oneness (*ekatva*), separateness (*pṛthaktva*), and largeness (*mahattva*)— yet is not devoid of the property of being an absence residing in time, because it is an object of cognition, like a jar.
Nor is there an impossibility of being a *kevalānvayin* (exclusively positive) because of the absence of a property that is devoid of residing in multiple things, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth;
for it is possible [to find] the absolute non-existence of being other than each of those colors and so on.

[The subject is] the substratum of that which is devoid of time, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction-ness, genus-ness, inherence-ness, substance-ness, and the state of being an absence residing in time.

Because it is an object of cognition (*meyatvāt*), like a jar. Time is the substratum of that which is devoid of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and the universals [of those], and which is not devoid of the absence residing in time—[an absence] that is itself devoid of the universals of being a universal, inherence, and substance;
because it is an object of cognition, like a jar.

Nor is there an impossibility of being a subject (*pakṣatva*) because of the absence of such a probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), [even] if it were based solely on the five qualities beginning with number (*saṃkhyā*), since one may take as [the locus of the probandum] the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of time and so forth.
Because it is established as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and because it is established as being equal to the subject (*pakṣa*) by taking into account its specific qualities.

Nor is there here the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) by means of [the opponent's] power (*śakti*) and so forth, for the very reason stated previously. Furthermore, there is no possibility of a counter-argument based on a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here.

"Because it is purely positive (kevalānvayin). Nor can one argue: "This jar possesses the absolute absence of something residing in some locus, which is devoid of being resident in this [jar] and others, and is devoid of being a sequence of qualities resident in eternal things, because it is knowable (meyatva), like a jar."

Alternatively, [the inference] is by means of a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) argument such as: "Time possesses a magnitude that resides in time, and it possesses unity and separateness that do not reside in non-time, and it possesses properties residing in other times and in itself, because it is an object of cognition (meyatva), like a jar. For instance, time—

It possesses existence (bhāva) that is devoid of being an effect, devoid of being a quality, and devoid of being inherence, because it is an eternal substance; for whatever is not thus is not so, like a jar;
and since it is not an impermanent substance, it is therefore so. Nor [is there any deviation] here by means of atoms.

This would be either a proof of what is already established or a proving of something irrelevant, because those [categories] are non-dependent due to being eternal substances. Or else: time possesses existence that is devoid of corporeality, quality-ness, action-ness, genus-ness, and inherence-ness.
Because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutvāt*); for that which is not thus is not thus, just as a jar [is not all-pervasive]; and this [self] is all-pervasive, therefore it is so.
Nor should it be said that, when such a state of being is established, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

This is because such a thing as the ether (gagana) and so forth is well-established. Nor can it be argued that there is the fallacy of an "unestablished qualification" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) on the grounds that even this kind of "state of being an entity" (bhāvatva) is unestablished; for that [qualification] consists in its connection with the subject (pakṣa) which is the locus of the probandum (sādhya).

For in all inferences, it is precisely that which is unestablished [prior to the inference] that is established. Nor does the existence of a similar instance (sapakṣa) in this way constitute a refutation of the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference;
for even when such an entity is established, [the probans] remains independent of it, as it belongs to that [subject].

Because a similar instance (sapakṣa) is impossible; because there is no sublation when proving merely such a state from the probans itself; and because that [state] is possible even for that which is dependent. Nor is there a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) such as "time does not possess such a state, because it is knowable" (meyatvāt).

For, in proving the absolute non-existence of such entities, one would fall into either the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), due to the absolute non-existence of space (*gaganātyantābhāva*). And likewise, in establishing the absolute non-existence of all such entities...
If, by the word "all," one intends to refer to all such entities as being dependent on something else,
then the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) and other such faults remain as they were.
However, if one intends to refer to all such entities regardless of whether they are dependent or independent, [the argument holds].
Because its qualification is unestablished;
for as long as such positive entities are not established, their absence remains unestablished,
and because as long as all such entities are not cognized, it is impossible to apprehend their absence.
Even in the proof of the absolute non-existence of such a state of being,
there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because such a state of being is unestablished prior to the establishment of the specific property (*viśeṣa*).

Because that absolute non-existence is unestablished; and in cases such as "this jar is devoid of qualities belonging to the ground," there is a negation of the possession of the jar and the possession of qualities.
Because the negation of all jars and all qualities is established, there is no room for an objection;
for even in a single jar and a single quality, it is impossible for the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of "jar-ness" or "quality-ness" to occur. Nor is it the case that...

Is "existence" (bhāvatva) itself the probandum, or is it the individual instance (vyakti) which is the substratum of such existence? Not the first, because since such existence is not established in time (kāla) and so forth, there would be a failure to establish the non-distinction [of the subject from the example].

Nor the second, because in proving an individual instance residing in any one of space (ākāśa) and so forth as being ascertained by valid cognition (yāvat-pramita), [the reason would be inconclusive].

[The opponent argues: "Because it would be sublated; and because, in proving an individual distinct from that [universal], there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

This is incorrect, because one proves an individual substrate of such a state of being (*bhāvatva*) precisely as it is, without being delimited by qualifications such as "being dependent" or "not being dependent."

And because that [entity] is unestablished. Even so, by the turn of fate, is this [entity] dependent or independent? In either case, the aforementioned fault follows from the proof-establishing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It cannot be the first [alternative], for it is not established by another means of valid cognition.
Because no such entity distinct from space and so forth is established by the means of valid cognition that establishes space and so forth; nor is the second [alternative] possible,
because of its non-existence, as perceived by the apprehending direct perception (*grāhakapratyakṣa*).
Because that [universal] is not apprehended by that which grasps all its individual instances due to the proximity of being its qualifier;
and because such a state of being (bhāvatva) is devoid of residing in anything other than what resides in things distinct from eternal substances, since it is an object of cognition (meyatvāt).

If it is argued that because [the probandum] is established by the inference beginning with "like a jar" (ghaṭavat), and since the specific [property] is established merely by proving the qualification,
the original inference is redundant— [we reply: no,
for by such an [inference], there is the establishment of other dependent non-eternal substances of this kind through the absence of dependence [on anything else].
Or, since the root inference which establishes the particular (viśeṣa) establishes it precisely as residing in such an eternal substance, it is indeed an establisher of the particular.
Or, let it be that the particular is established from the very establisher of the qualifier; even so, it is proven.
Our desired object.
It has been stated that some [categories] are both generalities and particulars, while others are particulars alone. In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes a generality, the Sūtra says:
"Existence" (bhāva). (1.2.4)

In this context, regarding the verbal root *as* in the sense of "being," that form which is produced from it denotes "existence" (*bhāva*), "becoming" (*bhavana*), or "being-ness" (*sattā*). Just as *sattā* is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it persists through substances, qualities, and actions, so too [is the case here].
Because it is excluded from universals, particulars, and inherence, even the particular (*viśeṣa*) [is a universal];
therefore, existence (*sattā*) is both a universal and a particular, and not merely a universal. That is not so, because it is not admitted that existence is excluded from universals.

Because existence (*sattā*) is established through perception and inference that apprehend its properties, and because it is devoid of exclusion from universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; or, if there were exclusion from universals and so forth, even then existence would not be a particular universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), since it lacks exclusion from the distinctness of substance, quality, and action.
Because it is impossible for existence (*sattā*) to be a particular (*viśeṣa*) characterized by being excluded from genus (*jāti*),
and because mere exclusion is not intended here as "particularity," therefore existence is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*), and not [a particular] while possessing corporeality (*mūrtitva*).

This is because the definition of a mere universal (*kevalasāmānya*) consists either in being devoid of exclusion from any one among substances, qualities, or actions while being inclusive, or in being devoid of exclusion from both universals and the possessors of universals while being inclusive.
This being the case, even "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the like would be a mere generality (*kevalasāmānya*). [Objection: This is a contradiction. [Response:

Or rather, let it be so; for even while being a generality-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), it possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttatva*), since the definition of a generality-particular is precisely this: being a generality that is also excluded. How then [is this so]?

The claim that "existence (sattā) is exclusively a universal" is a mere popular saying; for the author of the Sūtras does not state in any way that existence is exclusively a universal. If it is argued that the Sūtra "bhāva" [1.1.4] implies that existence is exclusively a universal—no, because of the Sūtra "abhāva" [1.1.5].
Because an object denoting existence (*sattā*) does not denote a mere universal form (*kevalasāmānyarūpatā*).

If it is argued that the intent of the sūtra "bhāva" (existence), which enters [the discussion] when there is the expectation "Is it the universal itself?", is that "existence is indeed the universal," then [one must ask]: what is the universal-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*)?
Because the introduction of the Sūtra occurs precisely when there is such an expectation [of inquiry].

If it is argued that this is the answer to the expectation "Is it only a universal?", we say no; for there is no such expectation as "Is it some kind of universal? Or, even if such an expectation were to exist—
It must be explained that the author of the Sūtras intended the answer to be precisely "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth. || 4 ||

But when existence (sattā) is itself a generality (sāmānya), then, in response to the inquiry as to what constitutes a "generality-cum-particular" (sāmānyaviśeṣa), the aphorism states: "Substantiality (dravyatva), quality-ness (guṇatva), and action-ness (karmatva) are generalities and particulars."
Thus [it is said]. But surely this is untenable, because the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*) consists in being eternal and inhering in many,
and because [the definition] of a non-existence (*abhāva*) consists in not being the locus of existence (*sattā*) which is devoid of residing in many.

Because they possess the characteristic of being specific (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa), and because those two cannot coexist in one and the same thing; for if they did coexist, it would follow that [the definition] is over-extensive (ativyāpaka). This is incorrect, even though [qualities such as] substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth possess the characteristic of being general (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).

Because there is an absence of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and because the employment of the word "specific" (*viśeṣa-pada*) is determined to have the purpose of excluding similarity to a specific [other], it is therefore figurative (*gauṇatva*).
Alternatively, the cause for the employment of the word "specific" is that which stands as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to a generality (*sāmānya*).
Exclusion from both [categories] and the absence of substantiality (dravyatva)—

this constitutes the primary status of substance and the rest as general-particulars (sāmānya-viśeṣa). If that is so, then [the same applies to] effects, substances, conjunction, disjunction, multiple numbers, and multiple distinctnesses as well.

If it is argued that universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth must be mere residues of their own essential natures because they are excluded [from others]—this is true. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras, in the section on the universal nature of effects, refuted the claim that causal substances and the like possess the nature of a universal. The word "and" (*ca*)...

This is for the purpose of including [categories such as] earthness, formness, and throwing-ness, which possess inherence that lacks an unmentioned existence (*sattā*). This is because it is precisely the inherence lacking existence that is to be established in this chapter. || 5 ||

If everything, like inherence (samavāya) which is devoid of existence (sattā), were to fall under the category of both universal and particular, then one might suspect that even ultimate particulars (antyaviśeṣas) would likewise be both universals and particulars;
it is to dispel this doubt that the following aphorism is stated:
Except for the ultimate particularities. (1.2.6)

Thus: by excluding [the category of] "other," it is established that all generalities (sāmānya) and particularities (viśeṣa), with the exception of the ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣa), possess inherence (samavāya) while being devoid of existence (sattā). What, then, is this ultimacy?

Regarding "at the end" (*ante*): Master Ātreya explains that because they exist at the end of production and destruction—that is, they abide at the final limit—the word "end" refers to eternal substances (*nityadravya*). Because they reside in those [substances], the word "ultimate" (*antya*) refers to the particularities (*viśeṣa*).

Alternatively, they are called "ultimate" (*antya*) because they exist at the end or conclusion of other particularities (*viśeṣa*). For instance, in relation to existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*) is a particularity; in relation to that, earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth are particularities; and in relation to those, that which resides in a single substance [is the ultimate particularity].

This is the distinction. Furthermore, there exists no differentiator other than the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), because it would be impossible for such a thing to persist [in multiple individuals]. Therefore, that very thing is called "ultimate" (*antya*) because it occurs at the end of all qualifiers.

Alternatively, they are called "final" (antya) because they occur at the end, namely at the time of universal liberation (*sarvamukti*). In that case, there exists no differentiator for the self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*) other than their final particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*).
Because general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*) do not serve to differentiate [substances], and because no particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) exist [in them].
Alternatively, by the word "end" (*anta*), time (*kāla*) is expressed; that which exists therein is called "final" (*antya*). It is not [the case that it does not exist].
For it is possible that only time (*kāla*) exists as the ultimate differentiator (*antya-vyāvartaka*),
because number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction are not differentiators;
otherwise, [the following would occur].
For otherwise, it would follow that doubts and misconceptions regarding the self could not arise at the time of its subsequent reflection and so forth.

The aphorism for the purpose of establishing the means of valid cognition regarding existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, is as follows:
"That [notion] from which [the cognition] 'it exists' arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions—that is existence. (1.2.7)

Existence (*sattā*) is that from which the application of the notions "there is substance," "there is quality," and "there is action" arise as qualifiers. This is merely an illustration; by extension, it refers to that from which the notion "substance" arises with respect to the nine [categories] beginning with earth—that is, substantiality (*dravyatva*). Likewise, it refers to that from which [the notion of "quality" arises].

The state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) resides in the twenty-four [categories] beginning with form (*rūpa*). "Action" (*karman*) is that which exists in throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth; thus is it to be understood for all universals (*jāti*).
In this manner, until the conclusion of the chapter, everything within the scope of existence (*sattā*) is also [to be understood].

"This should also be observed in the case of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth. [Objection: But even this is untenable; for the cognition and linguistic usage "it exists" (*sat*) arise from the individual's own nature (*vyakti-svarūpa*), inherence (*samavāya*), knowability (*prameyatva*), and so on.
