Otherwise, due to the lack of proficiency [in linguistic usage], there would be the undesirable consequence of not employing the term "existent" (*sat*) with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like;

for in those cases, the "existence" (*sattā*) intended by you is absent. If it is argued that the term "exists" is applied there because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of existence—[we reply: no, for since the uncontradicted practical usage of "truth" (*satya*) is established through its being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), that [superimposition] is unnecessary.
Because it lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, inference is not a means of valid cognition regarding existence (*sattā*).
If it is argued that substances, qualities, and actions possess a single generality (*sāmānya*) because they are "possessors of generality" (*sāmānyavat*), we say no;
for among substances, there is [the generality] "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), among qualities, "qualitiness" (*guṇatva*), and among actions, "actionness" (*karmatva*).

Because it would result in proving what is already established. If it is argued that a single, undivided universal (*sāmānya*) is being proven to exist within substances, qualities, and actions—and that this is not the case for substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) because these are distinct—[we reply]: no.
In the proof that [the subject] possesses a single generality residing in substance, quality, and action, the qualification is unestablished,
because existence itself has not yet been established.

Since a single universal residing in substances, qualities, and actions is not established, [the claim that] a universal is established in substances, qualities, and actions— [and that] by the force of its presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), it is established as being one alone—
is not correct; for the presence in the subject...

Because it is not a prover [of the probandum] other than that which is connected with the subject of the thesis (*sādhyapakṣa*). When generality (*sāmānya*) is established in substances, qualities, and actions, it is established as one alone due to the parsimony of postulation (*kalpanālāghava*).
If it is argued that it is like God (*īśvara*) in relation to the earth and so forth—no.
This is because the parsimony of conceptual construction (*kalpanālāghava*) is not accepted as an auxiliary factor for inference; otherwise,

[one would have to conclude that] earthiness (*pārthivatva*) and so forth are produced by the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), triads (*tryaṇuka*), and so on.
For, by means of arguments such as "because it is an effect, like a jar," combined with the principle of parsimony (kalpanālāghava),
there would follow the undesirable consequence that the inherent causes and non-inherent causes of the dyads of earth and other elements are one and the same.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that number, dimension, and so forth would be established as single entities in space, time, and the like, based on such arguments as: "Space and the rest possess number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction, because they are substances."
Nor is it the case that "space possesses a genus distinct from substantiality, because it possesses a genus and because it is a substance, like cowness";
for this argument is already satisfied by the establishment of [other] qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*), which are sub-classes of substantiality that prove the existence of *sattā*.

[This is] because [the probandum] is swallowed by another meaning. If it is argued that the probandum is qualified by the absence of any sub-class of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), we say no; for this would result in the example of the cow being deficient in the probandum. This applies to both the examples of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as the examples of cows and so forth.

If it is argued that they are similar to the subject (*pakṣa*), we say no; for if they possess substantiality (*dravyatva*), they lack the probans (*sādhanavikalatva*) [in the case of the first reason], and even in the case of other reasons as the probans, they lack the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) with respect to valid cognition (*pramā*). Therefore, [this applies] to that which is distinct from an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*).

If it is argued that this is an example based on cognition because cognitions are accepted as being knowledge despite the non-acceptance of their status as a genus (*jāti*), we say no; for against Śālikanātha Miśra and others, the fallacy of the probandum being absent (*sādhyavikalatva*) remains exactly as before, since they do not accept [the status of] cognitions as being knowledge.

If it is argued that "form and the other [categories] possess birth (jāti), because they exist as entities distinct from generality, particularity, and inherence, like a cow"—[we reply: no, because [the reason] is overqualified by the property of being a substance (dravyatva). [This is stated] by the Prābhākara.

If it is argued that "substantiality" (dravyatva) is not accepted [as a universal], we say no; for by that [term], the possession of qualities and so forth is itself admitted as substantiality. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas and others can maintain that the universal "substantiality" is merely adventitious (aupādhika). This is because [it is established] through its being an effect.

And because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor does this [condition] pervade the probans (*sādhana*), for it is excluded from eternal forms and the like which possess the probans of being a positive entity that is not distinct from a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, these two are not "otherness-of-the-pakṣa" (*pakṣetaratva*).

Because it is excluded even from the counter-example (vipakṣa), such as generality (sāmānya) and the like, which are devoid of possessing a genus (jātimattva); for instance, "substantiality (dravyatva) is excluded from genus because it does not reside in non-substances, like a cloth"—thus, the possession of a genus is established. If it is argued that substantiality does not pervade the probandum (sādhya), we say no.

Because the exclusion from substances (*dravyavyāvṛttatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the exclusion from that which possesses genus (*jātimadvyāvṛttatva*). Nor is this [condition] merely "otherness than the subject" (*pakṣetaratā*), because it is excluded from [properties] such as knowability (*prameyatva*), which lack the exclusion from that which possesses genus.
Because [properties] such as "knowability" (prameyatva) are excluded precisely by virtue of being non-excluded;
for there is no possibility of the qualification "substance-ness" (dravyatva) being that which is to be excluded, and thus it would be "other-than-the-pakṣa" (pakṣetaratva).
If this is argued, we say no, because there exists that which is to be excluded by the qualification "substance-ness," namely, the category of "existence" (bhāva) and so forth.
Because it is excluded from that [existence] due to its non-existence,

by means of the qualification "excluded," there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on the fact that [the reason] does not exclude substances, since it does not subsist pervasively (*avyāpyavṛtti*). This refers to action (*karma*).

Nor is it the case that [the probandum] is "being an effect residing in a genus residing in what is resident in a cow," because this is subject to the condition (*upādhi*) of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which establish existence (*sattā*).
Nor is there the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntaratā*) by means of a genus residing solely in effects.
Nor is it correct to argue: "The action inherent in impermanent qualities possesses a genus residing in a substance, because it is inherent in the impermanent,

like a cow," for this would result in proving something already established (*arthāntara*) by means of the genus residing solely in that which is inherent in the impermanent, such as *dravyatva* (substance-ness).

"And because it possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*). This is because the Prābhākara accepts [the existence of] dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. If it is argued that this is not a limiting condition because it would destroy the subsumption of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) under "generality" (*sāmānya*), we say no; for being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is not included within the definition of a limiting condition.
"The pot is the inherent cause of that which possesses a genus residing in the pot,

because it is an inherent cause, like a part of the pot"— this [inference] is subject to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), because of the genus residing solely in the absence of effects. For that [genus] as well...

Because it is inherent in an effect that is inherent in the cloth, and because it possesses the condition (*upādhi*) of having touch; and because this [reason] is excluded from ether (*gagana*) and so forth, even though they possess the probans (*sādhana*).
[This is said] with respect to [the reason] being distinct from the nature of the individual substance, inherence, knowability (*prameyatva*), and so on.
If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is incorrect; for existence residing in the jar is established through the perception, "This jar exists.
Nor is this [existence] merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of this jar, because it resides in it, just like its color.
Furthermore, because it exists even in another jar that lacks this [specific] jar;
nor is it a substance, a quality, or an action, because it resides in a quality; nor is it a particularity (viśeṣa), because it resides in an effect.

Furthermore, because it is perceptible to those who are not lords among yogis and is cognizable [by the senses], this [existence] is neither inherence nor non-existence; for, as in the case of color and so forth, existence is perceived directly, whereas non-existence lacks such perceptibility. Therefore, by the method of elimination, existence is simply the universal (jāti).

And from inference as well: "A pot possesses a genus that is devoid of the exclusion residing in the pot, because it possesses a genus, like a pot; this pot possesses a genus that is devoid of the exclusion residing in this [pot], because it possesses a genus, like a pot."
This is because the existence of a genus (jāti) devoid of exclusion [from its own instances] is established.
Nor are "substantiality" (dravyatva) or "being an effect" (kāryatva) limiting adjuncts (upādhi) here, because they are purely positive (kevalānvayin).
For instance, in the case of color and so forth, one may argue: "Color and the like possess a genus, because they are cognizable (meyatva), like a jar. Thus it is with respect to color and the like.

And because the pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is destroyed, there is no possibility of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here either, precisely because [the reason] is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). Nor is there a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*), because the absence of a purely positive probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). However, when...
The position is that "existence" (*sattā*) is a genus (*jāti*) which persists through substance, quality, and action; in that case,
a jar possesses a genus that is excluded from [other] genera, etc., which are themselves excluded from the substances, qualities, and actions residing in the jar.
This [subject] possesses a genus that is excluded from those genera and so forth which are devoid of exclusion from the qualities and actions residing in this [subject],
because it possesses a genus. A pot possesses a genus that is excluded from those genera and so forth which are devoid of exclusion from the genus residing in a pot, because it is a pot.

Because it possesses a genus (*jātimattvāt*). One should formulate the argument as follows: "This [subject] possesses a genus that is excluded from those genera which are devoid of exclusion from the genus residing in this [subject], because it possesses a genus, like a jar. And in this case, [the reasons] *dravyatva* (substanceness) and *kāryatva* (effectness) [do not apply].

The *upādhi* (limiting condition) is [the property of] possessing a genus such as *rūpatva* (color-ness). This is because it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in respect to color and the like, which possess the genus *rūpatva*. For instance, in the inference "Color is the locus of that which lacks the property of being a genus residing in color, because it is knowable" (*meyatva*), the possession of a genus is established in respect to color and the like.

Granted that existence (sattā) may exist, but substantiality (dravyatva) is not established, due to a lack of evidence. First of all, perception is not a means of knowledge here, because there is no experience of the form "this is a substance.
If it is argued that the very experience of independence is the experience of substantiality—no, [it is not].
The experience of independence is the experience of not being dependent;

this is unestablished in the case of a jar and so forth at that time. Or, even if it were established, it would be an error, because jars and the like are dependent. Or, if it were not an error, it would [be established] only as non-dependent.
Because that which has accomplished its purpose possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*). Likewise, experience (*anubhava*) is without an object because it is dependent;
furthermore, since that [dependence] does not prove its [the experience's] dependence, it is the differentiator.
And for cognitions and so forth, the general property (*sāmānya*) is the cognition, and it is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that acts as the differentiator.
Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is indeed experienced through perception immediately after the cognition of the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*).
If it is argued that "substantiality" is not [perceived] immediately after the cognition of the possession of the dewlap, which is the defining characteristic of a cow—[we reply:
no, for [it is perceived] even immediately after the reflection upon the possession of qualities.

Furthermore, the inclusive linguistic usage such as "substance because of substantiality," "experience," "fluidity," and "substance" is justified by the consideration of their possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*).
Nor can it be argued that, in this way, the linguistic usage of "cowness" would be established merely through the consideration of possessing a dewlap (*sāsnāvattva*).

It must be said that [the word] "cow" [is applicable]. For even in the case of a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) whose tail and snout have been cut off, the experience and linguistic usage of "cowness" (*gotva*) are established by direct experience.
This is because the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction, disjunction, and so forth, resides in this very individual (*vyakti*).

Because it would follow that [the universal] would be absent in other individuals. If it is argued that "substantiality is established because [the universal] resides in a limited number of individuals by virtue of grasping those respective substrata"—no, for its inclusion is possible through the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*). Even by another inclusive factor, it is substantiality itself [that is established].

This is because it is possible for the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) to reside in only a few individual instances; furthermore, if one were to require another inclusive category—just as one requires "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—it would lead to an infinite regress.
Moreover, what is being presented here regarding substance-ness: is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)?
Or is it the reasoning (*tarka*) that establishes that? Not the first, because the answer has already been stated. Not the second, because the formal argument (*prayoga*) cannot be defined.

Not the third, because the probandum (*āpādya*) and the probans (*āpādaka*) cannot be defined, since [the property of] conjunction and so forth belongs to the same class as earth and the other elements.
This restriction must be understood for the purpose of excluding the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Nor is it [the case that the definition is too narrow], because even in the absence of that [inherent cause] in each individual instance of earth and so forth, the status of being a genus (*jāti*) such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible; thus, there is no lack of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Nor...

Because it is impossible to establish a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), as no instance of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or similar category can possibly exist between a collection of manifested entities such as earth and so forth and another distinct collection of manifested entities such as earth and so forth; therefore, regarding the category of conjunction and the like...
If it is argued that "substantiality" (dravyatva) must be admitted in order to establish the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of earth and the other [elements]—
we say no; for their production occurs precisely through the nature of a quality (guṇatva),
and because a particular kind of conjunction itself serves as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of a particular substance.

Furthermore, since positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is possible even without a specific genus (*jāti*), and because perception, inference, and reasoning are not established even by this method regarding substantiality (*dravyatva*),
inference is not [established] due to its lack of definition.
If it is argued that "space possesses a genus that does not reside in qualities (aguṇavṛtti), because it possesses a genus, like a jar"— this is not so;

for if a genus such as "pervasiveness" (vibhutva) or "spatiality" (gaganatva) were established, the probandum would be qualified by its residing [in space], which would result in a deviation from the intended meaning (arthāntara).

Because the genus "possessing one sense-faculty" (*ekendriyatva*) and so forth would be established through a different object, and because it would be subject to a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the form of "possessing tangibility" (*sparśavattva*);

and because it would be excluded from that which possesses qualities (*guṇavat*). Furthermore, in the case of proving a genus that resides in qualities but is not excluded from that which possesses qualities...

Because it is a qualification of the subject (*siddha-viśeṣaṇatva*). Furthermore, if one attempts to prove that [the universal] is a genus that does not reside in qualities, does not reside in that which possesses qualities, and is devoid of exclusion from that which possesses qualities, the example would lack the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*). If it is argued that "action" (*karman*) is the example—no.

For that [position] as well, there is a deficiency regarding both the probandum and the probans, because the Prābhākara accepts action (*karman*) on account of the cognition and linguistic usage "this is an action."
This is because it is logically established as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction and disjunction;

furthermore, it possesses a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by virtue of being an effect. How then [could it be excluded] from the proof of a genus that resides in qualities and resides in actions, but does not reside in qualities, and which is established through a different object?

Furthermore, even if "not subsisting in action" is used as a qualification of the probandum (*sādhya*), the example would be deficient in the probandum; and because there is the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*), namely, that [the subject] possesses a genus (*jāti*) which does not subsist in qualities or actions and is not excluded from that which possesses qualities.
[The definition of the genus is: possessing a genus that does not subsist in quality-less things and is not excluded from that which possesses qualities.
If it is argued that [the reason] is to be proven (*sādhya*), we say no;
for it is counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*) by the absence of those two conditions— namely, having a non-tangible effect and being cooked— both of which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

If it is argued that by this [same reasoning] space possesses a genus distinct from existence (sattā), because it is a genus possessing another existence, or because it possesses qualities like a jar—and thus such arguments are employed—it follows that genera such as "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and so forth must likewise be refuted.

This is incorrect. For, through inference, there is established the existence of genera such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva), which reside in space and the like (which possess qualities that define them as substances), yet are excluded from those [qualities], and do not reside in what lacks those [qualities].

For instance, space possesses a genus that resides in its causes of qualities and is devoid of exclusion from that which possesses qualities; this is because it possesses a genus, like action. Nor is "possessing touch" a limiting adjunct (upādhi) here, [since it is absent] in that which possesses "action-ness" and so forth.

Because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of karma and so forth; nor because it does pervade the probandum in the case of color and so forth, which possess the nature of color (*rūpatva*) and so on; and because, according to our own view, it is established as being purely positive (*kevalānvayin*).

Furthermore, even in the case of "genus" (*jāti*), the status of being a genus (*jātitva*) is admitted. Nor can there be a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) here based on the absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because such an argument would fail due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases where the pervasion of the probandum by the limiting condition is broken, and because [the reason] is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*).

Nor can the non-substantiality (adravyatva) of the universal residing in the self be established merely by its being a universal that does not reside in anything devoid of qualities and that resides in the qualityless;
for the first qualification, "residing in that which possesses qualities," and the second qualification, "the quality-ness of that which possesses qualities," would both be redundant.
This must be stated: because the qualifier is well-established, either because the universal (jāti) "being devoid of exclusion from that which possesses qualities" is itself devoid of qualities,
or because it is devoid of subsistence in that which possesses qualities.
Not the first, because it is impossible for a genus that lacks subsistence in that which possesses qualities not to subsist in that which lacks qualities.
Not the second, [because...]
Because a universal that excludes qualities (guṇavyāvṛtta) yet does not reside in qualityless things (nirguṇāvṛtti), and which is distinct from substantiality (dravyatva),
is impossible; therefore, for this reason as well,
the possession of qualities (guṇavattva) is included within the second qualifier.

It must indeed be accepted for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*), and it is not [unacceptable] because of impossibility; for even in my view, there is no non-establishment of the probandum,

since [the subject] possesses the property of being a quality-possessor, being excluded from that which possesses qualities, being devoid of [the absence of] that which possesses qualities, and possessing the nature of action (*karmatva*) which does not reside in that which is devoid of qualities.

If it is argued that the [probandum] is established because of its being different from any genus that does not reside in quality-possessing things, yet resides in action, and is other than [the genus] "knowability," as in the case of a jar— this is not so.
Because prior to the establishment of substantiality (*dravyatva*), there is a failure of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), making it impossible to establish such a probandum;
and because such a formulation of the probandum can only be established subsequent to the establishment of substantiality.

This is because it does not constitute a flaw, as it does not act as an obstacle to the inference of substanceness (*dravyatva*). Nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), since even if a genus (*jāti*) residing in qualityless things (*nirguṇa*)— which is devoid of being excluded from that which possesses qualities (*guṇavat*)— is established, substanceness itself remains unproven.

Because the establishment of the definition of substance (*dravya*)— namely, that it is a genus residing in that which is devoid of qualities and excluded from that which possesses qualities— is itself the establishment of substantiality (*dravyatva*).
But surely this is not the definition of substantiality (dravyatva). [Thesis:
Substantiality is that which is other than a genus that does not reside in quality-less things and is not excluded from what is excluded from that which possesses qualities;
[Reason: because it is cognizable (meyatva); [Example: like a jar.
Because, when [the property] is established as a distinct genus, it does not serve to exclude that [other]; thus, since substantiality is unestablished,
the second inference is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

However, the establishment of a genus that excludes those possessing qualities and does not reside in qualityless things is unavoidable. Therefore, there exists another genus, established by the aforementioned inference,
which excludes that which is excluded from "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and does not reside in qualityless things.

Since "being an object of cognition" (*meyatva*) is [a reason] like a pot, once the second genus is established, "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is that genus which does not reside in quality-less things, yet resides in those devoid of exclusion from things possessing qualities.
If that is so, then [this is established] by the second inference.
In the first [definition], the definition of "genus" (*jāti*) characterized as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*).
Now, if "substantiality" is a genus established by the second inference, then [the same fault applies] to the genus established by the first inference.

The definition of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) characterized by the aforementioned [qualities] is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*); therefore, this is not a valid definition of substance-ness. Consequently, even if this [definition] were established, substance-ness itself would not be established. To that, we say: no.
Because the two universals (*jāti*) established by the first and second inferences possess the aforementioned definition of substancehood (*dravyatva*);
and because substancehood is the denotation of the word "substance" and is the basis for the application of that term to substances, it resides within substances.

Otherwise, because [the property] does not reside in the object itself, it would be over-extensive; for otherwise, the definitions of earth and so forth would result in being over-extensive due to their subsistence in a single instance of earth and so on.
Therefore, even if this [subject] were established as possessing such a definition...
Because the establishment of substanceness [in that case] is already accounted for,

there is no over-extension (*ativyāpaka*) due to the absence of [the reason's] exclusion from the locus; otherwise, since the proof of "being distinct from earth" would not contradict the non-sublation of "being another substance residing therein," it would follow that there is no opposition to its establishing substanceness residing therein.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that a proof establishing fire residing on this mountain would not be seen to establish another fire residing on this same mountain. As for the second and third [objections], the answer is simply that they are themselves the proofs [of the point]. Nor is "equal occurrence" (*tulyavṛttitva*) a fault here, because there is no evidence for its being a fault. Not...

Furthermore, duality (dvitīyatva) is not a universal (jāti). Nor is it impossible for there to be another fire residing on this mountain. The proof [of its existence] is as follows: "The fire residing on this mountain is distinct from the fire residing on this mountain [already perceived], because it is an object of cognition (meyatvāt), like a jar."

Is that [universal] a substance because it is manifold? Or is it a number because it lacks unity? Or is it the mutual absence of being a substance (*dravyatva-anyonyābhāva*)? Regarding the first [option], it is not so, because numbers are not admitted in the case of a universal (*jāti*). As for the second and third [options], the answer is simply that they are contradicted by the evidence. It is not [the case].

Furthermore, having an identical number of individual instances (*tulyavyaktitva*) is not a defect here, as there is no evidence for its being a defect. Nor is "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) not a genus (*jāti*),
because it possesses an identical number of individual instances while being distinct from the first occurrence of substance-ness.
Or rather, it should be stated that [the cow-ness] is like the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*). This is because [the alternative view] is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there a lack of evidence for two distinct universals (*jāti*), since inference has already been stated. And it does not follow that the second [entity] would become "cowness" merely by virtue of those two [universals] being stated; for there is no such sublation (*bādhaka*).

Because that too is desired; for if it were so, there would be no non-occurrence [of the property] from that very [cause], as it is devoid of being a genus that excludes those possessing qualities and does not reside in those devoid of qualities, because of its specific nature. That which is not thus is not thus, just like a jar.

Furthermore, the proof for a second substance is subject to the fallacy of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*). Nor does this [proof] suffer from the fault of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*);
for the qualification is "the state of being a distinct genus that does not reside in qualityless things and is devoid of exclusion from those possessing qualities."

This [universal] is a genus that does not reside in quality-less things and is devoid of exclusion from those possessing qualities, because it has as its counter-positive an absence distinct from mutual non-existence, since it is knowable, like a jar; thus, the qualification is established.

[The subject] is the substratum of that which is devoid of residing in anything other than what is excluded from the qualified by the possession of qualities and which does not reside in the qualityless;
because it is an object of cognition (*meyatva*), like a jar. This is also because [the opponent's reason] is counterbalanced (*satpratipakṣa*) by a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) inference.

"By such a kind" means either being devoid of residing in a genus other than such a genus, or being devoid of residing in that very genus. As for the first alternative, it is refuted by contradiction and sublation; as for the second alternative...

In that case, it would be so only if the subject (*pakṣa*) were not distinct from such a genus; otherwise, since that which resides in the subject is necessarily not resident in anything other than such a genus, its being devoid of that [genus] would result in a contradiction. Thus, regarding the subject:

"Thus, the difference in genus (*jātyanyatva*) of such a kind is unestablished; therefore, it is a different object (*arthāntara*). By this, the proofs for a second *gotva* (cowness) and so forth are refuted.
[Objection: But let there be no [such thing as] "being a genus that does not reside in qualityless things and is excluded from those possessing qualities."

The definition of a substance (*dravya*) suffers from the fallacy of being too narrow (*avyāpti*), because it excludes too much; furthermore, there will be the fallacy of the unestablished nature of its own essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*), due to the absence of any means of proving it. This is because that [substance], being unestablished, is not established by this very reason under discussion (*prakṛtahetu*). Moreover, that which pervades the reason under discussion is distinct from it.
And because that [existence] pervades it, its establishment cannot occur through the force of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

For the presence of the reason in the subject (*hetupakṣadharmatva*) does not establish anything beyond the presence of the property to be proven in the subject (*sādhyapakṣadharmatva*), as is the case with the possession of a genus (*jātimattva*) in respect to action and so forth.

Nor is there a lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because its establishment occurs through the failure of the [opposite] to be pervaded by that [reason], which constitutes a necessary implication (aparyavasāna). For there is no evidence that this necessary implication, as something distinct from the property of being present in the subject (pakṣadharmatā), is a constituent factor of inference.

Nor can it be established that the quality [in question] lacks the state of being excluded from that which possesses qualities— which is established by the inference under discussion— simply because it resides in that which possesses qualities;
for from the fact of its residing in that which possesses qualities, the absence of exclusion from that which possesses qualities is established.
It must be stated that because it possesses the property of subsisting in that which has qualities while being devoid of subsistence in that which lacks qualities,
its non-subistence in that which lacks qualities is established; and since the establishment of its being a universal (jāti) follows from the very inference under discussion,
the definition of substance (dravyatva) is thereby established.
If it is argued that once the definition of substance (dravyatva) is established through the first inference, the determination follows that [the subsequent reason] does not prove substance,
that is incorrect.

This is because the definition of substance (*dravyatva*) consists in possessing a genus that resides in things possessing qualities, excludes things possessing qualities, and does not reside in qualityless things; and because this [definition] is established by the inference under discussion. Nor is there any pointlessness (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) in the qualification, since it serves to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Because you yourself have stated that it is unestablished; for while the non-establishment of the reason is a defect of the inference, it is not a defect of its definition—if this is argued, we say no, because the definition itself constitutes a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference.
Nor is there here the fault of a redundant qualification.
Because [the definition] excludes that which lacks both the occurrence in what possesses qualities and the exclusion from what possesses qualities,

it serves the purpose of excluding jars and the like; whereas the property of being a universal (*jātitva*) serves the purpose of excluding existence (*sattva*), since existence does not occur in that which is devoid of qualities.
Because it serves the purpose of excluding [the presence of] qualities and so forth:

in the expression "devoid of being excluded from qualities residing in that which possesses qualities," the property of "residing in that which possesses qualities" (guṇavadvṛttitva) is redundant. Likewise, in the expression "devoid of residing in both that which possesses qualities and that which lacks qualities," the property of "residing in that which possesses qualities" [is likewise redundant].

If it is argued that [the qualification] is useless— no, because it lacks the status of being a qualifier of the reason (*hetu*), because there is no exclusion of that which possesses qualities from that which possesses qualities,
and because it is a qualifier of an existent entity (*bhāva*). And since there is no exclusion of that which possesses qualities...
Because the state of residing in that which possesses qualities (*guṇavadvṛttitva*) cannot be a qualifier;
for it is not employed as a qualifier of the reason (*hetu*),
and furthermore, it is impossible for it to be a qualifier of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Because [the properties of] "possessing the occurrence of qualities" and "being excluded from that which possesses qualities" serve as qualifiers of the probans (*hetu*).

If it is argued that, precisely because they are qualifiers, the qualifier of the probans is a fault known as the "uselessness of a qualifier"— we say no, because [the property of] possessing qualities...

If it is argued that the qualification "exclusion from that which possesses qualities" (guṇavadvyāvṛttitva) is redundant— just like the absence of the qualification "distinction from the cause"— we say no; for the exclusion from that which possesses qualities is itself excluded from that which exists in both the quality and the possessor of the quality, which are the qualifications of the reason.
Since it is impossible for there to be a mere apprehension of the occurrence of what possesses qualities without a simultaneous apprehension of its exclusion from what lacks those qualities,
nothing here is redundant.

Furthermore, [the probandum] is established precisely because there is no finality in either the absence of exclusion from qualities or the non-occurrence in that which lacks qualities. Nor is such lack of finality a constituent part of inference, for it would lead to the fallacy of the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*)—just as when fire on a mountain is inferred by means of "smokeness" [rather than a specific smoke]. And it is not the case that...
Establishment [of the probandum] occurs through the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*),

because you yourself have stated that the "property-of-the-subject" status of the reason lacks probative power apart from its being a property of the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-pakṣadharman*). Otherwise, [it would follow that] it is established by the force of the property-of-the-subject alone.

For it would follow that [the properties of] being devoid of exclusion from that which possesses qualities, being non-existent in that which lacks qualities, and being a genus (jāti) would also be established as "substance-ness" (dravyatva). Alternatively, let there be no establishment [of substance-ness] by the first inference through the reason "because of being denotable by the word 'substance' characterized by fluidity."
But the establishment of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is indeed unavoidable;

for, in this way, once the genus (jāti) has been established by that inference, the denotability of the word "substance"—characterized as substance-ness—is itself inferred from that very [inference]. Likewise, this...
This universal (jāti) is devoid of the property of being excluded from that which possesses qualities,

because it resides in that which possesses qualities and because it lacks the absence of exclusion from that which possesses qualities. This universal is devoid of the property of residing in that which possesses qualities.
Because it subsists in that which possesses qualities while not subsisting in that which lacks qualities, like a cow;

and because the status of being a *jāti* (universal) is established by the very means that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhaka*). Nor can each individual factor—such as "the absence of exclusion from qualities" or "the absence of being devoid [of qualities]"—be the definition, for it is the [composite] qualified entity that constitutes it.

It must be stated that because [the definition] is not established by anyone, there is a failure of the definition (*lakṣaṇāsiddhi*). This is because being excluded from distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being devoid of [the absence of] non-existence, not subsisting in qualities (*guṇa*), and being a universal (*jāti*) constitute the definition of substance (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, it is because even the qualified [substance] is perceptible.

Let it be that [color and so forth] possess substantiality (*dravyatva*); however, their possession of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is not accepted. This is because there is no perception such as "this is a quality" or "this is a quality" with respect to color, taste, and the like;
furthermore, the inclusive cognition [of them as qualities] occurs only subsequent to the investigation of the definitions and other criteria that establish what constitutes a quality.

Because that [inference] is established otherwise; nor is it correct to say that the establishment of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so forth occurs through the eye and other senses depending upon instruction. For does the instruction mean that [the object] possesses the definition of quality and is thus denotable by the word "quality," or rather that it possesses the definition of quality?

What does "possessing qualities" mean? Does it mean possessing the definition of a quality; or possessing a genus that resides in that which possesses the definition of a quality, excludes that which possesses qualities despite being excluded from what possesses the definition of a quality, and does not reside in that which lacks both [the definition and the quality]?

Not the first [alternative], because even with such another instruction, there is no cognition of anything other than being denotable by the word "quality" (guṇa-śabda-vācyatva); and because it is impossible to state that the absence of quality-nature (guṇatva) is established by the eye depending on the instruction "those possessing the definition of quality are denotable by the word 'quality'," since quality-nature is not perceived by the eye or other senses in any other location. Nor the second, because if quality-nature and so forth were established, the word "quality-nature" would be redundant; otherwise, if the absence of quality-nature in the eyes and so forth were established by depending on the instruction "those possessing the definition of quality are devoid of quality-nature," then quality-nature would still not be perceived by the eye or other senses in any other location.

Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the absence of such a genus [as "quality"] could be established by the eye—which depends on instruction stating that "those possessing the characteristics of quality do not possess this kind of nature" and so forth—and because the very establishment of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) would depend on those [characteristics].
Furthermore, [qualities] differ from the eye and other [senses] precisely because of the establishment of "quality-ness.

Moreover, if it were not expressible by the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), then "quality-ness" and so forth could not be established even by the eye and other senses aided by that [word], and thus inference would be impossible.

If it is argued: "Form (rūpa) possesses a genus distinct from its own nature (rūpatva) and its intermediate existence (sattā), because it possesses a genus, like a cow"—this is not so; for [the reason] would entail proving something else (arthāntara) once a genus residing solely in qualities and actions has been established.

If it is further argued that the probandum is qualified by the property of "residing in qualities and actions"—this is not so, because the qualification "distinct from existence" (sattātiriktavat) would then be rendered redundant.

If it is argued that the genus [intended] as residing in qualities and substances alone is established by the reason "because it does not reside in qualities and substances," and thus the probandum must be qualified—
[we reply: no, because if it were established as residing in color and taste alone, there would be the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (arthāntara).
If it is argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is also qualified by the absence of subsisting in only color and taste—
no, because if a genus (*jāti*) subsisting in only color, taste, and smell were established, there would be the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*).
[It might be argued that] the probandum is also qualified by not subsisting in only color, taste, and smell.

If [it is argued that it is] not so—[we reply: no, because [the universal] is established as residing only in color, taste, smell, and touch, since it would otherwise entail a different object. Thus, [this applies] up to the twenty-three qualities beginning with color.
Even by means of [the argument beginning with] "subsisting only in color, taste, smell,

and touch," although there is a qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*), once a genus (*jāti*) subsisting only in the word "color" or subsisting in the word "taste" and so forth is established, there is the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*).

Because of that state [of the subject], even when the probandum is qualified by such properties as "subsisting only in color and sound," there would be the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara) through the establishment of a genus that subsists only in color in general, or subsists only in specific colors, or subsists only in the inherence of color, or subsists only in the absence of color.

Because that state [of the subject] remains; and because, even by qualifying the probandum with "subsisting in a universal of form" and so forth, there would be the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) once the existence of an entity other than *sattā* (Being) is established. If it is argued that there is no fallacy of proving something else because such a genus (*jāti*) is unestablished precisely due to sublation (*bādha*), we say no, because that [sublation] is absent. Otherwise, [the same fault would apply].

Otherwise, it would follow that even the category of quality (*guṇatva*) would be unestablished. By this same reasoning, the following argument is refuted: "Color (*rūpa*) possesses a subordinate genus of existence that is devoid of residing solely in color itself, because it possesses a genus, like a cow."
If it is argued that "taste possesses a genus that occurs in both that which lacks the characteristics of a quality and that which possesses them,

because it has the characteristics of a quality, like color"— this is not so; for if a genus occurring only in color and taste were established, it would result in proving something other than what was intended.

Even if the probandum is qualified by such attributes as "subsisting only in color and taste," the aforementioned fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) remains in the same state; furthermore, this is because [the reason] has "being color" (*rūpatva*) as its limiting condition (*upādhi*). [The argument is: "Space possesses another universal (*jāti*) residing in both color and taste."

If it is argued that [the universal] is like a generality because it is devoid of the characteristics of a quality— no, for that would result in proving something other than the intended point, namely, the non-existence of another genus residing solely in color and taste.
This is because, if the qualification of the probandum were "being devoid of residing solely in color and taste," [the argument would fail].

Because of the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara) by means of the absolute non-existence of a universal residing solely in color, taste, and smell; and because [the argument] would fail to establish the absolute non-existence of a universal that is devoid of the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) found in the definition of a quality.
Because there would be the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara) once the absence of a universal residing only in qualities and actions is established;

and because even if the probandum is qualified by "residing only in qualities and actions," there would still be the fallacy of proving something else once the absence of a universal residing only in qualities and material things is established.

Even when the probandum is qualified by "not residing in any quality, action, or corporeal substance," there is the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), because [the probandum would then include] the absolute non-existence of a universal that resides only in qualities, actions, or corporeal substances.
Even when the probandum is qualified by "not residing in any quality, action, or corporeal substance" ...

Because it is a different object [from existence] due to the absolute non-existence of existence therein; because the notion "space exists" is sublated by perception. If it is argued that the absolute non-existence of existence is not established in space—no, for since space is imperceptible, there is no such cognition as "space exists. If [such a cognition] were present...
Or rather, it is because [the reason] can be accounted for even as an error, namely that a universal is existent;

furthermore, it is subject to a limiting condition (*upādhi*) due to the absence of possessing a genus (*jāti*). Nor is this [reason] merely "other than the subject" (*pakṣetara*), because it is excluded from the heterologous instances (*vipakṣa*) such as color, taste, and so forth, precisely by virtue of the absence of a limiting condition.
And it is because there is a counter-argument:
"Existence (sattā) is other than a universal that is distinct from that which possesses the characteristics of a quality, because it is cognizable,
like a jar"— this too is not tenable.
Because [the probans] would result in proving something other than the intended object— namely, that existence (*sattā*) is distinct from qualities, actions, and universals (*jāti*), etc.;

and even if it were established that [existence] is devoid of the occurrence of another [quality] and devoid of the occurrence of qualities, it would still not establish the property of being "devoid of occurring in what is not a quality," because being "devoid of occurring in what is not a quality" is distinct from being "devoid of the occurrence of another quality," and because the latter is pervaded by the former.

"Because its existence [as a substance] occurs even without that [quality]," and thus the inferences establishing the nature of quality (*guṇatva*) are also to be refuted; therefore, quality does not exist. This is incorrect, because color (*rūpa*) possesses the characteristic of quality and exists as that which has the characteristic of quality.
Because it possesses a genus that is not excluded from what is devoid of the characteristics of qualities— that is, because it possesses a genus— like a cow,
the nature of being a quality (guṇatva) is established. Nor is there any room for the objection of proving something other than the intended point (arthāntaratā) here,
since that has already been refuted previously.

In this same way, it should be understood that the proof of all universals (*jāti*) is to be seen through the establishment of the possession of a class-characteristic (*vṛttijāti*) devoid of those [specific] characteristics such as action (*karman*), by means of [showing] that action, etc., while possessing characteristics such as action, is likewise devoid of the exclusion of its own occurrence (*vṛttivyāvṛtti*).

Now, [this applies] to inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa); to qualities and actions which are causes of conjunction and disjunction; to substances, qualities, and actions which possess a genus characterized by non-motion;
to substances and qualities which possess a genus that is not a substratum of an effect; to qualities which possess their own genus; and to corporeal actions.

A universal (jāti) is not established by the aforementioned reasoning in the case of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), intangible substances (*asparśavat*), things possessing their own nature (*svarūpavat*), and tastes (*surasa*), nor in the case of general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*). This is because, in the absence of a sublation (*bādha*), its existence is indeed accepted; whereas, when a sublation exists, it is precisely due to that sublation that the universal is not established.
But even so, the establishment of Brahminhood is not achieved,
because Brahminhood residing in Devadatta and others— which is distinguished from Kṣatriyas and the like—
is not experienced through perception; for one thinks, "This person is a Brahmin" solely on the basis of his appearance.

If it is argued that "known" refers to the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the cognition of Brahminhood—no, for that too is unestablished. This is because even the form excluded from Kṣatriyas and others is unestablished, and thus the claim that it exists "by way of its form" is likewise unknown. [This would require] being accompanied by the comprehension of the defining characteristics of a Brahmin.

If it is argued that its experience occurs through the eye and other [senses]—no, because those do not exist. For this very reason, it is also unestablished by the logic previously stated. If it is argued that the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is being born from Brāhmaṇa parents—no, because [the status of] being born from Brāhmaṇa parents...
Because its conjunctions and disjunctions are over-extensive.
If it is argued that its definition is "having a body produced by a Brāhmaṇa mother and father," we say no; for this would be over-extensive in the case of deformed beings such as pigs and the like.
If it is argued that the definition [of a Brahmin] is being a human being born from Brahmin parents— no,

because this is non-pervasive (avyāpaka) in the case of Brahmins born at the beginning of creation, and also because it is non-pervasive in the case of Agastya who was born from a water-jar, Viśvāmitra who was born from a Kṣatriya, and others like them. Of these...
Furthermore, because the states of being "thus-become" (*tathābhūta*) and being a *brāhmaṇa* are established by the Purāṇas;

and because, in the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), these [definitions] would fail to apply to those born as *brāhmaṇas* on the second day or thereafter.
Furthermore, because it does not pervade those Brāhmaṇas who are born immediately after a previous Brāhmaṇa has perished due to the disappearance of each individual constituent part;
and because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), wherein the establishment of Brāhmaṇahood depends on the establishment of being born from Brāhmaṇa parents,
and the establishment of that [parentage] depends upon the establishment of Brāhmaṇahood.
By this, the definition of a Brahmin as "the state of being a human born of parents denoted by the word 'Brahmin'" is refuted.
If it is argued that its definition is "being produced by a specific unseen force (adṛṣṭa)," we say no, because such a thing is unestablished.

If it is argued that the inference [of the specific unseen cause] is based on the body and the activity of a Brāhmaṇa—no, for if Brāhmaṇahood is already established, then the fact of being produced by a specific unseen cause (adṛṣṭaviśeṣa) is established; and if that is not established, then Brāhmaṇahood itself is not established. Thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva). [End of section on] Brāhmaṇas.

Vādivāgīśvara [argues] that the proof of Brahminhood is established by the statement: "Non-Brahmin humans possess a class of livelihoods, because, while being distinct from Brahmin humans, they possess different constituent parts.
That too is not correct, because Brahminhood is unestablished in respect to Brahminhood.
Furthermore, even the class (*jāti*) of the human activity of being a Brāhmaṇa is unestablished.
If it is argued that "being born from Brāhmaṇa parents" is the inferential mark (*anumānāṅga*) for [proving] Brāhmaṇahood—it is not so; for if that were the case...

Because [the status of] being a Brāhmaṇa is common to those born from Brāhmaṇa parents, those born from non-Brāhmaṇa parents, and those produced at the beginning of creation or born from the jar (kalaśa), there is a logical fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) regarding the establishment of a sub-class of Brāhmaṇahood;

and because it is common to those born from Brāhmaṇa parents, those born from non-Brāhmaṇa parents, and those produced at the beginning of creation or born from the jar, there is a logical fallacy of proving what is already established regarding the establishment of a distinct sub-class of Brāhmaṇahood.
That is incorrect, because that [status] is established by direct perception itself in the form "this person is a Brahmin.
Nor is such direct perception unestablished, for it is established through the conventional usage "this person is a Brahmin. Nor is that [conventional usage] itself unestablished.

This is because it is established by the experience of all people; otherwise, even [categories] such as "cowness" (gotva) would be dissolved. Nor can its establishment be explained away by means of the definition of a Brahmin, since you yourself have demonstrated the absence of such a definition. In this same way, the Kṣatriyas and others are to be justified.
The proof for [the existence of] earthness is as follows:
A pot possesses a genus that resides in that which has odor, is excluded from that which lacks odor, and is devoid of residing in that which is devoid of qualities.

Because it possesses a genus (*jātimattvāt*). This pot possesses a genus that is (1) resident in a pot, (2) excluded from what lacks fragrance, (3) not resident in what lacks fragrance, and (4) devoid of [residing in] what lacks fragrance;
because it possesses a genus. This pot...

This possesses a genus that is devoid of subsistence in that which is odorless and yet not excluded from odors subsisting in this [substance], because it possesses a genus. This pot possesses a genus that is devoid of subsistence in that which is odorless and yet not excluded from odors subsisting in this [substance], because it possesses a genus.

"Because it possesses a genus (*jāti*), like karma," and so forth. That same means of valid cognition [establishes] the state of being water (*udakatva*) as well: [water] possesses a genus that is excluded from what is not present in river-currents, excluded from what is not cold, and excluded from what does not possess odor; and it is excluded from what is not present in that which is odorless and excluded from what is not cold.
Because it possesses a genus (*jāti*).
[The subject] possesses a genus that resides in what is cold and resides in what is neither hot nor cold, while being devoid of the genus residing in the coldness found in river-currents;
because it possesses a genus. This...

This [lamp] possesses a genus that exists in what is excluded from both cold and non-cold, and is devoid of the state of being excluded from the occurrence of cold; for it possesses a genus, like a cow, and so forth.
This is also a proof for the nature of fire (*tejastva*). The lamp [is the subject].
[The subject] possesses a genus that is excluded from heat and its exclusion, and is not excluded from heat and non-heat,
because it possesses a genus. A lamp possesses a genus that is excluded from the heat residing in a lamp and is not excluded from heat and non-heat.

Because it possesses a genus (*jāti*). This lamp possesses a genus that does not reside in heat, while being devoid of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the heat residing in it; because it possesses a genus, like "cowness" (*gotva*), and so forth.
The proof for the existence of air [is as follows]:

Air possesses a genus that does not reside in anything possessing color or touch, nor in anything excluded from that which possesses color or touch, and it does not reside in anything devoid of color and touch;
this is because it possesses a genus, like a jar and so forth. And so on.
The proof for the existence of the self:
The self possesses a genus that occurs in intelligent beings and is excluded from non-intelligent beings, while being devoid of the state of being excluded from intelligent beings;
this is because it possesses a genus. [For example,] a happy person.
This self possesses a genus that does not reside in pleasure, activity, or the intellect, yet does reside in that which is devoid of the exclusion from the intellect and the non-intellect,

because it possesses a genus. This self possesses a genus that does not reside in that which is devoid of the exclusion from the intellect and activity, yet resides in that which is devoid of color and touch, and is itself devoid of color and touch.

"Because it possesses a genus (jāti), like a jar," and so forth— this is the proof for the existence of the mind (*manas*). The mind possesses a genus that does not reside in tangible atoms, but does reside in intangible atoms, and which is excluded from those [atoms] that lack such a genus.
Because it possesses a genus:

the mind possesses a genus that does not reside in anything lacking the touch of mental activity or non-activity, nor in anything lacking the touch of an atom, nor in anything lacking the touch of an atom.

Because it possesses a genus (*jātimattvāt*), like a pot (*ghaṭavat*), and so forth. The proof for its being color (*rūpatva*) is as follows: Color is that which possesses a genus residing in a quality (*guṇa*) perceptible by the eye, which is excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by external senses other than the eye and which is not excluded from being excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by the eye; and which resides in that which is excluded from being excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by the eye and residing in a genus that is excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by external senses other than the eye and residing in a genus that is excluded from being excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by the eye; and which is excluded from residing in that which is excluded from being excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by the eye and residing in a genus that is excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by external senses other than the eye and residing in a genus that is excluded from being excluded from [the set of] qualities perceptible by the eye.

Because it possesses a genus (*jātimattvāt*). Blue possesses a genus that is excluded from being a quality graspable by the eye, which is itself excluded from qualities graspable by the eye that are not grasped by external sense organs and lack the property of residing in blue; and this [genus] is excluded from residing in anything other than those [qualities]. Because it possesses a genus. This...

This form possesses a universal that does not reside in [other] things, which is excluded from qualities graspable by the eye but not graspable by external senses other than the eye, and which is devoid of the state of being the eye itself; because it possesses a universal, like a pot, and so forth.
In this way, the definition of substances such as taste, independent of [the universals] such as tasteness (*rasatva*), applies to the qualities of taste and the rest.
Furthermore, regarding actions such as upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth,

the universals such as "tasteness" (rasatva) and others are to be established by means of an inference based on the possession of a universal that does not occur in those things lacking the aforementioned definition, yet occurs in those possessing that definition.

The universals such as "whiteness" (śuklatva) must be established solely on the basis of the inclusive perception (anugatapratyakṣa)— such as "this is white," "this is white"— regarding white objects and the like, which are devoid of any characteristic independent of birth (jāti).

If it is asked: "How is the existence of *saṃskāra* established— given that it is devoid of a characteristic independent of genus (*jāti*), given that the corresponding cognition has been forgotten, and given that it is devoid of enmity (*vaira*), and that its ultimate nature consists in the state of maintaining momentum (*vega*) and elasticity (*sthāpasthāpaka*)?"— it is not so, for it is established by inference alone.

[This is established] because of possessing a genus that is devoid of velocity (vega), non-velocity, the state of being devoid of velocity, the state of being devoid of the state of being devoid of the mental impression (bhāvanā), the state of being devoid of the state of being devoid of the elasticity (sthitisthāpaka), and the states of being devoid of velocity, the state of being devoid of the mental impression, and the state of being devoid of elasticity—just like a jar, and so forth.

If it is argued that since merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) are both "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) and thus constitute a single quality, the number of qualities as twenty-four would be untenable—we say no; for the number of qualities as twenty-four is tenable when one intends to express the non-difference between the states of being merit and being demerit.

If it is argued that the number twenty-four of qualities is untenable with respect to the sub-genuses of the genus "quality" (*guṇatva*), we say no; for since merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) also possess sub-genuses of the genus "quality," the intended meaning is the number twenty-four with respect to the direct sub-genuses of the genus "quality.
If it is further argued that by accepting [merit and demerit] as the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), merit and demerit do not possess direct sub-genuses of the genus "quality," we say no;

for since the categories of "specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) and "general quality" (*sāmānyaguṇatva*) are possible as direct sub-genuses of the genus "quality," it would follow that even color (*rūpa*) and the like could not possess direct sub-genuses of the genus "quality" simply because they are "unseen."
The author of the Sūtras intends the number twenty-four for the qualities with respect to the subordinate genus of qualityness itself;
let there be other means of proof for this.

The statement [in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra], "Existence (sattā) is a distinct entity from substance, quality, and action" (1.2.8), is untenable because it cannot withstand critical analysis. For instance, does this [sūtra] intend to state a thesis (pratijñā) or provide a reason (hetu)? Even in the first case, what is "existence"?

There are three propositions: existence is distinct from substance, existence is distinct from quality, and existence is distinct from action; or rather, [the argument is] because existence deviates [from these categories] and because it subsists in qualities and subsists in actions.
Because it is seized by the absence of an example, and because qualities, actions, and so forth— being equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*)— cannot serve as examples;
nor is the second [alternative] possible, because it would entail the extension of the probandum (*sādhyātideśāt*).
But Ātreyācārya,

having raised the objection that existence (*sattā*) is eternal because it inheres in many things, and having maintained the thesis that "existence is eternal," [proceeds to establish] its distinctness from substance, quality, and action.
He says that the reason is established by this sūtra; however, that too is incorrect,
because of the absence of an example, and also because of the absence of particularity and inherence.

Because its permanence is unestablished; for that very reason, even if it were established, the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) would remain as it was, and there is also the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). If [the object] were impermanent, then being one of the three—substance, quality, or action—and possessing a universal (*jātimattva*) would be indicated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
If this is argued—[we reply] no, because in the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), the pervasion with the probandum (*sādhyavyāpti*) would be broken.
Therefore, the aphorism (*sūtra*) is untenable.
That is not so, because this is a thesis-statement (*pratijñāsūtra*).

And thus, the proposition is that "existence (sattā) is distinct from substance, quality, and action. Nor is there a lack of a reason (*hetu*) here, because its subsistence in qualities and its subsistence in actions will be stated later.
If it is argued that those two [reasons] are simply the reasons for the two propositions "it is not a quality" and "it is not an action"—[we reply: no, for in this case as well...

Because its status as a cause is possible; nor is there an absence of examples, since qualities, actions, inherence, and absences serve as valid examples. Furthermore, because particulars and inherence themselves cannot serve as examples [for themselves].
Because those two [existence and inherence] are established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends their substrata as being distinct from substance, quality, and action. [Sūtra 1.2.9:
"Existence is not a substance, because it resides in a single substance," like color. This is incorrect, because of existence... [text fragment].
Because it is established that [color] does not reside in a single substance by virtue of residing in multiple substances such as jars and cloths,
the teacher Ātreya maintains that "residing in a single substance" means being perceived through contact with a sense organ that resides in a single substance.

That is not so, because of the deviation in the case of cloth and the like. If it is argued that cloth and such are perceived through multiple sense-object contacts with their constituent parts, we say no; for even existence (*sattā*) is perceived through multiple contacts with its constituent parts.
If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) is perceived even through contact with a single substance, whereas jars and the like are not, we say:
no;
for the perception of existence is produced by contact with a substance that does not depend on contact with many constituent parts (*avayava*).
Because there is no such measure [of distinction], since the existence of a cloth and so forth are identical due to the unity of the causal complex for their apprehension.
If it is argued that in the case of "the self exists," existence is apprehended through contact with a single substance—[we reply:
no, because the self is also apprehended here through contact with a single substance.
Because the deviation [of the reason] remains in that state. If it is argued that existence (*sattā*) is perceived through contact with a single word,

and therefore "being perceived through contact with a single substratum" is the reason for its not being a substance (*adravyatva*)— no, because this [reason] deviates in the case of the self (*ātman*), since that too...
If it is argued that the self is perceived through its own contact alone, even by means of contact with pleasure and so forth— because it is the substratum of existence and because it is unitary,
since it is perceived only as accompanied by pleasure and so forth— we say: no.

[The opponent argues: "Because the self is perceived as qualified by pleasure, pain, and so forth, and because [the term 'substance'] would be redundant if it were already grasped; therefore, the Sūtra is untenable. This is not so, because another meaning for the Sūtra is possible.
For substance is of two kinds:
that which consists of a single substance and that which consists of multiple substances.
Among these, that which consists of a single substance—such as space and so forth—is devoid of any sub-class of the genus "substance-ness."

Because it exists as a single unit. A substance composed of multiple substances (*anekadravya*) is that which possesses a sub-class of the genus "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), such as earth and so forth; this is because its individual instances (*vyakti*) are manifold.
Therefore, [the term] "possessing a single substance" (*ekadravyavattva*) refers to its being dependent on space (*ākāśa*), its being dependent on time (*kāla*), and so forth.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: because it is dependent on the directions, and because it is dependent on that which lacks a subordinate genus within the category of substance (dravyatva), like the qualities of space and so forth. || 9 ||

Nor is "the absence of inherence in more than one" a limiting condition (*upādhi*) here, as in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Nor is "the absence of inherence in more than one while being devoid of the property of quality (*guṇatva*)" a limiting condition, because it is merely "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), since there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) from which it could be excluded.

Because effect-substances (kāryadravya) are excluded [from being universals] precisely by the absence of inherence in multiple [substances], there is no counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) such as: "Existence is not a substance because it lacks the nature of a quality, like a cloth. Nor is there a fallacy of the "limiting condition" (sopādhitva), because [the reason] "being dependent on space" and so forth serves as such a condition.
But because it exists in qualities and actions, it is neither action nor quality.
(1-2-10) By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied: "What is substance? Therefore, existence (*sattā*) is not substance, and existence is not quality.
Existence (*sattā*) is not action (*karman*), because it subsists as a quality (*guṇa*), whereas action subsists [as a substance];
it is like the absence residing therein (*tadgatābhāva*).

Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so forth, because they are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣatulyatva*). Nor [is there a deviation] in the case of "quality-ness"...
The probans (*upādhi*) is "the absence of inherence in multiple [substances] while being devoid of substantiality" (*dravyatvarahitānekasamavetatvābhāva*);
for this is merely "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), since it is a qualification that lacks both a counter-example (*vyāvartya*) and a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
This is because qualities that inhere in multiple [substances] are already excluded by the very fact of their inhering in multiple [substances].

Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) is not a quality (*guṇa*), because it inheres in multiple things while being devoid of substantiality (*dravyatva*), like pleasure (*sambhoga*); thus, there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*). Moreover, [the reason] is characterized by a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*), namely the absence of functioning as a quality. Nor, in the case of non-successiveness (*akramatva*)...

The absence of that which is inherent in a jar devoid of the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is the *upādhi*. This is because, as in the previous case, it is a property of the subject itself (*pakṣetaratva*). Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) does not [possess this absence], because it is inherent in cloth-ness, which is devoid of action and the property of being a quality—just like the action of a jar.

There is the state of being countered by an equally valid opposing argument (*satpratipakṣatva*), because it is characterized by a limiting condition (*sopādhitva*) due to the absence of subsistence in action,
and because it is characterized by a limiting condition due to the property of not being audible;
and furthermore, there is sublation (*bādhā*) by perception which apprehends the absence of the nature of action (*karmatva*).
"And because of the absence of general and particular properties" (1-2-11).

General and particular properties are, in substances, such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth; and in actions, such as upward-throwingness (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth. By the existence of these...
The absence of substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness is inferred in existence (sattā).
Furthermore, in the reason for the negation of substance-ness, the qualification "being distinct from space, time, and ether" must be employed.

Furthermore, existence (sattā) is not a substance (dravya), because, while being distinct from space, time, and ether, it possesses earthness, fireness, and airness, yet lacks selfhood (ātmatva), just like color (rūpa). Existence is not a quality (guṇa), because it lacks the twenty-four universals such as colorness (rūpatva), tasteness (rasatva), and so forth.
"Like a jar": existence is not action,
because it is devoid of the properties of throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion, just like a jar.

Alternatively, the meaning of the sūtra is this: by the word "general" (sāmānya) the universal (jāti) is meant, and by the word "particular" (viśeṣa) a particular universal, namely existence (sattā). Through the absence of that [existence], the negation of substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness in respect to existence is inferred.
And thus, existence (sattā) is not a substance, nor a quality, nor an action;
and because it is devoid of a universal (jāti), it is like a non-entity (abhāva). This [argument] is according to the intention of the ancient teachers (pūrvācārya);
for we accept existence in both existence and non-existence, so that the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha).
Nor is it [the case] because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).
Others, however, hold that "generality" (*sāmānya*) refers to particularities such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*);
since existence (*sattā*) is devoid of these, it is neither substance, nor quality, nor action.

They explain the meaning of the Sūtra as follows: "That is incorrect, because it is unestablished that existence (*sattā*) is not a substance (*dravya*), since [the reason] 'because of being devoid of substantiality' (*dravyatvarahitatvāt*) and so forth is unproven. However, the Teachers (*ācāryāḥ*) in the Sūtra [state]:

They explain the meaning of the sūtra as follows: "Generality and particularity" refers to lower generality (*aparasāmānya*); because that [lower generality] is absent, existence (*sattā*) is a different entity from substance, quality, and action. That too—

No, because the absence of a universal is redundant due to the absence of deviation [from the probandum], and because the property of being devoid of both universal and particular is unestablished for the opponent. || 11 ||

Now, for the purpose of establishing that substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are distinct entities from substances, qualities, and actions, there are six sūtras:
