"Substance-ness is stated [to be distinct] because of its possessing a single substance. (1.2.12)

And because of the absence of commonalities and particularities. (1.2.13) Because it exists in qualities, "quality-ness" has been stated. (1.2.14) Because of the absence of commonalities and particularities. (1.2.15)
"Because it exists in actions, action-ness is stated" (1-2-16);
and "because of the absence of both generality and particularity" (1-2-17),
substance-ness is stated— and by implication, quality-ness and action-ness are stated— in this context.
The ellipsis is "it is a different entity from substance, quality, and action. The remainder is as before.
This is not untenable; for if one were to propose a separate sūtra merely on the basis of a difference in examples,
then [the same would apply] to each of the universals such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.
Because of the context of composing the Sūtras: once the method [of reasoning] has been established in one place, it arises elsewhere as well;
thus, there is the composition of all the Sūtras.
If it is argued that this is not so because the same [reasoning] applies to substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like, [we reply:
"Being (*bhāva*) is one, because there is no distinction in its mark (*liṅga*) and because there is an absence of any specific mark. (1.2.18)

What, then, is being established by this? We say that existence (*sattā*) is one and the same throughout all places, at all times, and in all individual manifestations (*vyakti*). Even so, the existence residing in this jar is not different from itself.
This is because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the existence of this jar does not, by itself, comprehend its difference [from others];
because there is no other means of valid cognition that establishes difference;
and because there exists a means of valid cognition that apprehends non-difference, namely, "this is devoid of being other than this. Likewise...
The existence residing in a cloth is not distinct from the existence residing in a jar;

for even by another means of valid cognition, that which is stated by the means of valid cognition apprehending the existence residing in the cloth would be [the same], since it does not involve the apprehension of any difference in that existence as it pertains to the jar.
Furthermore, because it is not ascertained that the existence residing in the cloth is non-different from the existence residing in the jar;

and because it is determined by perception that "the existence residing in the cloth is devoid of being other than the existence residing in the cloth"; since the absence of difference from the existence of the jar is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) for perception.
Because it is perceptible.

This has been stated: "Because there is no distinction in the mark of existence (*salliṅga*) and because there is an absence of a specific mark (*viśeṣaliṅga*), being (*bhāva*) is one" (VS 1.2.18). The term *sat* is an indication emphasizing the state of being (*bhāva*), while *liṅga* refers to the mark.

The term *pramāṇa* [is used here] because of the subsequent aphorism: "Cause (*hetu*), indication (*apadeśa*), mark (*liṅga*), sign (*nimitta*), and instrument (*kāraṇa*)—these are synonymous with *pramāṇa*.
And in this context, *pramāṇa* refers to...

The non-difference of particulars is indeed directly perceived. That [non-difference] is either the exclusion itself or that which makes exclusion known; for even by the means of valid cognition grasping existence (*sattā*), there is no apprehension of difference due to the particular (*viśeṣa*), and because of the apprehension of non-difference and the absence of any means of valid cognition establishing difference, they are one.
"Existence" (sattā) is the meaning of the Sūtra.

But when existence is not perceptible and is instead cognizable through inference, then [the argument is]: "A jar possesses a genus that is devoid of the exclusion residing in jars, because it is an object of knowledge (meyatvāt)."

Existence is inferred by means of [the reason] "like a jar" and so forth. At that time, since existence and oneness are established by the inference that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakānumāna*), and since the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend difference are rendered invalid by the sublation of the means of knowledge that apprehends the locus, there is only one existence for each [individual].

This has been stated: "Because there is no difference in the mark of existence (*salliṅga*) and because there is an absence of a specific mark, existence is one" (VS 1.2.18). Alternatively, the existence residing in a cloth is not different from the existence residing in a jar, because it is characterized as existence, just like the existence of a jar. Nor is it [different] from the existence of a cloth...
The counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) is that [the cloth] is distinct because it subsists in the cloth, like the color of the cloth;

however, this is fallacious due to the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the existence of a jar. For the existence of a jar subsists in the cloth, because it is cognizable (*meyatva*), just like the jar; thus, the subsistence of the jar's existence in the cloth is established.

Because it lacks the characteristic of existence (*sattā*) and because it possesses a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Nor is this [reason] "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), since it is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as the existence of a jar and so forth. This has been stated as follows:

"Because there is no distinction in the mark [that proves it]" means that since the mark proving the existence of a jar is indistinguishable everywhere, the existence of the jar is established everywhere.
By this, the omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) of existence (*sattā*) has been demonstrated.

Because the meaning of the word "all-pervading" (sarvagata) is precisely the state of residing in all individuals, and the meaning of the word "eternal" (nitya) is precisely the state of occurring at all moments.
As they say: "Eternality is existence at all times.
Nor does this entail the consequence that space and so forth would not be omnipresent, for those too lack the quality of being dependent upon everything.
Because it is accepted that [the self] is not omnipresent; nor does this entail the consequence of impermanence for space and so forth,
because [impermanence] consists in the absence of dependence upon every moment.

Because being everything is also desired; however, when the "all-pervasiveness" of space and so forth is intended to mean their conjunction with all corporeal substances, then [this applies] to existence (*sattā*).
Omnipresence is certainly not accepted [in that sense]. However, when imperishability itself is intended as permanence, then it is indeed accepted for space, existence, and so forth.

Nor does it follow that substances and the like would become omnipresent, for that is not accepted; since they are held to exist only where such features as the dewlap are present. Nor [does this imply] the destruction of existence (*sattā*).

There is no lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding perishability, because that [perishability] is established by the very same valid cognition that apprehends its subsistence in all future individuals.
Because it is untenable for [destruction] to reside in an individual that has arisen after another destruction;

and because of the following inference: "A pot is devoid of the state of being destructible while residing in a pot that lacks destruction, because it is cognizable (meyatva), just like existence (sattā) residing in a pot."
Furthermore, existence (sattā) is not perishable because it resides in a jar;
nor is there a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) based on the claim that existence and the like are perishable because they possess form, as in the case of the form residing therein.
Because of the absence of the first cause and the pervader, etc.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Vaiśeṣikasūtravārtika composed by the illustrious servant of Lord Hara, the supreme scholar, Nyāyācārya Bhaṭṭa Vādīndra.
First Āhnika of the Second Chapter.
In the first chapter, the definition of substance (*dravya*) was established as "that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause" (cf. 1.1.18).

It has also been stated that "that which subsists in a substance, possesses qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent," is the definition of a quality (cf. 1.1.15). Both of these [definitions] are untenable;

for in the case of earth and the other elements, the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) is unestablished due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves the existence of specific qualities.

Because the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); for the fact that color and other qualities reside in earth and the like is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). Furthermore, this follows from the inference: "Earth and the others possess qualities, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), like color. Thus, in the first [case]...
In this chapter, the classification of substances and qualities has been set forth, but it is untenable.
Since there is no distinction in the marks of substance and an absence of specific marks [to differentiate them], the oneness of substance is established.
Thus, earth is not distinct from water and the other elements, because it possesses the nature of substance and because it possesses qualities.

Water and so forth, as well as color and so forth, are not distinct from taste and so forth, because they possess the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*), just like taste and so forth. Nor is there a contradiction with perception regarding such cases, because that [perception] is erroneous;
the cognition of distinctions such as earth and so forth is false.

Because it is a cognition of difference, like the cognition of the difference between the moon and other objects; and because the difference between earth and other elements is false, due to its being a difference, like the difference in the appearance of the moon. Furthermore, there is no deficiency in the classification of substances, as there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for [the existence of] ether and the stars.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish [the existence of] viscidity and so forth, the classification of qualities and the like is also deficient. To resolve all of this, the second chapter is commenced.
Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch. || 1 ||
It is established that [the atom] has color, taste, and touch as its limiting conditions (*āvṛti*), and it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of color, taste, smell, and touch.
But how can the suffix *matup* have the sense of the locative case? It is by the force of the rule that it has the sense of the genitive case;
for when there is the intention to express the sense of the genitive, [the suffix *matup* is applied].

The meaning would be "due to the connection with color, taste, smell, and touch. And in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the reason] being contradictory (viruddha), because [the reason] would occur in the locus of the absence of the probandum—for instance, in the inference "earth is distinct from others because of possessing smell-ness" (gandhatva), the reason occurs in smell-ness itself). [Objection: There is no contradiction because of the intention to express the locative sense (saptamy-artha).
Odor also [is not established], because it is impossible for it to exist in the category of "odor-ness" due to its lack of effort toward odor and so forth;
one should cite the sūtra, "Those do not exist in space" (2.1.5), as the authority.
Therefore, by this [argument], the lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhatva*) regarding the reason "because of possessing qualities" must be avoided;

for the qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the earth. Nor is there a lack of being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*) for the quality of "residing in a substance," for that very same reason. Nor is it the case that [the earth] possesses color and so forth...

The perception of "earth" and so forth is not erroneous, because there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*); otherwise, it would follow that all perceptions are erroneous, which has already been refuted. [The opponent claims:
"Earth and the other elements do not possess qualities, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*). That is incorrect.

If the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) is not established, then its absence is likewise unestablished, resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). But if the possession of qualities is established, is it established in the existence of earth and the other [elements], or elsewhere?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that establishes the possession of qualities such as earthiness; nor is the second, because [the reason] is deviant with respect to knowability (*prameyatva*); and there is no impossibility regarding the division [of categories].
Because the distinction between earth and the other [elements] is established by perception;
because "cowness" (gotva) consists precisely of those formal properties residing in earth and so forth that are excluded from space and the like;
and because it is accepted that the superimposition of contradictory properties alone constitutes a differentiator.

The position that difference consists in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is also [tenable], because mutual non-existence that is perceptible to the senses is established by perception in the case of earth and so forth,
as is the case for mutual non-existence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is imperceptible.

This is because of the inference based on [the earth's] possession of odor and so forth; that entity, by virtue of possessing odor, allows for the inference of its distinction from either earth or [water]. However, this is not possible through [its] possession of taste and so forth, because these [qualities] belong to other things such as water.

If it is argued that this is because [the reasons] are contradictory—no, for by the possession of odor, earth is inferred to be distinct from water and the like; by the possession of taste, from fire and the like; by the possession of color, from wind and the like; and by the possession of touch, from ether and the like. And thus:
Earth is distinct from water and the other elements, because it possesses odor. Earth is distinct from water and the other elements, because it possesses taste. Earth is earth.

Earth is distinct from air and the other [elements], because it possesses color. Earth is distinct from space and the other [elements], because it possesses tangibility. In all cases, that which is not thus is not so, as for example:
Regarding the phrase "water and so forth":

as for what was stated—that the perception establishing non-difference is erroneous—that is not so, because there is no sublation. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the cognition of the difference between earth and so forth is erroneous—[that too is not so].

As for the argument "because it is a cognition of difference," that is not so. Is its erroneous nature (bhrāntatva) the state of being a misconception (viparyaya), or the state of being doubt (saṃśaya), or the state of being non-determination (anadhyavasāya), or the state of being a dream (svapna), or the absence of being a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇatvābhāva)? It is not the first [option], because there is no misconception, doubt, or non-determination regarding difference.
Because of the deviation [of the first definition] in dreams; nor the second, third, or fourth,
because doubtfulness, lack of determinacy, and the absence of being a dream do not exist in the determinations of the waking state regarding the earth and so forth.

Because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is it the case that, due to the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the nature of being a cognition of difference therein, validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not well-established in the case of the cognition of the non-dual Self; for if it is argued that there is no cognition of difference therein and thus no deviation, we say: no.
Because there is no means of valid cognition for a cognition of the self that is entirely devoid of all attributes such as "selfhood";
and because a cognition of the self as qualified by attributes such as "selfhood" necessarily has difference as its objective support,
[this applies] to the self in the form of space.

This is because properties such as distinctness (vyāvṛttātmatva) residing in the self constitute the difference between [ether and so forth], since it is precisely the superimposition of contradictory attributes that constitutes differentiation. Furthermore, the cognition of mutual non-existence is the cognition of difference; and that...
If it is argued that there is no deviation because [the reason] is "invariably concomitant" (*anugata*) therein— no;
for if the cognition of earth and so forth as qualified by a differentiating property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*), which has mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its object,
is taken as the subject (*dharmin*), then the reason— "being a cognition whose object is mutual non-existence"— is unestablished (*asiddha*).
And because the cognition of the distinction between the objects of mutual non-existence would itself be a subject (dharmin), it would be a different entity;
for [the subject] is precisely the state of not being the object of the superimposition of contradictory properties upon the objects of mutual non-existence.

Because it is presented as a means of establishing difference: if the knowability of self-cognition—which is devoid of all attributes—is not established, then, since that [self-cognition] is nonetheless well-known, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Or, if...
If it is determined [to be valid] by the absence of sublation, then by that very same [absence], the validity of the cognition of difference residing in earth and so forth is also determined;
thus, the inference has a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*). Now, [if one objects]:

Furthermore, because the absence of sublation residing in only a few persons constitutes a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and because the absence of sublation residing in all persons at all times cannot be ascertained—
since such ascertainment is impossible— it does not follow [the probans] from earth and so forth.
If you maintain that it is the determination of the validity of the cognition of difference [that establishes the self], then for that very reason,
because the self-cognition of the self as liberated from all attributes is itself determined to be valid,
the non-existence of that [difference] would simply have an unestablished qualifier (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva), due to the absence of any sublation (bādhābhāva).
Because of the ascertainment of its validity (*prāmāṇya*).
If it is asked, "How is the validity of the cognition of difference ascertained?"—we reply: "From mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)."

Because the cognition of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), just like the cognition of [any] object. If it is asked, "How then is the validity of that [second-order cognition] ascertained?"—it is from that very same mental perception.
Nor does an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follow from stating the means for ascertaining validity in that case, because there...

Alternatively, since the cessation of the determination of validity (pramātva) entails the cessation of that [object], otherwise there would be the presence of contradictory properties due to the unavoidable infinite regress of a series [of cognitions]. This is because of the distinction [between them].

[The opponent argues: "Because [difference] is defined by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas color and other qualities residing in earth and so forth are not defined by a counter-correlate. This is not correct, because properties that are excluded from ether and the like constitute difference, and [the property of] being excluded from ether and the like [is indeed present].
And [the reason] "because it is determined by being excluded from space and so forth" [is valid].

As for what was stated—that the difference between earth and the other elements is false because it is a difference, like the difference between the moon and its reflection—that is not so; for if the difference between earth and the others were not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be sublated by that very fact.

If [the difference] were established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Otherwise, [arguments] such as "because it possesses the property of being a sky-lotus, like that which is commonly accepted" would be unavoidable.
[Objection: It is the difference itself that is grasped by the means of valid cognition that apprehends difference, but not its existence.

If it is argued that [the world is real], no; for we do not admit a "totality" (sarvatva) distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that reality (*satyatva*) is the absence of falsity (*mithyātva*), no; for falsity is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).
Furthermore, is falsity the state of being an object of error (*bhrānti-viṣayatva*) or the state of being an object of sublation (*bādha-viṣayatva*)?

Is it (1) being the object of invalid cognition, or (2) the absence of being the object of valid cognition, or (3) unreality (*asatyatva*), or (4) the absence of being an object distinct from cognition? Not the first, because it is admitted that everything is the object of delusion. Not the second, for the same reason.
Because it is accepted that all errors are sublated, the third [alternative] is not tenable;
for since the property of being the absence of the object of valid cognition (*pramā*) is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because that too cannot be defined: what is meant by "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*)? Is it something that cannot be described?

Is it either existence or non-existence, or the property of being excluded from both existence and non-existence, or the state of possessing the absolute absence of both existence and non-existence? Not the first, because it is impossible to express [the object] by words such as "difference" (*bheda*) and so forth. Nor is the second [correct].
If "otherness from existent and non-existent" means "otherness from both existence and non-existence," then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*),
because you accept that difference consists in being other than the positive entity (such as a jar) and its subsequent destruction (non-existence). Now, if...

If what is intended is the "otherness" (anyatva) from all existents and non-existents, then the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because when neither existents nor non-existents are established, that which is other than them is likewise unestablished.

And because of contradiction: for the definition of non-existence is being other than all existents, and the definition of existence is being other than all non-existents. Furthermore, if "being other than existent and non-existent" means being other than that which is neither the locus of existence nor the locus of its absence, then even in that case, as before, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Furthermore, by the inclusion of all these qualifiers,

as in the previous case, there is a contradiction regarding the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). At that time, the distinctness from both existent and non-existent, or the distinctness from both cognizable and incognizable, would constitute an unestablished qualifier.

If its being immeasurable is unestablished, then its being other than that is also unestablished. Furthermore, if one establishes its being other than only a few knowable and unknowable things, it is a case of proving what is already established; and if all qualifiers are employed, the aforementioned fault persists. Now, suppose [the opponent claims] that "being other than the existent" applies to Brahman.

If [the probandum] is "otherness from that which is other than Brahman," even then it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the distinction between earth and so forth is admitted to be otherness from both Brahman and things other than it. This is because the previously mentioned fault applies if one intends "everything other than Brahman. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, [namely] being possessed of a property excluded from both existence and non-existence.

Because it would be proving what is already established; and because, if all the qualifiers were included, the qualifier would be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Nor is the fourth [alternative] possible, because of contradiction (*vyāghāta*), since existence and non-existence and their absolute absence are necessarily mutually exclusive.

Because the state of having an absolute non-existence of both existence and non-existence is excluded [from the subject], and because its difference [from the subject] is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

If it is argued that the qualifier is established in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like— no, for in the case of the mother-of-pearl shell, it is precisely because the silver is perceived as existent.
This is because it is accepted that in that case, what appears is precisely silver as it is commonly known from [ordinary] wives and so forth.
If it is argued that there is the establishment of the qualifier in the case of silver produced on the surface of a mother-of-pearl shell and the like— no,
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of silver there.
If it is argued that the cognition "this is silver" is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we say no,

because it is an error (*bhrānti*). If it is further argued that even an error establishes the existence of silver because all cognitions have distant objects as their domain, we say no, because this is true even of error.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction: if error were the means of establishment (*sādhaka*), it would follow that silver-ness is established [as real], since the error arises precisely as "this is real silver"; thus, error would be the establisher.
Moreover, being a means of establishment consists in being the cause of validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself, and not of the object. And of that...
Because it cannot coexist with error, and because at the time of error the presence of silver in front [of one] is perceived by another person;
now, the absence of silver residing in Bhaṭṭa and others [is located] in that which stands before [the observer].

It is apprehended by another person, but not the absence of the silver called "error," because the absence of that silver— which was perceived by a person in a village— is unfit for perception by another person due to its being restricted to a specific individual other than that person.

If you think that the determination [of the object] is by means of another person, that is not so; for if it were perceived by a specific individual, there would be a lack of consistency (nānābhāva). Silver, which is the object of error, is not perceived by a specific individual, because it is silver, like that which is commonly agreed upon.

This follows also from inference. Nor is there a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) here, because the silver is established for both disputants; for the error consists in the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "that which was apprehended by me as silver is this very same thing."

Furthermore, because there is no evidence for the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the silver that is the object of error— since perception does not apprehend it as such, given that it grasps only the piece of mother-of-pearl as its object—
and because there is likewise no evidence for it through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference;

[The opponent’s position is rejected] because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*), since that [cognition] which apprehends the substratum grasps its existence in the form "this is silver.
Otherwise, [counter-arguments] such as "this is not silver, because it is an object of knowledge" would be unavoidable. Nor is it the case that...

There is no inference for the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the silver within the scope of the erroneous cognition, because [propositions] such as "this [silver] is indeterminable" suffer from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because there is nothing that remains unaccounted for; for if it were existent, it would be sublated by the subsequent sublation of the error. And if it were existent...
If it is argued that "inexplicability" (anirvācyatva) is postulated because appearance and sublation are otherwise untenable—we say no, for they are tenable in another way as well.
To explain: is error itself untenable without a cause, or is it the object [that is untenable]?
Or [is it] without [them]? Not the first, because the defective sense organ and so forth alone are the cause.
Not the second, because the silver and so forth alone are the object. If it is argued that "if the silver and so forth exist, they could not be the objects of error"—[we reply: no.
Because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary]. If it is argued that whatever exists is not the object of error, just as Brahman is not—[we reply:
no, because there is no proof for the absence of Brahman being the object of error;
furthermore, there is the inference: "Brahman is the object of error, because it is knowable, like a jar."
Furthermore, the intended inference is: "Whatever is existent is not an object of error;
and since this 'silver in the mother-of-pearl' is existent, it is therefore not an object of error.
Alternatively, the intended reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) is: "If this silver were existent, then it would not be an object of error."
The intended [reason] is not the first, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*) and because there is sublation (*bādhā*).
Nor is it the second, because it does not result in a contrary conclusion (*viparyayāparyavasāna*);
for [the reason] "because this is the object of a non-existent error" and so forth is unestablished as a predicate (*vācyatvāsiddhatvāt*).
Because there is no concomitance (*vyāpti*) anywhere between being an object of error and the absence of existence—

since it is admitted that everything which is an object of error possesses existence— and because there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to Brahman, [the reason] "being its object" [is fallacious].

If it is argued that the intended reasoning (*tarka*) is "there would be no state of being an error," we say no, because it does not result in a contrary conclusion (*viparyayāparyavasāna*). This is because there is no apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) in such [propositions] as "this [cognition] does not have a real object, because it is an error. As for that (*sā*):

If it is argued that this [cognition] is not an error because its object is existent— just as the cognition of real silver is not— this is not so; for, since it is excluded even from the "similar instances" (sapakṣa), such as jars and the like, which lack the property of having an existent object, the reason is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).

Furthermore, since it is not admitted that cognitions of jars and the like possess either a real object or the status of valid knowledge (*pramātva*), they cannot function as negative examples (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). If you argue: "Whatever has a real object is not an error, just like the valid cognition of Brahman"—we say no, because Brahman is the object of error.

Because it is an object of knowledge, like that which is commonly accepted; thus, once error is established, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekivyāpti*) is broken. Furthermore, if "having that as its object" means "having Brahman as its object," then the logical argument (*tarka*) is that if it has Brahman as its object, it could not be an error. And so it is.

There is no end to such fallacies. For instance, the argument that "this [cognition] does not have Brahman as its object because it is an error" is refuted if one takes as the subject of the proposition an error whose object is an entity possessing existence (*sattā*). Furthermore, this remains untenable even if one takes as the subject an error whose object is an entity lacking existence.
Because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
Likewise, there is also sublation (*bādha*); for what reason? Because [the cognition] is untenable without a cause or without an object.
It is not the first case, because the sense organs and so forth are indeed the causes. Nor is it the second case.

For it is precisely the absence of silver and so forth that constitutes the object of sublation in such cognitions as "this is not silver. If it is argued that what is existent cannot be the object of sublation—no, for if by the word "existent" one means Brahman, then no misconception can result [since Brahman is never negated]. [In the case of the error] "this is silver," it is not Brahman [that is perceived].

Because [the reason] would result in proving what is already established in the case of the sun and so forth; and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman, which is the object of sublation in such statements as "The body is not Brahman"; and even if the word "existent" (*sat*) denotes a positive entity (*bhāva*), it does not result in the establishment of the opposite [of the probandum]; as in the case of "This is silver, it is not... [where the negation does not negate the existence of the silver].

If "existence" (*bhāva*) is taken as the subject in the argument beginning with "because it is sublatable" (*bādhyatvāt*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding Brahman. If it is argued that "Brahman is not the locus of existence" (*brahma na sattāśrayaḥ*), we say no; for by the perception "Brahman exists" (*brahma sat*), Brahman is indeed existent.

Furthermore, since existence is established in Brahman through the inference "because it is knowable" and "because it is not a substance," the term *sat* (existent) denotes the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If [existence] were defined by the term *prameya*, there would be no avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), as in the case of such arguments as "this silver is not an object of knowledge because it is sublated."

If it is argued that there is a *tarka* (reductio) to the effect that "if [the cognition] had a real object, it would not be sublatable," we say no; for this has already been refuted by the previously stated reasoning (*nyāya*), and because its root is weak. This is because there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between having a real object and the absence of sublation, since the realization of Brahman, which has a real object, is [nevertheless] sublatable. As for the phrase "having a real object" (*sadviṣaya*), [it refers to] the realization of Brahman.

Because of the acceptance of its being a cognition. Furthermore, it is not correct to say that in the first case (the theory of *anyathākhyāti*), the nature of being a manifestation (*khyātitva*) is untenable.

Is this [manifestation] untenable without a cause, or without an object? Not the first, because the sense organs and so forth are indeed the cause of that. As for the second, [it is untenable] only in the absence of silver, its absence, and so forth.

Because it is an object [of cognition], silver would not be perceived if it were non-existent. Non-existence (asattva) consists either in being other than Brahman, or in being devoid of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvatva), or in being devoid of existence (sattā), or in being devoid of causality, or in being devoid of knowability (prameyatva). Not the first.
Because its root is loose, because even things other than Brahman such as jars are perceived,
and because there is no finality in the reversal [of error]; for instance, the inference "this silver is Brahman because it is being perceived" is sublated in the case of a jar and so forth.
And because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because its foundation is weak;

for even the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāva*) and the like, though devoid of the nature of being (*bhāvatva*), are perceived, and because it does not result in a contradiction (*viparyaya*). "This is silver, not..."

This is because [the argument] "it is devoid of the nature of being (bhāvatva) because it is perceived," and so forth, is contradicted; furthermore, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a jar and other such things.
Nor is the third [alternative], because its foundation is weak, since even that which is devoid of existence (sattā) [is perceived].
Because universals, particulars, and so forth do appear, and because [the argument] does not terminate in a contrary conclusion;

and because [arguments such as] "this is silver, because it is perceived as real" result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to universals and the like.

Furthermore, on the view that existence (sattā) is a purely positive concomitant (kevalānvayin), there is a failure to establish the probans (apādaka) because the state of being devoid of existence is unestablished,
as well as a failure to establish the consequence (āpādya).
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because its root is lax;
for even that which lacks causality, such as the final liberation (*antyamukti*) and so forth, appears [as an object], and because it results in a contradiction. "This silver is the cause."
Because [the reason] "since it is being perceived" and so forth results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*),

and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicārāt*) in the case of final liberation (*antya-mukti*); for even if that [liberation] were a cause, causality would be a property of absolute positive concomitance (*kevalānvayitvena*).
Nor is the fifth [alternative] possible, because that which is devoid of being a cause is unestablished, and thus the probans (the *āpādaka*) is unestablished; furthermore,
there is no logical conclusion in the contrapositive (*viparyaya*).

This [proposition]—"this silver is an object of cognition"—is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) for those who accept the perceived [silver], and it suffers from a deficiency in its root (*mūlaśaithilya*). Furthermore, there is a lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) for the statement: "that which is devoid of cognizability (*prameyatva*) is not cognized. If it is argued that "the horn of a hare" serves as the example:
If that [non-existence] is not cognized, the example is unestablished; if it is cognized, it lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*).
If it is argued that what is intended is "that which is non-existent is directly cognized"—no, for even a hare’s horn is an object of its own direct perception, since it possesses horns.

If it is argued that this is what is intended to be expressed— no, for even when one is at a distance and does not perceive the distinguishing properties [of a horn], there is visual perception of the form "this possesses a horn"; therefore, neither the [non-existent] rabbit-horn nor its connection with this object exists here.

Or is it distinct? It cannot be the first or the second [options], because those two exist and are perceived. Nor can it be the third, because their relation—whether characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) or as the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*)—would likewise [be subject to the same critique].

Because it exists and because it is perceived. If it is argued that [the relation] does not exist between a hare and a horn because of their respective natures—that is not so; for the inherence (*samavāya*) of the five-worded formula is as indelible as adamantine glue (*vajralepa*) there. Furthermore, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) exists between the hare and the horn.

If it is argued that [the relation does not exist] because [the object] does not exist— no, for [relations such as] existence (*sattā*) and so forth can still function as the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). If it is argued that the state of being qualified by a horn does not exist in the rabbit, nor does the state of qualifying a horn exist in the rabbit— what follows from this?
Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because "being the qualificandum of a horn" and "being the qualifier of a rabbit" exist in a buffalo and so forth,
as well as in the qualities of a rabbit and so forth, and thus they would be perceived as existing.
Nor is it the fourth [alternative], since even a jar and the like possess "otherness from that."
Because it exists and because it is being perceived. By this, it is also logical that what is non-existent cannot be sublated.
Furthermore, is the fact that error must otherwise be inexplicable the reason for its being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent?
The means of proof is either the impossibility of [the appearance] otherwise than as an appearance and its sublation,
or the appearance [of an object] despite the impossibility of error and sublation, or the impossibility of sublation otherwise [than by the existence of the object].
Not the first, because error and sublation are established precisely through the absence of that [object].
Not the second, because appearance and sublation are accounted for by existence alone.

Nor the third, because they are accounted for by existence and non-existence respectively. If it is argued that the existence and non-existence of a single thing are contradictory—no, for [they belong to] a single...
Because even the existence and non-existence of existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory;

for the absence of existence is itself the referent of the term "non-existence," and the absence of non-existence is itself the referent of the term "existence," since each is necessarily determined by the other.
Furthermore, regarding the sublation of error, are the two cognitions of equal strength or of unequal strength?

Not the first, because if they were of equal strength, both would lack validity due to being counter-balanced by a valid opposite (satpratipakṣa). Nor the second, because when one is of superior strength, it sublates the other, thereby rendering the weaker one invalid.
The very fact of being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent constitutes the avoidance of both the counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣa*) and sublation (*bādha*). Furthermore,
since the inexpressibility [of the self] is established even by the mere fact that sublation would otherwise be inexplicable,
the inclusion of "the inexplicability of its being an error" is redundant.
If it is argued that the very impossibility of sublation (*bādhānupapatti*) is the proof for indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*), we say no;

for that [reason] is common to both one's own position and the opponent's position, and thus constitutes a "neutralized reason" (*prakaraṇasama*). By this same logic: "This is silver, because it is sublatable; for whatever is real is not sublatable, as for example Brahman."

Nor can it be argued that the establishment of indeterminability (anirvācyatva) is achieved through the force of two inferences— namely, "it is not non-existent because it is perceived, like Brahman"— for this too is refuted,
since the first inference suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

Because non-existence, which is the absence of being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*), is unestablished; for this very reason, the second inference also suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), since if non-existence is not established, its absence is likewise unestablished. However, if [silver] were existent, the proof would be: "This is silver..."
"Because it is being perceived as existent, like the self (ātman).

Nor is there a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like; for even in the case of a rabbit's horn, there exists the relation residing in the rabbit's horn, as well as things distinct from that relation. And it is not thus [that the reason is fallacious].

Because sublation would be untenable: for in the view that silver-ness is superimposed upon the object present before one, [the cognition] would have to apprehend the absolute absence of silver-ness in that which is present before one;
whereas in the view that identity with silver is superimposed upon the object present before one, [it would have to apprehend the absence of such identity] in that which is present before one.

For it is established that "this is not silver" functions as a sublation (bādha) by apprehending the absence of identity with silver; likewise, "this is mother-of-pearl" also functions [as a sublation] by apprehending the quality of being mother-of-pearl,
which is contrary to both the relation of silverness and the identity with silver.
Because its refutation is logically established.

Nor is it the fifth [alternative]. Is non-existence (asattva) the state of being an entity (bhāvatva), or being the counter-positive of an entity, or the absence of existence (sattā), or the state of not being a cause?
Alternatively, it is being the object of invalid cognition, or being the object of sublation,
or the absolute absence in the object of valid cognition, or being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in all things, or the three periods of time.
Is it counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*), or dependence on time (*kālāśritatva*), or being non-worldly (*alaukikatva*), or existence distinct from cognition (*jñānātiriktabhāva*)?
Not the first, because [the world] has the manifold of absences (*abhāvaprapañca*) as its substratum (*dharmin*).

The first [position] is not tenable, because since it is established through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is no sublation regarding the fact that positive entities possess the nature of conceptual proliferation;
furthermore, if it were the case that non-existence is itself an existence, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Nor is the second [position] tenable, because there is no dispute [regarding it].

Nor is the third [alternative] tenable: if the subject (*dharmin*) were a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). If the subject were a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, since existence (*sattā*) is unestablished in some cases, its absence (*tadabhāva*) would likewise be unestablished; furthermore, if its existence in a substance were established, there would be a contradiction (*bādhāt*).

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable; for if it were characterized by the manifoldness of individual instances of final liberation, there would be a contradiction with established fact, and if it were characterized by absolute liberation, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
Nor is the fifth [alternative] tenable, because it is admitted that everything is indeed the object of error.

Nor is it the sixth, because it is admitted that everything is the object of sublation (*bādha*). Nor is it the seventh, because if it were unestablished, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*);

for if it were established either elsewhere than the subject (*pakṣa*) or as something not cognized by a means of valid knowledge (*aprameya*), there would be a contradiction. [If it were established] in the subject itself...

Because if that [subject] were established, the means of proof would be redundant; and because if the subject is not cognized, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), whereas if it is cognized, there is a contradiction;
furthermore, if the inference of the absence of being cognized as residing in the subject were itself valid, there would be a contradiction.
Furthermore, since that [invalidity] is unestablished, and because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*);
for it is not experienced through perception that shell-silver is not the object of a valid cognition,
given that there is a subverting perception (*bādhakapratyakṣa*) regarding the object present before one, such as "this is not silver."

Alternatively, for one who seeks to establish the absence of the silver's identity with silver, the silver does not establish its status as an object of valid cognition; for the perception "this is mother-of-pearl" manifests the existence of the mother-of-pearl,
[not that of the silver].

Because it does not prove the absolute absence of being an object of valid cognition, and because there is no other perception [to establish such an absence]. The disputed cognition of silver has an object distinct from the existence of this [silver], because it is a cognition.

If it is argued that "like the cognition of a cloth" is the proof for the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), we say no; for even this [cognition] would involve a contradiction if it were to produce a valid cognition whose object is an absolute non-existence. And if it does not produce [such a cognition], it cannot establish that [theory]. However, if silver exists, the proof is as follows: "This..."

"Silver is an object of valid cognition (prameya), because it is knowable (jñeya), like a jar. If it is objected: "Is this silver cognized by valid means of knowledge (pramita) or not? In the first case, the probans (sādhana) is redundant;
in the second, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi)," we reply: No, for we accept that it is cognized by valid means of knowledge. It is not...

And there would be the futility of the proof, because it is being proven for the sake of another; and even if that other person were to accept it in that way, [it would still be for the sake of yet another].

Because no proof has been stated [to establish it]. If it is argued: "Since this is established by the cognition 'this is silver,' if [the substrate] were the apprehender of the locus (dharmin), there would be the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi); for this [cognition] is an error and thus not a means of valid knowledge, and because there is no other mental mode (vṛtti) that establishes this silver"—we say: no.
This is because it would entail the admission of another valid cognition (*pramiti*) having silver as its object;

for [the opponent] accepts that it is precisely the silver cognized by a means such as perception (*bhaṭṭa*, i.e., *pratyakṣa*) that appears here. Nor is it the eighth [alternative], because it would result in the establishment of several distinct [theories].
Nor is the ninth [alternative] tenable; because it fails to establish a locus distinct from time, it results in proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntaratva*).

Nor is the tenth [alternative] tenable; because it establishes merely that [the property] rests upon something other than the locus of time, it results in proving something other than the intended point across all three positions.

Furthermore, because it would result in proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*) by establishing merely that [the self] is non-dependent. Even if it were non-dependent, its existence would still be [unproven], like time, because it would be a dependent object of cognition (*prameya*), just like the qualities of time.
If you argue that this is not so because [the reason] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the color and other qualities of earth and so forth—[we reply: no, for those too...
If it is argued that [the qualities] reside in time— no, because that would entail the consequence of time being perceptible.

If it is argued that there is no inherence of color and so forth in time— no, because of the deviation in that very case, and because the definitions of earth and the other elements involve residing in time.

Because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*). Furthermore, even if [the object] were non-dependent (*anāśrita*), there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason in that very case. Nor is the eleventh [alternative] tenable, because "extraordinariness" (*alaukikatva*) cannot be defined. Extraordinariness would have to be either the absolute absence of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāviṣayatvātyantābhāva*) or the incapacity to produce an effect (*kāryājanakatva*). It cannot be the first, because...

Because it is refuted. Not the second [alternative], because it is contradicted by evidence and because the example of nacre-silver is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). For there is neither perception nor inference regarding this [nacre] being a producer of the effects of silver; [otherwise, one would have to accept] that "this is silver" is a producer of the effects of silver.
This is also established by the inference: "Because it is silver, like other silver.
Nor is "the absence of being the object of this cognition" a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) here, for even the ground and so forth are objects of this cognition.

Because it is pervaded by the probandum (sādhya) through its connection with the causal function of silver; nor does the objection follow that there would be the consequence of producing [actual] mother-of-pearl or silver if this were a producer of the effect of silver, for such a consequence is accepted.

This is because it is accepted that it is precisely the silver well-known from [the experience of] Bhaṭṭa and others that appears in the mother-of-pearl, and by means of that [silver], the production of a ring and so forth occurs. Even if one accepts the silver produced on the surface of the mother-of-pearl, there is no consequence that a ring could be fashioned from it; for [the production of the ring] occurs only prior to its [alleged] formation.
Because it is destroyed at the moment prior to sublation; otherwise, for you as well, it would follow that silver is absent at the time of sublation and so forth.
Nor is the twelfth [alternative] possible, because its qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvāt*). Knowledge-ness (*jñānatva*) is what is being proven.
If this is argued—[we reply]: no; for if the locus is the phenomenal world consisting of jars, universals (*jāti*), and so forth, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
If the locus is the phenomenal world of jars and so forth whose nature is ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is sublation (*bādha*).
And if the locus is the phenomenal world that is the subject of dispute regarding whether it is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) or ignorance (*ajñāna*)—this [is the case].

This knowledge is distinct from that which lacks the nature of being other than knowledge, because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), like any other knowledge; for there is no sublation of the established [proposition] regarding the alternative position of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*). If it were included within the subject (*pakṣa*), then the reason (*hetu*) of being an object of knowledge would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to that very [non-knowledge].

Furthermore, is this knowledge of ignorance (ajñāna) a cognition whose object is distinct from the cognition of its [own] object, because it is a cognition, like any other cognition? In this regard, is the established ignorance included within the subject (pakṣa) of the inference or not?
Not the first, because it would be contradicted by the evidence (bādhāt). Not the second, because there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very case.

Furthermore, what is this "cognitivity" (*jñānatva*)? Is it the ground for the exclusion of non-cognition (*ajñāna-vyāvṛtti-nimitta*)? Not the first, because for you [the opponent], since non-cognition is not established, there can be no exclusion of non-cognition.
Nor the second, because for you, the universal "cognitivity" (*jñānatva-jāti*) is not established.

And as for the universal "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva-jāti*), is it a universal that lacks the property of being excluded from cognition, or is it the exclusion from non-cognition while possessing the property of not being excluded from cognition?
[The first two options are rejected] because existence (*sattā*) is a different entity. It is not the third [option], either.
It is not the first [alternative], because the qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
It is not the third, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of existence (*sattā*), being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and so forth.
Nor is it the fourth, because if ignorance itself is unestablished, then the "otherness" (*itaratva*) relative to it cannot be established.
Not the fifth [alternative], because it is contradicted by the proof of non-difference from the manifestation of all knowledge;

nor [is it valid] for the proof of non-difference from a single manifestation of some knowledge, because there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to those manifestations of knowledge distinct from it. [If it is argued that] what is being proven is the non-difference from a manifestation of knowledge whose specific features have not been grasped—
If [you argue that it is not so], no; for the state of having its particulars always grasped is unestablished in any case whatsoever.

Since the state of having its particulars ungrasped at some time exists in all individual instances of cognition (*jñānavyakti*), the aforementioned defects and infinite regress (*anavasthā*) persist. And as for the property of being an individual instance of cognition...

The sixth [definition] is not tenable, because it is impossible to define "the state of being the locus of knowledge" (jñānatvāśrayatva) without first defining "knowledge-ness" (jñānatva) and so forth; and if those were defined, the aforementioned defects would ensue. Nor is it the case that "knowledge" (jñāna) is simply that which is known (jñāyate).

If the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is derived from the sense of an object (*karman*), then proving that it is denotable [by the word "knowledge"] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). If one intends to prove that it is denotable by the word "knowledge" as derived from the sense of a state (*bhāva*)—where "knowledge" means "the act of knowing"—then, since the nature of "being knowledge" (*jñaptitva*) cannot be defined, the aforementioned fault persists. Furthermore, if one intends to prove that it is denotable by the word "knowledge" without having grasped its specific [derivation], then even if it is established that it is denotable by the word "knowledge" derived from the sense of an object, this constitutes the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*).

Not the seventh [alternative], because if one intends to express the exclusion of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth by means of the word "cause of the application of the term 'knowledge'," the aforementioned fault remains. By this, the argument that "there is no difference between blue and the cognition thereof because they are necessarily perceived together" is refuted. Furthermore, blue is not the cognition of blue; therefore...
The intended meaning is either "because it is perceived simultaneously [with its object], like the cognition of blue," or alternatively,
"the cognition of blue is non-different from the blue,
because it is perceived only together with it, like the blue. It is not the first case, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Because even when the cognition of blue (*nīla-jñāna*) is not perceived, the appearance of blue is admitted; and because blue is not established in space. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, precisely because of non-establishment: for even when blue is not manifest, the cognition of blue is manifested by the mind (*manas*). Thus, there is a cognition having blue as its object.

If it is argued that "only that which is delimited by blue is admitted"— no, for it is impossible to apprehend what is delimited by blue without apprehending the external object; thus, there would be no manifestation of mere cognition.
Furthermore, it is untenable that there is no manifestation of a cognition qualified by "blue," because a qualified cognition is produced by the cognition of its qualifier.
Nor is the sixth [alternative] possible, due to the fault already mentioned.
In that regard, matter (rūpa) is of two kinds: luminous and non-luminous. The first belongs to fire.

The second is of two kinds: transparent and non-transparent. The first belongs to water; the second belongs to earth. Therefore, earth is that which possesses matter devoid of both luminosity and transparency.

The definition [of color]. That too is of seven kinds: black, white, blue, green, yellow, red, and variegated. Whiteness and the others are sub-classes of the genus "color-ness" (rūpatva). There are also luminosity and transparency.
[It is] a subordinate genus within whiteness. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the existence of "color-ness" (rūpatva);

for the visual organ and other [senses] that produce the experience "this is color, this is color" constitute proof for it. Nor should it be said that the experience "this is color, this is color" is unestablished; for [there is indeed] the experience "this is color, this is color."

Because its establishment [is known] through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and because conventional usage arises from that [perception], there would otherwise be a collapse of worldly experience. Furthermore, in this case, the object of apprehension (*ālambana*) cannot be "that which is perceivable by the eye alone," because when the eye is not being perceived, one cannot perceive the property of being "perceivable by the eye alone" by means of that very eye. Not...
And it should not be said that this experience is non-visual,
because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [vision] in a way that cannot be otherwise accounted for;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the experience of a jar and so forth would be non-visual.

Furthermore, even in the absence of a form (rūpa) that is perceptible by the eye alone, the cognition of the measurement of form would be untenable. Nor should it be said that "absence does not exist," because that would involve a contradiction, as will be shown later. And [if you argue] that it exists as a positive entity (bhāva)...

The state of being perceivable by the eye alone is the basis for the conventional designation "form" (rūpa) [for form], because that [designation] would otherwise apply to universals such as whiteness and blackness. Nor is there an absence of universals such as whiteness, since white qualities are each singular.
It should be stated as follows: "This white [object] is distinct from white, because it is an object of cognition (*meyatva*), like blue.
And: "The white cloth possesses a form other than white, because it is a cloth, like a black cloth.
Thus, once the distinction from white and so forth is established by the force of such experience as "white is white," etc.

The universal (jāti) of whiteness and so forth is established because of such cognitions as "slightly white," "whiter," and "whitest"; for the cognition of "slightly white" arises from the contact of a white substance with a substance that does not possess the [universal] of whiteness,
while [the cognition of "white"] arises from the contact with a substance that possesses only a small amount of blackness.
It must be said that the cognition of "whiter" arises from the non-contact with white substances,
while the cognition of "whitest" arises from the non-perception of contact with black substances.
Furthermore, because there is the cognition "white, white" with respect to a single object,

[it is argued that] "white is that which possesses a genus (jāti) residing in all white things, because it possesses a genus, like a pot"— thus, by virtue of the commonality of the absence of a genus in non-white things and so forth, it is established as a quality (guṇa), and so on.

Because quality-ness (guṇatva) is untenable in the absence of the defining characteristics of a quality, and because Prabhākara also accepts both existence (sattā) and quality-ness [as residing in qualities];
[and because] action, generality, inherence, number, similarity, and action [cannot be established] due to their not being substrata of effects.
Because, in the absence of specific distinctions, [the definitions] such as "a quality is distinct from a substance" and so forth would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) regarding those two;

furthermore, since power (*śakti*) is not established, its distinction [from other categories] is likewise not established; and because similarity (*sādṛśya*) and the like are already included within the categories of substance and so on.

Because the qualification "being distinct from similarity and so forth" would be redundant, and because it would result in [the universal] being a *jāti* by virtue of inhering in multiple [substances]. Furthermore,
that which possesses a universal cannot be perceived by the eye alone.

Alternatively, being a quality perceivable by the visual faculty alone (*cakṣurmātragrāhyaguṇatva*) cannot be the basis for the conventional usage of the term "form" (*rūpa*), because for you [the opponent], the universal "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavattva*) and the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatvajāti*) are unestablished.
Nor is it tenable to claim that "quality-ness" is simply the definition of a quality; for that would fail if the state of possessing a universal were unestablished.

That too is unestablished. Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the state of being perceivable by the eye while being distinct from a universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause for the conventional usage of the term "form" (*rūpa*), according to your own position.
Because there is no exclusion of the two qualifiers—being distinct from genus and being an existent—[the following applies]:

it is that which resides in white, devoid of the exclusion of black; it is that which resides in white, devoid of the exclusion of blue; it is that which resides in white, devoid of the exclusion of green; it is that which resides in white, devoid of the exclusion of yellow; and it is that which resides in white, devoid of the exclusion of what is not [white].

[The argument is: "That which possesses a genus (jāti) excluded from the subsistence of white, black, blue, green, yellow, red, and variegated [colors], because it possesses a genus, like a cow," and so forth; thus, by such inference, *rūpatva* (the nature of color) is established.
Nor is its being a genus (*jātitva*) unproven; for this [is a] pot...
This [subject] is other than that which possesses a genus devoid of the difference from "this pot" and "white," because it is an object of cognition (*meyatva*), like a pot;

thus [the property to be proven] is established. Nor are "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*) limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) here, because they do not pervade the probandum in cases such as "white" and so forth. In this same manner, "existence" (*sattva*) and other properties may be demonstrated.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for variegated color (*citrarūpa*), because the perception "the cloth is variegated" exists.

It should not be argued that the cognition of variegation regarding the cloth is due to the blue and other colors residing in the threads, rather than a variegated color existing in the cloth itself; for there is a cognition of variegated color as being inherent in the cloth.
Furthermore, because the forms of the threads are not perceived in the cloth and so forth; otherwise, if cognitions such as "the cloth is white" were accounted for by the forms of the threads alone,
it would follow that all cloths and the like would possess the color blue (or whatever color the threads happen to have).
For even if the threads were endowed with color as its cause,

it would follow that there is an absence of color pervading the cloth, since [the color] would exist only as non-pervasive properties belonging to the cloth. One who holds a contrary view [must admit] that the cloth possesses a pervasive variegated color, because otherwise it would be perceived as white.

Furthermore, since cognitions such as these [of "white," etc. can be accounted for by means of qualities that exist non-pervasively (avyāpyavṛtti) within the cloth, it would follow that there is an absence of pervasive (vyāpyavṛtti) qualities in the cloth. This is also established by the following inference: the subject under dispute, the cloth, possesses pervasive qualities, because it is a cloth, like a commonly accepted instance.
Furthermore, this cloth does not possess colors such as blue or yellow, because it is a cloth, like any [cloth] commonly agreed upon;
and there is no [contradiction] regarding its possession of colors such as blue or yellow.

In some cases, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) due to its being unestablished [in general]; however, this is not the case here, because it is established in an earth-atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*), since blue, yellow, and other colors produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise therein in succession. Nor is it the case that "this cloth possesses a blue color, because its parts are yellow."
By the statement beginning with "like a yellow cloth," there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva),

because while [the opponent] seeks to establish the possession of blue and yellow colors in the aggregate by means of proving each individual form such as blue, [the proponent] establishes the possession of both blue and yellow forms.
And because they do not produce a single cognition;
for when the two [cognitions] establishing the possession of blue color and the possession of yellow color are of equal strength,
they are mutually contradictory, or when they are of unequal strength, one of them [is sublated].

Because it is invalid due to being sublated; and because the presence of blue color is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the appearance of yellow color, while the absence of blue color is a limiting condition for [the appearance of] yellow and other colors;
even though [the former] does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of an earth-atom.

Because it pervades the relationship between the probandum and the probans; and because, if that [pervasion] were also to be proven, it would constitute a deviation from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
This applies both to the absence of yellow constituent parts in the case of possessing a blue color, and to the possession of yellow or other colors.

Furthermore, the absence of blue parts (*nīlāvayavatvābhāva*) constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Moreover, if that [absence] were also to be proven, it would lead to a contradiction (*bādha*), and because there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) such as: "This cloth is not blue, because it has yellow parts, like a yellow cloth," and so forth. It is not [the case].

This [argument] is subject to a counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣatva*), namely: "This is the color of the cloth, because it possesses a color other than this color of the cloth, like the color of another cloth. Even if the possession of multiple colors were established, the possession of specific colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth would still be established; for these would then be attributes residing in the cloth.
Because my [proposition] lacks a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*); and because if it were to have as its subject a form distinct from that [color], your [proposition] would lack a locus.

By this, [arguments] such as "this cloth possesses a color other than the color of this cloth, because it is a cloth, like another cloth," and so forth, are refuted; for even by the establishment of multiple forms of the same genus, this [cloth]— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument.]
Because its purpose has already been fulfilled, it cannot establish the possession of blue, yellow, and so forth.
Nor is it logical that the cognition of "variegated" (*citra*) arises from a form possessing universals such as blueness and yellowness;
for this is contradicted by perception, in that one perceives: "This cloth is not blue," and "This cloth is not yellow. This [is not...]
Furthermore, there is sublation by inference: "The blue [object] has drunk yellow, because it is cloth, like a white cloth.

Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), on the grounds that the color possessing both blueness and yellowness is unestablished; for if blueness and yellowness were unestablished, the negation of them would likewise be unestablished. Of one...
Since blue and yellow forms are well-known,
the possession of blueness and yellowness by an earth atom is established; and since the negation of those [qualities] is also well-known in the case of white cloth and the like.

Nor is there a shift in the subject matter (*arthāntaratā*) despite the negation of blueness and yellowness, because the possession of color as the substratum of blueness and yellowness is not thereby negated;
for [this would be impossible] without the negation of color as the substratum of blueness and yellowness.

Because the negation of possessing blueness and yellowness does not terminate; for as long as that [negation] exists, since this cloth possesses blueness by virtue of being blue and possesses yellowness by virtue of being yellow, the state of possessing both blueness and yellowness is unavoidable. Nor is it the case that...

The absence of having blue and yellow constituent parts (*nīlapītāvayavatvābhāva*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the absence of having blue and yellow color (*nīlapītarūpavattvābhāva*), because it is merely "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*). Nor is the absence of having blue constituent parts (*nīlāvayavatvābhāva*) and so forth a limiting adjunct, because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpakatva*) in cases such as a blue cloth. Nor [is it a limiting adjunct] by virtue of having blue and yellow constituent parts...

There is no counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*), because [the reason] is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of blue objects and the like on account of their having blue parts; for example: "This cloth is blue, because it has blue parts, just like a [previously] agreed-upon blue object";
likewise, "It is yellow, because it has yellow parts, just like a [previously] agreed-upon yellow object."

If it is argued that there is "counter-thesis" (satpratipakṣatva), [we reply]: no, because neither one individually proves [the property] of being possessed of blue or yellow; and as for their combination, if they possess equal strength, they are mutual counter-theses;
and if they possess unequal strength, the weaker one is sublated and thus lacks probative power.
Because the absence of yellow parts in that which possesses blueness, and the absence of blue parts in that which possesses yellowness and so forth, are themselves the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
[This applies] to the absence of yellowness in that which possesses blueness, and to [the absence of blueness] in that which possesses yellowness and so forth.
Furthermore, because the absence of blueness would itself be a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); for if that were also to be proven,
it would result in a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), since [the opponent] accepts that a cloth possesses color as the substratum of both blueness and yellowness.
This is because both blueness and yellowness are admitted [to exist in the cloth]; for instance,

the color of the cloth is blue because it has blue as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and likewise it is yellow because it has yellow as its non-inherent cause, just like [the colors] commonly accepted [in other cases].

If it is argued that there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva), we say no; for neither blueness nor yellowness individually proves [the existence of the cloth]. Even in the case of the form of the cloth, each one [of the colors] fails to prove it, and the collection of them also fails to prove it in the manner already stated.

Furthermore, because "not being produced by yellow" is an *upādhi* (limiting condition) for blueness, and "not being produced by blue" is an *upādhi* for yellowness and so forth; and because even if that [condition] were to be proven, there would be a sublation (*bādha*),
as well as a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) such as "it is produced by yellow," etc., regarding blueness.
Furthermore, because the absence of yellowness [is an upādhi] with respect to yellowness and so forth, and because the absence of blueness [is an upādhi] with respect to blueness and so forth;
and because there would be a deviation from one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) if that too were to be proven.

Nor is there a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva) such as: "This cloth is not possessed of blue and yellow [colors], because it consists of earth-atoms, because it is the locus of conjunction, like an earth-atom," since [the cloth] possesses atomicity and blue parts; [this is established] by its being a cloth and so forth.

Because it possesses a limiting adjunct (*sopādhitvāt*). Nor is the absence of this conjunction with the earth-atom (*pārthivaparamāṇu*) the limiting adjunct in the absence of the nature of blue and yellow color; for this conjunction does not reside in that which is devoid of blue and yellow, because it resides in this cloth.

This is established by the example of a cloth (*paṭavat*). [The probans] pervades the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyavyāpaka*) in that which is the substratum of this conjunction but is devoid of being blue or yellow; whereas it does not pervade the property to be proven in that very same substratum of the conjunction [if it possesses the color]. In that very case, there is the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) consisting of the possession of that conjunction.
And because of deviation; for blue, yellow, and so forth, are presented through mutual exclusion.
It is also not tenable to say, "This is a blue pot," [since] blueness and yellowness...
